A random process $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t),\, t \in \mathcal{T},$ taking values in Rn is called a process with independent increments if, for any n, t0 ≤ t1 ≤ ⋯ ≤ tn = T, the random vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t_{0}),\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t_{1}) - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t_{0}),\ldots,\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t_{n}) - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t_{n - 1})$ are mutually independent.

The vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t_{0})$ is called the initial state (value) of the process, and its probability distribution is called the initial distribution of the process. For defining a process with independent increments, it suffices to define an initial distribution $P_{0}(\mathcal{B}) = \mathbf{P}\left\{ \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t_{0}) \in \mathcal{B} \right\},$ a collection of distributions $P(t,h,\mathcal{B}) = \mathbf{P}\left\{ \Delta\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t,h) \in \mathcal{B} \right\}$ for the vector $\Delta\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t,h) = \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t + h) - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t),$ where t ∈ 𝒯, h > 0, and ℬ ∈ Rm is a set of elementary events.

If a distribution P(t, h, ℬ) does not depend on t, i.e., P(t, h, ℬ) = P(h, ℬ), then a corresponding process with independent increments is called homogeneous.

Consider examples of some processes with independent increments. Let us begin with Brownian motion. For this process, the probability distribution P(t, h, ℬ) is Gaussian. The physical model of the process is the motion of a small particle in a liquid, which can be observed using a high-power microscope. Such a particle has constant movements, and its path represents a very complicated polygonal line with chaotically directed segments. This motion is explained by the collisions of the particle with the molecules of the liquid. The particle has relatively large dimensions in comparison with the dimensions of each molecule and suffers from a huge number of collisions with them each second. The visible motion of the particle is called Brownian motion. In a rough approximation, the displacements of the particle caused by collisions can be considered mutually independent, and hence Brownian motion can be treated as a process with independent increments. Due to small displacements, we can hypothesize that their sum satisfies the central limit theorem; in other words, Brownian motion can be described by a Gaussian random process with independent increments.

In particular, a homogeneous Brownian random process is defined by two parameters m and σ:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{M}\left\{ x(t) \right\} = mt,\quad\mathcal{M}\left\{ x^{2}(t) \right\} = \sigma^{2}t.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.28)

For m = 0 and σ = 1, the Brownian motion process is called the standard Wiener process.

Now consider Poisson processes. A stochastically continuous process with independent increments that takes nonnegative integer values is called a Poisson process if, for any (s, t) > 0 and s < t, the variable $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t) - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(s)$ obeys the Poisson probability distribution.

Let x(t0) = 0. Then the variable x(t) has the probability distribution


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{P}\left\{ x(t) = m \right\} = \frac{a^{m}(t)}{m!}\exp( - a(t)),\quad\mathcal{M}\left\{ x(t) \right\} = a(t).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.29)

Hence, it follows that


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{P}\left\{ x(t) - x(s) = m \right\}} & {= \frac{{\lbrack a(t) - a(s)\rbrack}^{m}}{m!}\exp\left( {- \lbrack a(t) - a(s)\rbrack} \right),} \\ & {\quad m = 0,1,2,\ldots} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.30)

If the process is homogeneous, then


$$\begin{aligned} & {a(t) = at,} \\ {\mathbf{P}\left\{ x(t) - x(s) = m \right\}} & {= \frac{a^{m}{(t - s)}^{m}}{m!}\exp( - a(t - s)),} \\ {s < t,} & {m = 0,1,2,\ldots} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.31)

3. Markov processes

The concept of a Markov process is based on the hypothesis about nonhereditary systems (also known as systems “without aftereffect”). At each time t, such a system has some state $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t),$ which depends on its state $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(s)$ at a preceding time s < t only. All admissible states form a certain set B ∈ X, where X is the phase space of the system. Assume that the system evolves stochastically, i.e., its state at a time t is not uniquely defined by the state at a preceding time s, thereby being random. Denote by $P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},t,B)$ the probability of the event $\left\{ \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t) \in B(s < t) \right\}$ under the condition $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(s) = \overset{\rightarrow}{x},$ which is often called the transition probability or the conditional probability of the system state's belonging to a set B at a time t given its state $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}$ at a time s in the phase space X.

Suppose that there exists an intermediate state $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(u)$ between the states $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(s)$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t),$ where s < u < t. Denote by $P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},u,\overset{\rightarrow}{y},t,B)$ the conditional probability of the event $\left\{ \overset{\rightarrow}{x}(t) \in B \right\}$ given $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(s) = \overset{\rightarrow}{x}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{x}(u) = \overset{\rightarrow}{y}.$ Using the general properties of conditional probabilities, write


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},t,B) = {\int_{X}P}(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},u,\overset{\rightarrow}{y},t,B)\, P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},u,\overset{\rightarrow}{y})\, d\overset{\rightarrow}{y}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.32)

For a nonhereditary system, a natural assumption is


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},u,\overset{\rightarrow}{y},t,B) = P(u,\overset{\rightarrow}{y},t,B).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.33)

In this case, equality (2.34) takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},t,B) = {\int_{X}P}(u,\overset{\rightarrow}{y},t,B)\, P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},u)\, d\overset{\rightarrow}{y}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.34)

This is the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation, which underlies the theory of Markov processes [47, 65, 166].

A Markov process is called homogeneous if the transition probabilities depend on the difference of the arguments t and s only, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},t,B) = P(t - s,\overset{\rightarrow}{x},B) = P_{t - s}(\overset{\rightarrow}{x},B).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.35)

For the homogeneous Markov processes, the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation (2.34) can be written in the simpler form


$$\begin{array}{r} {P_{u + v}(\overset{\rightarrow}{x},B) = {\int_{X}P_{u}}(\overset{\rightarrow}{x})P_{v}(\overset{\rightarrow}{y},B)\, d\overset{\rightarrow}{y}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.36)

The definitions given in this section are wide, thereby embracing the Markov processes that differ in their sources and properties. In the sequel, we will discuss some classification principles and certain classes of Markov processes. The first attribute for classification consists in the phase space of the system in which a Markov process is observed. From this viewpoint the elementary Markov processes are the ones with finite or denumerable sets of admissible states. In the latter case, by imposing some analytical constraints on transition probabilities, we can linearize the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations and obtain their linearized counterparts. For general phase spaces, it is possible to define the classes of Markov processes in a wide sense, enduing transitional probabilities with more adequate properties in terms of real system behavior. This viewpoint allows introducing the following classes of Markov processes:

  1. Jump processes. They correspond to the idea of the processes that move to a certain point of a phase space, staying at this point during a random period of time, and then jump to another point of the space, and so on.

  2. Processes with discrete interference of events. These processes are generated by a dynamic system whose trajectories suffer from simple discontinuities with random jumps at random times.

  3. Diffusion processes. They represent the processes in finite-dimensional dynamic systems that have Brownian motion on small periods of time.

  4. Markov processes with independent increments. The sources of such processes are the finite-dimensional dynamic systems that behave as the processes with independent increments on small periods of time.

For the above-mentioned classes of Markov processes, it is also possible to perform linearization of the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation, transforming it to a linear partial differential equation or an integro-differential equation.

2.2Digital Source of Data

As a matter of fact, digital data are represented by arrays of decimal or binary numbers. They are generated using digital measuring devices. However, we often deal with an analog measuring device. Then these arrays are the result of a digital transformation of initial analog information about a studied object or phenomenon. In other words, an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) is placed after the studied object or phenomenon, as illustrated in Fig. 2.1. For example, if the studied object operates on a given time interval 𝒯, thereby generating a certain continuous process, an ADC transforms this process into digital arrays. An ADC performs the amplitude and time quantization of an initial continuous process. A photograph is another example in which a visual image acts as an analog source. However, a photograph is transformed into a digital array using a slightly different ADC with scanning.

2.2.1Amplitude and time quantization

Amplitude quantization decomposes a certain set of values of a function into a finite number of subsets. If the function under consideration is scalar, then the matter concerns quantization intervals. For a vector function, the concept of quantization has a close relation to the decomposition of the set of values of its components into elementary volumes. The simplest type of quantization is the division of a range Δϕ = ϕmax − ϕmin of an analog function by an integer number, with rounding up or down to the nearest integer number. As a rule, quantization runs in binary code. The range Δϕ is divided by 2n, where n denotes the register length (or the digit count). Each amplitude is coded by a sequence of zeros and ones of length n.

Time quantization, further termed time sampling (in our case, the argument of a function is time), is performed using a pulse generator. Note that sampling rate must be at least twice as large as the maximum frequency of the function spectrum.

Consequently, values of an analog function (information, signal) are represented by a sequence of binary numbers that corresponds to the values of this function at discrete times.

Amplitude quantization is a nonlinear transformation for the values of an analog function [197]. Figure 2.2 shows the characteristic of a nonlinear element that performs the amplitude quantization of an analog function. Amplitude quantization can be uniform and nonuniform. In the former case, the quantization step hk = yk + 1 − yk is a constant h. Under nonuniform amplitude quantization, this step depends on the amplitude. Nonuniform amplitude quantization reduces the relative error of digital data generation. Figures 2.3(a)–2.3(c) demonstrate the characteristics of quantizers with different rounding rules: a—rounding up to the nearest integer number, b—rounding down to the nearest integer and c—rounding to the middle of the elementary interval.

Time sampling causes no measurement errors whereas amplitude quantization is accompanied by an error ε due to rounding. For estimating this error, a certain model has to be chosen. Consider two models, namely, deterministic and stochastic ones. Within the framework of the first model, the above-mentioned rounding rules lead to the maximum error


$$\begin{array}{r} {\varepsilon_{max} = h.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.37)

In other words, it coincides with the quantization step h. Assuming the quantization error to be a random variable, we have to declare its probability density function (PDF). For example, let this variable obey the uniform distribution on the interval $\lbrack - \frac{h}{2},\frac{h}{2}\rbrack,$ i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {p(\varepsilon) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{h} & {\text{for}\,\left| \varepsilon \middle| \leq \frac{h}{2}, \right.} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\,\left| \varepsilon \middle| > \frac{h}{2}. \right.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.38)

Since the PDF has symmetry, the mean of the quantization error is zero whereas its variance is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sigma^{2} = \frac{1}{h}{\int\limits_{- h/2}^{h/2}\varepsilon^{2}}d\varepsilon = \frac{h^{2}}{12}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.39)

Interestingly, the derived estimate is considerably smaller than the one of the deterministic model (2.37). However, recall that this estimate of the quantization error proceeds from the hypotheses of uniform distribution and uncorrelatedness with the analog function.

2.2.2Audio data

The digital conversion of sound signals is performed by an ADC, which transforms an analog signal into digital audio data. These transformations use different types of digital modulation. Pulse code modulation (PCM) and delta modulation (DM) are most widespread.

PCM transforms a sequence of the instantaneous amplitudes of an analog signal x(t) (Fig. 2.4(a)) into the quantized values with a fixed step h that correspond to discrete times nΔ (Fig. 2.4(b)). Each value xPC[nΔ] is transformed into a binary code, as illustrated in Fig. 2.4(c). Such a modulator outputs packets of 0's and 1's with time binding.

The accuracy of PCM depends on the step h and the number N of quantization amplitudes. The largest quantized value is (N − 1)h. The number of binary code combinations makes up n = [log2(N − 1)h], where [ ⋅ ] denotes the integer part operator.

DM is a special type of PCM that also represents an analog signal in the form of discrete samples of time with amplitude quantization. By assumption, there exists a relation between the samples in an audio signal. Therefore, it is possible to use only one digit for quantization of neighbor samples. Figures 2.5(a)–2.5(b) illustrate operation of a delta modulator. As its output this modulator (see Fig. 2.5(a)) generates a binary sequence of pulses,  + 1 for positive difference and  − 1 for negative difference.

The digital representation of sound signals is used in two ways as follows. First, for improving the quality of sound and further conversion back to the analog form. Second, for forming quantitatively measured attributes that characterize sound signals [124]. In this context, above all attributes, note the spectral composition of a signal and its basic parameters.

Consider again an analog signal described by a continuous function x(t). Let this function be defined and square integrable on the infinite interval ( − ∞,  + ∞). Then the Fourier transform of the function is given by


$$\begin{aligned} {\Phi_{1}(\nu)} & {= {\int\limits_{- \infty}^{+ \infty}x}(t)\exp( - 2\pi\iota\nu t)dt = \Phi(2\pi\nu),} \\ {\Phi_{2}(\omega)} & {= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\int\limits_{- \infty}^{+ \infty}x}(t)\exp( - \iota\omega t)dt = \sqrt{2\pi}\Phi(\omega),} \\ {\Phi(\omega)} & {= {\int\limits_{- \infty}^{+ \infty}x}(t)\exp( - \iota\omega t)dt.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.40)

Here $\iota = \sqrt{- 1}$, ν denotes linear frequency (in Hz), and ω = 2πν is angular frequency (in rad/s). Formulas (2.40) incorporate the complex exponents


$$\begin{array}{r} {\exp( - \iota\omega t) = \cos(\omega t) - \iota\sin(\omega t).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.41)

The function Φ(ω) is continuous for ω ∈ ( − ∞,  + ∞).

A real analog signal is defined on a finite time interval 𝒯 = [0, T]. A digital transformation of this signal yields a sequence of quantized values called samples of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {x\lbrack n\Delta\rbrack = {\int\limits_{- \infty}^{+ \infty}x}(\tau)\,\delta(n\Delta - \tau)d\tau,} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.42)

where δ( • ) denotes the delta-function, $\Delta = \frac{T}{N - 1},$ and N is the number of samples. Therefore, the digital representation of an analog signal on a finite time interval 𝒯 is described by an N-dimensional vector x with the elements x[nΔ] (2.42). According to (2.40), the Fourier transform of this signal is given by


$$\begin{aligned} {\Psi(\omega) = \Psi\left( {\frac{2\pi}{T}k} \right)} & {= \Psi(k) = {\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{N - 1}x}\lbrack n\Delta\rbrack\,\exp\left( {- \iota\frac{2\pi}{T}k\, n} \right) =} \\ {= {\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{N - 1}x}\lbrack n\Delta\rbrack} & {\left\lbrack {\cos\left( {\frac{2\pi}{T}kn} \right) - \sin\left( {\frac{2\pi}{T}kn} \right)} \right\rbrack,} \\ & {\quad k = \overline{0,N-1},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.43)

and called the discrete Fourier transform (DFT). Clearly, the DFT as the discrete spectrum of a digital signal is characterized by a vector $\overline{\Psi}$ with the elements Ψ(k) (2.2.2). Note that the dimension of this vector coincides with that of the vector x composed of the digital samples (2.42); see Figs. 2.6(a) and 2.6(b).

The vector $\overline{\Psi}$ determines the frequency distribution of the energy of the sound signal under consideration. As a rule, the interval Δ is sufficiently small to preserve the informational characteristics of the analog signal on the time interval 𝒯. Subsequently, the vector $\overline{\Psi}$ has a rather high dimension, which complicates the use of the discrete spectrum in applications. On the basis of this vector, it is necessary to obtain a reduced vector z with an essentially smaller dimension in comparison with the initial vector $\overline{\Psi}.$ A simple (albeit, not most objective and informative) solution is to assign a small number of intervals [0, k1], [k1 + 1, k2], …, [ks + 1, N − 1] and to construct the so-called energy spectrum, i.e., a vector z with the elements


$$\begin{array}{r} {z_{j} = {\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{k_{1}}\Psi}(i) + {\sum\limits_{i = k_{(j - 1)} + 1}^{k_{j}}\Psi}(i),\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{2,m},\quad m \ll (N - 1).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.44)

Then the total energy takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {E = {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{N - 1}\Psi}(k).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.45)

2.2.3Graphical data

Graphical data are the result of digitizing 2D analog monochrome or color images. The examples of such images include paintings, manuscripts, photo and video images, etc. The images are transformed into graphical data in two ways, using bit image (raster) graphics and vector graphics.

Bit image graphical data represent a matrix of fixed-size pixels. The digitization of analog images is performed through spatial discretization. More specifically, an image is split into separate elements (pixels) and each pixel is associated with 2D coordinates and a grey gradation (for monochrome images) or a color palette (for color images). The coordinates and palettes have digital form. Spatial discretization expresses graphical data as a matrix of finite dimensions in which each row contains a definite number of pixels with an appropriate color in a digital scale. At the hardware level, the bit image conversion of an analog image is implemented by a scanner. An example of bit image graphical data is given in Fig. 2.7(a).

Vector graphical data involve a mathematical description of the elementary graphical objects called primitives. Among such objects, note points, straight lines, some curves, splines, circles, polygons, etc. An example of vector graphics primitives is shown in Fig. 2.7(b). The major advantage of vector data over bit image data consists in a rather simple scalability without compromise to the original quality of an image.

In most cases, analog images are transformed into digital for further automatic processing using digital devices such as computers, smartphones, video and photo cameras, and so on. Consider the images of standard (fixed-form) documents, e.g., billing and banking documents, fiscal documents, voting ballots and questionnaires. These documents have a definite structure with fields to be filled. In other words, useful graphical data is contained only in corresponding boxes. Hence, there is no need to scan the entire document, just the requisite fields only. Therefore, the bit image representation of such a document has a fixed structure and a bit image representation of its fields.

Note that vector formats are often transformed into bit image ones. At the same time, the converse transformation is computationally intensive.

2.2.4Text data

Text is a peculiar object for digitization that essentially differs from the above-mentioned ones. Information about audio, video and graphical objects is completely reflected by physical measurements. In contrast, text is the result of integration of some rules and human perceptions of these rules. Subsequently, text has meaning as its distinctive attribute, unlike the objects of the other types. As a matter of fact, the notion of meaning is ambiguous, which causes its implicit description in terms of numerical characteristics.

Therefore, text data are numerical data yielded by some model of text [167]. We will comprehend a model of text as a set of numerical indicators used for its characterization. Besides easily calculated indicators, there exist the so-called syntax trees (or diagrams) and semantic networks with construction procedures of giant computational complexity.

Text modeling involves different types of information about text, i.e., text-relevant information and external information. The following types of text-relevant information are widespread:

  • the frequency characteristics of text elements (in the elementary case, the presence or absence of words (terms) from a given list in a document);

  • the mutual position of words in a document. Words have a definite order in accordance with the syntax rules of a given language, thereby forming groups and sentences. The mutual position of words contain some useful information;

  • formatting of a document. As a rule, before publication a text is appropriately formatted. Separate words, sentences or even paragraphs can be set in different types (bold, italic, etc.) or aligned;

  • the logical structure of a document. A document often consists of chapters, sections, subsection and paragraphs. Such a logical structure of a document reflects the meaning of text;

  • references to other documents. Documents often refer to other documents (e.g., in the form of hypertext links or bibliographic citations).

External information includes information about the source, author, date of creation or modification of a document, subject classification, user's behavior with respect to a document (e.g., user's access rate, etc.).

The frequency characteristics of a document are most widely used, in the first place, the histogram of homogeneous attributes, e.g., the vector of entries of keywords [160]. In this case, a common glossary of terms has to be managed for all documents analyzed. Each document is represented as a vector whose elements show the occurrence of corresponding terms in the document. This vector has a very large dimension that matches the total number of terms in the glossary.

In the general setting, an element of this vector represents an informational weight of a term in a document. Actually, the informational weight of a term is treated in a wider sense with additional attributes, e.g., the informational weight of a short sequence of letters (e.g., a combination of two letters), syllables, words, or normal-form word combinations [175]. The weight of an element is often defined using some statistical characteristics of its occurrence in text, with certain coefficients that reflect the format and position of this element in a given document.

In the first stage of a numerical characterization of text, the extended term weight allows to separate out a set (bag) of most adequate words for a document. The bag-of-words model was suggested in 1975, still remaining a commonly used model of text [170]. Within the framework of this model, text is represented as a set of words, regardless of their order. A certain weight is assigned for each word in this set. Therefore, the model of a document consists of a finite set of word-weight pairs. Note that weights can be assigned to words (terms) or stems. There exist the following standard methods to assign weights [93]:

  • the binary method (BI). This method defines only the presence or absence of certain terms in a document;

  • the number of term entries in a document. If a term appears many times in text, the document under consideration is likely to have a semantic relation to this term;

  • the term frequency (TF). The term frequency is calculated as the number of term entries divided by the total number of words in a document;

  • the logarithmical term frequency (LOGTF). This method defines the weight of a term as 1 + log (TF), where TF is the term frequency. Due to the logarithmical scale of informational weight assignment, the model has higher stability against overestimation of documents; the inverse document frequency (IDF). This parameter is the inversion of the term frequency.

A conventional approach is to analyze texts using a collection of documents described by a term-weight matrix.

2.2.5Government statistical data

There exist many objects that are assessed by government statistics services using problem-oriented registers associated with definite time scales. In the first place, note the measurements and state assessments for the economic system (macroindices, labour resources, GDP, finances, etc.), the demographic system (fertility, mortality and migration rates), and the environmental system (atmosphere, earth, water, soil, and so on). A considerable part of statistical measurements are performed for different regions of a country.

A government statistics system implements the acquisition, analysis and structuring of all measured parameters, as well as their further transformation into data in accordance with an accepted register. Each of these stages, from the acquisition of information from existing sources to data structuring in tabular form, is accompanied by inevitable errors, also causing errors in government statistical data. There exist two types of errors, namely, systematic errors and coverage errors. The former occur due to imperfect methods for transforming initial information into data, whereas the latter due to the mismatch between the target object and the elements actually observed.

To elucidate this point, let us consider an example of data formation to calculate per capita national income. This problem seems trivial: just divide the annual GDP in monetary terms by the amount of able-bodied population. However, the annual GDP in monetary terms is calculated using generalized prices that are defined by certain models. The input variables and characteristics (parameters) of these models are measured and estimated with errors (often interpreted as random variables). Therefore, the annual GDP is the arithmetical mean by month with the estimated variance. A similar situation takes place for able-bodied population, as its size varies unpredictably in the course of a year. In other words, the calculated value of the annual GDP incorporates both types of errors.

Consider the following mathematical model of this situation. Denote by x an index of interest that is associated with a time t. Assume that this index depends on n factors, y1, …, yn. Such an assumption leads to coverage errors: there is no evidence that the accepted set of factors (i.e., their number and meaning) is complete for defining the index x.

The next stage in formation of the index x is to model a parameterized relation between the factors and x, that is,


$$\begin{array}{r} {x = F(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{a}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.46)

where a = {a1,…,ap} act as parameters. The function F and its parameterization are chosen via expertise. Exactly this stage introduces systematic errors due to limited, incomplete and subjective knowledge of experts.

As a matter of fact, a government statistics system has a distributed structure and involves various primary processing methods for initial information. In combination with the human factor, these features almost rule out the possibility of adequate estimation for the government statistics errors. A remaining alternative is to use expert appraisals, which have a rather large spread from 5% to 20%.

The existing errors essentially affect (a) the estimated characteristics of relations between the input and output data and also (b) the solutions of other problems involving government statistical data.

2.3Restoration Methods for Missing Data

Digital sources generate sequences of data that are bound to time scales. A common situation in practice is the existence of different time scales or omissions for a certain time scale. However, for further usage of data sequences, one often needs to perform their synchronization (reduction to the same scale) or to restore missing data. As a matter of fact, data synchronization and restoration are close problems and their solution employs similar methods. Consider some of the methods in detail.

2.3.1Interpolation

A digital source of data generates a sequence of values of an analog function x(t) for a finite set of values of its argument. As a rule, these values are associated with a certain time scale with a step h. Take another function y(t) with a generated sequence of values in a different time scale with a step s < h such that {h/s} is an integer. Then we naturally arrive at the synchronization of these functions, i.e., it is necessary to restore the values of x(t) within the intervals [ih, (i + 1)h] with the step s (the so-called data interpolation problem). The classical approach to solve this problem is to construct a rather simple function z(t) so that its values in the h-scale coincide with the values of the function x(t) in the same scale, that is, z[0] = x[0], ⋯, z[ih] = x[ih].

Consider an arbitrary real function x(t) ∈ R defined on an interval 𝒯 = [0, T]. In space R choose a finite collection of elementary (simple) functions {φk(t)}0n so that they are linearly independent. In most cases, this is a sequence of power functions 1, t, t2, …; or trigonometric functions 1, sin t, cos t, sin 2t, cos 2t, …; or exponential functions 1, exp (α1t), exp (α2t), …, where {αi} denotes a number sequence.

Using the first n + 1 functions {φk(t)}0n, construct all possible linear combinations


$$\begin{array}{r} {a_{0}\varphi_{0}(t) + a_{1}\varphi_{1}(t) + \cdots + a_{n}\varphi_{n}(t) = \psi(t)} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.47)

with real coefficients a0, …, an. In interpolation theory, these coefficients are calculated in the following way. Choose n + 1 values of the variable t, i.e., t0, …, tn, which are called interpolation nodes. Let the function x(t) and its interpolating function ψ(t) have the same values at these nodes. This leads to the system of linear equations


$$\begin{array}{r} {x(t_{j}) = a_{0}\varphi_{0}(t_{j}) + a_{1}\varphi_{1}(t_{j}) + \cdots + a_{n}\varphi_{n}(t_{j}),\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{0,n}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.48)

The nodes should be chosen so that the determinant


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Delta = \left| \begin{array}{lll} {\varphi_{0}(t_{0})} & \cdots & {\varphi_{n}(t_{0})} \\ \cdots & \cdots & \cdots \\ {\varphi_{0}(t_{n})} & \cdots & {\varphi_{n}(t_{n})} \\ \end{array} \right| \neq 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.49)

Then the system possesses the unique solution


$$\begin{array}{r} {a_{i} = \frac{{\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{n}x}(t_{j})\Delta_{ij}}{\Delta},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{0,n},} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.50)

where Δij gives the algebraic complement of element (ij). Thus, according to (2.47),


$$\begin{array}{r} {\psi(t) = x(t_{0})\Phi_{0}(t) + x(t_{1})\Phi_{1}(t) + \ldots + x(t_{n})\Phi_{n}(t).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.51)

The functions Φi(t) are linear combinations of the functions ϕi(t) and do not depend on the function x(t). Since the equalities x(tj) = ψ(tj) hold at the interpolation nodes, the functions Φi(t) satisfy the following conditions:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Phi_{i}(t_{j}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 0 & {\text{for}\, i \neq j,} \\ 1 & {\text{for}\, i = j.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.52)

See, e.g., the monograph [17] for a discussion of refined interpolation procedures and their properties.

As background information consider some classes of interpolating functions that are widely used in applications. First, the Lagrange interpolating polynomial. Consider a sequence of power functions 1, t, t2, ...., tn, ... as a basic one. This sequence is linearly independent on any interval. For defining the function ψ(t) (2.47), find the functions Φi(t) that are linear combinations of the functions ϕ0(t), …, ϕn(t) and satisfy conditions (2.52). In other words, using the elements of the basic sequence, it is required to construct a polynomial that vanishes at the points t0, …, ti − 1 and takes value 1 at the point ti. Such a polynomial has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Phi_{i}(t) = A(t - t_{0})(t - t_{1})\cdots(t - t_{i - 1})(t - t_{i + 1})\cdots(t - t_{n}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.53)

Since Φi(ti) = 1, it follows that


$$\begin{array}{r} {1 = A(t_{i} - t_{0})(t_{i} - t_{1})\cdots(t_{i} - t_{i - 1})(t_{i} - t_{i + 1})\cdots(t_{i} - t_{n}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.54)

Subsequently,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Phi_{i}(t) = \frac{(t - t_{0})(t - t_{1})\cdots(t - t_{i - 1})(t - t_{i + 1})\cdots(t - t_{n})}{(t_{i} - t_{0})(t_{i} - t_{1})\cdots(t_{i} - t_{i - 1})(t_{i} - t_{i + 1})\cdots(t_{i} - t_{n})}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.55)

And the Lagrange interpolating polynomial is given by


$$\begin{aligned} {\psi(t) = L_{n}(t)} & {= x(t_{0})\frac{(t - t_{1})\cdots(t - t_{n})}{(t_{0} - t_{1})\cdots(t_{0} - t_{n})} +} \\ & {+ x(t_{1})\frac{(t - t_{0})(t - t_{2})\ldots(t - t_{n})}{(t_{1} - t_{0})(t_{1} - t_{2})\ldots(t_{1} - t_{n})} + \cdots +} \\ & {+ x(t_{n})\frac{(t - t_{0})\ldots(t - t_{n - 1})}{(t_{n} - t_{0})(t_{n} - t_{1})\ldots(t_{n} - t_{n - 1})}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.56)

Introduce the function


$$\begin{array}{r} {\omega_{n}(t) = {\prod\limits_{i = 0}^{n}{(t - t_{i})}}} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.57)

and write the Lagrange interpolating polynomial as


$$\begin{array}{r} {L_{n}(t) = {\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{n}x}(t_{i})\frac{\omega_{n}(t)}{(t - t_{i})\omega_{n}^{\prime}(t_{i})}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.58)

In the sense of applications, the Lagrange interpolating polynomial is somewhat inconvenient, as adding a new node requires forming a new polynomial. This drawback takes no place for the interpolating polynomial in the Newton representation. More specifically, the Newton interpolating polynomial involves the notion of divided differences [17] as follows.

Consider (n + 1) nodes and as many values of a function x(t), i.e., x(t0), …, x(tn). The first divided difference of the function x(t) at nodes ti − 1, ti is the value


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Delta_{i - 1,i} = \frac{x(t_{i}) - x(t_{i - 1})}{t_{i} - t_{i - 1}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.59)

The higher-order divided differences are calculated recursively. The divided difference of order m has the general formula


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Delta_{i - 1,i,i + 1,\ldots,i + m} = \frac{\Delta_{i,i + 1,\ldots,i + m} - \Delta_{i - 1,i,i + 1,\ldots,i + m - 1}}{t_{i + m} - t_{i}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.60)

Express the the Lagrange interpolating polynomial as


$$\begin{array}{r} {L_{n}(t) = L_{0}(t) + (L_{1}(t) - L_{0}(t)) + \ldots + (L_{n}(t) - L_{n - 1}(t)).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.61)

Clearly, this is the identity Ln(t) = Ln(t). It is possible to show [17] that


$$\begin{array}{r} {L_{i}(t) - L_{i - 1}(t) = \Delta_{0,\ldots,i}\omega_{i}(t),} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.62)

where ωi(t) = (t − t0)⋯(t − ti). Then the Newton representation Nn(t) of the Lagrange interpolating polynomial can be written as


$$\begin{aligned} & {L_{n}(t) = N_{n}(t) = x(t_{0}) + \Delta_{0,1}(t - t_{1}) + \ldots +} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad} + \Delta_{0,\ldots,n}(t - t_{0})(t - t_{1})\cdots(t - t_{n - 1}).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.63)

Once again, note that an interested reader may derive deep knowledge of the interpolating polynomials from the monograph [17].

2.3.2Auxiliary dynamic models

In this subsection, we describe a restoration method for missing data (in a time scale) that is based on mathematical models of a data source. Let 𝒳hN = {x[0],x[h],…,x[Nh]} be a packet of numerical data bound to a time scale with a step h. Using these data, construct a step function x̃(t) of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\widetilde{x}(t) = x\lbrack ih\rbrack\quad\text{for~}ih \leq t < (i + 1)h,\quad i = \overline{0,N-1}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.64)

Consider a dynamic system with the above step function as its input and an output y(t) of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. y\lbrack nh\rbrack = \mathcal{L}(x\lbrack ih\rbrack,\mathbf{a}\, \middle| \, 0 \leq i < n). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(2.65)

In this expression, ℒ denotes a functional that characterizes the dynamic properties of the system with parameters a ∈ Rm, where m is the dimension of the parameter vector. The parameters a actually affect the function y(t), i.e., y(t, a). For some values of the elements of the vector a, the system outputs a packet 𝒴hN = {y[0,a],y[h,a],…,y[(N−1)h,a]} at discrete times ih.

Define the total residual between packets 𝒳hN, 𝒴hN as


$$\begin{array}{r} {J(\mathbf{a}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{N}{(x\lbrack ih\rbrack - y\lbrack ih,\mathbf{a}\rbrack)}^{2}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.66)

The minimum of this residual gives the optimal parameters under which the difference between the above-mentioned packets at the nodes of the h-scale is as small as possible (in terms of the functional J (2.66)), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a}^{*} = \arg\min J(\mathbf{a}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.67)

Substituting the optimal parameters into (2.65) yields the packet 𝒴sNr = {y*[0],y*[s],…,y*[(l−1)s],y*[h],y[h+s],…,y*[h+(l−1)s];y*[2h],y*[2h+s],…,y*[Nh]}, where s < h, h/s = r and r is an integer.

This method will be illustrated using an example of a linear dynamic system with a pulse response w(t, a), t ≥ 0. Let


$$\begin{array}{r} {w(t) = a_{1}\exp( - a_{2}t),} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.68)

where a1, a2 are interval-type unknown parameters, i.e., the ones belonging to some intervals 0 < a1 ≤ a1+ and a2− ≤ a2 ≤ a2+, respectively. Generally speaking, the limits of these intervals are unknown. A possible way to find them consists in the global minimization of J (2.66) in a1+, a2− and a2+ (or calculation of an admissible small value if the global minimum does not exist).

Supply the step function x̃(t) to the input of this system to generate the output


$$\begin{array}{r} {y(t) = a_{1}{\int\limits_{0}^{t}\exp}( - a_{2}(t - \tau))\widetilde{x}(\tau)d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.69)

The interval [0,t] contains an integer number of subintervals N = {t/h} and t = Nh + μ, where 0 ≤ μ < (N + 1)h. Then the expression (2.69) can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {y(t) = \frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}\exp( - a_{2}t)\,{\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{N}x}\lbrack ih\rbrack\exp(a_{2}ih)\left( {\exp(a_{2}h) - 1} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.70)

The system output at the nodes of the h-scale is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {y\lbrack ih\rbrack = \frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}\left( {\exp(a_{2}h) - 1} \right)\exp( - a_{2}ih)\,{\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{i}x}\lbrack jh\rbrack\exp(a_{2}jh).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.71)

Consequently, the total residual functional (2.66) takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. J(a_{1},a_{2}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{N}{\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{i}\left( {A_{i,j}(a_{1},a_{2})x\lbrack jh\rbrack} \right)^{2}}}\Rightarrow\min, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(2.72)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {A_{i,j} = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}\left( {\exp(a_{2}h) - 1} \right)\exp(a_{2}h(j - i))} & {\text{for}\, j < i,} \\ {\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}\left( {\exp(a_{2}h) - 1} \right) - 1} & {\text{~for}\, j = i.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.73)

Note that the functional (2.72) possesses a rather complicated structure for an analytical study of its properties such as unique minimum, convexity (concavity), and so on. Therefore, in applications the missing data should be restored (or synchronized with other data packets) using numerical global minimization methods.

As soon as the parameters a1 and a2 are calculated, the missing data with the step s can be restored by


$$\begin{aligned} {y\lbrack ih + ks\rbrack} & {= \frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}\exp( - a_{2}(ih + ks))\,{\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{N}x}\lbrack ih\rbrack\exp(a_{2}ih)\left( {\exp(a_{2}h) - 1} \right),} \\ i & {= \overline{0,N},\,\, k = \overline{0,M},\,\, M = \left\{ h/s \right\}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.74)

2.3.3Spatial entropy decomposition

As emphasized earlier, the data formed by government statistics services are associated with certain spatial units (regions), each having a set of attributes, i.e., indicators. The dimensions of such regions and information about the values of these indicators are often related to each other. In many cases, the smaller is a region under consideration, the less accessible is information about its indicators. This leads to a rather topical problem of “spreading” the available state indicators of large regions to small districts within them using some indirect information about the latter.

Consider an economic space 𝔼 consisting of I regions. Each region i contains Mi districts, as shown in Fig. 2.8. Let the regions i and districts within them (i, j) be characterized by unique homogeneous indicators Si and Sij, respectively. For example, the list of possible indicators includes population size, production density, service endowment, and so on. The regional and district indicators, Si and Sij, satisfy the balance constraints


$$\begin{array}{r} {S_{i} = {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}S_{ij}},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,I}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.75)

Each region and hence district produces the goods of r types or disposes of r types of resources. Assume that, for each type k of goods (resources), the production functions of region i depend on the state indicators of all regions, i.e., $\overset{\rightarrow}{S} = \left\{ S_{1},\ldots,S_{I} \right\}.$ Denote these functions by $Q_{ik}(\overset{\rightarrow}{S}),\, i = \overline{1,I},\, k = \overline{1,r}.$ The same hypothesis also applies to the districts; denote their production functions by qijk(𝕊), where 𝕊 = {S11,…,S1, M1;…;SI, 1,…,SI, MI}. Then the resource constraints have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}q_{ijk}}(\mathbb{S}) = Q_{ik}(\mathbf{S}),\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,I},\,\, k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.76)

Suppose that the regional indicators S are known whereas the district ones 𝕊 are unknown. The problem is to find the district indicators taking into account the balance and resource constraints given by (2.75) and (2.76). The total number of the district indicators makes up $m = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{I}M_{i}},$ as by assumption each district and region has a single indicator. In addition, the problem includes (r + 1)I balance and resource constraints totally, and m > (r + 1)I. Therefore, numerous collections of district indicators satisfy equalities (2.75, 2.76).

An approach to obtain a unique collection of district indicators proceeds from the entropy maximization principle. As a matter of fact, entropy is a measure of uncertainty in the distribution of regional indicators over corresponding districts [138], i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {H(\mathbb{S}) = - {\sum\limits_{i = 1,j = 1}^{I,M_{i}}S_{ij}}\ln\frac{S_{ij}}{a_{ij}e},} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.77)

where 𝕊 is a matrix with entries Sij that characterizes the distribution of district indicators. The distribution of highest uncertainty, S, answers the maximum value of the entropy H under the balance and resource constraints (2.75, 2.76). Any prior information about the districts within the regions of interest can be incorporated into the parameters aij of the entropy function H.

Thus, the distribution of the regional indicators over the districts, called entropy decomposition, is the solution of the optimization problem


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(\mathbb{S})\Rightarrow\max,\quad\mathbb{S} \in D, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(2.78)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {D = \left\{ S_{ij} \middle| {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}S_{ij}} = S_{i};\,\,{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}q_{ijk}}(\mathbb{S}) = Q_{ik}(S),\quad i = \overline{1,I},\,\, k = \overline{1,r} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.79)

In this general statement, all regions and districts are related to each other through corresponding production functions. Another extreme case is when all regions and districts are isolated, i.e., the regional and district production functions depend only on the state indicators of their own regions or districts:


$$\begin{array}{r} {q_{ijk}(\mathbb{S}) = q_{ijk}(S_{ij}),\quad Q_{ik}(\mathbf{S}) = Q_{ik}(S_{i});\,\, i = \overline{1,I}\,\, k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.80)

For the isolated regions, the entropy decomposition problem (2.78) is reduced to I optimization problems of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H_{i}(\mathbb{S}_{i})\Rightarrow\max,\quad\mathbb{S}_{i} \in D_{i}, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(2.81)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {H_{i}(\mathbb{S}_{i}) = - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}S_{ij}}\ln\frac{S_{ij}}{a_{ij}e},} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.82)


$$\begin{array}{r} {D_{i} = \left\{ S_{ij} \middle| {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}S_{ij}} = S_{i},\,\,{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}q_{ijk}}(S_{ij}) = Q_{ik}(S_{i}),\quad i = \overline{1,I},\,\, k = \overline{1,r} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.83)

The production functions qijk of these districts form nonlinear functions of their state indicators. However, if an economy is in a neighborhood of an equilibrium, then the linear representation of the production functions becomes a completely adequate description of these functions, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {q_{ijk}(S_{ij}) = c_{ijk}S_{ij},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,I},\,\, k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.84)

Here cijk indicate the specific outputs of good k in district (i, j). In this case, the admissible set Di (2.83) is given by the system of linear equalities


$$\begin{array}{r} {D_{i} = \left\{ S_{ij} \middle| {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}S_{ij}} = S_{i};\,\,\,{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{i}}c_{ijk}}S_{ij} = Q_{ik}(S_{i}),\quad i = \overline{1,I},\,\, k = \overline{1,r} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.85)

Consider the specifics of the entropy decomposition procedure with the linear production functions for one region (I = 1) and one type of resources (r = 1):


$$\begin{aligned} {H_{1}(\mathbb{S}_{1})} & \left. = - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{1}}S_{1j}}\ln\frac{S_{1j}}{a_{1j}e}\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{1}}S_{1j}} & {= S_{1},\quad{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M_{1}}c_{1j1}}S_{1j} = Q_{11}(S_{1}).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.86)

This problem is characterized by the following parameters: the prior probabilities a1j; the state indicator S1 of the region; the specific productivities c1j1 and production function Q11 of the region. The solution of the problem, i.e., the entropy-optimal distribution of the regional state indicators over their districts depends on these parameters.

Introduce new variables in order to slightly reduce the number of parameters in the problem. Denote


$$\begin{array}{r} {w_{1j} = \frac{S_{1j}}{S_{1}},\text{\quad\quad}h_{1j1} = \frac{c_{1j1}}{Q_{11}(S_{1})},\,\, j = \overline{1,M_{1}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.87)

If the regional indicator S1 is given, then the variables h1j1 are also fixed. With these notations, the entropy decomposition problem can be written as


$$\begin{aligned} {H(\mathbf{w})} & \left. = - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}w_{j}}\ln\frac{w_{j}}{a_{j}e}\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}w_{j}} & {= 1;\quad{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}h_{j}}\, w_{j} = q,} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.88)

where q = 1/S1 and the subscripts i = k = 1 are omitted.

Solve the problem using the Lagrange method of multipliers. The Lagrange function has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {L(\mathbf{w},\mu,\lambda) = H(\mathbf{w}) + \mu(1 - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}w_{j}}) + \lambda(q - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}h_{j}}\, w_{j}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.89)

The first-order optimality conditions of the Lagrange function yield the equations


$$\begin{aligned} w_{j} & {= a_{j}\exp( - \mu - \lambda\, h_{j}) = a_{j}\, u\, z^{h_{j}};} \\ & {u = \exp( - \mu),\, z = \exp( - \lambda).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.90)

Taking into account the balance and resource constraints in (2.88), write the following equation for the Lagrange multiplier λ:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}a_{j}}\, z^{h_{j}}\,(h_{j} - q) = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,M}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.91)

Set


$$\begin{array}{r} {c_{j} = a_{j}(h_{j} - q),\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,M},} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.92)

and transform equation (2.91) to


$$\begin{array}{r} {f(z) = {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}c_{j}}z^{h_{j}} = 0,\quad z > 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.93)

Order the parameters hj so that


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 < h_{1} < h_{2} < \cdots < h_{l} < q < h_{l + 1} < \cdots < h_{M}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.94)

As a result,


$$\begin{array}{r} {c_{j} < 0\quad\text{for~}j = \overline{1,l}\quad\text{and}\quad c_{j} > 0\quad\text{~for~}j = \overline{l+1,M}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.95)

Consider equation (2.93) with the coefficients cj of arbitrary sign. Note that it has the root z0 = 0. Hence, this equation can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {f(z) = z^{h_{1}}f_{1}(z) = 0,\,\,\, z > 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.96)

where the function


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{1}(z) = c_{1} + {\sum\limits_{j = 2}^{M}c_{j}}z^{h_{j} - h_{1}}} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.97)

has no zero roots.

Theorem 2.1. Assume that the positive numbers h1, …, hM satisfy condition (2.94). Then the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{1}(z) = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.98)

where f1(z) is defined by (2.96), has at most M − 1 nonzero solutions.

Proof. To establish this, take advantage of the Gauss principle in the following formulation. Let the equation ϕ(x) = 0, where ϕ is a differentiable sufficiently many times function and x is a scalar variable, have n roots; then the equation ϕ′(x) = 0 has n − 1 nonzero roots located between the roots of the original equation.

Analyze the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{1}^{\prime}(x) = {\sum\limits_{j = 2}^{M}c_{j}}(h_{j} - h_{1})z^{h_{j} - h_{1} - 1} = 0.} \\ \end{array}$$

Since minj(hj − h1 − 1) = h2 − h1 − 1 > 0, this equation has a zero root. Hence, by analogy with (2.96) it can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{1}^{\prime}(x) = z^{h_{2} - h_{1} - 1}f_{2}(z) = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$

where the function


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{2}(z) = c_{2}(h_{2} - h_{1}) + {\sum\limits_{j = 3}^{M}c_{j}}(h_{j} - h_{1})z^{h_{j} - h_{1} - 1}} \\ \end{array}$$

has no zero roots. Continue this procedure to obtain


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{M - 1}^{\prime}(z) = z^{h_{M} - h_{M - 1 - 1}}f_{M}(z) = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$

where the function


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{M}(z) = c_{M - 1}(h_{M - 1} - h_{1})\cdots(h_{M - 1} - h_{M - 2}) + c_{M}(h_{M} - h_{1})\cdots(h_{M} - h_{M - 1})z^{h_{M} - h_{M - 1}}} \\ \end{array}$$

possesses no zero roots too. Consider the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {f_{M}(z) = 0.} \\ \end{array}$$

It has the nonzero root


$$\begin{array}{r} {y_{M}^{*} = z_{*}^{h_{M} - h_{M - 1}} = - \frac{c_{M - 1}(h_{M - 1} - h_{1})\cdots(h_{M - 1} - h_{M - 2})}{c_{M}(h_{M} - h_{1})\cdots(h_{M} - h_{M - 1})z^{h_{M} - h_{M - 1}}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

The derivative fM − 1′(z) possesses one zero root and one nonzero root yM*. Due to the Gauss principle, the equation fM − 1(z) = 0 has at most three roots one of which is zero (i.e., no more than two nonzero roots). On the other hand, fM − 1(z) = fM − 2′(z). Subsequently, the derivative fM − 2′(z) possesses at most two nonzero roots. Using the Gauss principle again, it is easy to find that the function fM − 2(z) has at most three nonzero roots. Following this line of reasoning, we finally get the desired result. ■

Now consider equations (2.96, 2.97) in which the coefficients cj are ordered in accordance with (2.95), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {c_{j} < 0\,\,\text{for}\,\, j = 1,\ldots,l,\text{\quad\quad}c_{j} > 0\,\,\text{for}\,\, j = l + 1,\ldots,M.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.99)

Theorem 2.2. Under conditions (2.95), equation (2.98) has a unique positive solution.

Proof. Write equation (2.98) as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(z) = \frac{{\sum\limits_{i = l + 1}^{M}c_{i}}z^{h_{i}}}{{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l}c_{j}}z^{h_{j}}} = 1,\,\, z \geq 0.} \\ \end{array}$$

Study the qualitative properties of the function ϕ(z), expressing it as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(z) = z^{h_{l + 1} - h_{1}}\frac{{\sum\limits_{i = l + 2}^{M}c_{i}}z^{h_{i}} + c_{l + 1}}{{\sum\limits_{j = 2}^{l}c_{j}}z^{h_{j}} + c_{1}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Clearly, ϕ(0) = 0. Now reduce the function ϕ(z) to the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(z) = z^{h_{M} - h_{l}}\frac{{\sum\limits_{i = l + 1}^{M - 1}c_{i}}z^{h_{i} - h_{M}} + c_{M}}{{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l - 1}c_{j}}z^{h_{j} - h_{l}} + c_{l}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Due to condition (2.95), ϕ(∞) = ∞. Consider the derivative of the function ϕ(z), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi^{\prime}(z) = \frac{{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l}{\sum\limits_{i = l + 1}^{M}c_{j}}}c_{i}(h_{i} - h_{j})z^{h_{j} + h_{i}}}{{({\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l}c_{j}}z^{h_{j}})}^{2}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Condition (2.95) leads to hi − hj > 0 for i = l + 1, …, M,  j = 1, …, l, and therefore ϕ′(z) > 0. ■

Thus, it has been shown that equation (2.98) possesses a unique positive solution under conditions (2.95).

Example 2.1 For problems of transportation infrastructure modeling, analysis and prediction, a typical scenario is the spatial decomposition of a given territory into rather small districts (traffic cells) with state indicators measured only for their groups.

As an example, consider a region of China that contains 26 traffic cells [189]. The region under study occupies the area P = 47 km2 accommodating S = 0.430 million of people. This population is somehow distributed over the traffic cells. Denote the real distribution by ${\widetilde{S}}_{j},\,\, j = \overline{1,M}.$

The problem is to synthesize a model-based distribution $S_{j},\,\, j = \overline{1,M},$ using the entropy decomposition method and to assess its adequacy to the real distribution. In this example, the state indicator of a traffic cell is the population located in it.

By assumption, there exists no prior information about the distribution. Therefore, the prior probabilities aj in the entropy function (2.82) can be treated constant, i.e., aj = a. Then the entropy expression takes a simpler form:


$$\begin{array}{r} {H(\mathbf{S}) = - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}S_{j}}\ln S_{j}.} \\ \end{array}$$

The population distribution over the traffic cells must satisfy the constraints (2.83). Recall that the first group of constraints applies to balance, and the second to resources (in our case, there is only one resource). Choose the generalized accommodation cost Q of population in the given region as a resource that characterizes the distribution. Then the parameters cj of the resource constraints are interpreted as the specific cost, i.e., the accommodation cost per one resident in cell j. Assume that this specific cost is proportional to the spatial weight of cell j, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {c_{j} = c\frac{p_{j}}{P},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,M}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Here pj denotes the area of cell j, and c is a normalized coefficient of proportionality measured in cost units. Table 2.1 shows the corresponding values of the relative specific cost c̃j = cj/c.

2.3.4Randomized restoration method for missing data

1. Structure of randomized restoration procedure for missing data

Consider components and properties of the informational support (infoware) of machine learning problems. A learning collection consists of some data on the functioning of an object O (Fig. 2.10) as well as on the measured input x(t) ∈ Rm and output y(t) ∈ Rn of the object O. The variables x(t) and y(t) contain measurement errors η(t) ∈ Rm and ξ(t) ∈ Rn, respectively. As a rule, information about them have a hypothetical character. A common assumption is that they figure in a learning collective additively:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}^{0}(t) + \eta(t);\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{y}(t) = \mathbf{y}^{0}(t) + \xi(t),} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.100)

where x0(t) and y0(t) are pure variables.

Suppose that the input and output are measured in the same time scale t = kh with a step h and on the same time interval 𝒯 = [0, T]. Hence, a real learning collection consists of a data matrix describing the input and output of the object O.

Data arrays for the input and output may have omissions; see the interval [k−, k+] in Fig. 2.11. There are three possible cases of such omissions: omissions in output data, omissions in input data and omissions in both types of data (not necessarily at the same time instants).

The main idea of randomized restoration of missing data is to replace the existing omissions by a missing data ensemble (MDE), i.e., the random values of the input and output components (see Fig. 2.11) optimized taking into account the available measurements. This is done using a randomized parametric model (RPM) of the object, whose probabilistic characteristics (the probability density functions (PDFs) of its parameters) are obtained through maximum entropy estimation (MEE). Details will be presented in Appendix A.

The optimized MDE is generated by the sampling of the optimal PDFs [64]. This MDE can be directly used for solving different machine learning problems. Also, it is possible to determine numerical characteristics of the optimized MDE, such as mean, median, variance pipe, interquantile data sets, etc. Figure 2.11 gives an illustration of this approach.

If omissions occur in output data, the procedure employs the input data x[kh], the RPM-O model and the output data with omissions $\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack kh\rbrack$ for calculating the entropy-optimal PDFs (Fig. 2.12(a)) and also for generating the ensemble 𝒴 of the restored input data.

The existing omissions in input data are restored using an additional RPM-I model with the input represented by an optimized sequence of independent random vectors η[kh] and the input data with omissions $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}\lbrack kh\rbrack.$ The PDFs of the parameters and this sequence are obtained through MEE. These functions are then used to generate the ensembles ℰ of the random vectors η[kh] and an ensemble 𝒳 of the restored input data; see Fig. 2.12(b).

Finally, consider the case of omissions both in the input and output data. First, the ensembles ℰ of the random vectors η[kh] and the ensemble 𝒳 of the input data are restored. Second, they are adopted for restoring the ensembles 𝒴 of the output data (Fig. 2.12(c)).

The set of randomized restoration methods for missing data will be denoted by RRMD (Random Restored Missing Data).

2. Optimization algorithms for MDE

a. Omissions in output data

Consider a discrete observation time interval τ = [0, N] On this interval, there are a set of input data x ∈ Rm without omissions, x[0], …, x[N], and a set of output data y ∈ Rn with omissions, y[0], …, y[k− − 1], y[k+ + 1], …, y[N]. The data y[k−], …, y[k+] are missing.

Construct the matrix


$$\begin{array}{r} {X_{(k - \varrho)} = \left\lbrack {\mathbf{x}\lbrack k - \varrho\rbrack,\mathbf{x}\lbrack k - \varrho + 1\rbrack,\ldots,\mathbf{x}\lbrack k\rbrack} \right\rbrack} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.101)

from the input data set, where ρ < N is a parameter.

The output data contain additive errors ξ[k] ∈ Rn of the interval type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\xi\lbrack k\rbrack \in \Xi_{k} = \lbrack\xi^{-},\xi^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.102)

The probabilistic properties of errors are characterized by PDFs Qk(ξ[k]), $k = \overline{0,N},$ which are assumed to be continuously differentiable.

In the general case, the relation between the input and output of the object O is described by a randomized parametric dynamic model RDM-O of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\rbrack = \mathbb{B}\left( {\mathbf{a},X_{(k - \varrho)}} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.103)

where 𝔹 is a nonlinear functional with random parameters a ∈ Rr of the interval type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} = \lbrack\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{a}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.104)

The probabilistic properties of these parameters are characterized by a PDF P(a), which is assumed to be continuously differentiable.

The observed output of RDM-O is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{v}\lbrack k\rbrack = \hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\rbrack + \xi\lbrack k\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.105)

For determining the optimal PDFs, apply the randomized machine learning (RML) algorithm suggested in [148]. In the case under consideration, it has the form


$$\begin{aligned} & {\quad\mathcal{H}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\xi)\rbrack = - {\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})\ln P(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} -} \\ & \left. - {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{T}{\int_{\Xi_{k}}Q_{k}}}(\xi\lbrack k\rbrack)\ln Q_{k}(\xi\lbrack k\rbrack)d\xi\lbrack k\rbrack\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ & {\quad{\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} = 1;\quad{\int_{\Xi_{k}}Q_{k}}(\xi\lbrack k\rbrack)d\xi\lbrack k\rbrack = 1,\,\, k = \overline{0,N},} \\ & {\quad{\int_{A}P}(\mathbf{a})\mathbb{B}\left( {\mathbf{a},X_{(k - \varrho)}} \right)d\mathbf{a} + {\int_{\Xi_{k}}Q_{k}}(\xi\lbrack k\rbrack)\xi\lbrack k\rbrack d\xi\lbrack k\rbrack = \mathbf{y}\lbrack k\rbrack,} \\ & {\quad k \neq k^{-},\ldots,k^{+};k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.106)

The PDFs are continuously differentiable, and the problem (2.106) belongs to the class of Lyapunov-type functional optimization problems [77]. Hence, it is possible to construct an analytical solution parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers {θ(0),…,θk− − 1,θk+ + 1,…,θ(N)}:


$$\begin{aligned} & {P^{*}(\mathbf{a},\theta) = \frac{\exp\left\lbrack {- {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{N}\langle}\theta^{(k)},\mathbb{B}\left( \left. \mathbf{a},X_{(k - \varrho)} \right\rangle \right)} \right\rbrack}{\mathcal{P}(\theta)},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}Q_{k}^{*}(\xi\lbrack k\rbrack,\theta^{(k)}) = \frac{\exp\left( {- \left\langle \theta^{(k)},\xi\lbrack k\rbrack \right\rangle} \right)}{\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\theta^{(k)})},} \\ & {\quad\text{\quad\quad}k \neq k^{-},\ldots,k^{+};\quad k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.107)

Here


$$\begin{aligned} & {\mathcal{P}(\theta) = {\int_{\mathcal{A}}\exp}\left\lbrack {- {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{N}\langle}\theta^{(k)},\mathbb{B}\left( \left. \mathbf{a},X_{(k - \varrho)} \right\rangle \right)} \right\rbrack d\mathbf{a},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\theta^{(k)}) = {\int_{\Xi_{k}}\exp}\left( {- \left\langle \theta^{(k)},\xi\lbrack k\rbrack \right\rangle} \right)d\xi\lbrack k\rbrack,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\quad k \neq k^{-},\ldots,k^{+};\quad k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.108)

The Lagrange multipliers are determined from the system of equations


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\mathbf{M}_{k}(\theta)}{\mathcal{P}(\theta)} + \frac{\mathbf{N}_{k}(\theta^{(k)})}{\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\theta^{(k)})} = \mathbf{y}\lbrack k\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k \neq k^{-},\ldots,k^{+};k = \overline{0,N},} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.109)

where


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{M}_{k}(\theta) = \int_{\mathcal{A}}} & {\exp\left\lbrack {- {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{T}\left\langle \theta^{(k)},\mathbb{B}\left( {\mathbf{a},X_{(k - \varrho)}} \right) \right\rangle}} \right\rbrack\mathbb{B}\left( {\mathbf{a},X_{(k - \varrho)}} \right)d\mathbf{a},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.110)


$$\begin{aligned} & {\mathbf{N}_{k}(\theta^{(k)}) = {\int_{\Xi_{k}}\exp}\left( {- \left\langle \theta^{(k)},\xi\lbrack k\rbrack \right\rangle} \right)\xi\lbrack k\rbrack d\xi\lbrack k\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.111)

b. Omissions in input data

Restoring omissions in input data is more difficult than the ones in output data. Really, the origin mechanism of input data and the source of its excitation are both unknown. In terms of the approach adopted here, this means that the model generating input data and also the process exciting it are unknown. All these factors increase the level of uncertainty in the problem, motivating the choice of randomization.

The randomized approach consists in using a sequence of independent random vectors $\zeta\lbrack k\rbrack \in R^{q}\,\,(k\overline{0,N})$ with special probabilistic characteristics, and a randomized parametric model, the choice of which is determined by its complexity.

Well, consider the observation interval τ = [0, N] and an input data set x ∈ Rm with omissions x[0], …, x[k− − 1], x[k+ + 1], …, x[T]. The data x[k−], …, x[k+] are missing.

To restore the missing input data, assume that they are the result of transforming a sequence of independent random vectors ζ[k] ∈ Rq, k ∈ τ. Let the vectors ζ[k] be of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\zeta\lbrack k\rbrack \in \mathcal{Z}_{k} = \lbrack\zeta^{-}\lbrack k\rbrack,\zeta^{+}\lbrack k\rbrack\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N},} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.112)

Due to the uncertainty and insufficient knowledge about the process and its transformation, choose the randomized parametric (RPM-I) model


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathbf{x}}\lbrack k\rbrack = \mathbb{F}\left( {\mathbf{c},Z_{(k - \rho)}} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.113)

where 𝔽 is a nonlinear vector functional with random parameters c ∈ Rs and Z(k − ρ) is the input matrix of dimensions (q × ρ) composed of the column vectors ζ[k] ∈ Rq, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {Z_{(k - \rho)} = \left\lbrack {\zeta\lbrack k - \rho\rbrack,\zeta\lbrack k - \rho + 1\rbrack,\ldots,\zeta\lbrack k\rbrack} \right\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.114)

Introduce the matrix


$$\begin{array}{r} {Z = \left\lbrack {Z_{( - \rho)},Z_{(1 - \rho)},\ldots,Z_{(N - \rho)}} \right\rbrack,} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.115)

which characterizes the input of the RPM-I model (2.113) on the time interval $k = \overline{0,N}.$ The matrix Z is random and of the interval type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {Z \in \mathcal{Z} = {\underset{k = 0}{\overset{N}{\cup}}\mathcal{Z}_{k}} = \lbrack Z^{-},Z^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.116)

The random parameters of this model are


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{c} \in \mathcal{C} = \lbrack\mathbf{c}^{-},\mathbf{c}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.117)

The probabilistic properties of the parameters c and matrix Z (2.115) are characterized by a joint probability density function (PDF) W(c, Z) with the domain of definition


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{C}{\cup \mathcal{Z}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.118)

This function is assumed to be continuously differentiable.

Let the available input data x[k] contain errors η[k] ∈ Rm of the interval type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\eta\lbrack k\rbrack \in \mathcal{E}_{k} = \lbrack\eta^{-},\eta^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.119)

The probabilistic properties of the errors are characterized by PDFs $G_{k}(\eta\lbrack k\rbrack),k = \overline{0,N},$ which are assumed to be continuously differentiable as well.

The observed output of the RPM-I model is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{z}\lbrack k\rbrack = \hat{\mathbf{x}}\lbrack k\rbrack + \eta\lbrack k\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.120)

Clearly, the missing input data are restored using a model similar to RDM-O, but with the random input ζ[k].

Apply the RML algorithm [148] for determining the PDFs W(c, Z) and $G_{k}(\zeta\lbrack k\rbrack),\, k = \overline{0,N}.$ In the case under consideration, this algorithm has the form


$$\begin{aligned} & {\quad\mathcal{H}\lbrack W(\mathbf{c},Z),G(\eta)\rbrack = - {\int_{\mathcal{F}}W}(\mathbf{c},Z)\ln W(\mathbf{c},Z)\, d\mathbf{c}\, dZ -} \\ & \left. - {\sum\limits_{k \in \mathcal{K}}{\int_{\mathcal{E}_{k}}G_{k}}}(\eta\lbrack k\rbrack)\ln G_{k}(\eta\lbrack k\rbrack)d\eta\lbrack k\rbrack\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ & {\quad{\int_{\mathcal{F}}W}(\mathbf{c},Z)\, d\mathbf{c}\, dZ = 1;\quad{\int_{\mathcal{E}_{k}}G_{k}}(\eta\lbrack k\rbrack)d\eta\lbrack k\rbrack = 1,} \\ & {\quad{\int_{\mathcal{F}}W}(\mathbf{c},Z)\mathbb{F}\left( {\mathbf{c},Z_{(k - \rho)}} \right)d\mathbf{c}\, dZ + {\int_{\mathcal{E}_{k}}G_{k}}(\eta\lbrack k\rbrack)\eta\lbrack k\rbrack d\eta\lbrack k\rbrack = \mathbf{x}\lbrack k\rbrack,} \\ & {\quad k \in \mathcal{K},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.121)

where the indexing set $\mathcal{K} = \overline{0,N}$ does not include k = k−, …, k+.

This problem belongs to the same class as (2.106). Its solution is given by


$$\begin{array}{rll} & {W^{*}(\mathbf{c},Z,\lambda) = \frac{\exp\left\lbrack {- {\sum\limits_{k \in \mathcal{K}}\langle}\lambda^{(k)},\mathbb{F}\left( \left. \mathbf{c},Z_{(k - \rho)} \right\rangle \right)} \right\rbrack}{\mathcal{W}(\lambda)},} & \\ & {G_{k}^{*}(\eta\lbrack k\rbrack,\lambda^{(k)}) = \frac{\exp\left( {- \left\langle \lambda^{(k)},\eta\lbrack k\rbrack \right\rangle} \right)}{\mathcal{G}_{k}(\lambda^{(k)})},} & \\ & {k \in \mathcal{K},} & \\ \end{array}$$
(2.122)

where


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{W}(\lambda) = \int_{\mathcal{F}}} & {\exp\left\lbrack {- \sum\left\langle \lambda^{(k)},\mathbb{F}\left( \left. \mathbf{c},Z_{(k - \rho)} \right\rangle \right) \right.} \right\rbrack d\mathbf{c},\quad\mathcal{G}_{k}(\lambda^{(k)}) =} \\ & {\,\, = int_{\mathcal{E}_{k}}\exp\left( {- \left\langle \lambda^{(k)},\eta\lbrack k\rbrack \right\rangle} \right)d\eta\lbrack k\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.123)

In the equalities presented above, λ(k) is the vector of Lagrange multipliers corresponding to the kth balance constraint. This vector satisfies the system of equations


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{{\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}}_{k}(\lambda)}{\mathcal{W}(\lambda)} + \frac{{\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}}_{k}(\lambda^{(k)})}{\mathcal{G}_{k}(\lambda^{(k)})} = \mathbf{x}\lbrack k\rbrack,\quad k \neq k^{-},\ldots,k^{+};k \in \mathcal{K},} \\ \end{array}$$
(2.124)

where


$$\begin{aligned} & {{\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}}_{k}(\lambda) = {\int_{\mathcal{F}}\exp}\left\lbrack {- {\sum\limits_{k \in \mathcal{K}}\langle}\lambda^{(k)},\mathbb{F}\left( \left. \mathbf{c},Z_{(k - \rho)} \right\rangle \right)} \right\rbrack\mathbb{F}\left( {\mathbf{c},Z_{(k - \rho)}} \right)d\mathbf{c}dZ,} \\ & {{\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}}_{k}(\lambda^{(k)}) = {\int_{\mathcal{E}_{k}}\exp}\left( {- \left\langle \lambda^{(k)},\eta\lbrack k\rbrack \right\rangle} \right)\eta\lbrack k\rbrack d\eta\lbrack k\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(2.125)

3. Omissions in input and output data

In this case, the procedures described in the previous paragraphs have to be used sequentially: first, the algorithm (2.121), and then the algorithm (2.106).

The algorithms, applied either separately or sequentially, yield:

  • the entropy-optimal PDFs of parameters of the corresponding models, P*(a) and W*(c);

  • the entropy-optimal PDFs of the measurement noises, Qk*(ξ[k]) and Gk*(η[k]), where $k = \overline{1,N};$

  • the entropy-optimal PDF of the randomized input sequence, $K_{k}^{*}(\zeta\lbrack k\rbrack),\, k = \overline{1,N}.$

3. Sampling of optimal PDFs

Sampling transforms a PDF into an appropriate sequence of random vectors. In the procedure under consideration, this is a way of realizing the ensembles of random vectors on the segments of missing data.

The general method for generating sequences of random vectors with a given PDF was described in [36]. It is intended to sample the sequences of the corresponding random-parameter vectors of the RPM-O and RPM-I models and the sequences of the measurement noise vectors, as well as to generate the ensembles of restored data using the Monte Carlo method [159].

Some useful characteristics of ensembles are as follows:

  • —the empirical PDFs $\mathcal{P}_{k}({\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack)$ and $\mathcal{W}_{k}({\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack)$ for the restored output and input data, respectively;

  • —the empirical probability distributions


    $$\begin{aligned} {\mathfrak{P}_{k}({\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}^{(i)}\lbrack k\rbrack)} & {= {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{i}\mathcal{P}_{k}}({\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}^{(j)}\lbrack k\rbrack)\quad\text{(for~the~output~data)}} \\ {\mathfrak{W}_{k}({\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}^{(i)}\lbrack k\rbrack)} & {= {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{i}\mathcal{W}_{k}}({\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}^{(j)}\lbrack k\rbrack)\quad\text{(for~the~input~data)}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (2.126)

The sets of restored data representing the integral characteristics of an ensemble of random trajectories can be used for solving machine learning problems.

1. Data maximizing the PDFs of parameters and noises (max-pn)

  • —The restored output data:


    $$\begin{aligned} {{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack} & {= \mathbb{B}(\mathbf{a}^{*},X_{(k - \rho)}),\quad\mathbf{a}^{*} = \arg\max P^{*}(\mathbf{a}),} \\ {\xi_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack} & {= \arg\max Q_{k}^{*}(\xi\lbrack k\rbrack),} \\ {{\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack} & {= {\hat{\mathbf{y}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack + \xi_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (2.127)

  • —The restored input data:


    $$\begin{aligned} {{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack} & {= \mathbb{F}(\mathbf{c}^{*},Z_{(k - \rho)}^{*}),\quad\mathbf{c}^{*} = \arg\max W^{*}(\mathbf{a}),} \\ Z_{(k - \rho)}^{*} & {= \lbrack\zeta^{*}\lbrack k - \rho\rbrack,\ldots,\zeta^{*}\lbrack k\rbrack\rbrack,\quad\zeta^{*}\lbrack k\rbrack = \arg\max K_{k}^{*}(\zeta\lbrack k\rbrack),} \\ {\eta_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack} & {= \arg\max G_{k}^{*}(\eta\lbrack k\rbrack),} \\ {{\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack} & {= {\hat{\mathbf{x}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack + \eta_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (2.128)

2. Data maximizing the empirical PDFs of observed trajectories for $k = \overline{0,N}$ (max-ePDF)

  • —The restored output data:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\check{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack = \arg\max\mathcal{P}_{k}({\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack),\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (2.129)

  • —The restored input data:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\check{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack = \arg\max\mathcal{W}_{k}({\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack),\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (2.130)

3. Data corresponding to the mean trajectory (mean)

  • —The restored output data:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack = \frac{1}{M}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}^{(i)}}\lbrack k\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (2.131)

  • —The restored input data:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}\lbrack k\rbrack = \frac{1}{M}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{M}{\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}^{(i)}}\lbrack k\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (2.132)

    (Here M denotes the number of trajectories in an ensemble.)

4. Data corresponding to the median trajectory (med)

  • —The restored output data:


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. {\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}^{(j^{*})}\lbrack k\rbrack\Rightarrow{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{j^{*}}\mathfrak{P}_{k}}({\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}^{(j)}\lbrack k\rbrack) = {\sum\limits_{j = j^{*} + 1}^{M}\mathfrak{P}_{k}}({\hat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rst}^{(j)}\lbrack k\rbrack). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (2.133)

  • —The restored input data:


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. {\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}^{(j^{*})}\lbrack k\rbrack\Rightarrow{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{j^{*}}\mathfrak{W}_{k}}({\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}^{(j)}\lbrack k\rbrack) = {\sum\limits_{j = j^{*} + 1}^{M}\mathfrak{W}_{k}}({\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{rst}^{(j)}\lbrack k\rbrack). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (2.134)

    (Here M denotes the number of trajectories in an ensemble.)

Useful restored data can be of assistance when solving applied problems.

CHAPTER 3 DIMENSION REDUCTION METHODS

DOI: 10.1201/9781003306566-3

3.1Review of Dimension Reduction Methods

The arrays of problem-oriented data described in the previous sections may contain information of little significance. This hypothesis underlies dimension reduction methods. Although any reduction causes loss of information about a studied object, it is reasonable to consider reduction with “minimum loss.” The experience accumulated by solving different machine learning problems indicates that the dimension reduction problems and the problems solved on resulting reduced data are related to each other. Therefore, there exists no universal efficient approach applicable to any problem. Note that dimension reduction becomes a rather topical problem for RML procedures due to the specific properties of the equations yielding the optimal “randomized” estimates. This feature explains the choice of the reduction methods below.

As a matter of fact, the dimension reduction methods employ one of the three basic ideas as follows. The first idea is related to the matrix that describes data of unspecified origin. By assumption, this matrix has a certain core of smaller dimension that concentrates main information about a studied object. In this case, a reduction tool is the singular decomposition of the data matrix and ordering of its singular values in absolute magnitude.

The second idea is to treat existing data as random, sometimes with additional statistical properties. Then, further analysis is focused on covariance matrix using one of two standard approaches. Following the first approach, one should assign some connectivity threshold for variables and eliminate one of two variables whose coefficient of correlation exceeds this threshold. The second approach is based on the singular decomposition of the covariance matrix.

Finally, the third idea for dimension reduction consists in direct and inverse projection. Direct projection is performed onto a space of smaller dimension (on choice). As the name implies, inverse projection is the same operation back onto the original space, yielding the so-called inverse vector. Naturally enough, the inverse vector differs from the original one. Hence, it is necessary to choose an appropriate functional of distance between the original and inverse vectors to be minimized over corresponding projection operators.

3.1.1Singular decomposition method for data matrix

Consider a rectangular data matrix A of dimensions (m × s) and recall some definitions from [60]. The left singular vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{u}$ of this matrix A are the eigenvectors of the matrix AA′ of dimensions (m × m). The right singular vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{u}$ of this matrix A are the eigenvectors of the matrix A′A of dimensions (s × s). A nonnegative real value β is a singular value of A if there exist two unit-length vectors $\overset{\rightarrow}{u} \in R^{m}$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{v} \in R^{s}$ such that


$$\begin{array}{r} {A\overset{\rightarrow}{v} = \beta\overset{\rightarrow}{u},\text{\quad\quad}A^{\prime}\overset{\rightarrow}{u} = \beta\overset{\rightarrow}{v}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.1)

A singular decomposition of the matrix A is given by the representation


$$\begin{array}{r} {A = USV^{\prime},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.2)

where the diagonal matrix S of dimensions (m × s) contains the singular values of A, whereas the matrices U and V of dimensions (m × m) and (s × s), respectively, are unitary

By this definition of singular decomposition, the matrices U and V are not unique and hence can be chosen so that the diagonal elements of the matrix S have the form
