$$\begin{array}{r} {\beta_{1} \geq \beta_{2} \geq \cdots \geq \beta_{r} > \beta_{r + 1} = \cdots = \beta_{m} = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.3)

where r denotes the rank of the matrix S.

The chain of inequalities (3.3) plays a key role in principal component analysis. The first principal component is the one with the maximum singular value (in the current notation, β1). The second successive component corresponds to the singular value β2, and so on. The last principal component is associated with the last nonzero singular value βr and its index (subscript) coincides with the rank of the matrix A.

The singular values are calculated by solving the following problem. Consider an approximate linear representation of the matrix A of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {A = USV^{\prime} + C.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.4)

Minimize


$$\begin{array}{r} {\varepsilon^{2} = \text{tr}(CC^{\prime})} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.5)

subject to the normalization conditions


$$\begin{array}{r} {U^{\prime}U = VV^{\prime} = I.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.6)

If the matrix A has a rank r > min (m, s), then C ≈ 0. The minimum value r that satisfies equality (3.2) is the rank of the matrix A. To find the left and right singular vectors ${\overset{\rightarrow}{u}}_{k}$, ${\overset{\rightarrow}{v}}_{k}$ for k = 1, …, r, introduce auxiliary normalized vectors ${\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k},{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k}$ and define vectors ${\overset{\rightarrow}{u}}_{k}$, ${\overset{\rightarrow}{v}}_{k}$ as


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overset{\rightarrow}{u}}_{k} = \frac{{\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k}}{\|{\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k}\|},\text{\quad\quad}{\overset{\rightarrow}{v}}_{k} = \frac{{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k}}{\|{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k}\|}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.7)

Then the singular value is


$$\begin{array}{r} {\lambda_{k} = \|{\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k}{\|\|}{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k}\|.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.8)

The auxiliary vectors are given by the equalities


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k} = \frac{A\,{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k}}{{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k}\,{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k}^{\prime}},\quad{\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{k + 1} = \frac{{\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k}^{\prime}}{{\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k}^{\prime}\,{\overset{\rightarrow}{a}}_{k}},\quad k = 1,2,\ldots} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.9)

At step k = 1, the row ${\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}_{1}$ of the matrix A has the maximum norm. At steps k = 2, 3, …, this procedure is iteratively applied to the matrix $A_{k + 1} = A_{k} - {\overset{\rightarrow}{u}}_{k}\lambda_{k}{\overset{\rightarrow}{v}}_{k}.$ To construct the matrix Âr = UrSrV′, it suffices to calculate only r columns of the matrix U and r rows of the matrix V′.

3.1.2Principal component analysis

Apparently, principal component analysis is the most commonly used dimension reduction method for data arrays [10, 84, 127]. There exist at least three basic versions of this method, namely, data approximation by linear smaller-dimension manifolds; searching for smaller-dimension subspaces with the maximum data spread (variance) in the orthogonal projection onto them; searching for smaller-dimension subspaces with the maximum root-mean-square distance between points in the orthogonal projection onto them. The basic versions involve a data matrix $X = \lbrack{\overset{\rightarrow}{x}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overset{\rightarrow}{x}}^{(m)}\rbrack$ whose column vectors ${\overset{\rightarrow}{x}}^{(i)}$ have dimension s.

To clarify the idea of this method, first consider the case s = 2. Consider a data matrix composed of two-dimensional columns whose elements are the measured values of some variables (attributes of interest). Interpret them as points {x1(i),x2(i)} on the plane; see Fig. 3.1(a). Draw a line AB so that the maximum variation of data occurs along it. The line AB is the first principal component. Perform the projection of the initial points on this line and use it as a new coordinate axis (Fig. 3.1(b)). Take the points representing the difference between the initial points and their projections on axis AB and again draw a line CD so that the maximum variation of these differences occurs along it, as shown in Fig. 3.1(c). The line CD is the second principal component and so on.

In the general multidimensional case, principal component analysis is performed in accordance with the following procedure:

  • identify the center of the existing data set and place the origin (i.e., the zeroth principal component) to this center;

  • find the direction of the maximum data variation (the first principal component);

  • find the data projections onto the first principal component as well as their variance;

  • if the variance is large, find the new principal direction of maximum variations that is orthogonal to the first one, and so on.

This procedure allows to replace the initial data matrix X of dimensions (s × m) by two matrices T and P of dimensions (s × k) and (k × s), respectively, where k < m. This representation is obtained using the new variables


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overset{\rightarrow}{t}}^{\mspace{2mu}(j)} = {\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}^{\mspace{2mu}(j,1)}{\overset{\rightarrow}{x}}^{(1)} + \cdots + {\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}^{\mspace{2mu}(j,m)}{\overset{\rightarrow}{x}}^{(m)},\quad j = \overline{1,k},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.10)

where ${\overset{\rightarrow}{t}}^{\mspace{2mu}(j)}$ and ${\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}^{\mspace{2mu}(j,i)},\, i = \overline{1,m},$ denote the columns of the matrices T and P, respectively. The new variables (3.10) are called the principal components, and the matrix T is called the principal component matrix. An important property of the principal components consists in their orthogonality. Therefore, the matrix T is not reconfigured as we increase the number of principal components.

With these variables, the matrix X can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {X = \hat{X} + E = {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{k}{\overset{\rightarrow}{t}}^{(j)}}{\lbrack{\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}^{(j)}\rbrack}^{\prime} + E,\text{\quad\quad}\hat{X} = T\, P^{\prime}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.11)

Here E stands for the residue matrix of dimensions (s × m). The residual error is assessed in terms of some numerical characteristic of the residue matrix, e.g., the relative variance


$$\begin{array}{r} {D = 1 - \frac{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}e_{ji}^{2}}}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}x_{ji}^{2}}},\quad e_{ji} = x_{ji} - {\hat{x}}_{ji}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.12)

There exist many recursive algorithms to calculate the principal components, which are oriented towards the specifics of initial information and employ different data processing methods. First, the matrix X is centered, i.e., for each column the average value


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{x}}_{j} = \frac{1}{s}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}x_{i}^{(j)}}} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.13)

and the standard deviation


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sigma_{j} = \frac{1}{s}\sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{(x_{ji} - {\overline{x}}_{j})}^{2}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.14)

are calculated. The modified data matrix X̃ that is used to calculate the principal components consists of the elements


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\widetilde{x}}_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - {\overline{x}}_{j}}{\sigma_{j}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.15)

The algorithm for searching the principal components includes the following steps.

  1. Choose an initial vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{t}$ (3.10).

  2. Calculate ${\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}^{\mspace{2mu}\prime} = \frac{{\overset{\rightarrow}{t}}^{\mspace{2mu}\prime}E_{j}}{{\overset{\rightarrow}{t}}^{\prime}\overset{\rightarrow}{t}}.$

  3. Calculate $\overset{\rightarrow}{p} = \frac{\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}{{({\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}^{\prime}\overset{\rightarrow}{p})}^{1/2}}.$

  4. Calculate $\overset{\rightarrow}{t} = \frac{E_{j}\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}{{\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}^{\prime}\overset{\rightarrow}{p}}.$

  5. Find D using (3.12) and get back to Step 2.

The number of the principal components is defined by comparing the relative variance (3.12) with the admissible error.

As mentioned earlier, the singular decomposition (3.2) of a rectangular matrix and principal component analysis are related to one another. This relation has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {T = US,\quad P = V.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.16)

Principal component analysis and its modifications were considered in a vast literature, mostly with applications to the problems of classification and regression [188].

3.1.3Random projection method

Like principal component analysis, dimension reduction by means of random projections involves a linear transformation f:ℝn→ℝk of a data matrix and is applied in problems where objects are represented by points of the multidimensional Euclidean space [20].

The idea of the random projection method is based on the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma [83]: for a set X of points in a multidimensional space of a high dimension, there exists a subspace of a smaller, albeit rather high, dimension such that projection onto this subspace will save, on average, the relative distances between all points from the given set. The error of transformation is described by a value ε ∈ (0, 1):


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left( {1 - \varepsilon} \right)\left\| {x_{1} - x_{2}} \right\|^{2} \leq \left\| {f(x_{1}) - f(x_{2})} \right\|^{2} \leq \left( {1 + \varepsilon} \right)\left\| {x_{1} - x_{2}} \right\|^{2}} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.17)

for all vectors x1, x2 ∈ X.

Moreover, the original lemma also gives a lower bound on k, i.e., the dimension of the subspace onto which the objects are projected. For example, for a set of N points, the value k must satisfy the condition


$$\begin{array}{r} {k > \frac{8\ln N}{\varepsilon^{2}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.18)

In other words, the minimum possible dimension of the subspace for projection does not depend on the dimension of the original space, but depends only on the number of projected objects and the error of transformation. In various special cases, the lower bound on the value k was refined in [82, 86].

Consider a linear transformation f:ℝn→ℝk for projecting objects from a set X. It is defined by a rectangular matrix R of dimensions [k × n] (k <  < n) and has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {X_{k \times N}^{RP} = R_{k \times n}X_{n \times N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.19)

As it turned out, the elements of the matrix R for such a transformation can consist of random variables, which makes the projection random. In early works devoted to the random projection method [30, 76, 108], it was proposed to use random variables with the standard Gaussian distribution N(0, 1), and to construct the matrix R so that its row vectors are orthogonal and have unit length.

Later in [8], it was demonstrated that the matrix R can be obtained using the uniform distribution, under certain constraints dictated by storing information in databases, due to integer calculations. In this case, it was suggested to compose the matrix R from random elements rij of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {r_{ij} = \sqrt{3} \times \left\{ \begin{aligned} {+ 1} & {\text{with~probability~}\frac{1}{6},} \\ 0 & {\text{with~probability~}\frac{2}{3},} \\ {- 1} & {\text{with~probability~}\frac{1}{6}.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.20)

Thus, for calculating the projection XRP, it is necessary to multiply the matrices R and X, and this transformation has the complexity 𝒪(knN). In principal component analysis, the matrix for projection is square with dimensions [n × n], and the transformation to projections has the complexity 𝒪(n2N). Hence, for dimensionality reduction, the random projection method is preferable to principal component analysis in terns of computational efficiency.

Also, note the existing studies to speed up the transformation to projections. One line of research is focused on sparse matrices: as it was shown in [20], if the data matrix X has at most c nonzero components in each column, then the complexity of transformation is reduced to 𝒪(ckN). The influence of data sparsity on the efficiency of the random projection method was studied in the papers [38, 87]. Another approach to accelerating projection is based on the Fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss Transform (FJLT) [9], a randomized Fourier transform.

The range of possible applications of the random projection method for dimension reduction includes a wide class of problems with multidimensional data. Since the relative distances between different objects of a given set are preserved in the smaller dimension space, the structure of this set is also preserved, which is especially important when dividing objects into groups, e.g., in classification and clustering. Therefore, random projections become an effective dimension reduction solution in metric data analysis methods, such as the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) for clustering [30], support vector machine (SVM) for classification [27], and the least squares (LS) method for regression [116].

Random projections turn out to be especially effective when dealing with large collections of multidimensional sparse data, such as images, text, audio and video data, etc. In the field of signal processing, a separate line of research devoted to the use of random projections for data analysis and restoration is called Compressed Sensing; for example, see [29, 46].

Regardless of the field of application, the nature and dimension of the original data represented by a set of points in a multidimensional space, the use of random projections allows reducing the dimension while preserving the data structure. Moreover, the random projection method is easily interpreted and does not require significant computing resources, even in the case of high and ultrahigh-dimensional data, in contrast to alternative dimension reduction methods such as PCA and SVD.

However, note that random projections are intended only for the problems in which analysis and calculations are performed on data of reduced dimension, but the data are not used for visualization or restoration. For example, in the case of images, dimension reduction with random projections can lead to visual degradation of the image, for both the human eye and computer vision systems.

3.1.4Direct and inverse projection

Consider the space RNM of all real matrices A(N × M) whose elements take random values.

The transition from the original space RNM to the smaller-dimension one RNm causes the losses of information contained in the former's elements. For estimating these losses, it is necessary to return to the original space by means of inverse projection: RNm⇒RNM. This operation is performed using a projector matrix J(m × M), which gives the matrix X(N × M) = D(N × m)J(m × M) ∈ RNM. The matrices X(N × M) and A(N × M) are elements of the same space. Hence, the quality of compression of the original matrix can be estimated in terms of an appropriate criterion.

In the sequel, the quality of data compression, which depends on the projector matrices S(N × m) and J(m × M), will be estimated in entropy terms. More specifically, introduce the information entropy [139] of a matrix X(N × M) with respect to a matrix A(N × M),


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(X\, \middle| \, A) = - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}x_{ij}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}}{a_{ij}} = tr\left( {X^{\intercal}Y} \right), \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.21)

where tr denotes the matrix trace and Y is a matrix of dimensions (N × M) consisting of the elements


$$\begin{array}{r} {y_{ij} = \ln\frac{x_{ij}}{a_{ij}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.22)

Hereinafter, this entropy will be called the information cross-entropy[158]. The direct-inverse projection method described above is the core of the compression method of random data matrices. Consider a nonnegative data matrix U of dimensions (m × s). It is required to compress the matrix to a matrix Z of dimensions (n × r), where r < s and n < m. This problem will be solved sequentially, in two stages as follows. First, reduce the matrix U(m × s) to a matrix Y(m × r), and then compress the latter to a matrix Z(n × r). The approach presented below will be called the entropy dimension reduction (EDR) method.

Stage 1 Introduce a matrix Q(s × r) and perform direct projection for obtaining the column-compressed matrix


$$\begin{array}{r} {Y_{(m \times r)} = U_{(m \times s)}Q_{(s \times r)}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.23)

Next, introduce a matrix T(r × s) and perform inverse projection, which yields the matrix


$$\begin{array}{r} {X_{(m \times s)} = U_{(m \times s)}Q_{(s \times r)}T_{(r \times s)}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.24)

The matrix X(m × s) has the same dimension as the original matrix U(m × s) and characterizes the effect (losses) of direct and inverse projections in Stage 1.

The reduction of a data matrix is accompanied by the losses of information contained in it or by an increase of the relative information entropy [139]. For Stage 1 of this method, the information cross-entropy of a matrix X(m × s) with a fixed original matrix U(m × s) is given by


$$\begin{aligned} \left. H_{1}(X\, \middle| \, U) \right. & \left. = - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}x_{ij}}}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U)\ln\frac{\left. x_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{u_{ij}} = \right. \\ & \left. \quad = H_{1}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U)\Rightarrow\max_{(Q,T) \geq 0}, \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.25)

where, according to (3.24),


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. x_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{\mu = 1}^{r}{\sum\limits_{\nu = 1}^{s}t_{\mu,j}}}q_{\nu,\mu}u_{i\nu}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.26)

The maximization of the function (3.1.4) finally yields the entropy-optimal projector matrix Q(s × r)* and the compressed first-stage matrix


$$\begin{array}{r} {Y_{(m \times r)}^{*} = U_{(m \times s)}Q_{(s \times r)}^{*}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.27)

Stage 2 The second-stage data matrix Y(m × r) has a reduced number r < s of columns. It is required to compress this matrix to a given number n < m of rows. Introduce matrices B(n × m) and A(m × n) for performing the direct and inverse projection operations, respectively, by analogy with Stage 1:


$$\begin{array}{r} {Z_{(n \times r)} = B_{(n \times m)}Y_{(m \times r)},\text{\quad\quad}G_{(m \times r)} = A_{(m \times n)}Z_{(n \times r)}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.28)

The matrix G(m × r) has the same dimension as the original second-stage matrix Y(m × r) and characterizes the effect (losses) of direct and inverse projections in Stage 2. These losses are estimated by the information cross-entropy


$$\begin{aligned} \left. H_{2}(G\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right. & \left. = - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}g_{ij}}}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y)\ln\frac{\left. g_{ij}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{y_{ij}} = \right. \\ & \left. \quad H_{2}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*})\Rightarrow\max_{(B,A) \geq 0}, \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.29)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. g_{ij}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) = {\sum\limits_{\beta = 1}^{n}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{m}a_{i,\beta}}}b_{\beta,\alpha}y_{\alpha,j}^{*} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.30)

and


$$\begin{array}{r} {y_{\alpha,j}^{*} = {\sum\limits_{eta = 1}^{s}u_{\alpha,\eta}}q_{\eta,j}^{*}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.31)

3.2Entropy Optimization of Sequential Procedure

The first stage of the sequential procedure is to determine the optimal elements of the nonnegative matrices Q and T:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. (Q^{*},T^{*}) = \arg\max_{(Q,T) \geq 0}H_{1}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.32)

This problem will be solved numerically using an iterative algorithm based on projected gradient descent, which represents a combination of the standard gradient descent method and the truncation of all negative elements.

3.2.1Optimality conditions and algorithm

The gradient of the function H1(Q,T | U) with respect to the elements of the matrices Q and T has the components


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\left. \partial H(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial q_{\nu,\mu}} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\frac{\left. \partial h_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial x_{ij}}}}\frac{\left. \partial x_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial q_{\nu,\mu}},} \\ & {\quad\nu = \overline{1,s},\,\mu = \overline{1,r},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.33)


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\left. \partial H(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial t_{\mu,j}} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}\frac{\left. \partial h_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial x_{ij}}}}\frac{\left. \partial x_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial t_{\mu,j}},} \\ & {\quad\mu = \overline{1,r},\, j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.34)

where


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. h_{ij}(T,Q\, \middle| \, X) = x_{ij}\ln\frac{x_{ij}}{u_{ij}}, \right. \\ & {\frac{\left. \partial h_{ij}(T,Q\, \middle| \, X) \right.}{\partial x_{ij}} = \ln\frac{x_{ij}}{u_{ij}} + 1,\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.35)


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\left. \partial x_{ij}((Q,T\, \middle| \, U)) \right.}{\partial q_{\nu,\mu}} & {= t_{\mu,j}\, u_{i,\nu},\text{\quad\quad}\nu = \overline{1,s},\mu = \overline{1,r};} \\ \frac{\left. \partial x_{ij}((Q,T\, \middle| \, U)) \right.}{\partial t_{\mu,j}} & {= {\sum\limits_{\nu = 1}^{s}q_{\nu,\mu}}u_{i,\nu},\text{\quad\quad}\mu = \overline{1,r};} \\ i & {= \overline{1,m},\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.36)

Perform the vectorization of the matrices Q and T (see [115]) to obtain the corresponding vectors q and t. Denote by ∇Q(q, t) the gradient of the information cross-entropy functional H(Q,T | U) with the components (3.2.2), and by ∇T(q, t) the gradient of the information cross-entropy functional H(Q,T | U) with the components (3.33–3.36).

The algorithm max H1 has the following structure.

  • a). Initial step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{0} > \mathbf{0},\quad\mathbf{t}^{0} > \mathbf{0}.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • b). nth iterative step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {X^{n} = U\, Q^{n}\, T^{n},} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(Q^{n},T^{n}\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}x_{ij}^{n}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}^{n}}{u_{ij}} = H^{n}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{q}}\nabla_{Q}(\mathbf{q}^{n},\mathbf{t}^{n})\text{if}\,\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{q}^{n}\text{if}\,\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0};} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow Q^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{t}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{t}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{t}}\nabla_{T}(\mathbf{q}^{n},\mathbf{t}^{n})\text{if}\,\mathbf{t} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{t}^{n}\text{if}\,\mathbf{t}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0}.} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{t}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow T^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {X^{(n + 1)} = U\, Q^{(n + 1)}\, T^{(n + 1)};} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(Q^{(n + 1)},T^{(n + 1)}\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}{u_{ij}} = H^{(n + 1)}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$

  • c). Stopping condition:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\text{If}\,\, H^{(n + 1)} - H^{(n)} \leq \delta,\,\text{then}\, STOP.} \\ \end{array}$$

3.2.2Approximation of information cross-entropy functional

In some cases, the elements of the reduced matrix Q can be determined with sufficient accuracy using the logarithmic function approximation in the neighborhood of a point x0 = a, where a ≥ amin:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\ln x < \ln a + \frac{1}{a_{min}}(x - a).} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.37)

For a = xij, this formula gives the following approximate expression for the information cross-entropy functional:


$$\begin{aligned} \left. H_{1}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \approx \sum_{i = 1}^{s}\sum_{j = 1}^{m} \right. & {\left\lbrack x_{ij}^{2}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) - x_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U)u_{ij} \right\rbrack =} \\ & \left. \widetilde{H}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U). \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.38)

This equality can be written in the matrix form

where ⌈A, B⌋ denotes the Frobenius inner product [115],

The elements of the matrices Q and T will be found by minimizing the functional H̃1(Q,T | U) on the set of all nonnegative matrices Q and T under a fixed data matrix U, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. ({\widetilde{Q}}^{*},{\widetilde{T}}^{*}) = \arg\min_{(Q,T) \geq 0}{\widetilde{H}}_{1}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.41)

This problem is solved by an algorithm involving the components of the gradient of the functional H̃1(Q,T | U) with respect to the matrices Q and T.

Recall some differentiation rules for scalar functions of matrices [115]. Consider the linear space of all matrices A of dimensions (m × n). In this space, the scalar product and the Frobenius norm are given by

and

respectively. According to these definitions, a matrix is treated as a vector composed of its adjoining rows (the so-called matrix vectorization). For a scalar function of a matrix, the gradient is defined as follows. The increment of a scalar function f(A) is written as

Here o(Δ) denotes the remainder term of the Taylor series. The gradient of the function f(A) with respect to the matrix A is


$$\begin{array}{r} {\bigtriangleup_{A}f(A) = H.} \\ \end{array}$$

Some simple and useful examples of scalar functions of a variable are

and


$$\begin{array}{r} {f(A) = \| A\|^{2},\text{\quad\quad} \bigtriangleup_{A}f(A) = 2A.} \\ \end{array}$$

Using the matrix differentiation rules described above, derive the following expressions for the gradients of the functional H̃1(Q,T | U) (3.41):


$$\begin{array}{r} {\bigtriangleup_{Q}(Q,T) = \frac{\left. \partial{\widetilde{H}}_{1}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial X}\frac{\partial X}{\partial Q} = 2TPQT - TP,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.42)


$$\begin{array}{r} {\bigtriangleup_{T}(Q,T) = \frac{\left. \partial{\widetilde{H}}_{1}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{\partial X}\frac{\partial X}{\partial T} = 2Q^{\intercal}PQT - Q^{\intercal}P,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.43)

where P = XX⊺ and △Q(Q, T) and △T(Q, T) mean the gradients with respect to the matrices Q and T, respectively. According to (3.42, 3.43), the gradients of the function H̃(Q,T | U) with respect to the matrices Q and T are matrices of dimensions (s × r).

For maximizing the functional H̃1(Q,T | U), apply gradient descent with the nonnegativity check of the matrices U and T.

The algorithm max H̃1 has the following structure.

  • a) Initial step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {T^{0} > 0,\quad Q^{0} > 0.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • b) nth iterative step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {X^{n} = U\, Q^{n}\, T^{n},} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(Q^{n},T^{n}\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}x_{ij}^{n}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}^{n}}{u_{ij}} = H^{n}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {Q^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{aligned} \left. Q^{n} + \gamma_{Q} \bigtriangleup_{Q}(\widetilde{H}(Q^{n},T^{n}\, \middle| \, U) \geq 0 \right. & {\text{if~}Q^{(n + 1)} \geq 0,} \\ Q^{n} & {\text{if~}Q^{(n + 1)} < 0;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {T^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{aligned} \left. T^{n} + \gamma_{T} \bigtriangleup_{T}(\widetilde{H}(Q^{n},T^{n}\, \middle| \, U) \geq 0 \right. & {\text{if~}T^{(n + 1)} \geq 0,} \\ T^{n} & {\text{if~}T^{(n + 1)} < 0;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {X^{(n + 1)} = U\, Q^{(n + 1)}\, T^{(n + 1)};} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(Q^{(n + 1)},T^{(n + 1)}\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}{u_{ij}} = H^{(n + 1)}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$

  • c) Stopping condition:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\text{If}\,\, H^{(n + 1)} - H^{n} \leq \delta,\,\,\text{then}\, STOP.} \\ \end{array}$$

The algorithm max H1 or max H̃1 yields the entropy-optimal projector matrix Q(s × r)*. Hence, it is possible to determine the matrix Y(m × r)* (1.5) for passing to the second stage of the compression procedure of the matrix U, which is characterized by the projector matrices B(n × m) and A(m × n).

The optimal elements of the nonnegative matrices B and A are given by


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. (B^{*},A^{*}) = \arg\max_{(B,A) \geq 0}H_{2}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.44)

By analogy with Stage 1, this problem will be solved using the iterative algorithm based on projected gradient descent (a combination of gradient descent and the truncation of all negative elements).

The gradient of the function H2(B,A | Y*) with respect to the elements of the matrices B and A has the components


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\left. \partial H_{2}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{\partial a_{i,\beta}} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}\frac{\left. \partial s_{ij}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{\partial g_{ij}}}}\frac{\left. \partial g_{ij}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{\partial a_{i,\beta}},} \\ & {\quad i = \overline{1,n},\, j = \overline{1,r},\,\beta = \overline{1,n},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.45)


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\left. \partial H_{2}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{\partial b_{\beta,\alpha}} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}\frac{\left. \partial s_{ij}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{\partial g_{ij}}}}\frac{\left. \partial g_{ij}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{\partial b_{\beta,\alpha}},} \\ {i =} & {\overline{1,n},\, j = \overline{1,r},\,\beta = \overline{1,n},\,\alpha = \overline{1,m},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.46)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\left. \partial s_{ij}(B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) \right.}{\partial g_{ij}} = \ln\frac{g_{ij}}{y_{ij}^{*}} + 1,\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,n},\, j = \overline{1,r};} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.47)


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\left. \partial g_{ij}((B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*})) \right.}{\partial a_{i,\beta}} & {= {\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{m}b_{\beta,\alpha}}y_{\alpha,j}^{*},\text{\quad\quad}\beta = \overline{1,n};} \\ \frac{\left. \partial g_{ij}((B,A\, \middle| \, Y^{*})) \right.}{\partial b_{\beta,\alpha}} & {= a_{i,\beta}y_{\alpha,j}^{*},\text{\quad\quad}\beta = \overline{1,n},\alpha = \overline{1,m};} \\ i & {= \overline{1,m},\quad j = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.48)

Perform the vectorization of the matrices B and A, and introduce the corresponding vectors b and a. Denote by ∇B(b, a) the gradient of the relative information entropy H2(B,A | Y*) with the components (3.46–3.48), and by ∇A(q, t) the gradient of the relative entropy functional H2(B,A | Y*) with the components (3.48).

The algorithm max H2 has the following structure.

  • a) Initial step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{b}^{0} > \mathbf{0},\quad\mathbf{a}^{0} > \mathbf{0}.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • b) nth iterative step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {G^{n} = A^{n}B^{n}Y^{*},} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(B^{n},A^{n}\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}g_{ij}^{n}}}\ln\frac{g_{ij}^{n}}{y_{ij}^{*}} = H^{n}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{b}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{b}}\nabla_{B}(\mathbf{b}^{n},\mathbf{a}^{n})\text{if}\,\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{b}^{n}\text{if}\,\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0};} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow Q^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{a}}\nabla_{A}(\mathbf{b}^{n},\mathbf{a}^{n})\text{if}\,\mathbf{a} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{a}^{n}\text{if}\,\mathbf{a}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0};} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{a}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow A^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {G^{(n + 1)} = A^{(n + 1)}B^{(n + 1)}Y^{*};} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(B^{(n + 1)},A^{(n + 1)}\, \middle| \, Y^{*}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}g_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}}\ln\frac{g_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}{y_{ij}^{*}} = H^{(n + 1)}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$

  • c) Stopping condition:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\text{If}\,\, H^{(n + 1)} - H^{(n)} \leq \delta,\,\text{then}\, STOP.} \\ \end{array}$$

3.3Entropy Optimization of Parallel Procedure

3.3.1Definition and structure

The parallel implementation of the direct-inverse projection procedure leads to the matrix equalities


$$\begin{array}{r} {U_{(m \times s)}Q_{s \times r} = Y_{(m \times r)},\quad B_{(n \times m)}Y_{(m \times r)} = Z_{(n \times r)},} \\ {Z_{(n \times r)}W_{(r \times s)} = D_{(n \times s)},\quad E_{(m \times n)}D_{(n \times s)} = X_{(m \times s)}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.49)

The first chain in these formulas, related to the direct projection with a matrix Q(s × r) and the inverse projection with a matrix B(n × m), yields a reduced matrix Z(n × r). The second chain, related to the direct projection with a matrix W(r × s) and the inverse projection with a matrix E(m × n), yields a matrix X(m × s).

From equalities (3.49), it follows that


$$\begin{array}{r} {X_{(m \times s)} = E_{(m \times n)}\left\{ {\left\lbrack {B_{(n \times m)}\left( {U_{(m \times s)}Q_{(s \times r)}} \right)} \right\rbrack W_{(r \times s)}} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.50)

Here the round, square and curly brackets indicate the sequence of the projection operations. The elements of the matrix X(m × s) have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {x_{ij} = {\sum\limits_{\mu = 1}^{n}e_{i,\mu}}{\sum\limits_{\nu = 1}^{r}w_{\nu,j}}{\sum\limits_{\beta = 1}^{m}b_{\mu,\beta}}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{s}u_{\beta,\alpha}}q_{\alpha,\nu},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.51)

3.3.2Optimality conditions and algorithm

For measuring the deviation of the transformed matrix X(m × s) from the original one U(m × s), choose the information cross-entropy


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathcal{H}(X\, \middle| \, U) = - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}s_{ij}}}(X\, \middle| \, U), \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.52)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {s_{ij} = x_{ij}\ln\frac{x_{ij}}{u_{ij}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.53)

Due to (3.51), the information cross-entropy (3.52) is a scalar function of the matrices (Q, B, W, E) ≥ 0, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}(Q,B,W,E).} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.54)

The optimal elements of the matrices are obtained by maximizing the function ℋ:


$$\begin{array}{r} {(Q^{*},B^{*},W^{*},E^{*}) = \arg\max_{(Q,B,W,E) \geq 0}\mathcal{H}(Q,B,W,E).} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.55)

This problem will be solved using the coordinate-wise scheme of projected gradient descent.

In the parallel procedure, there are a pair of matrices (Q, B) for reducing the original matrix U with respect to the first variable (r < s) and a pair of matrices (W, E) for compressing the matrix U with respect to the second variable (n < m). Each iterative step in the coordinate-wise scheme of projected gradient descent consists of two sub-steps, related to iterations over the (Q, B)-gradients and over the (W, E)-gradients, respectively.

According to (3.51–3.53), the gradient of the function ℋ(Q, B, W, E) has the components


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial\mathcal{H}}{\partial q_{\alpha,\nu}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\frac{\partial s_{ij}}{\partial x_{ij}}}}\,\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial q_{\alpha,\nu}},} \\ {\frac{\partial\mathcal{H}}{\partial b_{\mu,\beta}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\frac{\partial s_{ij}}{\partial x_{ij}}}}\,\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial b_{\mu,\beta}},} \\ {\frac{\partial\mathcal{H}}{\partial w_{\nu,j}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\frac{\partial s_{ij}}{\partial x_{ij}}}}\,\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial w_{\nu,j}},} \\ {\frac{\partial\mathcal{H}}{\partial e_{i,\mu}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\frac{\partial s_{ij}}{\partial x_{ij}}}}\,\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial e_{i,\mu}},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.56)

where


$$\begin{aligned} & {\frac{\partial s_{ij}}{\partial x_{ij}} = \ln\frac{x_{ij}}{u_{ij}} + 1,} \\ & {\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial q_{\alpha,\nu}} = w_{\nu,j}{\sum\limits_{\mu = 1}^{n}e_{i,\mu}}{\sum\limits_{\beta = 1}^{m}b_{\mu,\beta}}u_{\beta,\alpha},\text{\quad\quad}\alpha = \overline{1,s},\,\nu = \overline{1,r};} \\ & {\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial b_{\mu,\beta}} = e_{i,\mu}{\sum\limits_{\nu = 1}^{r}w_{\nu,j}}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{s}u_{\beta,\alpha}}q_{\alpha,\nu},\text{\quad\quad}\mu = \overline{1,n},\,\beta = \overline{1,s};} \\ & {\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial w_{\nu,j}} = {\sum\limits_{\mu = 1}^{n}e_{i,\mu}}{\sum\limits_{\beta = 1}^{m}b_{\mu,\beta}}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{s}u_{\beta,\alpha}}q_{\alpha,\nu},} \\ & {\frac{\partial x_{ij}}{\partial e_{i,\mu}} = {\sum\limits_{\nu = 1}^{r}w_{\nu,j}}{\sum\limits_{\beta = 1}^{m}b_{\mu,\beta}}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{s}u_{\beta,\alpha}}q_{\alpha,\nu},\text{\quad\quad}\mu = \overline{1,n}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.57)

Applying matrix vectorization, pass to the corresponding vectors q, b, w and e. Denote by ∇q, ∇b, ∇w and ∇e the components of the gradient with respect to these vectors.

The algorithm max ℋ has the following structure.

  • a) Initial step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{0} > \mathbf{0},\quad\mathbf{b}^{0} > \mathbf{0},\quad\mathbf{w}^{0} > 0,\quad\mathbf{e}^{0} > 0.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • b) nth iterative step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {X^{n} = E^{n}\left\{ {\left\lbrack {B^{n}\left( {UQ^{n}} \right)} \right\rbrack W^{n}} \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{H}^{n} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}x_{ij}^{n}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}^{n}}{u_{ij}};} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{q}}\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{q}^{n},\mathbf{b}^{n},\mathbf{w}^{n},\mathbf{e}^{n})\,\text{if}\,\mathbf{q} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{q}^{n}\,\text{if}\,\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0};} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow Q^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{b}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{b}}\nabla_{\mathbf{b}}(\mathbf{q}^{n},\mathbf{b}^{n},\mathbf{w}^{n},\mathbf{e}^{n})\,\text{if}\,\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{b}^{n}\text{if}\,\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0};} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow B^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{w}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{w}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{w}}\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)},\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)},\mathbf{w}^{n},\mathbf{e}^{n})\,\text{if}\,\mathbf{w} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{w}^{n}\text{if}\,\mathbf{w}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0};} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{w}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow W^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{e}^{(n + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{e}^{n} + \gamma_{\mathbf{e}}\nabla_{\mathbf{e}}(\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)},\mathbf{b}^{(n + 1)},\mathbf{w}^{n},\mathbf{e}^{n})\,\text{if}\,\mathbf{e}^{(n + 1)} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ {\mathbf{e}^{n}\text{if}\,\mathbf{e}^{(n + 1)} < \mathbf{0};} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{e}^{(n + 1)}\Rightarrow E^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {X^{(n + 1)} = E^{(n + 1)}\left\{ {\left\lbrack {B^{(n + 1)}\left( {UQ^{(n + 1)}} \right)} \right\rbrack W^{(n + 1)}} \right\};} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{H}^{(n + 1)} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}{u_{ij}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • c) Stopping condition:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\text{If}\,\,\mathcal{H}^{(n + 1)} - \mathcal{H}^{(n)} \leq \delta,\,\text{then}\, STOP.} \\ \end{array}$$

3.4Entropy Reduction under Matrix Norm and Information Capacity Constraints

When applying the entropy reduction of a data matrix, it is desirable to obtain a reduced matrix with definite properties. In terms of the EDR method, this means introducing some restrictions on the class of projector matrices, which indirectly affect the resulting reduced matrix. Consider some useful characteristics of projector matrices.

1. Frobenius norms of matrices Above, it has been supposed that the direct Q and inverse T projector matrices have nonnegative elements. Such an assumption is due to the use of cross-entropy to characterize the “distance” between them. However, in applications-relevant machine learning problems, it often makes sense to narrow the class of projector matrices. This can be achieved by considering the Frobenius matrix norm:

2. Information capacity of data matrix In the course of reduction, some information contained in a data matrix is lost. Therefore, it should be measured somehow. Introduce the concept of the information capacity ℐ(A) of a nonnegative matrix An × q, which is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{I}(A) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{q}a_{ij}}}\ln a_{ij}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.59)

Clearly, the information capacity corresponds to the entropy taken with the opposite sign.

3. Cross-entropy reduction algorithm The dimension reduction procedure of a data matrix is to minimize the cross-entropy:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(Q,T\, \middle| \, U)\Rightarrow\min\limits_{Q,T}, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.60)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}x_{ij}}}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U)\ln\frac{\left. x_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) \right.}{u_{ij}}, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.61)


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. x_{ij}(Q,T\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{\mu = 1}^{r}{\sum\limits_{\nu = 1}^{s}t_{\mu,j}}}q_{\nu,\mu}u_{i,\nu},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,m};\, j = \overline{1,s}, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.62)

subject to the following constraints:

  • —the nonnegative values of the projector matrices,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {Q \geq 0,\text{\quad\quad}T \geq 0;} \\ \end{array}$$
    (3.63)

  • —the upper bounds (a, b) on the norm of the projector matrices,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {n_{Q}(Q) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}q_{ij}^{2}}} \leq a,\quad n_{T}(T) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{r}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}t_{ij}^{2}}} \leq b;} \\ \end{array}$$
    (3.64)

  • —the δ-admissible decrease of the information capacity,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\left. \mathcal{I}(U) - \mathcal{I}(Y(Q \middle| U)) \right.}{\mathcal{I}(U)} \leq \delta.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (3.65)

In this inequality,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathcal{I}(Y(Q\, \middle| \, U)) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}y_{ij}}}(Q\, \middle| \, U)\ln y_{ij}(Q\, \middle| \, U), \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.66)


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. y_{ij}(Q\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{\nu = 1}^{s}u_{i,\nu}}q_{\nu,j}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.67)

Due to the properties of the objective function (an entropy-bilinear form) and the constraints specified by quadratic entropy inequalities, the cross-entropy reduction problem (3.60)–(3.64) is nonconvex; for details, see [134, 171]. Therefore, there exists a certain (a priori unknown) number of local optimums, and this problem should be treated as a global optimization one.

Consider the problem (3.60)–(3.64) as a local minimization problem on the nonnegative orthant R+2sr. Here the variables are the elements of the matrices Q and T each containing rs entries. Using matrix vectorization, i.e., the transition to a complex vector through the sequential joining of rows, construct the vectors q, t and u, corresponding to the matrices Q, T and U, respectively. Then the cross-entropy minimization problem can be represented as


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{u})\Rightarrow\min, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.68)


$$\begin{aligned} & {(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t}) \in R_{+}^{(2sr)},} \\ & {N_{Q}(\mathbf{q}) = - {\widetilde{N}}_{Q}(\mathbf{q}) + a \geq 0,\quad N_{T}(\mathbf{t}) = - {\widetilde{N}}_{T}(\mathbf{t}) + b \geq 0,} \\ & \left. \mathcal{I}_{Y}(\mathbf{q}) = I_{Y}(\mathbf{q}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{u}) - \gamma(\delta) \geq 0,\quad\gamma(\delta) = (1 - \delta)I_{U}. \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.69)

Recall that the problem (3.68) is considered as a local optimization one, for which the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions are necessary. The Lagrange function for this problem has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {L(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\alpha,\beta,\gamma) = \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) - \left\langle \alpha,\mathbf{q} \right\rangle - \left\langle \beta,\mathbf{t} \right\rangle,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.70)

where α = {α1,…,αrs}, β = {β1,…,βrs}, and γ = {γ1,γ2,γ3} are the Lagrange multipliers related to the corresponding constraints.

The function


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) = \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t}) - \gamma_{1}N_{Q}(\mathbf{q}) - \gamma_{2}N_{T}(\mathbf{t}) - \gamma_{3}\mathcal{I}_{Y}(\mathbf{q})} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.71)

will be called the truncated Lagrange function.

Assume that there exists a local minimum point (q*, t*) in the problem (3.68, 3.70) and a neighborhood


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbf{q}^{*},\mathbf{t}^{*})}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t}) \in \|\mathbf{q}^{*} - \mathbf{q}\|^{2} + \|\mathbf{t}^{*} - \mathbf{t}\|^{2} \leq \varrho} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.72)

such that the problem (3.68), (3.70) becomes convex on the set (3.72). Then the Kuhn–Tucker conditions [134] are satisfied on the set (3.72) in terms of the truncated Lagrange function (3.71), i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} & {\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) \geq \mathbf{0},\text{\quad\quad}\nabla_{\mathbf{t}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ & {\mathbf{q} \otimes \nabla_{\mathbf{q}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) \geq \mathbf{0},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{t} \otimes \nabla_{\mathbf{t}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ & {\mathbf{q}^{*} \geq \mathbf{0},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{t}^{*} \geq \mathbf{0},} \\ & {\nabla_{\gamma}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) \leq \mathbf{0},\text{\quad\quad}\gamma \otimes \nabla_{\gamma}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) = \mathbf{0},} \\ & {\gamma \geq \mathbf{0}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.73)

This system of equations and inequalities can be solved using the multiplicative algorithm [143]. Introduce the following notations:


$$\begin{aligned} & {\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) = \mathbf{1} - \theta\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma),} \\ & {\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) = \mathbf{1} - \theta\nabla_{\mathbf{t}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma),} \\ & {\mathbf{K}_{\gamma}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma) = \mathbf{1} + \theta\nabla_{\gamma}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t},\gamma).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.74)

The multiplicative algorithm, further referred to as Minimum Cross-Entropy with constraints (MCEC), has the following structure.

  • a) Initial step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{0} > \mathbf{0},\quad\mathbf{t}^{0} > \mathbf{0}.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • b) nth iterative step:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)} = \mathbf{q}^{n} \otimes \mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{q}^{n},\mathbf{t}^{n},\gamma^{n}),} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{t}^{(n + 1)} = \mathbf{t}^{n} \otimes \mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{q}^{n},\mathbf{t}^{n},\gamma^{n});} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{t}^{(n + 1)}\rightarrow T^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\gamma^{n + 1} = \gamma^{n} \otimes \mathbf{K}_{\gamma}(\mathbf{q}^{n},\mathbf{t}^{n},\gamma^{n})} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{q}^{(n + 1)}\rightarrow Q^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{t}^{(n + 1)}\rightarrow T^{(n + 1)}; \right. \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} {X^{(n + 1)} = U\, Q^{(n + 1)}\, T^{(n + 1)};} \\ \end{array}$$


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(Q^{(n + 1)},T^{(n + 1)}\, \middle| \, U) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}}\ln\frac{x_{ij}^{(n + 1)}}{u_{ij}} = H^{(n + 1)}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$

  • c) Stopping condition:


    $$\begin{array}{r} {H^{(n + 1)} - H^{(n)} \leq \Delta.} \\ \end{array}$$

This algorithm converges to a local minimum if the initial point is positive [143].

3.5Estimating Efficiency of Dimension Reduction for Linear Model Learning

Linear static models are widely used to describe objects in RML problems. Consider this description in detail for the original and reduced input learning collections.

3.5.1Linear model

A linear static object has a single output z and s inputs u ∈ Rs. The state of this object is characterized by s attributes with parametric weights a. The object's mathematical model is randomized, i.e., parameters a are random of the interval type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} = \left\{ \mathbf{a}^{-} \leq \mathbf{a} \leq \mathbf{a}^{+} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.75)

The probabilistic properties of these parameters are characterized by a probability density function (PDF) P(a). Since the object is linear and static, the output z of its model has a linear relation to the inputs:


$$\begin{array}{r} {z = \left\langle \mathbf{u},\mathbf{a} \right\rangle,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.76)

where ⟨,⟩ denotes the scalar product of vectors.

Suppose that there is an input learning collection 𝒰 of m such objects, whose state is characterized by vectors u(1), …, u(m) from the attribute space Rs and output is characterized by a vector y = {y1,…,ym}. Due to the object's linearity, the output of the model has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{z} = U\mathbf{a},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z} = \left\{ z_{1},\ldots,z_{m} \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.77)

where U = U(m × s) is a nonnegative matrix of dimensions (m × s) and


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z} = \lbrack\mathbf{z}^{-},\mathbf{z}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z}^{-} = U\mathbf{a}^{-};\,\,\mathbf{z}^{+} = U\mathbf{a}^{+}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.78)

A common assumption is that the outputs of the objects contain measurement errors described by a random vector $\overline{\xi} = \left\{ \xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{m} \right\}$ of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\overline{\xi} \in \mathcal{K} = \left\{ {\overline{\xi}}^{-} \leq \overline{\xi} \leq {\overline{\xi}}^{+} \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.79)

with a probability density function $L(\overline{\xi}).$ In addition, let the PDFs of the model parameters and measurement noises be continuously differentiable.

The observed output of the model is distorted by some noises and has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{z} + \overline{\xi} = U_{(m \times s)}\,\mathbf{a} + \overline{\xi}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.80)

The vector v belongs to the m-dimensional parallelepiped


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{V} = \lbrack\mathbf{v}^{-},\mathbf{v}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{v}^{-} = \mathbf{z}^{-} + {\overline{\xi}}^{-};\,\,\mathbf{v}^{+} = \mathbf{z}^{+} + {\overline{\xi}}^{+}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.81)

RML procedures produce the estimates P̂(a) and $\hat{L}(\overline{\xi})$ of the corresponding PDFs. This is done using the learning collection (𝒰,y) and the randomized model (3.80). The resulting estimates serve for implementing this model, i.e., for generating an ensemble 𝒱 of the random vectors v ∈ Rm. The generation of such ensembles is one of the randomized machine-learning problems [145], further referred to as the s-problem of RML.

In many cases, the dimension s of the attribute space turns out to be very high for the existing computational capabilities. Therefore, it makes sense to reduce this space to a given dimension r < s.

Introduce an input data matrix W(m × r), which will characterize a collection 𝒲 of m objects in the reduced attribute space Rr, and a randomized model with parameters b = {b1,…,br} ∈ Rr:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{w} = W_{(m \times r)}\mathbf{b},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{b} \in R^{r},\,\,\mathbf{w} \in R^{m}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.82)

The parameter vector b consists of random components of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B} = \lbrack\mathbf{b}^{-},\mathbf{b}^{+}\rbrack,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.83)

with a PDF B(b). The observed vector has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{w} + \overline{\zeta},\text{\quad\quad}\overline{\zeta} \in R^{m}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.84)

The random vector $\overline{\zeta}$ describes measurement errors and is of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\overline{\zeta} \in \mathcal{J} = \lbrack{\overline{\zeta}}^{-},{\overline{\zeta}}^{+}\rbrack,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.85)

with a PDF $Q(\overline{\zeta}).$ Finally,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{t} \in \mathcal{T} = \lbrack\mathbf{t}^{-},\mathbf{t}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{t}^{-} = W\mathbf{b}^{-} + {\overline{\zeta}}^{-},\,\,\mathbf{t}^{+} = W\mathbf{b}^{+} + {\overline{\zeta}}^{+}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.86)

All the PDFs characterizing the model parameters and measurement noises are assumed to be continuously differentiable functions. The estimation of the PDF B(b) and the generation of a corresponding ensemble 𝒯 is another randomized machine-learning problem, called the r-problem of RML.

3.5.2Comparing s- and r-problems of RML

These problems will be compared via a three-stage method as follows. In the first stage, the s- and r-problems solved by the RML procedures using the learning collections (𝒰,y) and (𝒲,y), respectively. This stage yields the entropy-optimal PDFs of the model parameters and measurement noises, P*(a) and $L^{*}(\overline{\xi})$ for the s-problem as well as B*(b) and $Q^{*}(\overline{\zeta})$ for the r-problem, respectively. In the second stage, the linear models (3.80, 3.84) are used for calculating the PDFs Fs(v) and Fr(t) normalized on the set 𝒞 = 𝒱 ∩ 𝒯. Finally, in the third stage, the Kullback–Leibler relative entropy [102] is calculated, which characterizes the absolute divergence between the PDFs Fs(v) and Fr(t). This method will be called the s \&r comparison (SRC).

Consider the first stage, and recall the RML procedure for solving the s-problem; see the model described by (3.80).

For obtaining the best estimates under maximum uncertainty (the highest quality of learning), maximize the entropy functional defined on the PDFs P(a) and $L(\overline{\xi}),$


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathcal{H}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),L(\overline{\xi})\rbrack = - {\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})\,\ln P(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} - {\int_{\mathcal{K}}L}(\overline{\xi})\ln L(\overline{\xi})d\overline{\xi}\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.87)

subject to the constraints


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} = 1,\text{\quad\quad}{\int_{\mathcal{K}}L}(\overline{\xi})d\overline{\xi} = 1,} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.88)

and


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{M}\left\{ \mathbf{z} \right\} = {\int_{\mathcal{A}}U}P(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} + {\int_{\mathcal{K}}\overline{\xi}}L(\overline{\xi})d\overline{\xi} = \mathbf{y}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.89)

This is an entropy-linear functional programming problem [138]. Its solution has the form


$$\begin{aligned} & {P^{*}(\mathbf{a}) = \pi^{- 1}(\overline{\theta})\exp\left\langle - \overline{\theta},U\,\mathbf{a} \right\rangle,} \\ & {L^{*}(\overline{\xi}) = \varpi^{- 1}(\overline{\theta})\exp\left\langle - \overline{\theta},\overline{\xi} \right\rangle,} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.90)

where


$$\begin{aligned} {\pi(\overline{\theta})} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{A}}\exp}\left\langle - \overline{\theta},U\,\mathbf{a} \right\rangle d\mathbf{a},} \\ {\varpi(\overline{\theta})} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{K}}\exp}\left\langle - \overline{\theta},\overline{\xi} \right\rangle d\overline{\xi}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.91)

The Lagrange multipliers $\overline{\theta}$ are found from the balance equations (3.89):


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\mathcal{A}}U}P^{*}(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} + {\int_{\mathcal{K}}\overline{\xi}}L^{*}(\overline{\xi})d\overline{\xi} = \mathbf{y}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.92)

Thus, the solution of the s-problem of RML gives the two entropy-optimal PDFs P*(a) (model parameters) and $L^{*}(\overline{\xi})$ (measurement noises).

In the second stage, the linear model (3.80) is used, which has independent parameters and measurement noises. The probability density function F(v) of the observed vector v has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {F(\mathbf{v}) = {\int_{\mathcal{K}}G}(\mathbf{v} - \overline{\xi})L^{*}(\overline{\xi})d\overline{\xi},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.93)

where G( • ) is the density of the vector z (3.80). According to this equality,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} = {(U^{\intercal}U)}^{- 1}\, U^{\intercal}\mathbf{z}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.94)

Therefore,


$$\begin{array}{r} {P^{*}({(U^{\intercal}U)}^{- 1}\, U^{\intercal}\mathbf{z}) = \eta(\mathbf{z}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.95)

where the vector z is defined on the set 𝒵 (3.78). Normalizing this function, obtain the PDF


$$\begin{array}{r} {G(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{\eta(\mathbf{z})}{{\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\eta}(\mathbf{z})}d\mathbf{z}} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.96)

of the vector z, which is normalized on the set 𝒵 (3.78).

Well, equality (3.93) gives the PDF F(v), v ∈ 𝒱 (3.81) for the randomized model of the s-problem. Denote it by Fs(v).

Using a similar procedure for the r-problem (3.82–3.84) with the reduced data matrix W (3.75), find the PDF Fr(t) normalized on the set 𝒯 (3.86).

For comparing the PDFs Fs(v) and Fr(t), introduce the set


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{V}{\cap \mathcal{T}},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.97)

and normalize these functions on it. The normalized PDFs have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\widetilde{F}}_{s}(\mathbf{c}) = \frac{F_{s}(\mathbf{c})}{{\int_{\mathcal{C}}F_{s}}(\mathbf{c})d\mathbf{c}},} \\ {{\widetilde{F}}_{r}(\mathbf{c}) = \frac{F_{r}(\mathbf{c})}{{\int_{\mathcal{C}}F_{r}}(\mathbf{c})d\mathbf{c}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

In the third stage, the PDFs will be compared using the Kullback–Leibler divergence as a measure of the absolute information error Δ between the PDFs F̃r(c) and F̃s(c):


$$\begin{array}{r} {KL({\widetilde{F}}_{s},{\widetilde{F}}_{r}) = {\int_{\mathcal{C}}{\widetilde{F}}_{r}}(\mathbf{c})\ln\frac{{\widetilde{F}}_{r}(\mathbf{c})}{{\widetilde{F}}_{s}(\mathbf{c})} = \Delta \geq 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.98)

Note that the minimum Δ = 0 is achieved at F̃r(c) = F̃s(c).

In addition, introduce the relative information error δ in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\delta = \frac{\Delta}{H_{s} + H_{r}},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.99)

where


$$\begin{aligned} H_{s} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{C}}{\widetilde{F}}_{s}}(\mathbf{c})\ln{\widetilde{F}}_{s}(\mathbf{c})d\mathbf{c},} \\ H_{r} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{C}}{\widetilde{F}}_{r}}(\mathbf{c})\ln{\widetilde{F}}_{r}(\mathbf{c})d\mathbf{c}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.100)

These equalities are the information entropies of the PDFs F̃s and F̃r defined on the support 𝒞 (3.97).

3.6Estimating Efficiency of EDR for Binary Classification Problems

The EDR method will be characterized and compared by efficiency with principal component analysis (PCA) and the random projection (RP) method using a computational experiment on real data for the binary classification problem with a linear classifier.

3.6.1Linear classifier

Recall some necessary results from the theory of linear classification [21, 57, 188]. The classifier's model has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {z(t_{k}) = \text{sign}({\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}a_{i}}u_{i}(t_{k})).} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.101)

Here the parameters a ∈ Rs are unknown deterministic weights of the attributes, and


$$\begin{array}{r} {\text{sign}(x) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {+ 1,} & {{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}a_{i}}u_{i}(t_{k}) \geq 0,} \\ {- 1,} & {{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}a_{i}}u_{i}(t_{k}) < 0.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.102)

Let ℒ(y, U(m × s)) be a collection of learning data. The components of the vector y ∈ Rm are equal to  + 1 if the object with number tk belongs to the first class and equal to  − 1 if this object belongs to the second class. The rows of the matrix Um × s contain the values of the attributes of all objects tk, $k = \overline{1,m}.$

The classifier (3.101) is learned by minimizing the empirical risk


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. J(\mathbf{a}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{z}(}}\mathbf{a}\, \middle| \, U_{(m \times s)})\|^{2} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.103)

over the parameters a. The components of the vector z are generated by the classifier's model (3.101).

The learned classifier is tested using another data collection 𝒯 = (x, V(n × s), where x ∈ Rn. The classifier


$$\begin{array}{r} {w(t_{k}) = \text{sign}({\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{s}{\hat{a}}_{i}}v_{i}(t_{k})),\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,n}} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.104)

outputs w(tk) =  + 1 or w(tk) =  − 1 depending on the rows of the matrix V(n × s). They are compared with the test vector x, and the number of matches (correct classification) is calculated:


$$\begin{array}{r} {I = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}\Lambda}(w(t_{k}) - x(t_{k})),} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.105)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Lambda(y) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 1 & {\text{for}\, y = 0,} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\, y \neq 0.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.106)

Then the classification accuracy ε can be characterized by the ratio


$$\begin{array}{r} {\varepsilon = \frac{I}{n}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.107)

3.6.2Scheme of computational experiment

Following [162, 190], the EDR method was experimentally studied by solving the binary classification problem in the original and reduced attribute spaces, with subsequent comparison of this method with PCA and the RP method in terms of the classification accuracy (3.107). For making the results stable, Monte Carlo simulations and cross-validation were used.

The experiment consisted of several stages:

  1. solving the classification problem in the original space;

  2. solving the classification problem in the PCA-reduced spaces;

  3. solving the classification problem in the RP-reduced spaces;

  4. solving the classification problem in the EDR-reduced spaces.

Stages 2–4 were sequentially implemented for the dimension reduced by 1, i.e., r = s − 1, …, 1, where r denotes the dimension of the reduced spaces. Stage 4 was implemented for various values of δ (an admissible decrease of information capacity).

The Python program for the experimental study was developed in OS Linux using the numpy 1.14.3, scipy 1.1.0, sklearn 0.19.1 libraries. Dimension reduction by principal component analysis and the random projection method was carried out using the corresponding classes of the scikit-learn library [128], PCA and GaussianRandomProjection. The classification problem was solved using support vector machines [70], i.e., the SVC class with the linear kernel.

The experimental study was based on two data sets as follows. The first one (simulation) was a synthetic data set of 100 objects with 10 attributes. The data were generated by the make_classification function [26] with the parameters n_classes=2, n_clusters_per_class=2, n_informative=10, n_redundant=0 and class_sep=1.0. This function generates points in the space of the dimension n_informative that are normally distributed (with zero mean and unit variance) around the edges of a hypercube with sides 2 * class_sep with some noise added.

The second data set (heart) consisted of the real data collected during heart disease research [2]. This data set contains 270 objects with 13 attributes.

In all experiments, the data were normalized to the interval [0,1].

3.6.3Results of experiment

All experiments involved cross-validation using the bootstrap method [70]. More specifically, 30 objects were randomly selected 2 times from the original data set; 20 of them were used to learn the classifier, whereas the remaining 10 were used for testing; the results for each sample were averaged. Then the experiment was repeated 10 times, the results were also averaged. Dimension reduction at each stage was carried out for the entire learning sample (30 objects).

The problem (3.32)–(3.35) was solved using the constrained optimization method SLSQP [97] on the nonnegative orthant, implemented in the scipy library by the minimize function with the parameters ftol=1e-4 and maxiter=1000. Note that for some values of δ the method yielded no solution for the given optimization parameters. In such cases, the last solution found was used.

1. Dependence of ε on number of objects (sample size m) It is important to study this dependence for the three reduction methods in order to identify the areas of their application. As is well known, entropy maximization methods and their derivatives, in particular, the EDR method, are usually used with a limited amount of data compared to the dimension of the attribute space. In the case of “big data,” there exist no fundamental restrictions on their application, but the computational difficulties will significantly increase. As for PCA, for large amounts of data (sufficiently great m) and their heterogeneity, the method becomes unstable [136].

The dependence of the classification accuracy on small sample sizes for the simulation data set was examined. The results are presented in Table 3.1, Table 3.2, Table 3.3 for $m = \overline{5,10}.$ For each of these sets, the attribute space was reduced to the size $r = \overline{5,10}.$
