The results of the computational experiment allow drawing the following conclusions:

  • The EDR method is operable for any amounts of data in the learning and testing data collections; PCA does not work when the amount of data is smaller than the dimension of the attribute space; the operability of the RP method requires additional research.

  • The level of information losses when applying the EDR method is retained up to the two-fold reduction of the attribute space; for PCA and the RP method, the level of information losses grows significantly with decreasing the dimension of the attribute space.

  • Thanks to the control parameter δ in the EDR method, the level of relative information losses can be regulated. At the same time, this possibility is absent in PCA and the RP method.

3.7Entropy Methods for Random Projection

3.7.1Statements of Entropy Randomized Projection Problems

1. Point-set representation of data matrices: indicator of compactness

Consider a data matrix describing some objects and their attributes:


$$\begin{array}{r} {U_{(m \times s)} = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{u}^{(1)} \\ \cdots \\ \mathbf{u}^{(m)} \\ \end{array} \right),\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{u}^{(i)} = \left\{ u_{1}^{(i)},\ldots,u_{s}^{(i)} \right\} \in R^{s},\,\, i = \overline{1,m}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.109)

Here m and s are the numbers of objects and their attributes, respectively; Rs denotes the attribute space. Assume that the elements of this data matrix are standardized, i.e., $u_{ij} \in \lbrack 0,1\rbrack,\, i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s}.$

The point-set representation of a matrix U(m × s) in the attribute space R(m)s is the set 𝔘ms of the points {u(1),…,u(m)}.

For example, the set 𝔘1002 of 100 two-dimensional points represents a matrix U(100 × 2).

The spread of points in a set 𝔘ms can be characterized by the indicator of compactness ρU, which will be defined as the arithmetic average of the distances between the points:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\rho_{U} = \frac{2}{m(m - 1)}{\sum\limits_{(\alpha,\beta) = 1,\mspace{2mu}\alpha \neq \beta}^{m}\varrho}(\mathbf{u}^{(\alpha)},\mathbf{u}^{(\beta)}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.110)

where 𝜚(u(α), u(β)) gives the distance between the points u(α) and u(β). If the elements of the data matrix are standardized, then


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 \leq \varrho(\mathbf{u}^{(\alpha)},\mathbf{u}^{(\beta)}) \leq \sqrt{2}\text{\quad\quad}\text{for~all}\,\,(\alpha,\beta) = \overline{1,m},} \\ {0 \leq \rho_{U} \leq 1.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.111)

Introduce the following classes of transformations for data matrices:

  • (mr) -class: U(m × s)→Y(m × r), the set 𝔜mr is in the space R(m)r;

  • (ns) -class: U(m × s)→B(n × s), the set 𝔅ns is in the space R(n)s;

  • (nr) -class: U(m × s)→Z(n × r), the set ℨnr is in the space R(n)r.

2. Random projector matrices and their probabilistic characteristics

1. Projection onto the space R(m)r (generation of the set 𝔜mr) This operation will be performed using a projector matrix Q(s × r):


$$\begin{aligned} & {Y_{(m \times r)} = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{y}^{(1)} \\ \cdots \\ \mathbf{y}^{(m)} \\ \end{array} \right) = U_{(m \times s)}Q_{(s \times r)};} \\ & {\quad y_{j}^{(i)} = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{s}u_{ik}}q_{kj},\,\, i = \overline{1,m};\, j = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.112)

The projector matrix Q(s × r) is random and of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {Q_{(s \times r)} \in \mathcal{Q} = \lbrack Q^{-},Q^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.113)

The probabilistic properties of the projector matrix are characterized by a continuously differentiable probability density function (PDF) P(Q), defined on 𝒬.

The vectors y(i) form the set 𝒴mr of r-dimensional points, m in total. Define the distance 𝜚(y(α),y(β) | Q(s × r)) between them and the indicator of compactness


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \rho_{Y}(Q) = \frac{2}{m(m - 1)}{\sum\limits_{(\alpha,\beta) = 1,\mspace{2mu}\alpha \neq \beta}^{m}\varrho}(\mathbf{y}^{(\alpha)},\mathbf{y}^{(\beta)}\, \middle| \, Q_{(s \times r)}). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.114)

Since the elements of the projector matrix have random values, the average distance (3.114) is random as well.

Hence, define the mathematical expectation of the indicator of compactness:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\rho}}_{Y} = {\int_{\mathcal{Q}}P}(Q)\rho_{Y}(Q)dQ.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.115)

2. Projection onto the space R(n × s) (generation of the set 𝔅ns) This operation will be performed using a projector matrix T(n × m) with random elements:


$$\begin{aligned} B_{(n \times s)} & {= \left( \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{b}^{(1)} \\ \cdots \\ \mathbf{b}^{(n)} \\ \end{array} \right) = T_{(n \times m)}U_{(m \times s)};\quad b_{j}^{(i)} = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{m}t_{ik}}\, u_{kj},} \\ & {\quad i = \overline{1,n};\, j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.116)

The projector matrix T(n × m) is random and of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {T_{(n \times m)} \in \mathcal{T} = \lbrack T^{-},T^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.117)

Its probabilistic properties are characterized by a PDF W(T) defined on 𝒯.

The vectors b(i) form the set 𝔅ns of s-dimensional points, n < m in total. Define the indicator of compactness


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \rho_{B}(T) = \frac{2}{n(n - 1)}{\sum\limits_{(\alpha,\beta),\mspace{2mu}\alpha \neq \beta}^{n}\varrho}(\mathbf{b}^{(\alpha)},\mathbf{b}^{(\beta)}\, \middle| \, T) \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.118)

and its mathematical expectation


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\rho}}_{B} = {\int_{\mathcal{T}}W}(T)\rho_{B}(T)dT.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.119)

3. Projection onto the space R(n)r (generation of the set ℨnr) This operation will be performed using random projector matrices Tn × m and Q(s × r):


$$\begin{aligned} Z_{(n \times r)} & {= \left( \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{z}^{(1)} \\ \cdots \\ \mathbf{z}^{(n)} \\ \end{array} \right) = T_{(n \times m)}U_{(m \times s)}Q_{(s \times r)};} \\ z_{j}^{(i)} & {= {\sum\limits_{p = 1}^{m}t_{ip}}\,{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{s}u_{pk}}\, q_{kj},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,n};\, j = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.120)

These projector matrices are of the interval type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {T_{(n \times m)} \in \mathcal{T} = \lbrack T^{-},T^{+}\rbrack,} \\ {Q_{(s \times r)} \in \mathcal{Q} = \lbrack Q^{-},Q^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.121)

The probabilistic properties of the projector matrices are characterized by a joint PDF F(T, Q) defined on the set


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{T} \otimes \mathcal{Q}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.122)

The vectors z(i) form the set ℨnr of r-dimensional points. The indicator of compactness for this set is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \rho_{Z}(T,Q) = \frac{2}{n(n - 1)}{\sum\limits_{(\alpha,\beta),\mspace{2mu}\alpha \neq \beta}^{n}\varrho}(\mathbf{z}^{\alpha},\mathbf{z}^{\beta}\, \middle| \, T,Q). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.123)

The mathematical expectation of the indicator of compactness has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\rho}}_{Z} = {\int_{\mathcal{F}}F}(T,Q)\rho_{Z}(T,Q)dTdQ.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.124)

Depending on the relations between the dimensions (m, s) of the original data matrix and the dimensions (m, r), (n, s) and (n, r) of the projector matrices, the former is compressed (if r < s and n < m) or expanded (if r > s and n > m).

3.7.2Algorithms for Entropy Randomized Projection

Consider projection onto the space R(n)r, which transforms a data matrix simultaneously by both parameters.

The entropy randomized projection (ERP) algorithm consists in the maximum entropy estimation (MEE) of the PDF F(T, Q) with the additional condition that the data matrix U(m × s) and the projection Z(n × r) have equal values of their indices of compactness.

The MEE-estimate of the function F(B, Q) (see Chapter A) is calculated as


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{H}\lbrack F(T,Q)\rbrack} & \left. = - {\int_{\mathcal{F}}F}(T,Q)\,\ln\, F(T,Q)\, dTdQ\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ & {{\int_{\mathcal{F}}F}(T,Q)dTdQ = 1,} \\ & {{\int_{\mathcal{F}}F}(T,Q)\rho_{Z}(T,Q)dTdQ = \rho_{U}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.125)

The problem (3.125) is a functional constrained optimization problem of the Lyapunov type: all components of such problems are integral functionals [77].

Due to the integral form of this problem, the optimality conditions involve the following Lagrange functional with scalar Lagrange multipliers:


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{L}\lbrack F(T,Q)\rbrack} & {= \mathcal{H}\lbrack F(T,Q)\rbrack + \mu(\left( {1 - {\int_{\mathcal{F}}F}(T,Q)dTdQ} \right) +} \\ & {+ \lambda\left( {\rho_{U} - {\int_{\mathcal{F}}F}(T,Q)\rho_{Z}(T,Q)dTdQ} \right).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.126)

The first-order optimality conditions for this functional in terms of the Gâteaux derivative [77] (𝔊F) have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathfrak{G}_{F}\mathcal{L}\lbrack F(T,Q)\rbrack = 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.127)

The entropy-optimal PDF of the projector matrices is given by


$$\begin{aligned} \left. F^{*}(T,Q\, \middle| \,\lambda) \right. & {= \frac{\exp\left( {- \lambda\,\,\rho_{Z}(T,Q)} \right)}{\mathbb{F}(\lambda)},} \\ {\mathbb{F}(\lambda)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{F}}\exp}\left( {- \lambda\,\,\rho_{Z}(T,Q)} \right)dTdQ.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.128)

According to (3.128), the structure of the PDF depends on the distance (3.123) and is independent of the parameter λ. This parameter satisfies the balance equation for the indicators of compactness:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Phi(\lambda) = {\int_{\mathcal{F}}\exp}\left( {- \lambda\,\rho_{Z}(T,Q)} \right)\left( {\rho_{Z}(T,Q) - \rho_{U}} \right)dTdQ = 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.129)

Since λ is a scale parameter, it may be sufficient to find its approximate value from the linearized equation (3.129):


$$\begin{array}{r} {\widetilde{\lambda} = \frac{{\int_{\mathcal{F}}\left( {\rho_{Z}(T,Q) - \rho_{U}} \right)}dTdQ}{{\int_{\mathcal{F}}\rho_{Z}}(T,Q)\left( {\rho_{Z}(T,Q) - \rho_{U}} \right)dTdQ}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.130)

Example Let a data matrix and the indicators of compactness based on the Euclidean and Manhattan distances be


$$\begin{array}{r} {U_{(3 \times 2)} = \left( \begin{array}{ll} 0.1 & 0.8 \\ 0.5 & 0.4 \\ 0.9 & 0.2 \\ \end{array} \right);\text{\quad\quad}\rho_{U}^{E} = 0.506,\quad\rho_{U}^{M} = 0.933.} \\ \end{array}$$

Consider projection onto the space R(1)2:


$$\begin{array}{r} {Z_{(2 \times 1)} = \mathbf{z}^{(2)} = T_{(2 \times 3)}U_{(3 \times 2)}\mathbf{q}(2),} \\ \end{array}$$

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{T} = \lbrack T^{-},T^{+}\rbrack,\quad T^{-} = \left( \begin{array}{lll} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{array} \right);\,\, T^{+} = \left( \begin{array}{lll} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \end{array} \right)} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{Q} = \lbrack\mathbf{q}^{-},\mathbf{q}^{+}\rbrack,\quad\mathbf{q}^{-} = \left( \begin{array}{l} {- 1} \\ {- 1} \\ \end{array} \right),\,\mathbf{q}^{+} = \left( \begin{array}{l} 1 \\ 1 \\ \end{array} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$

The vector z(2) consists of the components


$$\begin{array}{r} {z_{1} = q_{1}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}t_{1j}}u_{j1} + q_{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}t_{1j}}u_{j2},\quad z_{2} = q_{1}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}t_{2j}}u_{j1} + q_{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}t_{2j}}u_{j2}.} \\ \end{array}$$

The two types of distances between the elements of z are:

  • —the Euclidean distance


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\rho_{Z}^{E}(T,\mathbf{q}) = {(z_{1} - z_{2})}^{2} = \left\lbrack {q_{1}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}u_{j1}}(t_{1j} - t_{2j}) - q_{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}u_{j2}}(t_{1j} - t_{2j})} \right\rbrack^{2};} \\ \end{array}$$

  • —the Manhattan distance


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \rho_{Z}^{M}(T,\mathbf{q}) = \middle| z_{1} - z_{2} \middle| = \middle| q_{1}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}u_{j1}}(t_{1j} - t_{2j}) - q_{2}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{3}u_{j2}}(t_{1j} - t_{2j}) \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$

The entropy-optimal PDFs (3.128) of the random projector matrices have the following form:

  • —for the Euclidean distance,


    $$\begin{aligned} \left. F_{E}^{*}(T,\mathbf{q}\, \middle| \,\lambda) \right. & {= \frac{\exp\left( {- \lambda\,\,\rho_{Z}^{E}(T,\mathbf{q})} \right)}{\mathbb{F}(\lambda)},} \\ {\mathbb{F}_{E}(\lambda)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{F}}\exp}\left( {- \lambda\,\rho_{Z}^{E}(T,\mathbf{q})} \right)\, dT\, d\mathbf{q};} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (3.131)

  • —for the Manhattan distance,


    $$\begin{aligned} \left. F_{M}^{*}(T,\mathbf{q}\, \middle| \,\lambda) \right. & {= \frac{\exp\left( {- \lambda\,\,\rho_{Z}^{M}(T,\mathbf{q})} \right)}{\mathbb{F}(\lambda)},} \\ {\mathbb{F}_{M}(\lambda)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{F}}\exp}\left( {- \lambda\,\rho_{Z}^{M}(T,\mathbf{q})} \right)\, dB\, d\mathbf{q}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (3.132)

The parameter λ satisfies the following equations for the Euclidean and Manhattan distances, respectively:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\mathcal{F}}\exp}\left( {- \lambda\,\rho_{Z}^{E}(T,\mathbf{q})} \right)\left( {\rho_{Z}^{E}(T,\mathbf{q}) - \delta\,\rho_{U}^{E}} \right)\, dT\, d\mathbf{q} = 0,} \\ {{\int_{\mathcal{F}}\exp}\left( {- \lambda\,\rho_{Z}^{M}(T,\mathbf{q})} \right)\left( {\rho_{Z}^{M}(T,\mathbf{q}) - \delta\,\rho_{U}^{M}} \right)\, dT\, d\mathbf{q} = 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.133)

In equalities (3.131–3.133),


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{T} \otimes \mathcal{Q}.} \\ \end{array}$$

A qualitative picture of the morphology of the multidimensional PDFs (3.131, 3.132) can be obtained using some of their sections.

  • a) The projector matrix T is given:


$$\begin{array}{r} {T^{*} = \left( \begin{array}{lll} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \end{array} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$

The corresponding sections of the unnormalized functions (3.131, 3.132) have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. F_{E}^{*}(B^{*},\mathbf{q}) \right.\sim\exp\left\lbrack {- \lambda\,{(0.41q_{1} - 0.28q_{2})}^{2}} \right),\quad(q_{1},q_{2}) \in \lbrack - 1,1\rbrack,} \\ \end{array}$$

and


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. F_{M}^{*}(B^{*},\mathbf{q}) \right.\sim\exp\left\lbrack \left. - \lambda\, \middle| 0.41q_{1} - 0.28q_{2} \right| \right),\quad(q_{1},q_{2}) \in \lbrack - 1,1\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$

The graphs of these functions for different values λ are shown in Fig. 1(a,b,c) and Fig. 2(a,b,c).

  • b) The projector matrix T and the projector vector q(2) are given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {T = \left( \begin{array}{lll} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ t_{21} & 0 & 1 \\ \end{array} \right),\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{q}^{(2)} = \left( \begin{array}{l} q_{1} \\ {- 1} \\ \end{array} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$

The corresponding sections of the unnormalized functions (3.131, 3.132) have the form


$$\begin{aligned} {\left. F_{E}^{*}(T^{*},\mathbf{q}) \right.\sim\exp} & {\left\lbrack {- \lambda\,{( - 0.1q_{1}t_{21} - 0.4q_{1} + 0.8t_{21} + 0.2)}^{2}} \right),} \\ & {q_{1} \in \lbrack - 1,1\rbrack,\quad t_{21} \in \lbrack 0,1\rbrack,} \\ \end{aligned}$$

and


$$\begin{aligned} {\left. F_{M}^{*}(B^{*},\mathbf{q}) \right.\sim\exp} & {\left\lbrack \left. - \lambda\, \middle| - 0.1q_{1}t_{21} - 0.4q_{1} + 0.8t_{21} + 0.2 \right| \right),} \\ & {q_{1} \in \lbrack - 1,1\rbrack,\quad t_{21} \in \lbrack 0,1\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$

The graphs of these functions for different values λ are presented in Figs. 3a–c and Figs. 4a–c.

Note that these PDFs of random projectors are entropy-optimal for the corresponding data matrix and differ significantly from the Gaussian distribution recommended for random projection. For example, see [181].

3.7.3Implementation of random projectors and their numerical characteristics

A standard approach to implement random projectors is to sample the entropy-optimal PDFs P(Q), W(T) and F(T, Q), which preserve the inter-vector distance of the data matrix in its projector matrices. As the result of sampling, the PDFs are transformed into a sequence of random projector matrices:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. F^{*}(T,Q)\Rightarrow(T^{(1)},Q^{(1)}),(T^{(2)},Q^{(2)}),\ldots,(T^{(N)},Q^{(N)}),\ldots \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.134)

A general method for generating random sequences with a given PDF was proposed in [36]. The balance property (see above) may be not satisfied for each separate element of this sequence, but it will surely hold “on the average.” Therefore, the empirical projector for implementation can be the matrix


$$\begin{array}{r} {\overline{T} \approx \frac{1}{N}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}T^{(i)}},\text{\quad\quad}\overline{Q} \approx \frac{1}{N}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}Q^{(i)}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.135)

The exact values of the “average” projector matrices are given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\overline{T} = {\int_{\mathcal{F}}T}\, F(T,Q)dTdQ,\text{\quad\quad}\overline{Q} = {\int_{\mathcal{F}}Q}\, F(T,Q)dTdQ.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.136)

Although the integrals in these equalities are multidimensional, integrands are exponentials of polynomials. This often provides analytical formulas for calculating multidimensional integrals.

In addition, the problem of calculating multidimensional integrals can be solved by approximate methods, such as the Monte Carlo simulations and the polynomial approximation of integrands.

The PDF F*(T, Q) is defined on the bounded set ℱ (3.122). Therefore, the projector for implementation can be the pair of matrices


$$\begin{array}{r} {(T^{*},Q^{*}) = \arg\max_{\mathcal{F}}F(T,Q).} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.137)

3.7.4Random projector matrices with given values of elements

1. The set of (0, 1)-projector matrices and its ordering

Consider a projection procedure onto the space R(m)r performed by a projector matrix Q(s × r) with random elements taking values 0 or 1.

Write this matrix as a row vector of length sr. The number of different sequences composed of zeros and ones, i.e., the number of different row vectors, is N = 2rs. For example, for s = 3 and r = 1, there are 8 vectors of this type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {000,100,010,001,110,011,101,111;} \\ \end{array}$$

for s = 4 and r = 1, 16 vectors of this type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {0000,1000,0100,0010,0001,1100,0110,0011,} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {1001,0101,1010,1111,1110,0111,1011,1101.} \\ \end{array}$$

For a projector matrix Q(s × r), there exists a finite set ℚ of its (0, 1)-realizations:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{Q}} = \left\{ Q^{(1)},\ldots,Q^{(N)} \right\},\text{\quad\quad}N = 2^{sr}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.138)

Suppose that the realizations are random, then their probabilistic properties can be characterized by a discrete distribution function (DDF) W(α) with a discrete support α ∈ 𝒜 = [1, N], where


$$\begin{array}{r} {W(\alpha) = \mathbf{w} = \left\{ w_{\alpha}\,\alpha = \overline{1,N} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.139)

The projector matrix is given by


$$\begin{aligned} {Y_{(m \times r)}^{(\alpha)} = \left( \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{y}_{(1)}^{(\alpha)} \\ \cdots \\ \mathbf{y}_{(m)}^{(\alpha)} \\ \end{array} \right)} & {= U_{(m \times s)}Q_{(s \times r)}^{(\alpha)};\quad y_{j}^{(\alpha,i)} = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{s}u_{ik}}q_{kj}^{(\alpha)},} \\ & {\quad i = \overline{1,m};\, j = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.140)

The indicator of compactness of the set 𝔜(α) has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}(Q) = \frac{2}{m(m - 1)}{\sum\limits_{(\kappa,\beta) = 1,\mspace{2mu}\kappa \neq \beta}^{m}\varrho^{(\alpha)}}(\mathbf{y}^{(\kappa)},\mathbf{y}^{(\beta)}\, \middle| \, Q_{(s \times r)}^{(\alpha)}). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.141)

Order the sequence (3.138) in accordance with the sequence of inequalities


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 < \rho_{Y}^{(1)}(Q) < \rho_{Y}^{(2)}(Q) < \cdots < \rho_{Y}^{(N)}(Q).} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.142)

2. MEE-estimate of DDFs

The MEE-estimate of the DDF W(α) is calculated as


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(\mathbf{w}) = - {\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}w_{\alpha}}\ln w_{\alpha}\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(3.143)

subject to the following constraints:

  • —the normalization conditions


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}w_{\alpha}} = 1;} \\ \end{array}$$
    (3.144)

  • —the balance conditions for the indicators of compactness


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}w_{\alpha}}\,\rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}(Q) = \rho_{U}.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (3.145)

The problem (3.143)–(3.145) is a finite-dimensional constrained optimization problem with a concave objective function (information entropy) and linear equality constraints.

Consider the Lagrange function


$$\begin{array}{r} {L(\mathbf{w},\lambda) = H(\mathbf{w}) + \mu\left( {1 - {\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}w_{\alpha}}} \right) + \lambda\left( {\rho_{U} - {\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}w_{\alpha}}\rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}(Q)} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.146)

From the first-order optimality conditions, for this function, it follows that the entropy-optimal discrete probability distribution is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {w_{\alpha}^{*} = \frac{\exp\left( {- \lambda\rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}(Q)} \right)}{{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}\exp}\left( {- \lambda\rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}(Q)} \right)},\text{\quad\quad}\alpha = \overline{1,N},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.147)

where the parameter λ satisfies the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}\exp}( - \lambda\rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}(Q))(\rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}(Q) - \rho_{U}) = 0,\text{\quad\quad} - \infty < \lambda < \infty.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.148)

Introduce the change of variable z = exp ( − λ). Then equation (3.148) can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\varphi(z) = {\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{N}z^{h_{\alpha}}}\, c_{\alpha} = 0,\,\,\, z \geq 0;\quad c_{\alpha} = (h_{\alpha} - \rho_{U}),\,\, h_{\alpha} = \rho_{Y}^{(\alpha)}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.149)

Theorem 3.1 Assume that there exists α = l such that


$$\begin{aligned} & {c_{\alpha} < 0\quad for\,\,\alpha = 1,\ldots,l,} \\ & {c_{\alpha} \geq 0\quad for\,\,\alpha = l + 1,\ldots,N,} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(3.150)

and, according to (3.142),


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 < h_{1} < h_{2} < \cdots < h_{l} < h_{l + 1} < \cdots < h_{N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.151)

Then equation (3.149) has a unique positive solution z* > 0.

Proof Using conditions (3.150, 3.151), write equation (3.149) as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(z) = \frac{{\sum\limits_{\alpha = l + 1}^{N}z^{h_{\alpha}}}c_{\alpha}}{{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{l}z^{h_{\alpha}}}c_{\alpha}} = 1.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.152)

Due to (3.151), hl + 1 − h1 > 0, and


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(z) = z^{(h_{l + 1} - h_{1})}\frac{{\sum\limits_{\alpha = l + 2}^{N}z^{h_{\alpha}}}c_{\alpha} + c_{l + 1}}{{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 2}^{l}z^{h_{\alpha}}}c_{\alpha} + c_{1}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.153)

Hence, ϕ(0) = 0. Now represent the function ϕ(z) in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(z) = z^{(h_{N} - h_{l})}\frac{{\sum\limits_{\alpha = l + 1}^{N - 1}z^{h_{\alpha} - h_{N}}}c_{\alpha} + c_{N}}{{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{l - 1}z^{h_{\alpha} - h_{l}}}c_{\alpha} + c_{l}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.154)

As is easily checked, ϕ(∞) =  + ∞. Consider its derivative:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi^{\prime}(z) = \frac{{\sum\limits_{\beta = 1}^{l}\,}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = l + 1}^{N}\,}c_{\beta}\, c_{\alpha}(h_{\alpha} - h_{\beta})z^{(h_{\beta} - h_{\alpha})}}{\left( {{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{l}c_{\alpha}}\, z^{h_{\alpha}}} \right)^{2}} > 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.155)

Therefore, the function ϕ(z) is monotonically increasing, and equations (3.149), (3.151) have a unique positive solution z* > 0. ■

3.7.5Choice of appropriate projector matrix from ℚ (3.138)

The entropy-optimal DDF $W^{*}(\alpha) = w_{\alpha}^{*},\,\alpha = \overline{1,N},$ (3.149) characterizes the probabilities of implementing the elements (projector matrices) from the set ℚ (3.138). However, for obtaining a particular projector matrix Y(m × r), a particular projector matrix from the set ℚ is needed. Particular matrices can be chosen using different strategies as follows.

1. Projector matrix with maximum probability Let the difference Δρ = ρY(N) − ρY(1) in (3.142) be sufficiently large. This means that the maximum value of probability in the DDF (3.149) is appreciably greater than the minimum one. Then the implemented projector matrix has the number


$$\begin{array}{r} {\alpha^{*} = \arg\max_{1 \leq \alpha \leq N}w_{\alpha}^{*}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.156)

2. Average projector matrix If Δρ = ρY(N) − ρY(1) is small, the sequence {ρ(α)} increases with a low rate. In this case, the projector matrix for implementation should be obtained by averaging:

where ⌊ • ⌋ denotes the integer part of a number  • .

3. Median projector matrix is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{\alpha^{*}}w_{\alpha}^{*}} = {\sum\limits_{\alpha = \alpha^{*} + 1}^{N}w_{\alpha}^{*}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.158)

4. Averaging of projector matrices This strategy consists of the following stages. In the first stage, subsets of projector matrices with definite properties are selected. In the second stage, a subset of the corresponding projector matrices is formed. Then the average projector matrix is calculated.

Whereas the second and third stages are related to standard calculations for mathematical statistics, the first one requires additional comments. The subsets of projector matrices are selected in accordance with rules reflecting their desired properties. Depending on the rule for selecting such subsets, the so-called variance and interquartile subsets of projector matrices will be studied below.

First, consider the variance subsets. For this, find the root mean square (RMS) value of the variable α:

Define the variance interval


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{I}_{\alpha} = \lbrack\alpha^{*} - \sigma_{\alpha}^{*},\alpha^{*} + \sigma_{\alpha}^{*}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.160)

The variance subset has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\widetilde{\mathbb{Q}} = \left\{ Q^{(\alpha^{*} - \sigma_{\alpha}^{*})},\ldots,Q^{(\alpha^{*} + \sigma_{\alpha}^{*})} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.161)

For each element of this subset, calculate the corresponding projector matrices:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\widetilde{\mathcal{Y}} = \left\{ Y_{(m \times r)}^{(\alpha^{*} - \sigma_{\alpha}^{*})},\ldots,Y_{(m \times r)}^{(\alpha^{*} + \sigma_{\alpha}^{*})} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.162)

In the last stage, find the average projector matrix on the variance set:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{Y}}_{(m \times r)}^{D} = \frac{1}{2\sigma_{\alpha}^{*}}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = \alpha^{*} - \sigma_{\alpha}^{*}}^{\alpha^{*} + \sigma_{\alpha}^{*}}Y_{(m \times r)}^{(\alpha)}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.163)

Now analyze the formation of the interquantile subsets. The entropy-optimal probability distribution function (see (3.147)) has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {F^{*}(\kappa) = {\sum\limits_{\alpha = 1}^{\kappa}w_{\alpha}^{*}},\text{\quad\quad}\kappa \in \lbrack 0,1\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.164)

Recall that the κ*-quartile of a random variable α is the set 𝒜(κ*) of its values [1, κ*].

Consider two quartile sets, 𝒜(κ1*) and 𝒜(κ2*), where κ1* > κ2*. The subsets of projector matrices are associated with each of these sets:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{Q}}(\kappa*_{1}) = \left\{ Q^{(1)},\ldots,Q^{(\alpha(\kappa_{1}^{*}))} \right\},} \\ {{\mathbb{Q}}(\kappa*_{2}) = \left\{ Q^{(1)},\ldots,Q^{(\alpha(\kappa_{2}^{*}))} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.165)

Construct the subset of projector matrices


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{Q}}(\kappa_{1}^{*} - \kappa_{2}^{*}) = \left\{ Q^{(\alpha(\kappa_{2}^{*}))},\ldots,Q^{(\alpha(\kappa_{1}^{*}))} \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.166)

which is the (κ1* − κ2*)-interquantile subset ℐ(κ1* − κ2*) of the entropy-optimal projector matrices. The number of elements in this subsets is M(κ1* − κ2*) = α(κ1*) − α(κ2*).

For each element of the subset 𝒬(κ1* − κ2*) (3.166), calculate the corresponding projector matrices


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{Y}(\kappa_{1}^{*} - \kappa_{2}^{*}) = \left\{ Y_{(m \times r)}^{\alpha(\kappa_{2}^{*})},\ldots,Y_{(m \times r)}^{\alpha(\kappa_{1}^{*})} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.167)

The average projector matrix on the subset ℐ(κ1* − κ2*) is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{Y}}_{(m \times r)}^{K} = \frac{1}{M_{(\kappa_{1}^{*} - \kappa_{2}^{*})}}{\sum\limits_{\alpha = \alpha(\kappa_{2}^{*})}^{\alpha(\kappa_{1}^{*})}Y_{(m \times r)}^{\alpha}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(3.168)

Averaging over interquantile sets yields projector matrices with given (κ1, κ2)-quantiles.

CHAPTER 4 RANDOMIZED PARAMETRIC MODELS

DOI: 10.1201/9781003306566-4

An important component of the RML procedures is a model with random parameters, which will be called the randomized parametric model (RPM). In this way, we emphasize that the random parameters in this model are artificial and have optimal probabilistic characteristics. The optimality of the probabilistic characteristics of the RPM parameters is considered in terms of an quality functional and a set of admissible parameter values in a specific problem. As the RML procedures are used for a wide range of machine learning problems, we will study static and dynamics RPMs.

4.1Definition, Characteristics and Classification

A randomized parametric model (RPM) transforms input data into an ensemble of output data, which is generated by the model in accordance with given probability density functions (PDFs) of its parameters.

Consider a case in which the input data represent a one-dimensional array, i.e., a vector x ∈ Rn, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1(a). Its elements are some characteristics x1, …, xn of a studied object. An RPM has randomized parameters a ∈ Rr whose probabilistic properties are described by a PDF P(a). An RPM generates an ensemble 𝒴 of vectors y ∈ Rm with the given PDF P(a).

Next, let the input data be defined by a two-dimensional array, i.e., a matrix X composed of column vectors $\mathbf{x}^{(j)},\, j = \overline{1,s}$ (see Fig. 4.1(b)). For example, such an array results from measuring the object's state vector at s different times. For each measured vector x(j) from the input array, an RPM with the above-mentioned properties generates an ensemble 𝒴(j) of random vectors y(j) ∈ Rm with the given PDF P(a).

As a last example, consider a set 𝒳τ composed of three-dimensional input data arrays containing measurements of a vector function $\mathbf{x}^{(j)}(\tau),\, j = \overline{1,s},$ where τ ∈ 𝒯 = [0, T]. Here, for each measurement, an RPM generates three-dimensional ensembles 𝒴(j) of random vector functions y(j)(t), t ≥ τ, with the given PDF P(a).

In all examples above, an RPM transforms deterministic input data into an ensemble of randomized output data. Such a transformation will be characterized by a mapping


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbb{M}(P(\mathbf{a}),\tau,t,T) = :\mathcal{X}_{\tau}\overset{P(\mathbf{a})}{\rightarrow}\hat{\mathcal{Y}},} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.1)

and a corresponding RPM will be assigned the “input–output ensemble” [I–OE] class; see Fig. 4.2(a).

Sometimes, it is useful to structure the mapping 𝕄(P(a), τ, T). In particular, we can represent it as two mappings 𝕄1(P1(a(1)), τ, λ, t, T) and 𝕄2(P2(a(2)), t, λ) within a feedback loop (see Fig. 4.2(b)), i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbb{M}_{1}(P_{1}(\mathbf{a}^{(1)}),\tau,\lambda,t,T)} & {= :(X_{\tau},{\hat{\mathcal{Z}}}_{\lambda})\overset{P_{1}(\mathbf{a}^{(1)})}{\rightarrow}\mathcal{Y};} \\ {\mathbb{M}_{1}(P_{2}(\mathbf{a}^{(2)}),t,\lambda)} & {= :\hat{\mathcal{Y}}\overset{P_{2}(\mathbf{a}^{(2)})}{\rightarrow}{\hat{\mathcal{Z}}}_{\lambda}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.2)

Here (λ, τ, t) ∈ 𝒯 = [0, T]. The models described by the mappings (4.1, 4.2) will be classified as the “(input, feedback)–output ensemble” [(I,FB)–OE] RPMs.

These RPMs have randomized interval-time parameters, that is,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} = \lbrack\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{a}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{a}^{\pm} = \left\{ a_{1}^{\pm},\ldots,a_{r}^{\pm} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.3)

In addition, the RPMs of both classes will be divided into subclasses, in terms of their temporal properties and mathematical modeling methods. Based on the first classification attribute, there exist static and dynamic RPMs. For the static models, τ = t in the mapping (4.1), i.e., an ensemble generated by such a model at a time t depends on the data at this time only. In the dynamic RPMs, an ensemble $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}$ depends on the data Xτ, where t0 ≤ τ ≤ t.

For further classification in terms of mathematical modeling methods, we will employ a standard approach by considering linear and nonlinear models, functions and functionals, differential and integral equations, and different approximations of nonlinearities. The classification tree is demonstrated in Fig. 4.3.

4.2“Single Input–Ensemble Output” Randomized Parametric Model

4.2.1Static models

For this class of models, an ensemble of output data at a time t depends on the input data at this time and also on a realization of the randomized parameters. Therefore, the index t can be omitted, and such mappings can be described using vector functions of the random argument a.

Consider an input data array, which is characterized by a matrix $\left. X = \lbrack x_{ij}\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,n},\, j = \overline{1,s}\rbrack. \right.$ This array consists of s measurements of an input vector x(j) = {x1(j),…,xn(j)}, where $j = \overline{1,s}.$ The elements of this vector are the elements of column j in the matrix X.

A static RPM transforms the input matrix X into an output matrix $\left. \hat{Y} = \lbrack{\hat{y}}_{kj}\, \middle| \, k = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s}\rbrack. \right.$ The columns of this matrix are the elements of the jth vector ${\hat{\mathbf{y}}}^{(j)} = \left\{ {\hat{y}}_{1}^{(j)},\ldots,{\hat{y}}_{m}^{(j)} \right\},$ where $j = \overline{1,s}.$

Introduce a matrix $\left. A = \lbrack a_{hp}\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,m},p = \overline{1,n}\rbrack, \right.$ composed of randomized parameters. The elements of this matrix are random variables taking values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A}_{hp} = \lbrack a_{hp}^{-},a_{hp}^{+}\rbrack,} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.4)

which form the (m × s)-dimensional parallelepiped


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A} = \otimes_{h = 1}^{m} \otimes_{p = 1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{hp}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.5)

By assumption, there exists a continuously differentiable PDF P(A) on this set.

A relation between the input X and the output ensemble $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}$ of a static RPM is described by a vector function ℱ that has the randomized parameters A with the PDF P(A), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathcal{Y}} = \mathcal{F}\left( {X,A,P(A)} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.6)

In other words, for a fixed input data array X, a static RPM generates an ensemble $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}$ of random matrices Ŷ with the above-mentioned properties.

An important special case of the RPMs (4.6) is the model with n inputs and one output. In this case, the model generates a vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \left\{ y_{1}^{(1)},\ldots,y_{m}^{(s)} \right\},$ and its randomized parameters are characterized by a vector a = {a1,…,ar} with interval-type elements


$$\begin{array}{r} {a_{h} \in \mathcal{A}_{h} = \lbrack a_{h}^{-},a_{h}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{A} = \otimes_{h = 1}^{r}\mathcal{A}_{h}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.7)

Then equality (4.6) takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathcal{Y}} = \mathcal{F}\left( {X,\mathbf{a},P(\mathbf{a})} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.8)

where $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}$ denotes an ensemble of random vectors $\hat{\mathbf{y}}.$

1. Linear static RPMs. This class of the models involves a linear vector function F (4.6) of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathcal{Y}} = A\, X,} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.9)

where A is a matrix of dimensions (m × n) with the randomized elements (4.4, 4.5) and the probabilistic properties characterized by a PDF P(A).

If the RPM (4.6) has n inputs and one output, then the output ensemble consists of the values of a random variable


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y} = \left\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{a} \right\rangle.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.10)

2.Nonlinear static RPMs. The nonlinear RPMs form a significantly wider class than the linear ones. The nonlinear processes that occur in nature are modeled using appropriate laws. If a certain relation between an input and output of an object surely exists but its form is unknown, then a more of less universal approach lies in approximation. Here it is necessary to define a structure and parameters of an approximating function. As a result, to design a nonlinear static RPM means to search for appropriate parameter values. Consider some types of approximations and also the underlying hypotheses on the properties of the “Single Input–Ensemble Output” relations.

2.1. Analytical nonlinearities. By a prevailing hypothesis, there exists an analytical relation between the input and output matrices, X and Y. This hypothesis allows us to perform approximation using the Taylor monomial


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathcal{Y}} = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}B^{(h)}}\, Z^{(h)}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.11)

Here B(h) denotes a matrix of dimensions (s × φ(h)) with interval-type randomized elements, and Z(h) is a matrix of dimensions (φ(h)) × r whose entries represent the products of degree h from the elements of the input matrix X. The matrices B(h) are defined on the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{B}_{h} = \lbrack\mathcal{B}_{h}^{-},\mathcal{B}_{h}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}h = \overline{1,R}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.12)

For a one-dimensional static object (with one input and one output), equality (4.11) takes the simpler form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y} = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}b_{h}}x^{h},} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.13)

where the parameters b1, …, bR are randomized and independent. The domain of definition of the parameters b1, …, bR is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{h} \in \mathcal{B}_{h} = \lbrack b_{h}^{-},b_{h}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}h = \overline{1,R}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.14)

2.2. Continuous nonlinearities. In fact, the existence of an analytical relation between an input and output of a static nonlinearity is a bold hypothesis. Following a more realistic approach, assume that the input is bounded and the nonlinearity Φ(x) has no discontinuities of the second kind (infinite jumps). Numerous approximation methods with orthogonal polynomials were developed on the basis of these hypotheses.

Recall some fundamental concepts of the corresponding methods. Consider a one-dimensional static object with a bounded input and a nonlinear characteristic that has no discontinuities of the second kind:


$$\begin{array}{r} {x^{-} \leq x \leq x^{+}.} \\ \end{array}$$

By assumption, there exists a certain function w(x) on this interval, which is often interpreted as a weight characteristic for the values of the variable x. Since the nonlinearity Φ(x) of the static object is considered on the same interval without discontinuities of the second kind,


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{x^{-}}^{x^{+}}w}(x)\Phi^{2}(x)dx < \infty.} \\ \end{array}$$

To obtain orthogonal polynomials, choose a system of power functions 1, x, x2, … and apply the following orthogonalization procedure:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\psi_{0}(x) = c_{0},} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\psi_{1}(x) = c_{0} + c_{1}x,} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\psi_{2}(x) = c_{0} + c_{1}x + c_{2}x^{2},} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\cdots = \cdots + \cdots + \cdots} \\ \end{array}$$

The coefficients c0, c1, c2, … in these formulas are adjusted so that


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{x^{-}}^{x^{+}}w}(x)\psi_{i}^{2}(x)dx = 1,\text{\quad\quad}i = 0,1,2,\ldots} \\ \end{array}$$

and


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{x^{-}}^{x^{+}}w}(x)\psi_{i}(x)\psi_{i - 1}(x)dx = 0,\text{\quad\quad}i = 1,2,\ldots} \\ \end{array}$$

This procedure yields a system of orthogonal polynomials. The weight function w(x) defines the class of a corresponding orthonormal polynomial. Some classes are presented in Table 4.1.

Table 4.1: Orthonormal polynomials.

Using the system of orthonormal polynomials, construct an approximating polynomial with the parameters a0, …, aR by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\Phi}(x) = {\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{R}a_{i}}\psi_{i}(x).} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.15)

In contrast to the classical approach to approximation, the parameters of an approximating function will be treated as randomized ones taking values within an interval [a−, a+].

4.2.2Functional description of dynamic models

An output ensemble of dynamic models at a time t is characterized by a mapping 𝕄[P(a), τ, t] of the form (4.1) and depends on the input data on a time interval [t − τ, t] and a realization of the randomized parameters.

Denote by x(τ) an input vector composed of independent observations x1(τ), …, xn(τ) that are defined on a time interval 𝒯t = [0, t], where τ ∈ 𝒯t. At each time t > 0, the model outputs a vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t)$ composed of observations ŷ1(t), …, ŷm(t), where t ∈ 𝒯 = [0, T]. A relation between the input x(τ | τ∈𝒯t) and the output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t)$ is described by a functional ℬ, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \hat{\mathbf{y}}(t) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}(\tau),\mathbf{a}\, \middle| \,\tau \in \mathcal{T}_{t}),\text{\quad\quad}t \in \mathcal{T} = \lbrack 0,T\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.16)

Assume that this functional is parameterized by a vector a = {a1,…,ar} of random elements that belong to intervals


$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{A}_{i} & {= \lbrack a_{i}^{-},a_{i}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}i \in \lbrack 1,r\rbrack;} \\ \mathcal{A} & {= {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{r}\mathcal{A}_{i}}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.17)

Three classes of the dynamic “Single Input–Ensemble Output” RPMs will be considered, namely, the linear ones, as well as the nonlinear ones with the power and polynomial nonlinearities.

4.2.3Linear dynamic models

Consider a dynamic RPM with an input x(τ), τ ∈ 𝒯t and an output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t),\, t \in \mathcal{T}.$ The input vector elements $x_{i}(\tau),\, i = \overline{1,n},$ are continuous time-varying functions. A relation between the input and output of this RPM is described by a linear functional ℬ with the parameters a (4.16), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t) = {\int_{0}^{t}B}(t,\tau,\,\mathbf{a})\mathbf{x}(\tau)d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.18)

In this formula, the matrix B(t, τ, a) of dimensions (m × n) consists of pulse characteristics $\left. \lbrack b_{ij}(t,\tau\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}^{(ij)}),\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,n}\rbrack \right.$ with random parameters a(ij) = {a1(ij),…,akij(ij)}, where kij is the number of parameters for a pulse characteristic bij(t, τ).

According to a general concept, the parameters a(ij) are interval-type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a}^{(ij)} \in \mathcal{A}^{(ij)} = \lbrack\mathbf{a}_{-}^{(ij)},\mathbf{a}_{+}^{(ij)}\rbrack,\quad\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\prod\limits_{j = 1}^{n}\mathcal{A}^{(ij)}}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.19)

The model (4.19) generates an ensemble ${\hat{\mathcal{Y}}}_{\mathcal{T}}$ of random trajectories $\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t),\, t \in \mathcal{T}.$ These pulse characteristics can be parameterized in different ways. Some of them will be discussed below.

1.1. Given functions with unknown parameters. As a rule, pulse characteristics are exponential functions or harmonic functions with exponential decay, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{ij}(t,\tau) = \alpha_{ij}(t)\exp\left( {- \beta_{ij}(t)\tau} \right)\text{or}b_{ij}(t,\tau)\exp\left( {- \beta_{ij}\tau} \right)\,\sin(\omega_{ij}(t)\tau + \phi_{ij}(t)),} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.20)

where, e.g., time-varying parameters have the form


$$\begin{aligned} {\alpha_{ij}(t)} & {= \alpha_{ij}^{0} + \alpha_{ij}^{1}t;\quad\beta_{ij}(t) = \beta_{ij}^{0} + \beta_{ij}^{1}t,} \\ {\omega_{ij}(t)} & {= \omega_{ij}^{0}\ln t;\text{\quad\quad}\phi_{ij}(t) = \phi_{ij}^{0} + \phi_{ij}^{1}t.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.21)

In these expressions, αij0, αij1, βij0, βij1, ωij0, ϕij0 and ϕij1 are random variables that take values within corresponding intervals.

1.2. Approximation by given family of functions with unknown weights. Consider a family ℛv of v deterministic functions, further referred to as the basis functions:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{R}_{v} = \left\{ \phi_{1}(t,\tau),\ldots,\phi_{v}(t,\tau) \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.22)

Then the pulse characteristics are written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{ij}(t,\tau) = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K_{ij}}b_{k}^{(ij)}}\,\phi_{k}(t,\tau),} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.23)

where the coefficients bk(ij) are randomized independent variables that take values within some intervals.

To a large extent, a proper choice of basis functions depends on the properties of an object under study. Here a widespread approach is to employ the families of basis functions formed by the exponential functions exp (α(t, τ)), the polynomial-exponential functions βtpexp (α(t, τ)) (with integers p), or the polynomial-exponential-harmonic functions βtpexp (α(t, τ) sin (ω(t, τ)).

Example 3.1 Consider a linear dynamic system with random time-varying parameters. The input vector consists of two elements {x1(τ),x2(τ)}, which are continuous functions on the time interval 𝒯. The output vector has one element of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {y_{1}(t) = {\int_{0}^{t}\left( {b_{11}(t,\tau)x_{1}(\tau) + b_{12}(t,\tau)x_{2}(\tau)} \right)}d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$

The pulse characteristics in this equality are given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{11}(t,\tau) = A\exp\left( {- \alpha(t)\tau} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{12}(t,\tau) = C(t)\exp( - \beta\tau).} \\ \end{array}$$

This model incorporates the constant parameters A = 2.0 and β = 0.5, as well as the random time-varying parameters α(t) = α0 + α1t and C(t) = C0 + C1t, where α0, α1, C0 and C1 are independent random variables taking values within the following intervals:


$$\begin{array}{r} {- 0.1 \leq \alpha_{0} \leq 0.2;\quad - 0.05 \leq \alpha_{1} \leq 0.10;} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {1.0 \leq C_{0} \leq 2.0;\quad - 0.5 \leq C_{1} \leq 0.5.} \\ \end{array}$$

They obey the uniform distributions on the corresponding intervals, i.e., the PDFs are given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {p(\alpha_{0}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 3.3 & {\text{for}\, - 0.1 \leq \alpha_{0} \leq 0.2,} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\, - 0.1 > \alpha_{0} > 0.2;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.\text{\quad\quad}p(\alpha_{1}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 6.6 & {\text{for}\, - 0.05 \leq \alpha_{1} \leq 0.10,} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\, - 0.05 > \alpha_{1} > 0.10;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {p(C_{0}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 1.0 & {\text{for}\, 1.0 \leq C_{0} \leq 2.0,} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\, 1.0 > C_{0} > 2.0;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.\text{\quad\quad}p(C_{1}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {1,0} & {\text{for}\, - 0.5 \leq C_{1} \leq 0.5,} \\ 0 & {\text{for} - 0.5 > C_{1} > 0.5.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

The pulse characteristics b11(t, τ) and b12(t, τ) are functions of two random variables, as illustrated in Figs. 4.4(a) and 4.4(b). Their graphical representations are the corresponding surface ensembles ℬ11(t, τ) and ℬ12(t, τ). At the time t = 0, the pulse characteristics depend on the variable τ only. The cutsets of these surfaces, i.e., the ensembles ℬ11(0, τ) and ℬ12(0, τ) are generated by the random parameters α0 and C0, respectively.

If the elements of the matrix B have random time-invariable parameters, the expression (4.18) takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{y}(t) = {\int_{0}^{t}B}(t - \tau)\,\mathbf{x}(\tau)d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.24)

The elements of the matrix B, which has dimensions (m × n), are the pulse characteristics bij(τ) with the independent randomized time-invariable parameters.

Example 3.2 For the linear dynamic system of Example 3.1, let the pulse characteristics be given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{11}(\tau) = A\exp\left( {- \alpha\tau} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{12}(\tau) = C\exp( - \beta\tau).} \\ \end{array}$$

In this model, A = 2.0 and β = 0.5 act as the constant parameters, whereas α and C are the random parameters taking values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {- 0.1 \leq \alpha \leq 0.2\text{\quad\quad}\text{and}\text{\quad\quad}1.0 \leq C \leq 2.0.} \\ \end{array}$$

The parameters are independent and have the uniform distributions, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {p(\alpha) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 3.3 & {\text{for}\, - 0.1 \leq \alpha \leq 0.2,} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\, - 0.1 > \alpha > 0.2;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.,\text{\quad\quad}p(C) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 1.0 & {\text{for}\, 1.0 \leq C \leq 2.0,} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\, 1.0 > C > 2.0.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

Figures 4.5(a) and 4.5(b) demonstrate ensembles ℬ11(τ) and ℬ12(τ) of the pulse characteristics b11(τ) and b12(τ), respectively.

1.3.Discrete input functions. In most cases, the input and output of an object are measured at discrete times with a fixed step Δ. An object operates on finite time intervals, and hence the available information about its input and output is represented as one-dimensional numerical data arrays. These arrays are used to form the vectors of lattice functions, x[kΔ] = x[k] and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\Delta\rbrack = \hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\rbrack$ for the object's input and output, respectively. For details, the reader is referred to [176].

In a linear approximation, a dynamic relation between the input and output lattice function vectors, x[k] and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\rbrack,$ can be described by a matrix B[k,q] composed of the lattice pulse characteristics bij[k, q] for the RPM with time-varying parameters or by a matrix composed of the lattice pulse characteristics bij[q] for the RPM with constant parameters. In both statements, the RPM contain independent random parameters taking values within given intervals. The pulse characteristics are assumed to have the so-called finite memory. For the RPMs with time-varying parameters, this means that


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{ij}\lbrack k,q\rbrack = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {b_{ij}\lbrack k,q\rbrack} & {\text{if}\, 0 \leq l \leq L_{ij}\,\text{and}\, k \geq 0,} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\, l > L_{ij}\,\text{and}\, k \geq 0;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.25)

for the RPM with constant parameters,


$$\begin{array}{r} {b_{ij}\lbrack q\rbrack = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {b_{ij}\lbrack q\rbrack} & {\text{if}\, 0 \leq l \leq L_{ij},} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\, l > L_{ij}.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.26)

Then the RPM with discrete inputs and outputs is described by the following formulas:

  • for the time-varying parameters,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{q = 0}^{L^{*}}B}\lbrack k,q\rbrack\,\mathbf{x}\lbrack q\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k \geq L^{*};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.27)

  • for the constant parameters,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{q = 0}^{L^{*}}B}\lbrack q\rbrack\,\mathbf{x}\lbrack k - q\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k \geq L^{*}.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.28)

Here L* = maxij Lij.

In contrast to the linear RPMs with continuous input functions, in this case the parameters can be the ordinates of the corresponding pulse characteristics.

Example 3.3 Consider a one-dimensional RPM with discrete input and memory of capacity 2, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y}\lbrack k\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{q = 0}^{1}b_{1,1}}\lbrack q\rbrack\, x\lbrack k - q\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k \in \lbrack 1,10\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$

Write this representation as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y}\lbrack k\rbrack = a_{0}\, x\lbrack k\rbrack + a_{1}\, x\lbrack k - 1\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}a_{0} = b_{1,1}\lbrack 0\rbrack;\,\, a_{1} = b_{1,1}\lbrack 1\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$

The parameters a0 and a1 are random and take values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A}_{0} = \lbrack - 0.5,\, 2.5\rbrack\text{\quad\quad}\text{and}\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{A}_{1} = \lbrack - 1.0,\, 6.0\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$

The PDF of the parameters has the following form:

  • –for the dependent parameters,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {P(a_{0},a_{1}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\left( {- \frac{a_{0}^{2} + a_{1}^{2} - 2a_{0}\, a_{1}}{8}} \right)} & {\text{if}\,(a_{0},a_{1}) \in \mathcal{A}_{0} \times \mathcal{A}_{1},} \\ 0 & {\text{if}(a_{0},a_{1}) \in \mathcal{A}_{0} \times \mathcal{A}_{1};} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

  • –for the independent parameters,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {P(a_{0},a_{1}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\left( {- \frac{a_{0}^{2} + a_{1}^{2}}{8}} \right)} & {\text{if}\,(a_{0},a_{1}) \in \mathcal{A}_{0} \times \mathcal{A}_{1},} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\,(a_{0},a_{1}) \in \mathcal{A}_{0} \times \mathcal{A}_{1}.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

4.2.4Nonlinear dynamic models with power nonlinearities

Most of real objects are intrinsically nonlinear. A nonlinear object may demonstrate “almost” linear properties under a small variation of its input. An approach to describe the nonlinear properties of real objects in terms of the “Single Input–Ensemble Output” models is based on their approximation using functional power series. The elements of such series represent power functionals of different structure that depends on the nonlinear properties of an object and also on the properties of input functions. Particularly, if the object's nonlinearities are continuous functions and the object's input signals are continuous time-varying functions, then the RPM of such an object can be defined by a functional Volterra series [177, 184].

Consider a dynamic system that operates on a time interval 𝒯t = [0, t] and is characterized by a continuous functional ℬ(x(τ)) | τ∈𝒯t). Let the input vector x(τ) = {x1(τ),…,xn(τ)} be belonging to the space 𝒳𝒯T of continuous time-varying functions. According to [100, 146, 184, 185], the functional ℬ(x(τ)) (equivalently, the RPM output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t)$) can be represented as a convergent functional series, i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t)} & \left. = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}(\tau))\, \middle| \,\tau \in \mathcal{T}_{t}) = \right. \\ {= {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{\infty}{\int_{0}^{t}\cdots}}} & {{\int_{0}^{t}W^{(h)}}(t - \tau_{1},\ldots,t - \tau_{h}) \times} \\ {\times \mathbf{x}^{(h)}} & {(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{h})d\tau_{1}\cdots d\tau_{h}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.29)

Here x(h)(τ1, …, τh) denotes the vector composed of the lexicographically ordered products {xi1(τj1)⋯xin(τjh)}, where $(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}) \in \overline{1,n}$ and $(j_{1},\ldots,j_{h}) \in \overline{1,h}.$ The dimension of the vector x(h) is


$$\begin{array}{r} {l(n,h) = n^{h}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.30)

The matrix W(h)(t1, …, th) has dimensions (m × l(m, h)), and its elements are multidimensional weight functions (pulse characteristics) wkh(h)(t1, …, th), where $k_{h} = \overline{1,l(n,h)}$.

Figure 4.8 illustrates the structure of the functional series (4.28). The blocks ∏h in Fig. 4.8 indicate the lexicographical ordered products from the elements of the vector x of power h.

The weight functions contain random parameters a(h) of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a}^{(h)} \in \mathcal{A}^{(h)} = \left\{ \mathbf{a}_{-}^{(h)} \leq \mathbf{a}^{(h)} \leq \mathbf{a}_{+}^{(h)} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.31)

Since the parameters are random, they have a PDF Ph(a(h)) on corresponding intervals.

Example 3.4 Consider the quadratic dynamic system (4.2.4) with two inputs x(τ) = {x1(τ),x2(τ)} and two outputs $\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t) = \left\{ y_{1}(t),y_{2}(t) \right\},$ which are continuous functions. A relation between them is described by a continuous functional ℬ with random parameters, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t) = {\int_{0}^{t}W^{(1)}}(t - \tau)\mathbf{x}(\tau)d\tau + {\int_{0}^{t}\,}{\int_{0}^{t}W^{(2)}}(t - \tau_{1},t - \tau_{2})\mathbf{x}^{(2)}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Here


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{x}^{(2)}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) = \left\{ x_{1}(\tau_{1})x_{1}(\tau_{2}),x_{1}(\tau_{1})x_{2}(\tau_{2}),x_{1}(\tau_{2})x_{2}(\tau_{1}),x_{2}(\tau_{1})x_{2}(\tau_{2}) \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$

The matrices of the weight functions (pulse characteristics) have the following elements:

  • the linear block is characterized by the four weight functions


    $$\begin{array}{r} {w_{ij}^{(1)}(\tau) = A_{ij}\exp\left( {- \alpha_{ij}\tau} \right),\quad(i,j) = 1,2;} \\ \end{array}$$

  • the quadratic block is characterized by the eight two-dimensional weight functions


    $$\begin{array}{r} {w_{ij}^{(2)}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) = B_{ij}\exp\left( {- \gamma_{ij}\tau_{1} - \rho_{ij}\tau_{2}} \right),\text{\quad\quad}i = 1,2;\, j = 1,2,3,4.} \\ \end{array}$$

For obtaining the graphical representations of the random weight functions, consider some of them in the linear (w11(1)(τ), w22(1)(τ)) and nonlinear (w21(2)(τ1, τ2), w13(2)(τ1, τ2)) blocks.

The linear block has the constant parameters A22 = 1.0, α11 = 0.5 and also the random parameters A11 ∈ [ − 0.5, 0.5], α22 ∈ [ − 0.5, 1.0] with the uniform distribution on the corresponding intervals. The ensembles 𝒲11(1) and 𝒲22(1) are shown in Figs. 4.9(a) and 4.9(b).

The nonlinear block has the constant parameters γ21 = 0.5, B13 = 1.5 and also the random parameters B21 ∈ [0.5, 1.5], ρ21 ∈ [ − 0.5, 0.5], B13 = 1.5, γ13 ∈ [0.1, 0.8] and ρ13 ∈ [ − 0.5, 0.5]. The PDFs of all random parameters are uniform on the corresponding intervals. The random surface ensembles 𝒲21(2) and 𝒲13(2) are demonstrated in Figs. 4.10(a) and 4.10(b).

The functional ℬ (4.2.4) can be often written as a functional series with structured weight matrices (pulse characteristics). Under structuring we mean a sequence of linear dynamic and nonlinear static operations. The block diagram of an RPM in which each channel represents a serial connection of a linear dynamic block and a power nonlinearity is shown in Fig. 4.11(a). The output of this model is defined by the following modification of the functional Volterra series:


$$\begin{aligned} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t)} & \left. = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}(\tau))\, \middle| \,\tau \in \mathcal{T}_{t}) = \right. \\ & {= {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{\infty}\left( {{\int_{0}^{t}W^{(h)}}(t - \tau)\,\mathbf{x}(\tau)\, d\tau} \right)^{h}}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.32)

For the one-dimensional RPM, the last-mentioned equality takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y}(t) = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{\infty}{\int_{0}^{t}\cdots}}{\int_{0}^{t}{\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{h}\,}}\left( {w(t - \tau_{i})\, x(\tau_{i})d\tau_{i}} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.33)

The block diagram in Fig. 4.11(b) corresponds to an RPM with the inverse sequence of the linear and nonlinear operations in each channel: first the input undergoes a power transformation and then a dynamic linear transformation. The RPM output is described by another modification of the functional Volterra series:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t) = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{\infty}{\int_{0}^{t}W}}(t - \tau)\mathbf{x}^{(h)}(\tau)\, d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.34)

Here, the vector x(h)(τ) consists of the lexicographically ordered elements formed by all possible products of the elements of the vector x(τ).

Example 3.5 Consider a one-dimensional RPM with a structured quadratic nonlinearity of the following form:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\hat{y}}_{1}(t) = {\int_{0}^{t}{\int_{0}^{t}w_{1}^{(2)}}}(t - \tau_{1})\, w_{2}^{(2)}(t - \tau_{2})\, x_{1}(\tau_{1})\, x_{1}(\tau_{2})\, d\tau_{1}\, d\tau_{2}.} \\ \end{array}$$

In this case, the quadratic pulse characteristic is also structured—it represents the product of the pulse characteristics:


$$\begin{array}{r} {w^{(2)}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) = w_{1}^{(2)}(\tau_{1})\, w_{2}^{(2)}(\tau_{2}).} \\ \end{array}$$

The pulse characteristics have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {w_{1}^{(2)}(\tau) = A\exp( - \alpha\tau)\cos(\omega\tau);\quad w_{2}^{(2)}(\tau) = C\exp( - \beta\tau).} \\ \end{array}$$

Hence,


$$\begin{array}{r} {w^{(2)}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) = A\, C\,\exp( - \alpha\tau_{1} - \beta\tau_{2})\,\cos(\omega\tau_{2}).} \\ \end{array}$$

The constant parameters are AC = 2.0, whereas the random parameters α, β and ω obey the uniform distributions on the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\alpha \in \lbrack - 0.5,0.5\rbrack;\,\,\beta \in \lbrack 0.8,1.6\rbrack;\,\,\omega \in \lbrack 1,2\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$

The ensemble 𝒲(2) is shown in Fig. 4.12.

Consider an RPM with a finite memory K; the input and output of this model are measured at discrete times tk with step Δ. Letting k = [tk/Δ],


$$\begin{aligned} {\hat{\mathbf{y}}\lbrack k\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{\infty}{\sum\limits_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) = 0}^{K}W^{(h)}}}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,} & {n_{h}\rbrack\,\mathbf{x}^{(h)}\lbrack k - n_{1},\ldots,k - n_{h}\rbrack,} \\ {k \geq} & {K.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.35)

The vector x(h)[k − n1, …, k − nh] has the elements xi1[k − n1]⋯xin[k − nh], which are the lexicographically ordered all possible products of $(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}) = \overline{1,n}$ elements of the vector x at the times $(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) = \overline{0,K}.$ The dimension of the vector x(h)[k − n1, …, k − nh] is


$$\begin{array}{r} {l(n,h) = \frac{(n\, K + h - 1)!}{h!(n\, k - 1)!}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.36)

The parameter K defines the memory capacity of the RPM, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {W^{(h)}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {W^{(h)}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack} & {\text{if~all}\,(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) \leq K,} \\ 0 & {\text{if~at~least~one}\, n_{j} > K.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.37)

The elements of the matrix W(h)[n1, …, nh] are discrete random weight functions (pulse characteristics) $w_{i,k_{h}}^{(h)}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack,\,\, i = \overline{1,m};\,\, k_{h} = \overline{1,l(n,h)}.$ They reflect the dynamic and nonlinear properties of the RPM. Note that the nonlinear properties are formulated in terms of multidimensional functions (pulse characteristics), not in terms of structurally representable nonlinear elements.

The pulse characteristics wi, kh(h)[n1, …, nh] have the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {w_{i,k_{h}}^{(h)}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack \in \mathcal{W}_{i,k_{h}}^{(h)} = \left\lbrack {{\widetilde{w}}_{i,k_{h}}^{(h, - )}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack,\,{\widetilde{w}}_{i,k_{h}}^{(h, + )}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack} \right\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.38)

In this expression, w̃i, kh(h,  ± )[n1, …, nh] are given functions that describe the left and right limits of the above intervals. For example, they can be defined as the exponential functions


$$\begin{aligned} {{\widetilde{w}}_{i,k_{h}}^{(h, - )}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack} & {= {\prod\limits_{j = 1}^{h}\beta_{(i,k_{h})}^{(h, - )}}(j)\,\exp\left( {- \alpha_{(i,k_{h})}^{(h, - )}(j)\, n_{j}} \right),} \\ {{\widetilde{w}}_{i,k_{h}}^{(h, + )}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack} & {= {\prod\limits_{j = 1}^{h}\beta_{(i,k_{h})}^{(h, + )}}(j)\,\exp\left( {- \alpha_{(i,k_{h})}^{(h, + )}(j)\, n_{j}} \right).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.39)

A convenient approach is to treat their ordinates as the RPM parameters. This allows us to transform the nonlinear RPM to its linear analog of considerably higher dimension. The transformation procedure for the one-dimensional RPM (with one input and one output) is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y}\lbrack k\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{H}\sum\limits^{K}}(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) = 0w^{(h)}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack\,{\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{h}x}\lbrack k - n_{i}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k \geq K.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.40)

Introduce a lexicographical ordering of the variables {n1,…,nh} by reassigning numbers from 0 to th = (K + 1)h − 1 to the resulting sets. Then


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \left\{ n_{1},\ldots,n_{h} \right\}\rightarrow i^{(h)},\text{\quad\quad}i^{(h)} \in \lbrack 0,t_{h}\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.41)

In accordance with this numbering scheme, define the following indexes for the random parameters that correspond to the values of the pulse characteristics at the discrete times 0, 1, …, K:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. a_{i^{(h)}}^{(h)}\rightarrow w^{(h)}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}i^{(h)} \in \lbrack 0,t_{h}\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.42)

Construct a random vector


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a}(h) = \left\{ a_{0}^{(h)},\ldots,a_{t_{h}}^{(h)} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.43)

The elements of the vector a(h) —see (4.38)—take values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A}^{(h)}(i^{(h)}) = \left\lbrack {a_{-}^{(h)}(i^{(h)}),\, a_{+}^{(h)}(i^{(h)})} \right\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.44)

By analogy with (4.41), introduce a lexicographical ordering of the variables k − n1, …, k − nh, where k is a fixed parameter and the indexes n1, …, nh take values within the interval [0,K].

For each fixed k, renumber the resulting sets as follows:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \left\{ k - n_{1},\ldots,k - n_{h} \right\}\rightarrow(k,i^{(h)}). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.45)

Then the lexicographically ordered products of the variables x[k − n1], …, x[k − nh] with fixed k form the vector


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{x}^{(h)}\lbrack k\rbrack = \left\{ {x_{k,0}^{(h)},\ldots,x_{k,t_{h}}^{(h)}} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.46)

Consequently, the expression (4.40) can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y}\lbrack k\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{H}\left\langle \mathbf{a}^{(h)},\,\mathbf{x}^{(h)}\lbrack k\rbrack \right\rangle},} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.47)

where ⟨•, •⟩ denotes the scalar product of vectors ∙ and  • .

Consider a one-dimensional RPM with structured nonlinearities (see Fig. 4.11(a)) and the following discrete time-varying functions as its input:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y}\lbrack k\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{H}\left( {{\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{K}w^{(h)}}\lbrack n\rbrack x\lbrack k - n\rbrack} \right)^{h}},\text{\quad\quad}k \geq K.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.48)

The pulse characteristics w(h)[n] have a finite memory K and random parameters. Again, as the latter choose their ordinates, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {w^{(h)}\lbrack n\rbrack = a_{n}^{(h)},\quad n = \overline{0,K}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.49)

Construct the vector


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a}^{(h)} = \left\{ a_{0}^{(h)},\ldots,a_{K}^{(h)} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.50)

The parameters an(h) are random, independent, and take their values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(h)} = \lbrack - A_{n}^{(h)},\, A_{n}^{(h)}\rbrack,\quad A_{n}^{(h)} = \beta_{n}^{(h)}\exp( - \alpha_{n}^{(h)}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.51)

The PDFs $p_{n}^{(h)}(a_{n}^{(h)}),\,\, n = \overline{0,K},$ are defined on these intervals.

Get back to equality (4.48) and introduce the following notations:

  • the index set


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{I}_{h}(K) = \left\{ i_{n}:\,{\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{K}i_{n}} = h,\, i_{n} = \overline{0,K} \right\};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.52)

  • the vector


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{i} = \left\{ i_{0},\ldots,i_{K} \right\};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.53)

  • the function


    $$\begin{array}{r} {C_{(k,i_{n})}(x) = \frac{1}{i_{n}!}\, x^{i_{n}}\lbrack k - n\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.54)

Then formula (4.48) can be written as


$$\begin{aligned} {\hat{y}\lbrack k\rbrack} & {= {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{H}V_{k}^{(h)}}(\mathbf{a}^{(h)},x),} \\ {V_{k}^{(h)}(\mathbf{a}^{(h)},x)} & {= {\sum\limits_{\mathbf{i} \in \mathcal{I}_{h}(K)}\,}{\prod\limits_{n = 0}^{K}\,}C_{(k,i_{n})}(x)\,{\lbrack a_{n}^{(h)}\rbrack}^{i_{n}}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.55)

Hence, unlike the RPM (4.40), the model under consideration is nonlinear with power nonlinearities.

4.2.5Nonlinear dynamic models with polynomial nonlinearities

In machine learning problems, it is often necessary to deal with dynamic objects whose observable output has jumps at certain times or under certain values of its input. In other cases, there exists prior information about the object's properties that defines its structure as illustrated in Fig. 4.13(a) or Fig. 4.13(b). The nonlinear blocks in these diagrams are described by orthonormal polynomials of different classes (see Table 4.1).

Consider an RPM with the structure presented in Fig. 4.13(a). Using orthogonal polynomials gk(x), let us write this RPM in the following form:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \hat{y}(t) = {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{K}c_{k}}{\int_{0}^{t}w}(t - \tau\, \middle| \mathbf{b})\, g_{k}(x(\tau))d\tau, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.56)

where the coefficients c0, …, cK are independent random variables of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {c_{k} \in \mathcal{C}_{k} = \lbrack c_{k}^{-},c_{k}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{0,K}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.57)

The parameters b of the pulse characteristic w(t |b) are randomized and belong to the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B} = \lbrack\mathbf{b}^{-},\mathbf{b}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.58)

Example 3.6 Consider a nonlinear RPM (Fig. 4.13(a)) in which the randomized model of the nonlinear element is based on the four Hermite polynomials from Table 4.1, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {z(t) = c_{0} + c_{1}x(t) + c_{2}(x^{2} - 1) + c_{3}(x^{3}(t) - 3x(t)).} \\ \end{array}$$

The coefficients c0, c1, c2 and c3 are random, independent and take values within the interval 𝒞 = [c−, c+], where c− =  − 1 and c+ = 1. All the coefficients have the same PDF


$$\begin{array}{r} {f(c) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {A\exp( - c^{2})} & {\text{if}\, - 1 \leq c < 1,} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\, - 1 > c \geq 2.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

The normalization constant is A = 1.71. Then the joint PDF takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {F(c_{0},\ldots,c_{3}) = A^{4}\exp( - c_{0}^{2} - c_{1}^{2} - c_{2}^{2} - c_{3}^{2}).} \\ \end{array}$$

The pulse characteristic of the linear dynamic element is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {w(\tau) = \exp( - \alpha\tau),} \\ \end{array}$$

where α denotes a random parameter with the uniform distribution on the interval [ − 0.5, 0.5], i.e., its PDF has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {b(\alpha) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 1 & {\text{if}\, - 1 \leq \alpha < 1,} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\, - 1 > \alpha \geq 1.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

Therefore, the RPM is described by the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{y}(t) = {\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{3}c_{i}}{\int_{0}^{t}\exp}( - \alpha(t - \tau))\, H_{i}(x(\tau))d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$

Here Hi(x) stand for the Hermite polynomials, ci and α are the random parameters, and x(t) = 1. Figure 4.14 demonstrates the ensemble of all trajectories, as well as the mean and median trajectories, which match one another.

Now get back to the block diagram in Fig. 4.13(b). Obviously, the linear and nonlinear dynamic elements of the object have interchanged their places. The object's input is a function x(t). Let us construct the RPM of this object using the pulse characteristic with random parameters w(τ | b) for the linear element and a collection of orthogonal polynomials with random coefficients for the nonlinear element. Then the RPM can be written as


$$\begin{aligned} {\hat{y}(t) = \sum_{k = 1}^{K}\,\sum_{i = 0}^{k}} & \left. c_{k}a_{ki}\int_{0}^{t}\cdots\int_{0}^{t}w(t - \tau_{0} \middle| \mathbf{b})\cdots w(t - \tau_{i} \middle| \mathbf{b}) \times \right. \\ & {\times x(\tau_{0})\cdots x(\tau_{i})d\tau_{1}\cdots d\tau_{i}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.59)

In this equation, aki denote the coefficients of the orthonormal polynomials (see Table 4.1); c1, …, cK are the independent random coefficients of the randomized model of the nonlinear element. They are of the interval type (4.57).

Example 3.7 Consider a nonlinear RPM with the structure presented in Fig. 4.13(b), where the randomized model of the nonlinear element is given by the four Hermite polynomials (see Example 3.6). The pulse characteristic of the linear dynamic element is the same as in Example 3.6. The RPM output has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {y(t) = c_{0} + c_{1}{\int_{0}^{t}\exp}( - \alpha(t - \tau))x(\tau)d\tau +} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {+ c_{2}\left( {{\int_{0}^{t}{\int_{0}^{t}\exp}}( - \alpha(t - \tau_{1}))\exp( - \alpha(t - \tau_{2}))x(\tau_{1})x(\tau_{2})d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2} - 1} \right) +} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {+ c_{3}{\int_{0}^{t}{\int_{0}^{t}{\int_{0}^{t}\exp}}}( - \alpha(t - \tau_{1}))\exp( - \alpha(t - \tau_{2}))\exp( - \alpha(t - \tau_{3})) \times} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\times x(\tau_{1})x(\tau_{2})x(\tau_{3})d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}d\tau_{3} -} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {- 3c_{3}{\int_{0}^{t}\exp}( - \alpha(t - \tau))x(\tau)d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$

The ensemble of all trajectories, as well as the mean and median trajectories, are shown in Fig. 4.15.

If the input and output of this RPM is characterized by the lattice functions, then the following equations hold:

  • for the RPM in Fig. 4.13(a),


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \hat{y}\lbrack n\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{K}\,}{\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{k}c_{k}}a_{ki}{\sum\limits_{m = 0}^{n}w}\lbrack n - m\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b}\rbrack\, x^{i}\lbrack m\rbrack; \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.60)

  • for the RPM in Fig. 4.13(b),


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \hat{y}\lbrack n\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{K}{\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{k}c_{k}}}a_{ki}{\sum\limits_{(m_{0},\ldots,m_{i}) = 0}^{n}{\prod\limits_{j = 0}^{i}w}}\lbrack n - m_{j}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b}\rbrack\, x\lbrack m_{j}\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.61)

In these formulas, the coefficients ck are the independent random variables distributed on the corresponding intervals (4.57) in accordance with the given PDFs. The parameters b1, …, bs of the pulse characteristic are also random, independent and take values within the corresponding intervals with the given PDF.

4.2.6Randomized neural networks

Neural networks are a kind of parameterized models used in machine learning procedures. A structural foundation of a neural network is the Kolmogorov theorem [94], which states that a continuous function of n variables on the nonnegative unit cube can be written as the superposition of one-variable functions with summation:


$$\begin{array}{r} {f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{(2n + 1)}h_{k}}\left( {{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\phi_{ik}}(x_{i})} \right);} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.62)

here the variables h1, …, h2n + 1 depend on the function f, whereas the functions ϕik(xi) do not. This theorem claims the existence of such a representation but gives no technical details to find it.

On the one hand, the universalism of neural networks can be explained by a structural analogy with the Kolmogorov theorem; on the other, by a simplified (statistical) analogy with operation of a biological neuron [122]. The general structure of the neuron's statistical model is illustrated in Fig. 4.16(a). It consists of three serially connected blocks, namely, synaptic coefficients w = {w1,…,wn}, an adder and a nonlinear transformation block with an activation function ϕ(u, b), where b are the activation function parameters. Figure 4.16(b) shows an example of this model, in which the nonlinear transformation block has an activation function ϕ(u, Δ) with a threshold Δ. In the general case, the activation function ϕ(u) may contain several parameters, further denoted by b1, …, bq. Besides the function ϕ(u) in Fig. 4.16(b), the following activation functions are widespread:

  • —the linear activation function (see Fig. 4.17(a))


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(u) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 0 & {\text{if}\, u \leq \Delta,} \\ u & {\text{if}\, u \geq \Delta;} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.63)

  • —the sigmoidal activation function (see Fig. 4.17(b))


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(u) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(u - \Delta)};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.64)

  • —the tangent activation function (see Fig. 4.17(c))


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(u) = \tan(u).} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.65)

A network with the structure presented in Fig. 4.16(b) is called a single-layer neural network. A serial connection of single-layer neural networks yields a multilayer neural network. Its internal layers are called hidden whereas the last one is called the output layer. Most applications involve one hidden layer, as illustrated in Fig. 4.18. The input layer has a set of synaptic coefficients w11, …wnh; the hidden layer, g11, …, ghs.

Thus, single- and multilayer neural networks (Figs. 4.16 and 4.18) are statistical systems, i.e., the network's input at a current time theoretically depends on its input at this time. For example, the output of a single-layer neural network has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {y(t) = S\left( \mathbf{x}(t)\, \middle| \,\mathbf{w},\mathbf{b} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.66)

where w and b are network parameters.

By assumption, a randomized neural network incorporates random parameters that take values within given intervals, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{W} = \lbrack\mathbf{w}^{-},\mathbf{w}^{+}\rbrack;\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B} = \lbrack\mathbf{b}^{-},\mathbf{b}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.67)

The probabilistic properties of the parameters on these intervals are characterized by probability density functions Pw(w) and Pb(b). The output of a randomized neural network represents an ensemble of the values of the random variable y.

Example 3.7 Consider a randomized neural network with the structure shown in Fig. 4.16 and the sigmoidal activation function. The equations of this network have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {u = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{3}w_{i}}x_{i},\text{\quad\quad}y = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(u - \Delta)},} \\ \end{array}$$

where Δ = 0.5 and the coefficients wi ∈ [ − 0.5, 1.5] are random and independent with the PDF


$$\begin{array}{r} {P_{w}(\mathbf{w}) = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{3}p_{w}}(w_{i}),} \\ \end{array}$$

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {p_{w}(w_{i}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} & {\text{for}\, - 0.5 \geq w_{i} \leq 1.5,} \\ 0 & {\text{for}\, - 0.5 \leq w_{i} \geq 1.5.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

A probability density of the output of the network generated in the course of 1000 Monte Carlo simulations with the PDF Pw(w) can be observed in Fig. 4.19. For this ensemble, the mean value and variance are m = 0.55094 and σ = 0.053719.

4.3“(Single Input, Feedback)–Ensemble Output” Dynamic Randomized Parametric Model

4.3.1Definition and structure

For a structural design of many dynamic RPMs, it is insufficient to define an input-output relation. In such cases, we have to reflect some internal mechanisms of the processes or objects under modeling. A mathematical framework that can be used to describe these mechanisms involves different classes of equations. Their general structure is represented by a certain block with a parameterized mapping 𝔾 and a feedback loop characterized by a parameterized mapping ℂ, see Fig. 4.20.

In this figure, x ∈ Rn denotes the model input; y ∈ Rm is the model output; finally, z ∈ Rd gives the feedback block output.

The mappings 𝔾 and ℂ describe the internal mechanisms of the processes running in an object. Using a functional description for these mappings, introduce the following notations:


$$\begin{aligned} \mathbb{G} & {= \mathcal{G}\left( \mathbf{x}(\tau),\mathbf{z}(\tau),\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a};\,\tau \in \mathcal{T} \right),} \\ {\mathbb{C}} & {= \mathcal{C}\left( \mathbf{y}(\tau),\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c};\,\tau \in \mathcal{T} \right).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.68)

The functionals 𝒢 and 𝒞 contain random parameters a ∈ Rr and c ∈ Rh, respectively, with independent elements that belong to the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} = \lbrack\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{a}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{c} \in \mathcal{S} = \lbrack\mathbf{c}_{-},\mathbf{c}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.69)

Consequently, the [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM can be written as
