$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{y}(t)} & {= \mathcal{G}\left( \mathbf{x}(\tau),\mathbf{z}(\tau)),\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a};\,\tau \in \mathcal{T} \right),} \\ {\mathbf{z}(t)} & {= \mathcal{C}\left( \mathbf{y}(\tau),\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c};\, \middle| \,\tau \in \mathcal{T} \right).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.70)

The functionals in these equations may have different mathematical models, depending on the declared properties of objects under analysis.

4.3.2Linear dynamic models

The linear [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM have the structure illustrated in Fig. 4.20, except for its blocks are described by linear functionals 𝒢 and 𝒞 with random parameters. Assume that the input vector consists of continuous time-varying functions and the parameters are time-invariable. Then the integral form of the linear [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM can be written as


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{y}(t)} & \left. = {\int_{\mathcal{T}}G}(t - \tau\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})\,\mathbf{x}(\tau)\, d\tau + {\int_{\mathcal{T}}F}(t - \tau\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b})\,\mathbf{z}(\tau)\, d\tau, \right. \\ {\mathbf{z}(t)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{T}}C}(t - \tau)\,\mathbf{y}(\tau)\, d\tau.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.71)

Recall that these equalities involve vectors x ∈ Rn, y ∈ Rm and z ∈ Rd, as well as the matrices $\left. G(t\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}) = \lbrack g_{ij}(t\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}),\, i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,n}\rbrack;\, F(t\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b}) = \lbrack f_{il}(t\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b}),\, i = \overline{1,m}\rbrack,\, l = \overline{1,d};\, C(t\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b}) = \lbrack c_{h,k}(t\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}),\, h = \overline{1,d},\, k = \overline{1,m}\rbrack. \right.$ As their elements the matrices contain the pulse characteristics gij(t | a), fil(t | b) and ch, k(t | c) with random parameters described by the vectors a, b and c; the elements of these vectors are independent and take values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} = \lbrack\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{a}^{+}\rbrack,\quad\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B} = \lbrack\mathbf{b}^{-},\mathbf{b}^{+}\rbrack,\quad\mathbf{c} \in \mathcal{C} = \lbrack\mathbf{c}^{-},\mathbf{c}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.72)

The [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM can be transformed into the [SI–EO] RPM. In our case, a most convenient approach is to employ the Fourier transform. First, eliminate the vector z in (4.71) to get the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{y} = {\int_{\mathcal{T}}G}(t - \tau\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})\,\mathbf{x}(\tau)\, d\tau + {\int_{\mathcal{T}}F}(t - \tau\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b})\,{\int_{\mathcal{T}_{\tau}}C}(t - \lambda\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})\,\mathbf{y}(\lambda)\, d\tau d\lambda. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.73)

Using the Fourier transform [43], write the solution of this equation in the frequency domain (i.e., in terms of image functions):


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. \mathbf{Y}(s) = K(s\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})\,\mathbf{X}(s), \right. \\ & \left. K(s\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}) = \left( I - F(s\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b})C(s\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}) \right)^{( - 1)}G(s\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}). \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.74)

Here s = α + ιω and $\iota = \sqrt{- 1},$ whereas α and ω are real variables. Transition from the frequency domain to the time domain yields the following integral equation for an equivalent [SI–EO] RPM:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{y}(t) = {\int_{\mathcal{T}}K}(t - \tau\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})\,\mathbf{x}(\tau)\, d\tau, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.75)

where the matrix


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. K(t\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}) = \mathcal{L}^{( - 1)}\left\{ K(s\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}) \right\}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.76)

Example 3.8 Consider a one-dimensional [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM with the structure shown in Fig. 4.20:


$$\begin{array}{r} {y(t) = {\int_{0}^{t}\exp}( - \lambda(t - \tau))(x(\tau) - z(\tau))\, d\tau -} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {- {\int_{0}^{t}\exp}( - \lambda(t - \tau))\left( {{\int_{0}^{\tau}\exp}( - \alpha(\tau - \mu))\, y(\mu)\, d\mu} \right)d\tau.} \\ \end{array}$$

The parameters λ and μ are random, independent, and belong to the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\lambda \in \lbrack - 1,2\rbrack,\quad\mu \in \lbrack 0.1,0.5\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$

The PDFs of these parameters have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {p(\lambda) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {1/3} & {\text{if}\, - 1 \leq \lambda < 2,} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\, - 1 \geq \lambda \geq 2,} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.\text{,}\quad u(\mu) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} 0.25 & {\text{if}\, 0.1 \geq \mu < 0.5,} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\, 0.1 \leq \mu \geq 0.5.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$

Consider the differential form of the linear [(SI,FB)–EO] RPMs. Introduce the following notations: x(t) = {x1(t),…,xn} as the input vector; z(t) = {z1(t),…,zd} as the state vector; y(t) = {y1(t),…,ym(t)} as the output vector; $\left. A = \lbrack a_{i}j\, \middle| \,(i,j) = \overline{1,d}\rbrack \right.$ as a transition matrix; $\left. B = \lbrack b_{kl}\, \middle| \, k = \overline{1,d},l = \overline{1,n}\rbrack \right.$ as the input matrix; finally, $\left. C = \lbrack c_{ht}\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,m},t = \overline{1,d}. \right.$ The elements of these matrices are independent random variables that take values within the intervals


$$\begin{aligned} a_{ij} & {\in \mathcal{A}_{ij} = \lbrack a_{ij}^{-},a_{ij}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}(i,j) = \overline{1,d};} \\ b_{kl} & {\in \mathcal{B}_{kl} = \lbrack b_{kl}^{-},b_{kl}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,d},\, l = \overline{1,n};} \\ c_{ht} & {\in \mathcal{C}_{ht} = \lbrack c_{ht}^{-},c_{ht}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}h = \overline{1,m},\, t = \overline{1,d}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.77)

Due to independence, perform the direct product of these intervals for defining the matrix intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A} = \lbrack\mathcal{A}^{-},\mathcal{A}^{+}\rbrack,\quad\mathcal{B} = \lbrack\mathcal{B}^{-},\mathcal{B}^{+}\rbrack,\quad\mathcal{C} = \lbrack\mathcal{C}^{-},\mathcal{C}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.78)

As a result, the differential form of the linear [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM is given by


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d\mathbf{z}(t)}{dt} & {= A\mathbf{z}(t) + B\mathbf{x}(t),\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z}(0) = \mathbf{z}^{0},} \\ {\mathbf{y}(t)} & {= C\,\mathbf{z}(t),} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.79)

where the matrices A,B, and C have random elements of the interval type (4.78).

The linear [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM can be written in the input–output representation using the fundamental solution matrix[85]


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. W(A \middle| t - \tau) = \exp\lbrack A(t - \tau)\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.80)

In this case,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{y}(t) = CW(A \middle| t)\mathbf{z}^{0} + C{\int_{0}^{t}W}(A \middle| t - \tau)B\mathbf{x}(\tau)d\tau. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.81)

Let the input, output and feedback vectors consist of the lattice functions x[s], z[s] and y[s], respectively, and also let the matrices G,F and C consist of the corresponding lattice pulse characteristics $\left. g_{ij}\lbrack s\rbrack,\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,n},\, j = \overline{1,m};\, f_{il}\lbrack s\rbrack,\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,n},\, l = \overline{1,d};\, c_{hk}\lbrack m\rbrack,\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,d},\, k = \overline{1,m}. \right.$ In addition, assume that the input functions have discrete time, i.e., are lattice functions. Under all these hypotheses, the integral form (4.71) can be transformed into the additive one, i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{y}\lbrack s\rbrack} & \left. = {\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{s}G}\lbrack t,\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}\rbrack\,\mathbf{x}\lbrack s - t\rbrack + {\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{s}F}\lbrack t,\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b}\rbrack\,\mathbf{z}\lbrack s - t\rbrack, \right. \\ {\mathbf{z}\lbrack s\rbrack} & \left. = {\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{s}C}\lbrack t,\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}\rbrack\,\mathbf{y}\lbrack s - t\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.82)

As a rule, the lattice pulse characteristics have finite memory: they are nonzero if s ∈ [0, M]. In this case, equations (4.82) take the following form:


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{y}\lbrack s\rbrack} & \left. = {\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{M}G}\lbrack t,\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}\rbrack\,\mathbf{x}\lbrack s - t\rbrack + {\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{M}F}\lbrack t,\, \middle| \,\mathbf{b}\rbrack\,\mathbf{z}\lbrack s - t\rbrack, \right. \\ {\mathbf{z}\lbrack s\rbrack} & \left. = {\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{M}C}\lbrack t,\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}\rbrack\,\mathbf{y}\lbrack s - t\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}s \geq M. \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.83)

4.3.3Nonlinear dynamic models with power nonlinearities

Consider an object whose [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM has the structure shown in Fig. 4.20. Let the functionals 𝒢 and 𝒞 be continuous. Then they can be represented using the framework of functional Volterra series [184]; see Section 3.1.

This framework will be adopted for the one-dimensional [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM (Fig. 4.20), which is described by the system of equations


$$\begin{aligned} {y(t)} & {= \mathcal{G}\left( \varepsilon(\tau)),\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a};\,\tau \in \mathcal{T} \right),} \\ {z(t)} & {= \mathcal{C}\left( y(\tau),\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c};\, \middle| \,\tau \in \mathcal{T} \right),} \\ {\varepsilon(t)} & {= x(t) - z(t).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.84)

Assume that the time-varying functions x(t), z(t), and y(t), as well as the functionals 𝒢(ε, | a) and 𝒞(y, | c), are continuous. In this case, they can be expressed as the functional series with the corresponding weight functions (pulse characteristics), i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} {y(t) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{\infty}{\int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}\cdots}}} & \left. {\int_{\tau_{i} \in \mathcal{T}}\,}g_{i}(t - \tau_{1},\ldots,t - \tau_{i}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}^{(i)}) \times \right. \\ {\varepsilon(\tau_{1})} & {\cdots\varepsilon(\tau_{i})\, d\tau_{1}\cdots d\tau_{i},} \\ {z(t) = {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{\infty}{\int_{\lambda_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}\cdots}}} & \left. {\int_{\lambda_{j} \in \mathcal{T}}\,}c_{j}(t - \lambda_{1},\ldots,t - \lambda_{j}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}^{(j)}) \times \right. \\ {\times y(\lambda_{1})} & {\cdots y(\lambda_{j})\, d\lambda_{1}\cdots d\lambda_{j},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.85)


$$\begin{array}{r} {\varepsilon(t) = x(t) - z(t).} \\ \end{array}$$

Here the pulse characteristics have random parameters, namely, the random independent vectors a(i) and c(j) with independent elements taking values within the intervals


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{a}^{(i)} \in \mathcal{A}^{(i)}} & {= \lbrack\mathbf{a}_{-}^{(i)},\,\mathbf{a}_{+}^{(i)}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}i \in \lbrack 1,\infty),} \\ {\mathbf{c}^{(j)} \in \mathcal{S}^{(j)}} & {= \lbrack\mathbf{c}_{-}^{(j)},\,\mathbf{c}_{+}^{(j)}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}j \in \lbrack 1,\infty).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.86)

As a matter of fact, there exists a certain relation between the [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM (4.3.3) and the [SI–EO] RPM (4.2.4) with continuous nonlinearities. Recall that the latter model is described by a continuous functional ℬ, which can be also written as a functional Volterra series, i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{y}(t)} & \left. = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}(\tau),\, \middle| \,\tau \in \mathcal{T}) = \right. \\ {+ {\sum\limits_{k}^{\infty}{\int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}\cdots}}} & {{\int_{\tau_{k} \in \mathcal{T}}\,}w_{k}(t - \tau_{1},\ldots,t - \tau_{k}) \times} \\ \times & {x(\tau_{1})\cdots x(\tau_{k})\, d\overline{\tau}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.87)

Define the pulse characteristics in this formula so that equations (4.3.3) turn into identities [146]. First, substitute the last-mentioned equation into the first one to obtain an integral equation in the variable y(t):


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. y(t) = {\int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}g_{1}}(t - \tau_{1}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})\lbrack x(\tau_{1}) - {\int_{\lambda_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}\,}c_{1}(\tau_{1} - \lambda_{1}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})\, y(\lambda_{1})\, d\lambda_{1} + \right. \\ & \left. \quad + {\int_{\lambda_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}{\int_{\lambda_{2} \in \mathcal{T}}\,}}c_{2}(t - \lambda_{1},t - \lambda_{2}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})\, y(\lambda_{1})y(\lambda_{2})\, d\lambda_{1}d\lambda_{2} + \ldots \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.88)

Then construct the solution in the form of the functional series (4.3.3): substitute it into the left- and right-hand sides of equation (4.3.3), collecting and comparing the terms with the same powers of the variable x. These manipulations lead to the following system of integral equations for the cores wk(τ1,…,τk)=wk(τ1,…,τk | a,c) of (4.3.3):


$$\begin{aligned} \left. {\int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}w_{1}}(t - \tau_{1}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) \right. & \left. x(\tau_{1})\, d\tau_{1} = {\int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}g_{1}}(t - \tau_{1}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})\,\lbrack x(\tau_{1})\, d\tau_{1} - \right. \\ {- {\int_{\lambda_{1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\tau_{1}}}\,}c_{1}(\tau_{1}} & \left. - \lambda_{1}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})\,{\int_{\mu_{1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\lambda_{1}}}\,}w_{1}(\lambda_{1} - \mu_{1}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) \times \right. \\ & {\times x(\mu_{1})\, d\tau_{1}d\lambda_{1}d\mu_{1},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.89)


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. \int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}\int_{\tau_{2} \in \mathcal{T}}\, w_{2}(t - \tau_{1},t - \tau_{2}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c})\, x(\tau_{1})x(\tau_{2})\, d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2} = \right. \\ {- \int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}} & \left. g_{1}(t - \tau_{1} - \tau_{2}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})\int_{\lambda_{1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\tau_{1}}}\int_{\lambda_{2} \in \mathcal{T}_{\tau_{2}}}\, c_{2}(\tau_{1} - \lambda_{1},\tau_{2} - \lambda_{2}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}) \times \right. \\ \times & \left. \int_{\mu_{1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\lambda_{1}}}\int_{\mu_{2} \in \mathcal{T}_{\lambda_{2}}}\, w_{1}(\lambda_{1} - \mu_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c})w_{1}(\lambda_{2} - \mu_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) \times \right. \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad} \times x(\mu_{1})x(\mu_{2})\, d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}d\lambda_{1}d\lambda_{2}d\mu_{1}d\mu_{2} -} \\ & \left. \text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad} - \int_{\tau_{1} \in \mathcal{T}}\int_{\tau_{2} \in \mathcal{T}}\, g_{2}(t - \tau_{1},t - \tau_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}) \times \right. \\ & \left. \text{\quad\quad} \times \int_{\lambda_{1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\tau_{1}}}\int_{\lambda_{2} \in \mathcal{T}_{\tau_{2}}}c_{1}(\tau_{1} - \lambda_{1})c_{1}(\tau_{2} - \lambda_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})\, \times \right. \\ & \left. \text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad} \times \int_{\mu_{1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\lambda_{1}}}\int_{\mu_{2} \in \mathcal{T}_{\lambda_{2}}}\, w_{1}(\lambda_{1} - \mu_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) \times \right. \\ & \left. \text{\quad\quad}w_{1}(\lambda_{2} - \mu_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c})\, d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}d\lambda_{1}d\lambda_{2}d\mu_{1}d\mu_{2},\cdots. \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$

This system consists of homogeneous (with respect to the powers of x) integral equations with a recursive structure. Using the multidimensional Fourier transform (see the details in [42, 178]), write the final expressions


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. \text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}W(s_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) = \frac{\left. G_{1}(s_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}) \right.}{\left. 1 + G_{1}(s_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})C(s_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}) \right.}, \right. \\ & \left. \text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}W(s_{1},s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) = \right. \\ & {\quad = \frac{\left. - G_{1}(s_{1} + s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})\, C_{2}(s_{1},s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})\, W_{1}(s_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c})W_{1}(s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) \right.}{\left. 1 + .G_{1}(s_{1} + s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})C_{1}(s_{1} + s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{c}) \right.} +} \\ & {+ \frac{\left. G_{2}(s_{1},s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})W_{1}(s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c})\lbrack C_{1}(s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})W_{1}(s_{1}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}) - 2C_{1}(s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{c})\rbrack \right.}{\left. 1 + G_{1}(s_{1} + s_{2}, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})C_{1}(s_{1} + s_{2}), \middle| \,\mathbf{c} \right.},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\cdots} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.90)

Here s1, …, si are the complex parameters of the multidimensional Fourier transform.

Therefore, the [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM (4.3.3) can be written as the [SI–EO] RPM (4.2.4). This transformation may be fruitful in machine learning problems for randomized dynamic regression models.

4.3.4Nonlinear dynamic models with polynomial nonlinearities

In the previous subsection, we have studied the procedure of using the orthogonal polynomials in the [SI–EO] RPMs. Now consider this procedure subject to the [(SI,FB)–EO] RPMs. For the [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM with the structure shown in Fig. 4.21(a),


$$\begin{aligned} {y(t)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{T}}w}(t - \tau)\,{\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{K}w_{k}}g_{k}(\varepsilon(\tau))\, d\tau,} \\ {z(t)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{T}}c}(t - \tau)\,{\sum\limits_{m = 0}^{M}v_{m}}c_{m}(y(\tau))\, d\tau,} \\ {\varepsilon(t)} & {= x(t) - z(t).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.91)

Another [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM (see Fig. 4.21(b)) is described by the following system of equations:


$$\begin{aligned} {y(t)} & {= {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{K}w_{k}}g_{k}(u(\tau))\, d\tau,} \\ {u(t)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{T}}w}(t - \tau)\,\varepsilon(\tau)\, d\tau,} \\ {e(t)} & {= {\int_{\mathcal{T}}c}(t - \tau)\, y(\tau)\, d\tau,} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.92)


$$\begin{aligned} {z(t)} & {= {\sum\limits_{m = 0}^{M}v_{m}}c_{m}(e(\tau))\, d\tau,} \\ {\varepsilon(t)} & {= x(t) - z(t).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.93)

The parameters of these RPMs, w and v, are random, independent and take values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{W} = \lbrack\mathbf{w}^{-},\mathbf{w}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{V} = \lbrack\mathbf{v}^{-},\mathbf{v}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.94)

Recall that the orthogonal polynomials can be applied for approximating the continuous nonlinear functions and, moreover, the discontinuous nonlinearities, which forms their distinctive feature. However, the orthogonal property of the polynomials holds only on a certain set (the domain of definition) and in a certain functional space.

The usage procedure of the orthogonal polynomials from Section 3.2 is naturally extended to the [(SI,FB)–EO] RPMs.

Example 3.9 Consider the [(SI,FB)–EO] RPM with the block diagram shown in Fig. 4.22(a). The corresponding equations have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {y(t) = {\int_{0}^{t}w}(t - \tau)\phi(\varepsilon(\tau))d\tau,} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {z(t) = \psi\left( {{\int_{0}^{t}c}(t - \tau)y(\tau)d\tau} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\varepsilon(t) = x(t) - z(t).} \\ \end{array}$$

The nonlinear elements of this model are described by the Hermite polynomials


$$\begin{array}{r} {H_{1}(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon,\text{\quad\quad}H_{3}(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon^{3} - 3\varepsilon,} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi(\varepsilon) = w_{1}H_{1}(\varepsilon) + w_{3}H_{3}(\varepsilon),\quad\psi(e) = v_{1}H_{1}(e) + v_{3}H_{3}(e).} \\ \end{array}$$

The coefficients w1, w3, v1 and v3, acting as parameters, represent independent random variables distributed on the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {w_{1} \in \lbrack - 1,1\rbrack,\, w_{3} \in \lbrack - 0.1,0.1\rbrack,\quad v_{1} \in \lbrack - 2,2\rbrack,\, v_{3} \in \lbrack - 1,1\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$

Their PDFs are uniform on the corresponding intervals. The properties of the dynamic elements are reflected by the pulse characteristics


$$\begin{array}{r} {w(\tau) = \exp( - 0.5\tau)\cos(2\tau),\text{\quad\quad}c(\tau) = \tau\exp( - 0.5\tau).} \\ \end{array}$$

The input function has the form x(t) = 2sin (2t).

The ensemble of all trajectories, as well as the mean and median trajectories and the variance pipe, are shown in Fig. 4.22(b).

4.4Probabilistic Characteristics of Randomized Parameters and Ensembles

The models used in the RML procedures have realizations of randomized parameters, which generate the ensembles of random objects (vectors, trajectories, events) at the output of these models. The properties of both are described in terms of appropriate probabilistic characteristics.

1. Probabilistic characteristics of randomized parameters

The RPMs under study involve randomized interval-type parameters with desired probabilistic properties. We will discriminate between

  • the original parameters a = {a1,…,an}, which take values within the n-dimensional parallelepiped 𝒜 with arbitrary-size faces, i.e.,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A} = \lbrack\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{a}^{+}\rbrack = \otimes_{i = 1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i} = \lbrack a_{i}^{-},a_{i}^{+}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\text{and}} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.95)

  • the relative nonnegative parameters u = {u1,…,un}, which take values within the n-dimensional nonnegative parallelepiped 𝒰 with the unit faces, i.e.,


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{U} = \lbrack\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (4.96)

The relative nonnegative parameters are related to the original ones by


$$\begin{aligned} a_{i} & {= a_{i}^{-} + u_{i}\delta_{i},\quad\delta_{i} = a_{i}^{+} - a_{i}^{-},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,n},} \\ \mathbf{a} & {= \mathbf{a}^{-} + \Delta\mathbf{u},\text{\quad\quad}\Delta = \text{diag}\lbrack(a_{i}^{+} - a_{i}^{-})\,,\, i = \overline{1,n}\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(4.97)

The model parameters of these types undergo randomization in accordance with the desired probabilistic characteristics, more specifically, in accordance with the PDFs, P(a) for the original parameters a and W(u) for the relative nonnegative parameters u. In the general case, the elements of the vectors a and u can be related to each other. Their PDFs represent multivariable functions of general form. If the parameters are independent, then the corresponding PDFs have the multiplicative structure:


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(\mathbf{a}) = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}P_{i}}(a_{i}),\text{\quad\quad}W(\mathbf{u}) = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}w_{i}}(u_{i}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.98)

For making presentation compact, let us introduce the following terminological abbreviations:

  • RPM-Orig for the randomized parametric models with the original parameters a and the PDF P(a);

  • RPM-Rel for the randomized parametric models with the relative nonnegative parameters u and the PDF W(u).

2. Empirical probabilistic characteristics of ensembles

The randomized models output the ensembles of random vectors (static models), the ensembles of time-varying functions, i.e., trajectories (dynamic models), or the ensembles of random events. For each model, these ensembles appear as the result of generating its the randomized parameters. The ensembles can be described in quantitative terms using the well-known probabilistic characteristics of mathematical statistics.

Consider an arbitrary ensemble ${\hat{\mathcal{Y}}}_{T}$ of trajectories ŷ(t) on a finite time interval 𝒯 = [0, T], that is, generated by the one-dimensional RPM-Orig model with a given PDF. An example of such an ensemble is presented in Fig. 4.23. Assume that it contains N trajectories. Denote by ŷ(t*) its cutset under a fixed value t = t*. This cutset forms a collection of values (realizations) of the random variable ŷ(t*), which will be used for empirical estimation.

A) The evolution of mean trajectory. The mean value of the random variable ŷ(t*) is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\overline{y}(t^{*}) = \frac{1}{N}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{N}{\hat{y}}^{(k)}}(t^{*}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.99)

where ŷ(k)(t*) denote the realizations of the random variable ŷ(t*).

Calculating these means for different times t* ∈ 𝒯, we obtain a collection of empirical estimates $\overline{y}(t_{u}^{*}),\, u \in \overline{1,U}.$ They can be approximated using a continuous curve $\overline{y}(t),$ which forms the mean trajectory [104].

B) The evolution of the empirical variance pipe. Take the ensemble ${\hat{\mathcal{Y}}}_{T}$ illustrated in Fig. 4.23, and consider its cutset ŷ(t*). Define the random variable


$$\begin{array}{r} {D(t^{*}) = {\lbrack\hat{y}(t^{*}) - \overline{y}(t^{*})\rbrack}^{2}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.100)

The mean of this random variable (i.e., the variance of the random variable ŷ(t*)) is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\overline{D}(t^{*}) = \frac{1}{N - 1}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{N}D^{(k)}}(t^{*}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.101)

where D(k)(t*) denote the realizations of the random variable D(t*) (4.100).

Introduce the standard deviation of the random variable ŷ(t*) from its mean $\overline{y}(t^{*})$:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sigma(t^{*}) = \sqrt{\overline{D}(t^{*})}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.102)

Under an assumption that t* takes values within the interval 𝒯, let us approximate the resulting points using a continuous curve—the standard deviation trajectory σ(t).

Define two trajectories, $\delta_{\pm} = \overline{y}(t) \pm \sigma(t).$ The domain


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{D} = \left\{ \hat{y}:\delta_{-}(t) \leq \hat{y}(t) \leq \delta_{+}(t) \right\}} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.103)

will be called the standard deviation pipe. Figure 4.23 demonstrates the standard deviation pipe 𝒟 about the mean trajectory $\overline{y}(t).$

C) The evolution of the empirical probability density function. The empirical estimates of the PDFs can be constructed using the random variable realizations ŷ(t*) at a fixed time t*.

The empirical PDF, i.e., the histogram p[ŷ(t*)], is constructed in accordance with the well-known rules [104]. Denote by ŷ−(t*) and ŷ+(t*) the left and right limits, respectively, for the random variable ŷ(t*). Next, divide the interval [ŷ−(t*), ŷ+(t*)] into J subintervals $\eta_{j},\,(j = \overline{1,J})$ of the length (ŷ+(t*) − ŷ−(t*))/J. The empirical probability density function is the frequency with which the values of the random variable ŷ(t*) get into the subinterval $\eta_{j},\,(j = \overline{1,J}),$ i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {p_{j} = \frac{M_{j}}{M},} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.104)

where Mj gives the number of values ŷ(t*) within the subinterval ηj and M is the total number of trajectories in the ensemble. Figure 4.24 provides an example of the histogram p[ŷ(t*)]. The evolution of the histogram can be observed by varying the time t*. As a rule, an ensemble contains very many trajectories. Therefore, the histogram can be approximated with good accuracy using a continuous curve P̂[ŷ(t*)].

D). The evolution of the empirical median trajectory. Often the empirical PDF has no symmetry. In such cases, the median trajectory seems to be more informative. Consider the PDF P̂[ŷ(t*)], and define a value z(t*) such that


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{{\hat{y}}^{-}(t^{*})}^{z(t^{*})}\hat{P}}(x)dx = {\int_{z(t^{*})}^{{\hat{y}}^{-}(t^{*})}\hat{P}}(x)dx.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.105)

The value z(t*) of the random variable ŷ(t*) is called the median for the time t*. Performing these calculations for all t* ∈ 𝒯, obtain a continuous curve, which will be called the median trajectory of the ensemble.

E). The evolution of the α-quantiles of the empirical PDF. For a fixed time t*, introduce the empirical probability density function


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\hat{F}}_{t^{*}}(y) = {\int_{{\hat{y}}^{-}(t^{*})}^{y}{\hat{P}}_{t^{*}}}(v)dv.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.106)

According to the definition given in [104], the αt*-quantile (αt* ∈ [0, 1]) of the distribution F̂t*(y) of a random variable y is the number yαt* satisfying the inequalities


$$\begin{array}{r} {Pb\left\{ y \leq y_{\alpha_{t^{*}}} \right\} \leq \alpha_{t^{*}}} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.107)

and


$$\begin{array}{r} {Pb\left\{ y > y_{\alpha_{t^{*}}} \right\} \leq 1 - \alpha_{t^{*}},} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.108)

where Pb denotes probability. The αt*-quantile is illustrated in Fig. 4.25(b). By analogy with items A)–C), consider different cutsets t* ∈ 𝒯 of the ensemble to get the αt-quantile trajectory, see Fig. 4.25(b).

F). The evolution of the empirical confidence intervals and confidence levels. The αt*-quantile allows us to define an interval (known as the confidence interval) that covers the values of the random variable ŷ(t*) with the probability αt* (the confidence level).

By definition, the confidence interval


$$\begin{array}{r} {C_{t^{*}} = \lbrack y_{1 - \alpha_{t^{*}}/2},y_{1 + \alpha_{t^{*}}/2}\rbrack} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.109)

covers the values of the random variable ŷ(t*) with the confidence level


$$\begin{array}{r} {P\lbrack\hat{y}(t^{*}) \in C_{t^{*}}\rbrack = \alpha_{t^{*}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.110)

Letting t* = t ∈ 𝒯 in both formulas, construct the confidence domain C(t), as illustrated in Fig. 4.25(c).

3. The moment characteristics of the ensemble

Consider a one-dimensional ensemble ${\hat{\mathcal{Y}}}_{T}$ consisting of random trajectories ŷ(t | a), where t ∈ 𝒯. The parameters a are randomized with a given PDF P(a). Let t = t* be fixed. Then ŷ(t* | a) represents a function of the random argument a.

Define its kth moments by


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. M_{k}(t^{*}) = \mathcal{M}\left\{ y(t^{*}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a}) \right\} = {\int_{\mathcal{A}}y^{k}}(t^{*}\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})P(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(4.111)

Introduce the k-means of these moments in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {m_{k}(t^{*}) = M_{k}^{1/k}(t^{*}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(4.112)

For k = 1, the moment coincides with its mean, i.e., M1 = m1.

Assuming t* to be a variable that takes values within the interval 𝒯, find the kth moment trajectory Mk(t) and the k-mean trajectory mk(t).

In some applications, the object's output vector consists of the elements acting as the average functionals with random parameters. For example, consider option trading [15, 182]. Each of r financial derivatives contains p random parameters a1, …, ap, which are realized in the course of trading with some PDF P(a). The relations between the financial derivatives and parameters are described by functionals 𝒢1(a), …, 𝒢r(a). As a rule, they belong to the class of power functionals; in the elementary statement, these functionals have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{G}_{1}(\mathbf{a}) = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{p}c_{k}}a_{k},} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{G}_{2}(\mathbf{a}) = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{p}c_{k}}a_{k} + {\sum\limits_{k_{1} = 1}^{r}{\sum\limits_{k_{2} = 1}^{r}c_{k_{1}k_{2}}}}a_{k_{1}}a_{k_{2}},} \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} \ldots \\ \end{array}$$


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{G}_{r}(\mathbf{a}) = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}c_{k}}a_{k} + {\sum\limits_{k_{1},k_{2}}c_{k_{1},k_{2}}}a_{k_{1}}a_{k_{2}} + \ldots + {\sum\limits_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}}c_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}}}a_{k_{1}}\cdots a_{k_{r}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

The more efficient models that are used to predict future mean prices involve the integral power functionals; their cores depend on the time variables, c(τ), c(τ1, τ2), ….

In both statements, the relations under consideration give the mean prices of the financial derivatives, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{G}_{1}}(\mathbf{a})P(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a},\,{\int_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{G}_{2}}(\mathbf{a})P(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a},.....} \\ \end{array}$$

These mean price formulas represent the combinations of the weighted moments of the random vector a. In the option trading models, the object's output y is the predicted mean prices for the corresponding financial derivatives.

CHAPTER 5 ENTROPY-ROBUST ESTIMATION PROCEDURES FOR RANDOMIZED MODELS AND MEASUREMENT NOISES

DOI: 10.1201/9781003306566-5

The main stage of each randomized machine learning procedure is to estimate the probability density functions. Estimation involves input and output data arrays. According to a common hypothesis, output arrays contain errors due to imperfect measurements. The core of the estimation procedures consists in a model with randomized interval-type parameters, which can be original or relative. A static model with randomized parameters generates an ensemble of random vectors, whereas a dynamic model an ensemble of random trajectories. They are characterized in terms of different-order moments, which serve for balancing the model's output with its input data.

The PDF estimation problem is formulated as the problem to find the “best” functions under maximum uncertainty. The latter is measured using the information entropy of the model and measurement noises. Maximizing the entropy, we construct the entropy-optimal PDFs of the model parameters and the “worst” PDFs of the noises in the sense of this criterion.

5.1Structure of Entropy-Robust Estimation Procedure

Consider the general phenomenological structure of the estimation procedure. It represents a sequence of stages shown in Fig. 5.1. This procedure yields the estimated PDFs of the model parameters and noises—P*(a) and $Q(\overline{\xi}),$ respectively.

1. Data source (DS) generates an array of input data vectors x(t1), …, x(ts) and a corresponding array of output data vectors y(t1), …, y(ts), where s denotes the number of measurements, x ∈ Rn and y ∈ Rm. Sometimes, it seems convenient to write these data arrays in the form of matrices $\left. X = \lbrack\, x_{ij}\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,n};\, j = \overline{1,s}\,\rbrack \right.$ and $\left. Y = \lbrack\, y_{ij}\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,m};\, j = \overline{1,s}\,\rbrack. \right.$ By a standard assumption, input data are measured perfectly and output data with errors, and this aspect should be taken in account for estimation procedure design.

2. Randomized parametric model (RPM) generally represents a dynamic system with randomized original parameters a ∈ Rr that take values within the r-dimensional parallelepiped


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A} = \lbrack\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{a}^{+}\rbrack \in R^{r},\quad\mathcal{A} = {\underset{i = 1}{\overset{r}{\cup}}\mathcal{A}_{i}},\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{A}_{i} = \lbrack a_{i}^{-},a_{i}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.1)

The probabilistic properties of the randomized original parameters are described by the PDF P(a). The models of this class will be referred to as the RPM-Orig models.

In many cases, it is reasonable to use nonnegative relative randomized parameters u ∈ ℐ = [0, 1]; ℐ ∈ R+r. Recall that they have the following relation to the original parameters:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a}^{-} + A\,\mathbf{u},\quad\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{I},} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.2)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {A = \text{diag}\,\lbrack a_{i}^{+} - a_{i}^{-}\, i = \overline{1,r}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.3)

The probabilistic properties of the randomized relative parameters are characterized in terms of the PDF W(u). The models of this class will be mentioned as the RPM-Rel models.

For each realization of the randomized parameters, the models generate trajectories with the given PDFs, which have the following functional descriptions:

  • for the RPM-Orig model,


    $$\begin{aligned} \left. \mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack \right. & {= \mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}(t_{j},\tau),\mathbf{a},P(\mathbf{a});(t_{j},\tau) \in \mathcal{T}\rbrack,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.4)

  • for the RPM-Rel model,


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{z}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack = \mathcal{D}\lbrack\mathbf{x}(t_{j},\tau),\,\mathbf{a}^{-} + A\,\mathbf{u},\, W(\mathbf{u});(t_{j},\tau) \in \mathcal{T}\rbrack,j = \overline{1,s}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$

In formulas (5.4, 5.5), ℬ and 𝒟 are integral functionals.

At the discrete measurement times, the randomized models output the ensembles of corresponding trajectories, i.e.,

  • for the RPM-Orig model,


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathcal{Y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack = \left\{ \mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, P(\mathbf{a}) \right\},\text{\quad\quad}t_{j} \in \mathcal{T},\, j = \overline{1,s}, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (5.5)

  • for the RPM-Rel model,


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathcal{Z}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack = \left\{ \mathbf{z}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}t_{j} \in \mathcal{T},\, j = \overline{1,s}. \right. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (5.6)

3. Measurement error generator (MEG) is intended to simulate the measurement errors in output data. This device produces the ensembles of random vectors with certain probabilistic properties. It consists of a vector randomizer (VR) with a standard PDF and a converter (C) of these vectors into the ones with the given PDFs. The standard PDF is the density of the random vectors that have the uniform distribution on the unit nonnegative m-dimensional cube. The converter transforms these vectors into the random vectors with a PDF that is defined by the machine learning of the model.

Thus, the MEG outputs the random noise vectors $\overline{\xi}(t_{j}) = {\overline{\xi}}^{(j)},\,(j = \overline{1,s}\,),$ where ${\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \in R^{m}.$ In the same way, describe the noise arrays that appear as the result of data accumulation using a matrix $\left. \Xi = \lbrack\,\xi_{ij}\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,m};\, j = \overline{1,s}\,\rbrack. \right.$

The elements of the noise vectors are assumed to be independent and belonging to the intervals


$$\begin{aligned} {\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} & {\in \mathcal{K}_{j} = \lbrack{\overline{\xi}}_{-}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}_{+}^{(j)}\rbrack,\quad j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \Xi & {\in \mathcal{K} = \otimes_{j = 1}^{s}\mathcal{K}_{j}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.7)

It is often useful to introduce the relative nonnegative vectors ${\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}$ that take values within the unit nonnegative m-dimensional cube ℰj = [0, 1]. In addition, define the auxiliary variable matrix $\left. E = \lbrack\,\eta_{ij}\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,m};\, j = \overline{1,s}\,\rbrack. \right.$ The transformation of the random vectors ${\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}$ into the vectors η(j) runs as follows:


$$\begin{aligned} {{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} = {\overline{\xi}}_{-}^{(j)} +} & {K_{j}\,{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)},\quad K_{j} = \text{diag}\,\lbrack\xi_{i, +}^{(j)} - \xi_{i, -}^{(j)}\rbrack,} \\ & {\, i = \overline{1,m};j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.8)

The probabilistic properties of the noises are characterized by the PDF $Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})$ defined on 𝒦j (5.7) or by the PDF $G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})$ defined on the unit cube ℰ. If these density functions are specified, then the MEG produces the ensembles of random vectors that simulate

  • the original noises


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{Q}_{j}\lbrack Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\rbrack = \left\{ {\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\lbrack Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\rbrack \right\},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (5.9)

  • the nonnegative relative noises


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{G}_{j}\lbrack G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\rbrack = \left\{ {\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}\lbrack G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\rbrack \right\},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (5.10)

4. Measurement model (MM) simulates the influence of the measurement errors on the estimation results. By assumption, this influence is described well by the additive measurement model. The ensembles of the measurement model outputs have the following form:

  • for the RPM-Orig model,


    $$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{V}_{j}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\rbrack} & {= \mathcal{Y}_{j}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack + \mathcal{Q}_{j}\lbrack Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\rbrack,} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.11)

  • for the RPM-Rel model,

5. Moment evaluator (ME) performs online calculations for the moment characteristics of the ensembles generated by the measurement model.

For the randomized models, the ensembles consist of the following random trajectories:

  • for the RPM-Orig model,


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{v}(t_{j}) = \mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack + {\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\lbrack Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\rbrack; \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (5.12)

  • for the RPM-Rel model,


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{f}(t_{j}) = \mathbf{z}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack + {\overline{\xi}}_{-}^{(j)} + K_{j}{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}\lbrack G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (5.13)

As the numerical characteristics of the ensembles 𝒱j and ℱj, adopt the vectors composed of the k-means of the kth moments (see (4.111, 4.112)), i.e.,

  • for the RPM-Orig model,


    $$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{m}^{(k)}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack} & {= \left\{ {\lbrack M_{i}^{(k)}(j)\rbrack}^{1/k},\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,m} \right\},} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.14)

  • for the RPM-Rel model,


    $$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{n}^{(k)}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)},j)\rbrack} & {= \left\{ {\lbrack N_{i}^{(k)}(j)\rbrack}^{1/k},\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,m} \right\},} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.15)

In these formulas, the kth moments of the corresponding vector elements are given by


$$\begin{aligned} {M_{i}^{(k)}(j) =} & \left. \int_{\mathcal{A}}y_{i}^{k}(t_{j},\, \middle| \,\mathbf{a})P(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} + \int_{\Xi_{j}}{\lbrack\xi_{i}^{(j)}\rbrack}^{k}Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})d\xi_{i}^{(j)}, \right. \\ N_{i}^{(k)} & \left. (j) = \int_{\mathcal{U}}z_{i}^{k}(t_{j},\, \middle| \,\mathbf{u})W(\mathbf{u})d\mathbf{u} + {\lbrack\xi^{(j})}_{-}\rbrack_{i}^{k} + \right. \\ & {+ K_{ji}\int_{\mathcal{E}}{\lbrack\eta_{i}^{(j)}\rbrack}^{k}G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})d\eta_{i}^{(j)}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.16)

6. Balancing model (BM) is used to compare available output data y with the accepted characteristics of ensembles 𝒱 or ℱ.

For the randomized models, the balance constraints have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{m}^{(k)}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}),\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.17)


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{n}^{(k)}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)},j)\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}),\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.18)

7. Machine learning algorithm (ML-A) is intended to form optimal estimates for the PDFs of the parameters and measurement noises. As repeatedly mentioned earlier, the randomized machine learning procedure has to estimate the PDFs under the maximum uncertainty characterized by information entropy. Thus, the ML-A is searching for its constrained maximum on an admissible set in the form of the balance constraints (5.17, 5.18).

The information entropy functional ℋ is defined over the class of continuously differentiable PDFs $P(\mathbf{a}),Q_{1}({\overline{\xi}}^{(1)}),\ldots,Q_{s}({\overline{\xi}}^{(s)}),$ which describe the probabilistic properties of the randomized parameters and noises simulating the measurement errors, respectively. The entropy functional generalizes the finite-dimensional concept of information entropy.

In 1865, German physicist R. Clausius introduced a physical quantity to characterize a thermodynamic system, called entropy.


$$\begin{array}{r} {S = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T}.} \\ \end{array}$$

In 1877, L. Boltzmann established a relation between the thermodynamic entropy S (or the physical entropy E) and the statistical weight Z for the macrostate (ΔQ, T) of a thermodynamic system. Later on, using the hypothesis of equiprobable microstates, M. Planck wrote this relation in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {S = k\ln Z = E.} \\ \end{array}$$

Here k = 1.38 ⋅ 10 − 23 denotes the Boltzmann constant. The statistical weight of the macrostate (ΔQ, T) is measured by the number of all possible microstates (combinations) that make up this macrostate. Recall that these terms apply to the so-called (mono- or polyatomic) gas model, which considers a system (macrosystem) of very many indistinguishable particles (molecules). The space of the system's macrostates consists of m nonintersecting subsets with given capacities G1, …, Gm (i.e., the number of states that can be occupied by the particles). Behaving stochastically, the particles are distributed in a random way over the states in these subsets, with the same probability and independently of each other. Let each particle be uniquely labeled, and list the resulting subsets for all labeled particles; in fact, this list is the system's microstate. Of course, the list under consideration is of a huge volume. The sublists with the same number of particles Nk in the kth subset can be extracted. The number of particles Nk is an element of the system's macrostate N = {N1,…,Nm}. The number of elements in a sublist (the number of microstates that induce a given macrostate) is called its statistical weight Z = Z(Nk).

To find a relation between the statistical weight Z and the macrostate characteristic Nk (the number of particles that fill the kth subset), we will need a certain generalization of the macrosystem model. This generalization involves information about the prior probabilities a1, …, am with which the particles are distributed over the subsets of the macrostate space, as well as information about the properties of states in these subsets. Note that in the gas model the prior probabilities are assumed to be equal and the state properties are not described.

Consider a macrosystem in which each state can be occupied by one particle only (otherwise, the state is unfilled). The numbers of such states in the subsets are G1, …, Gm. The distribution mechanism has the following organization. Each particle may occupy Nk states in the kth subset with the prior probability ak randomly and independently of the other particles; hence, (Gk − Nk) states remain free with the prior probability (1 − ak). Denote this event by {Nk,(Gk−Nk)}. Due to the independence of all particles in this distribution mechanism, the probability of the event makes up


$$\begin{array}{r} {a_{k}^{N_{k}}\,{(1 - a_{k})}^{(G_{k} - N_{k})}.} \\ \end{array}$$

The number of filled states Nk can be achieved in different distributions of the particles over the kth subset, i.e., different microstates. The number of such microstates Z(Nk) is the number of Nk-combinations of Gk particles:


$$\begin{array}{r} {C_{N_{k}}^{G_{k}} = \frac{G_{k}!}{N_{k}!\,(G_{k} - N_{k})!}.} \\ \end{array}$$

The event {Nk,(Gk−Nk)} can be realized either by the 1st microstate, or by the 2nd microstate, …, or by the CNkGk th microstate. Therefore, the event {Nk,(Gk−Nk)} occurs with the probability


$$\begin{array}{r} {P_{k}(N_{k}) = \frac{G_{k}!}{N_{k}!\,(G_{k} - N_{k})!}\, a_{k}^{N_{k}}\,{(1 - a_{k})}^{(G_{k} - N_{k})}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Because all participants of the distribution mechanism are independent, the probability of the corresponding macrostate of this macrosystem is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(\mathbf{N}) = {\prod\limits_{k = 1}^{m}P_{k}}(N_{k}) = {\prod\limits_{k = 1}^{m}\frac{G_{k}!}{N_{k}!\,(G_{k} - N_{k})!}}\, a_{k}^{N_{k}}\,{(1 - a_{k})}^{(G_{k} - N_{k})}.} \\ \end{array}$$

According to Planck's definition, physical entropy is proportional to the logarithm of the probability distribution function, since the statistical weight is an unnormalized distribution. Therefore,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. S \right.\sim lnP(\mathbf{N}).} \\ \end{array}$$

Then it follows that


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. S \right.\sim{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{m}\ln}G_{k}! - \ln(G_{k} - N_{k})! - \ln N_{k}! + N_{k}\ln a_{k} + (G_{k} - N_{k})\ln(1 - a_{k}).} \\ \end{array}$$

As the values Nk are large, employ Stirling's approximation


$$\begin{array}{r} {\ln N! = N(\ln N - 1).} \\ \end{array}$$

In this case, the right-hand side of the expression for S can be written as the sum of a constant and a function of the macrostate:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. S \right.\sim C + H_{F}(\mathbf{N}).} \\ \end{array}$$

The function


$$\begin{array}{r} {H_{F}(\mathbf{N}) = - {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{m}\left\lbrack {\, N_{k}\frac{N_{k}}{{\widetilde{a}}_{k}} + (G_{k} - N_{k})\ln(G_{k} - N_{k})\,} \right\rbrack},\quad{\widetilde{a}}_{k} = \frac{a_{k}}{1 - a_{k}},} \\ \end{array}$$

is called the generalized Fermi information entropy. For this function, the domain of definition is the m-dimensional parallelepiped 𝒩 = [0, G], i.e., the set of admissible macrostates. If the parameters a and G satisfy the conditions


$$\begin{array}{r} {G_{k}a_{k} = \text{const},\text{\quad\quad}N_{k} \ll G_{k},} \\ \end{array}$$

then HF(N) can be transformed into the entropy function


$$\begin{array}{r} {H_{B}(\mathbf{N}) = - {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{m}N_{k}}\ln\frac{N_{k}}{a_{k}G_{k}e},} \\ \end{array}$$

which is called the generalized Boltzmann information entropy. This function is defined on the nonnegative orthant 𝒩 ∈ R+m, which represents the set of admissible macrostates.

The random distribution of the indistinguishable particles over the subsets in the state space consumes r types of resources (energy, time, finances, etc.). The available quantities of these resources are q1, …, qr. Resource consumption is characterized by consumption functions Φ1(t, N), …, Φr(t, N), which have parameters t (specific consumption rates) and depend on the macrostate vector N.

As the distribution process requires resources, it is possible to realize only those macrostates that satisfy the conditions


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Phi_{i}(\mathbf{t},\mathbf{N}) = q_{i},\quad i = \overline{1,s};\text{\quad\quad}\Phi_{i + s}(\mathbf{t},\mathbf{N}) = q_{i + s},\quad i = \overline{1,r-s}.} \\ \end{array}$$

These constraints define the so-called resource set 𝒟. The intersection of this set with the corresponding sets of admissible macrostates gives the admissible set


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{N}{\cap \mathcal{D}}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Using the above concepts and terminology, we can state the generalized variational principle as follows. The macrostate that is realized in the macrosystem corresponds to the constrained maximum of the generalized information entropy, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H(\mathbf{N})\Rightarrow\max\text{~subject~to~}\,\,\mathbf{N} \in \mathcal{F}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$

5.2Entropy-Robust Estimation Algorithms for Probability Density Functions

The estimation algorithms of the PDFs form the core of the randomized machine learning procedure. They are oriented towards the corresponding classes of the randomized parametric models, the RPM-Orig and RPM-Rel models. The two classes of randomized models have technical differences. First, some estimation algorithms for the RPM-Orig model will be considered, including the general problem statement and the structure of the resulting solutions. Then these estimation algorithms will be adapted to the RPM-Rel model.

5.2.1Estimation algorithms for RPM-Orig model

According to (5.4, 5.12), the observable output of the RPM-Orig model at a time instant tj is described by


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{v}(t_{j}) = \mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}} & \left| \, P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack + {\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\lbrack Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\rbrack, \right. \\ \left. \mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack = \mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x} \right. & \left. ((t_{j},\tau_{l}),\, \middle| \, l = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack, \right. \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.19)

Here, ℬ denotes a matrix functional of dimensions (m × n) that characterizes an existing relation between the model's output y(tj) and the array composed of the input vectors x(tj, τ1), …, x(tj, τ(j − 1)). The measurement errors are simulated by the noise vectors ${\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}.$ The RPM-Orig model output (5.2.1) depends on the randomized parameters a with a PDF P(a) and also on the randomized noise vectors ${\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}$ with a PDF $Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)});$ see (5.2.1). The available prior information about these PDFs (if any) is represented in the form of prior PDFs P0(a) and $Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}).$ By assumption, the PDFs belong to the class ℂ1 of all continuously differentiable functions.

For the RPM-Orig model (5.4), the entropy-robust estimation problem of the PDFs of its parameters and measurement noises is formulated as follows:

  • maximize the generalized Boltzmann information entropy functional [149]


    $$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{H}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),\overline{Q}(\xi)\rbrack =} & {- {\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})\,\ln\frac{P(\mathbf{a})}{P_{0}(\mathbf{a})}\, d\,\mathbf{a} -} \\ {- {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\,}{\int_{\Xi_{j}}Q_{j}}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})} & \left. \ln\frac{Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})}{Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})}d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\Rightarrow\min_{P,Q_{1},...,Q_{s}} \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.20)

  • subject to:

    • –the normalization conditions for the PDFs, i.e.,


      $$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} = 1,\quad{\int_{\Xi_{j}}Q_{j}}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\, d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} = 1,\quad j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
      (5.21)

      and

    • –the balance constraints for the k-means of the output of the RPM-Orig model (5.14) and the measurements of the object's output, i.e.,


      $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{m}^{(k)}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}),\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
      (5.22)

      Due to (5.13), the vector $\mathbf{m}^{(k)}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack$ in these equality constraints has the components


      $$\begin{aligned} & {m_{i}^{(k)}\lbrack j\rbrack = \left\lbrack {\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})y_{i}^{k}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack\, d\mathbf{a} \right\rbrack^{1/k} +} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad} + \left\lbrack {{\int_{\Xi_{j}}\,}Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\,{\lbrack\xi_{i}^{(j)}\rbrack}^{k}\, d\xi_{i}^{(j)}} \right\rbrack^{1/k},} \\ & {\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
      (5.23)

Consider the case in which the balance constraints involve the 1-mean of the RPM-Orig model output:


$$\begin{aligned} \left\lbrack {\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})\mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack\, d\mathbf{a} \right\rbrack & {+ \left\lbrack {{\int_{\Xi_{j}}\,}Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\,{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\, d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}} \right\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}),} \\ & {\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.24)

In this optimization problem, the functional constraints extract the subset $\Omega\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\overline{\xi})\rbrack$ of all admissible functions, where $Q(\overline{\xi}) = \left\{ Q_{1}({\overline{\xi}}^{(1)}),\ldots,Q_{s}({\overline{\xi}}^{(s)}) \right\},$ from the class ℂ1. In fact, the problem (5.2.1)–(5.24) is a functional entropy-linear programming problem [149]. It belongs to the class of the Lyapunov-type optimization problems [77, 174], in which the admissible set of functions is described by a system of linear integral functionals.

For the RPM-Orig model, the entropy-robust RML algorithm has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left\lbrack {P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\overline{\xi})} \right\rbrack^{*} = \arg\max_{\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\overline{\xi})\rbrack}\left\{ \mathcal{H},\, \middle| \,\lbrack\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{a}),\mathcal{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack \in \Omega \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.25)

where the admissible set Ω is given by the normalization conditions (5.21) and the empirical balance constraints (5.24).

5.2.2Estimation algorithms for RPM-Rel model

In the RPM-Rel model, the randomized parameters include the nonnegative relative parameters u and the measurement noises $\left\{ {\overline{\eta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\eta}}^{(s)} \right\}.$ According to (5.13), the observable output of the RPM-Rel model at a time instant tj is described by


$$\begin{aligned} \left. \mathbf{f}(t_{j}) = \mathbf{z}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack \right. & {+ {\overline{\xi}}_{-}^{(j)} + K_{j}{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}\lbrack G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\rbrack,} \\ \left. \mathbf{z}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack = \mathcal{D}\lbrack\mathbf{x}(t_{j},\tau), \right. & {\mathbf{a}^{-} + A\,\mathbf{u},\, W(\mathbf{u});(t_{j},\tau) \in \mathcal{T}\rbrack,} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.26)

Here, 𝒟 denotes a matrix functional of dimensions (m × n) that characterizes an existing relation between the model's output z(tj) and the array composed of the input vectors x(tj, τ1), …, x(tj, τ(j − 1)). The RPM-Rel model output (5.2.2) depends on the randomized relative parameters u with a PDF W(u) and also on the randomized relative noise vectors ${\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}$ with a PDF $G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)});$ see (5.2.2). The available prior information about these PDFs (if any) is represented in the form of prior PDFs W0(u) and $G_{j}^{0}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}).$ By assumption, the PDFs belong to the class ℂ1 of all continuously differentiable functions.

For the RPM-Rel model (5.1), the entropy-robust estimation problem of the PDFs of its parameters and measurement noises is formulated as follows:

  • maximize the generalized Boltzmann information entropy functional


    $$\begin{aligned} & {\quad\mathcal{H}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),\overline{G}(\eta)\rbrack = - {\int_{\mathcal{U}}W}(\mathbf{u})\,\ln\frac{W(\mathbf{u})}{W_{0}(\mathbf{u})}\, d\,\mathbf{u} -} \\ & \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\,}{\int_{\mathcal{E}_{j}}G_{j}}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\,\ln\frac{G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})}{G_{j}^{0}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})}d{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}\Rightarrow\min_{W,\overline{G}} \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.27)

  • subject to:

    • –the normalization conditions for the PDF, i.e.,


      $$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\mathcal{U}}W}(\mathbf{u})d\mathbf{u} = 1,\text{\quad\quad}{\int_{\mathcal{E}_{j}}G_{j}}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\, d{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)} = 1,\quad j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
      (5.28)

      and

    • –the balance constraints for the k-means of the output of the RPM-Rel model (5.15) and the measurements of the object's output, i.e.,


      $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{n}^{(k)}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}),\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
      (5.29)

    Due to (5.15), the vector $\mathbf{n}^{(k)}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack$ in these equality constraints has the components


    $$\begin{aligned} {n_{i}^{(k)}\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \left\lbrack {\int_{\mathcal{U}}W}(\mathbf{u})z_{i}^{k}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack\, d\mathbf{u} \right\rbrack^{1/k} +} \\ & {\left\lbrack {{\int_{\mathcal{E}_{j}}\,}G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\,{\lbrack\eta_{i}^{(j)}\rbrack}^{k}\, d\eta_{i}^{(j)}} \right\rbrack^{1/k},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\quad i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.30)

Consider the case in which the balance constraints involve the 1-mean of the RPM-Rel model output:


$$\begin{aligned} {\left\lbrack {\int_{\mathcal{U}}W}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{z}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack\, d\mathbf{u} \right\rbrack +} & {\left\lbrack {{\int_{\mathcal{E}_{j}}\,}G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\,{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}\, d{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}} \right\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}),} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.31)

Like in the optimization problem presented above, the functional constraints extract the subset $\Psi\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G(\overline{\eta})\rbrack$ of all admissible functions, where $G(\overline{\eta}) = \left\{ G_{1}({\overline{\eta}}^{(1)}),\ldots,G_{s}({\overline{\eta}}^{(s)}) \right\},$ from the class ℂ1. The problem (5.27-5.31) is also of the Lyapunov type.

For the RPM-Rel model, the entropy-robust RML algorithm has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left\lbrack {W(\mathbf{u}),\overline{G}(\overline{\eta})} \right\rbrack^{*} = \arg\max_{\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),\overline{G}(\overline{\eta})\rbrack}\left\{ \mathcal{H},\, \middle| \,\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G(\overline{\eta})\rbrack \in \Psi \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.32)

where the admissible set Ψ is given by the normalization conditions (5.28) and the empirical balance constraints (5.31).

5.2.3Estimation algorithms for RPM-F model with measurement errors of input and output

The previous sections have studied cases of measurement errors figuring in the output only. However, in many applications, there are input data collections containing errors as well. Hence, the general RML procedure should be modified accordingly.

If errors occur in the input data, the observed output of the RPM-F model takes the following form:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathbf{v}(t_{j}) = \mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, F(\mathbf{a},{\overline{\mu}}^{(j)})\rbrack + \overline{\xi}\lbrack Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\rbrack, \right. \\ \left. \mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, F(\mathbf{a},{\overline{\mu}}^{(t_{j})})\rbrack = \mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}(t_{j},\tau) + {\overline{\mu}}^{(t_{j})}\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(5.33)

Here ${\overline{\mu}}^{(j)}$ denotes the vector of input noises at a time instant tj, which are of the interval type:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\mu}}^{(j)} \in \mathcal{M} = \lbrack\mu^{-},\mu^{+}\rbrack\quad\text{for~all}\, t_{j}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.34)

From the RPM-F model equations (5.33) it follows that the random elements are the parameters a and the input noise $\overline{\mu}.$ Their probabilistic properties are characterized by a joint probability density function $F(\mathbf{a},{\overline{\mu}}^{(t_{j})}).$ If there exists some information about this function, it is represented in the form of a prior PDF $F_{0}(\mathbf{a},{\overline{\mu}}^{(t_{j})}).$

For the RPM-F model (5.33), the entropy-robust estimation problem of the PDFs of its parameters and input and output measurement noises is formulated as follows:

  • maximize the generalized Boltzmann information entropy functional


    $$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{H}\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu}),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack} & {= - \int_{\mathcal{R}}F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu})\,\ln\frac{F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu})}{F_{0}(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu})}\, d\,\mathbf{a}\, d\,\overline{\mu} -} \\ {- \sum_{j = 1}^{s}\,\int_{\Xi_{j}}} & \left. Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\,\ln\frac{Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})}{Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})}d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\Rightarrow\max_{F,\overline{Q}} \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.35)

  • subject to:

    • —the normalization conditions for the PDFs, i.e.,


      $$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\mathcal{R}}F}(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu})\, d\mathbf{a}\, d\,\overline{\mu} = 1,\text{\quad\quad}{\int_{\Xi_{j}}Q_{j}}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\, d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} = 1,\quad j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{array}$$
      (5.36)

    • —the balance constraints for the k-means of the observed output (5.33) and the real data, i.e.,


      $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{m}^{(k)}\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu}),Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}),\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
      (5.37)

    Due to (5.15), the vector $\mathbf{m}^{(k)}\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu}),Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),j\rbrack$ in these equality constraints has the components


    $$\begin{aligned} {m_{i}^{(k)}\lbrack j\rbrack =} & {\left\lbrack {\int_{\mathcal{R}}F}(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu})\mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, F(\mathbf{a},{\overline{\mu}}^{(t_{j})})\rbrack\, d\mathbf{a}d\overline{\mu} \right\rbrack^{1/k} +} \\ & {\left\lbrack {{\int_{\Xi_{j}}\,}Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\,{\lbrack\xi_{i}^{(j)}\rbrack}^{k}\, d\xi_{i}^{(j)}} \right\rbrack^{1/k},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\quad i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.38)

Consider the case in which the balance constraints involve the 1-mean of the RPM-F model output:


$$\begin{aligned} {m_{i}^{(1)}\lbrack j\rbrack =} & \left. {\int_{\mathcal{R}}F}(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu})\mathbf{y}\lbrack t_{j}\, \middle| \, F(\mathbf{a},{\overline{\mu}}^{(t_{j})})\rbrack\, d\mathbf{a}d\overline{\mu} + \right. \\ & {{\int_{\Xi_{j}}\,}Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\,\lbrack\xi_{i}^{(j)}\rbrack d\xi_{i}^{(j)},} \\ & {\quad i = \overline{1,m},\, j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.39)

Like in the optimization problem presented above, the functional constraints extract the subset $\Gamma\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu}),Q(\overline{\xi})\rbrack$ of all admissible functions, where $Q(\overline{\xi}) = \left\{ Q_{1}({\overline{\xi}}^{(1)}),\ldots,Q_{s}({\overline{\xi}}^{(s)}) \right\},$ from the class ℂ1. The problem (5.2.3—5.2.3) is also of the Lyapunov type.

For the RPM-F model with input and output data errors, the entropy-robust RML algorithm has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left\lbrack {F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu}),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})} \right\rbrack^{*} = \arg\max_{\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu}),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack}\left\{ \mathcal{H},\, \middle| \,\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\overline{\mu}),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack \in \Gamma \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.40)

where the admissible set Γ is given by the normalization conditions (5.36) and the empirical balance constraints (5.2.3).

5.3Optimality Conditions for Lyapunov-Type Problems

A comprehensive study of the Lyapunov-type functional programming problems, including a possible application of Lagrange's method of multipliers, can be found in the monographs [77, 174]. This section will briefly describe a mathematical framework based on the cited results and the Gateaux derivative [114].

A minimization problem with integral nonlinear functionals (a Lyapunov-type problem) can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \mathcal{J}\lbrack f(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = {\int_{\mathcal{X}}\Phi}\left\lbrack {f(\mathbf{x})} \right\rbrack d\mathbf{x}\Rightarrow\min_{f(\mathbf{x})} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(5.41)

subject to the constraints


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{G}_{i}\lbrack f(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = {\int_{\mathcal{X}}\Psi_{i}}\left\lbrack {f(\mathbf{x})} \right\rbrack d\mathbf{x} = 0,\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,m}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.42)

Here x ∈ Rn, the functions Φ[ • ], Ψ1[ • ], …, Ψm[ • ] and also the desired function f( • ) that minimizes the functional 𝒥[ • ] belong to the class ℂ1 of all continuously differentiable functions.

Define the Lagrange functional by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{L}\lbrack f(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = {\int_{\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{J}}\lbrack f(\mathbf{x})\rbrack - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\lambda_{i}}{\int_{\mathcal{X}}\Psi_{i}}\left\lbrack {f(\mathbf{x})} \right\rbrack d\mathbf{x}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.43)

The first-order optimality condition claims that the variation of this functional with respect to the function f(x) is zero, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\delta\mathcal{L} = 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.44)

Because the function under variation belongs to the class ℂ1, condition (5.44) is equivalent to the zero value of the Gateaux derivative of the functional ℒ.

Recall the definition of the Gateaux derivative. Consider a functional ℰ[w(u)], where w(u) ∈ ℂ1 is a scalar function, u ∈ Rn. Take an arbitrary function h(u) ∈ ℂ1, and introduce a linear combination w*(u) + αh(u), where α denotes a real variable and w*(u) is a certain fixed function from ℂ1 that possesses some necessary properties (e.g., minimizes the functional ℰ). For a chosen function h(u), the functional ℰ becomes a function of the real variable α. The Gateaux derivative of the functional ℰ is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. D\mathcal{E} = \frac{d}{d\alpha}\mathcal{E}\lbrack w^{*}(\mathbf{u}) + \alpha h(\mathbf{u})\rbrack \middle| {}_{\alpha = 0}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(5.45)

Getting back to the Lagrange functional (5.43), consider an arbitrary function h(x) from the class ℂ1 and the real variable α. Denote by f*(x) the function that yields minimum in the problem (5.41, 5.42). Represent an arbitrary function f(x) as the linear combination


$$\begin{array}{r} {f(\mathbf{x}) = f^{*}(\mathbf{x}) + \alpha h(\mathbf{x}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.46)

Under fixed f*(x) and h(x), the Lagrange functional (5.43) turns out to be a function of the real variable α, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{L} = {\int_{X}\Phi}\left\lbrack {f^{*}(\mathbf{x}) + \alpha h(\mathbf{x})} \right\rbrack d\mathbf{x} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\lambda_{i}}{\int_{X}\Psi_{i}}\left\lbrack {f^{*}(\mathbf{x}) + \alpha h(\mathbf{x})} \right\rbrack d\mathbf{x}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.47)

Then the first-order optimality condition for the Lagrange functional takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {D\mathcal{L} = {\int_{X}h}(\mathbf{x})\left( {\frac{d\Phi(y)}{dy} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\lambda_{i}}\,\frac{d\Psi_{i}(y)}{dy}} \right)d\mathbf{x} = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.48)

where y is a scalar argument of the functions Φ and Ψ1, …, Ψm. For this integral expression to vanish, a necessary condition is that its integrand takes zero value for any function h(x) ∈ ℂ1.

Consequently, the first-order optimality condition in the problem (5.41, 5.42) can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{d\Phi(y)}{dy} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\lambda_{i}}\frac{d\Psi_{i}(y)}{dy}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.49)

Here the derivatives of the functions Φ, Ψ1, …, Ψm depend on f*(x), the function that minimizes the functional (5.41), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {d\Phi(y)dy = \phi\lbrack f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}d\Psi_{i}(y)dy = \psi_{i}\lbrack f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack,\quad i = \overline{1,m}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.50)

Hence, equality (5.49) can be transformed into


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi\lbrack f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\lambda_{i}}\psi_{i}\lbrack f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.51)

This equality defines a parameterization of the optimal function f*(x) by the Lagrange multipliers λ1, …, λm. In some cases, the parameterization can be expressed in an analytical form. Particularly, let the function Φ in (5.41, 5.42) be quadratic, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Phi\lbrack f(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = a_{0} + a_{1}f(\mathbf{x}) + a_{2}f^{2}(\mathbf{x}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.52)

and also let the functions Ψ1, …, Ψm be linear, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Psi_{i}\lbrack f(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = b_{0}^{i} + b_{1}^{i}f(\mathbf{x}),\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,m},} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.53)

which leads to the functional quadratic programming problem. Then


$$\begin{array}{r} {\phi\lbrack f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = a_{1} + a_{2}f^{*}(\mathbf{x}),\text{\quad\quad}\psi_{i}\lbrack f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\rbrack = b_{1}^{i},} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.54)

and the optimality conditions (5.51) yield the following parametric representation for the optimal function f*:


$$\begin{array}{r} {f^{*}(\mathbf{x}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\lambda_{i}}b_{1}^{i}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.55)

The role of parameters is played by the Lagrange multipliers λ1, …, λm.

5.4Optimality Conditions and Structure of Entropy-Optimal Probability Density Functions

The entropy-robust estimation problems (5.2.1–5.22) and (5.27–5.29) are constrained maximization problems of an integral functional in functions from the class ℂ1 on an admissible set defined by integral equalities. To establish optimality conditions and perform a structural analysis of the resulting solution (optimal PDFs), we will take advantage of Lagrange's method of multipliers and the Gateaux derivatives.

5.4.1Randomized models of the RPM-Orig class with output errors

Consider the problem (5.2.1–5.22). Define the Lagrange functional in the form


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{L}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\overline{\xi})\rbrack} & {= \mathcal{H}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\overline{\xi})\rbrack + \lambda p\lbrack P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack + \left\langle \overline{\mu},\mathbf{q}\lbrack Q(\overline{\xi}\rbrack \right\rangle +} \\ & {+ \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{l}^{(j)}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\overline{\xi})\rbrack \right\rangle,} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.56)

where λ, μ1, …, μs, and θ1, …, θs denote the Lagrange multipliers for the corresponding constraints, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {p\lbrack P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack = 1 - {\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})d\mathbf{a} = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.57)


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{l}^{(j)}\lbrack P(\mathbf{a}),Q(\overline{\xi})\rbrack =} & {\mathbf{y}^{(j)} - \left\lbrack {{\int_{\mathcal{A}}P}(\mathbf{a})\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t_{j},\mathbf{a})\, d\mathbf{a}} \right\rbrack +} \\ {+ {\int_{\Xi_{j}}\,}Q_{j}} & {({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\,{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\, d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} = 0,} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.59)

To obtain optimality conditions for the Lagrange functional, use the Gateaux derivative-based method described in Section 4.3.

Let the PDFs P*(a) and $Q_{1}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(1)}),\ldots,Q_{s}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(s)})$ satisfy the first-order optimality conditions for the functional (5.56). Consider arbitrary functions h(a) and $g_{1}({\overline{\xi}}^{(1)}),\ldots,g_{s}({\overline{\xi}}^{(s)}),$ all from the class ℂ1, as well as real variables α and β1, …, βs. Write the PDFs in (5.56) in the form


$$\begin{aligned} {P(\mathbf{a}) = P^{*}(\mathbf{a}) + \alpha h(\mathbf{a});} & {Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}) = Q_{j}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}) + \beta_{j}g_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),} \\ & {\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.60)

Then the Lagrange functional becomes a function of the real variables 𝕎 = {α;β1,…,βs}. The Gateaux derivatives in these variables are given by


$$\begin{aligned} \left. \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\alpha} \middle| {}_{\mathbb{W} = 0} = \right. & {- {\int_{\mathcal{A}}h}(\mathbf{a})(\ln\frac{P^{*}(\mathbf{a})}{P_{0}(\mathbf{a})} + 1 + \lambda +} \\ {+ {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\langle}{\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{B}^{(j)}} & {\left. \lbrack\mathbf{x}(t_{j},\tau_{h},\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle)d\mathbf{a},} \\ \left. \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\beta_{j}} \middle| {}_{\mathbb{W} = 0} = - {\int_{\Xi_{j}}g_{j}}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}) \right. & {\left\lbrack {\ln\frac{Q_{j}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})}{Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})} + 1 + \mu_{j} + \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.61)

For these integrals to vanish for any functions $h(\mathbf{a}),g_{1}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}),\ldots,g_{s}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}) \in {\mathbb{C}}^{1},$ a necessary condition is that the bracketed expressions all take zero value, i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} & {\left. \ln\frac{P^{*}(\mathbf{a})}{P_{0}(\mathbf{a})} + 1 + \lambda + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{B}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}( \right.}\tau_{h},\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle = 0,} \\ & {\ln\frac{Q_{j}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})}{Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})} + 1 + \mu_{j} + \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.62)

The solution of these equations within the Lagrange multipliers λ, μ1, …, μs, and ${\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)}$ has the form


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\,\,\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}P^{*}(\mathbf{a}) = P_{0}(\mathbf{a}) \times} \\ & {\times \exp\left\lbrack \left. - 1 - \lambda - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{B}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.},\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}Q_{j}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}) = Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\exp\left\lbrack {- 1 - \mu_{j} - \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.63)

The Lagrange multipliers λ and μ1, …, μs can be eliminated using the normalization conditions (5.21). Then formulas (5.4.1) yield the following entropy-optimal estimates for the PDFs of the RPM-Orig model parameters and measurement noises:


$$\begin{aligned} & {P^{*}(\mathbf{a}) = P_{0}(\mathbf{a})\frac{\exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{B}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.},\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack}{\mathcal{P}({\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)})},} \\ & {Q_{j}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}) = Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\frac{\exp\left\lbrack {- \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack}{\mathcal{Q}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}),}\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.64)

Here


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{P}({\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)}) = {\int_{\mathcal{A}}P_{0}}(\mathbf{a}) \times} \\ & {\times \exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{B}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.},\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack d\mathbf{a},} \\ & {\quad\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{Q}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = {\int_{\Xi}Q_{j}^{0}}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\exp\left\lbrack {- \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.65)

Clearly, the entropy-optimal PDFs are parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers and represent exponential functions. However, they may have any form, depending on the parameters a. Figure 5.2, Figure 5.3, Figure 5.4, Figure 5.5 demonstrate some examples of the estimated PDFs of the model parameters. For the linear RPM-Orig model, the estimated PDFs are always exponential functions; see Fig. 5.2. Note that their form is affected by the input and output measurements.

For the nonlinear RPMs, the estimates have a wider variety of structural forms. For example, the estimated PDFs for the RPM-Orig models with the quadratic, quadratic-linear and cubic nonlinearities are shown in Fig. 5.3, Fig. 5.4, Figure 5.5.

5.4.2Randomized models of the RPM-Rel class with output errors

To construct optimality conditions for this class of the randomized models, introduce similar notations as (5.57–5.4.1), i.e.,

  • the Lagrange multiplier λ for the first constraint in (5.21), writing it in the form


    $$\begin{array}{r} {w\lbrack W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack = 1 - {\int_{\mathcal{U}}W}(\mathbf{u})d\mathbf{u};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (5.66)

  • the vector $\overline{\mu} = \left\{ \mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{s} \right\}$ composed of the Lagrange multipliers for the second group of constraints in (5.21), writing them in the form
