    $$\begin{aligned} & {\mathbf{g}\lbrack G(\overline{\eta})\rbrack = \left\{ g^{(1)}\lbrack G_{1}({\overline{\eta}}^{(1)})\rbrack,\ldots,g^{(s)}\lbrack G_{s}({\overline{\eta}}^{(s)})\rbrack \right\},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}g^{(j)}\lbrack G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\rbrack = 1 - {\int_{\mathcal{E}}G_{j}}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\, d{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s};} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.67)

  • the vectors ${\overline{\theta}}^{(j)} = \left\{ \theta_{1}^{(j)},\ldots,\theta_{m}^{(j)} \right\},\, j = \overline{1,s},$ composed of the Lagrange multipliers for the constraints (5.22), writing them in the form


    $$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{h}^{(j)}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\rbrack = \mathbf{y}(t_{j}) -} \\ & \left. - {\int_{\mathcal{U}}W}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{D}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}),\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + A\,\mathbf{u}\rbrack\, d\mathbf{u} - \right. \\ & {+ {\int_{\mathcal{E}_{j}}\,}G_{j}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\,{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}\, d{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)},\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.68)

Using these notations, define the Lagrange functional


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{L}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G(\overline{\eta})\rbrack} & {= \mathcal{H}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G(\overline{\eta})\rbrack + \lambda w\lbrack W(\mathbf{u})\rbrack + \left\langle \overline{\mu},\mathbf{g}\lbrack G(\overline{\eta})\rbrack \right\rangle +} \\ & {\left. + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{h}^{(j)}\lbrack W(\mathbf{u}),G_{j}( \right.}{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\rbrack \right\rangle.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.69)

To get optimality conditions for the Lagrange functional, we will again employ the Gateaux derivative-based method; see (5.60, 5.4.1). The corresponding first-order optimality conditions have the form


$$\begin{aligned} {\ln\frac{W^{*}(\mathbf{u})}{W_{0}(\mathbf{u})}} & {+ 1 + \lambda +} \\ \left. + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{j},\mathbf{D}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.},\, \middle| \, h = \right. & {\left. \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + A\,\mathbf{u}\rbrack \right\rangle = 0,} \\ {\ln\frac{G_{j}^{*}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})}{G_{j}^{0}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})} + 1 + \mu_{j}} & {+ \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)} \right\rangle = 0,} \\ {j =} & {\overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.70)

The solution of these equations within the Lagrange multipliers λ, μ1, …, μs, and ${\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)}$ is given by


$$\begin{aligned} {W^{*}(\mathbf{u}) = W_{0}} & {(\mathbf{u})\exp\lbrack - 1 - \lambda -} \\ {{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{j},\mathbf{D}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.},} & {\,\left| \, r = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + A\,\mathbf{u}\rbrack \right\rangle\rbrack,} \\ {G_{j}^{*}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}) = G_{j}^{0}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})} & {\exp\left\lbrack {- 1 - \mu_{j} - \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack,} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.71)

The Lagrange multipliers λ and μ1, …, μs can be eliminated using the normalization conditions (5.28). Then formulas (5.4.2) yield the following entropy-optimal estimates for the PDFs of the RPM-Rel model parameters and measurement noises:


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}W^{*}(\mathbf{u}) = W_{0}(\mathbf{u}) \times} \\ & {\times \frac{\exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{j},\mathbf{D}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{r}) \right.},\, \middle| \, r = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + \Delta\,\mathbf{u}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack}{\mathcal{W}({\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)})},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\quad\quad G_{j}^{*}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)}) = G_{j}^{0}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\frac{\exp\left\lbrack {- {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)} \right\rangle}} \right\rbrack}{\mathcal{G}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)})},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.72)

where


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{W}({\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)}) = {\int_{\mathcal{U}}W_{0}}(\mathbf{u}) \times} \\ & {\times \exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{D}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{r}) \right.},\, \middle| \, r = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + \Delta\,\mathbf{u}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack d\mathbf{u},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\mathcal{G}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = {\int_{\mathcal{E}}G_{j}^{0}}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\exp\left\lbrack {- \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack d{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.73)

Like for the randomized models of the RPM-Orig class (see (5.4.1)), the entropy-optimal PDFs are parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers and represent exponential functions.

5.4.3Randomized models of the RPM-Orig class with input and output errors

Consider the problem (5.2.3, 5.36, 5.2.3) and write out the Lagrange functional:


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{L}\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\mu),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack} & {= \mathcal{H}\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\mu),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack + \lambda w\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\mu)\rbrack + \left\langle \overline{\eta},\mathbf{q}\lbrack\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi}\rbrack \right\rangle +} \\ & {+ \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{c}^{(j)}\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\mu),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack \right\rangle,} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.74)

where $\lambda;\overline{\eta};\overline{\theta}$ —Lagrange multipliers for corresponding constraints:


$$\begin{array}{r} {w\lbrack P(\mathbf{a})\rbrack = 1 - {\int_{\mathcal{R}}F}(\mathbf{a},\mu)d\mathbf{a}d\mu = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.75)


$$\begin{aligned} & {\mathbf{c}^{(j)}\lbrack F(\mathbf{a},\mu),\overline{Q}(\overline{\xi})\rbrack = \mathbf{y}^{(j)} - \left\lbrack {{\int_{\mathcal{R}}F}(\mathbf{a},\mu)\hat{\mathbf{y}}(t_{j},\mathbf{a},\mu)\, d\mathbf{a}\, d\mu} \right\rbrack +} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad} + {\int_{\Xi_{j}}\,}Q_{j}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\,{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}\, d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} = 0,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.77)

To get optimality conditions for the Lagrange functional, we will again employ the Gâteaux derivative-based method. The corresponding first-order optimality conditions have the form


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}F^{*}(\mathbf{a},\mu) = F_{0}(\mathbf{a},\mu) \times} \\ & {\times \frac{\left. \exp\lbrack - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{B}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.} + \mu(t_{j},\tau_{h}),\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle\rbrack}{\mathcal{F}({\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)})},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}Q_{j}^{*}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)}) = Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\frac{\exp\lbrack - \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle\rbrack}{\mathcal{Q}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)})},\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.78)

where


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{F}({\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)}) = {\int_{\mathcal{R}}F_{0}}(\mathbf{a},\mu) \times} \\ & {\exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathbf{B}^{(j)}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.} + \mu(t_{j},\tau_{h}),\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack d\mathbf{a},} \\ & {\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{Q}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = {\int_{\Xi}Q_{j}^{0}}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\exp\left\lbrack {- \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(5.79)

The obtained PDF functions are parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers $\overline{\theta},$ which are determined from the balance equations.

5.5Equations for Lagrange Multipliers

All entropy-optimal PDFs belong to the class of exponential functions parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers ${\overline{\theta}}^{1},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{s};$ see the formulas derived in the previous section. For calculating the Lagrange multipliers, we have to solve the equations that are obtained from the balance constraints (5.24, 5.31) with the entropy-optimal PDFs (5.64, 5.4.2).

1. RPM-Orig model with output errors

To form the corresponding equations, introduce the following auxiliary notations.

  • the mean output of the model with the entropy-optimal randomized parameters


    $$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\mathbb{Y}_{j}(\overline{\theta}) = \mathcal{P}^{( - 1)}(\overline{\theta}){\int_{\mathcal{A}}P_{0}}(\mathbf{a}) \times} \\ {\times \exp} & {\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.}\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack \times} \\ & \left. \quad \times \mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h})\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack d\mathbf{a}; \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.80)

  • the mean entropy-“worst” measurement noises


    $$\begin{aligned} {{\mathbb{Q}}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = \mathcal{Q}_{j}^{( - 1)}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)})\int_{\Xi_{j}}} & {Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\exp\left\lbrack {- \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)},} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.81)

In these expressions, $\overline{\theta} = \lbrack{\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)}\rbrack.$

Using the balance constraints (5.24), write the equations of the Lagrange multipliers in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbb{Y}_{j}(\overline{\theta}) + {\mathbb{Q}}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = \mathbf{y}^{(j)},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.82)

2. RPM-Rel model with output errors

By analogy with the previous case, introduce the following auxiliary notations:

  • the mean output of the model with the entropy-optimal randomized parameters


    $$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad{\mathbb{Z}}_{j}(\overline{\theta}) = \mathcal{W}^{( - 1)}(\overline{\theta}){\int_{\mathcal{U}}W_{0}}(\mathbf{u}) \times} \\ & \left. \times \exp\lbrack - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathcal{D}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.}\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + \right. \\ & {\left. \text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad} A\,\mathbf{u}\rbrack \right\rangle\rbrack \times} \\ & \left. \times \mathcal{D}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h})\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + A\,\mathbf{u}\rbrack d\mathbf{u}; \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.83)

  • the mean entropy-“worst” measurement noises


    $$\begin{aligned} {\mathbb{G}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = \mathcal{G}_{j}^{( - 1)}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)})\int_{\mathcal{E}}} & {G_{j}^{0}({\overline{\eta}}^{(j)})\exp\left\lbrack {- \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack d{\overline{\eta}}^{(j)},} \\ & {\, j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.84)

Using the balance constraints (5.31), write the equations of the Lagrange multipliers in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{Z}}_{j}(\overline{\theta}) + \mathbb{G}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = \mathbf{y}^{(j)},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.85)

3. RPM-Orig model with input and output errors

To form the corresponding equations, introduce the following auxiliary notations.

  • the mean output of the model with the entropy-optimal randomized parameters


    $$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\quad\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathbb{Y}_{j}(\overline{\theta}) = \mathcal{F}^{( - 1)}(\overline{\theta}){\int_{\mathcal{R}}F_{0}}(\mathbf{a},\mu) \times} \\ & {\times \exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.} + \mu(t_{j},\tau_{h})\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack \times} \\ & \left. \text{\quad\quad} \times \mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) + \mu(t_{j},\tau_{h})\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack d\mathbf{a}d\mu. \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.86)

  • the mean entropy-“worst” measurement noises


    $$\begin{aligned} {{\mathbb{Q}}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = \mathcal{Q}_{j}^{( - 1)}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)})\int_{\Xi_{j}}} & {Q_{j}^{0}({\overline{\xi}}^{(j)})\exp\left\lbrack {- \left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack d{\overline{\xi}}^{(j)},} \\ & {j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (5.87)

Then, write the equations of the Lagrange multipliers in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbb{Y}_{j}(\overline{\theta}) + {\mathbb{Q}}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}) = \mathbf{y}^{(j)},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(5.88)

As a matter of fact, equations (5.82, 5.85, 5.88) possess some specifics. They incorporate functions that depend on the Lagrange multipliers; in turn, the latter are calculated by integration over the multidimensional domains of definition of the parameters and measurement noises. To be fair, these domains have a simple structure, representing multidimensional parallelepipeds. In the sequel, they will be called the parameterized integral components (PICs) in order to underline their specifics. PICs calculation and solution of the balance equations are separate and nontrivial problems. Some approaches to solve these problems will be considered in detail in Chapter 6.

CHAPTER 6 ENTROPY-ROBUST ESTIMATION METHODS FOR PROBABILITIES OF BELONGING IN MACHINE LEARNING PROCEDURES

DOI: 10.1201/9781003306566-6

The constrained maximization of entropy functionals represents an efficient tool for solving various problems, including the estimation of the probabilities of belonging to certain intervals for the model parameters and measurement noises. The original model parameters and measurement noises of the interval type are transformed into auxiliary nonnegative variables lying within the unit interval, which are treated as the probabilities of belonging [67]. Such a probabilistic interpretation of the auxiliary parameters and measurement noises justifies the applicability of entropy functionals to find best values of the auxiliary and original variables. The estimation algorithms for the probabilities of belonging are machine learning algorithms. The estimation problem is formulated as an entropy-linear programming problem with an admissible set that is constructed using available learning data arrays.

6.1Entropy-Robust Estimation Algorithms for Probabilities of Belonging

An important class of the parameterized models used in ML procedures consists of the models with the interval-type quasi randomized parameters; their values are defined by the probabilities of belonging to corresponding intervals. Denote this class of models by RPM-QuaRand and their parameters by c. These models have deterministic parameters with unknown values. Hence, the RPM-QuaRand models can be considered as randomized models with the PDFs R(c) = Rδ(c* − c).

The parameters c are of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{c} \in \mathcal{C} = \otimes_{i = 1}^{n}\mathcal{C}_{i} = \lbrack c_{i}^{-},c_{i}^{+}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.1)

Introduce the probability pi that the parameter ci takes some value within the interval 𝒞i. The values pi will be called the probabilities of belonging (PO). Then a parameter ci can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. c_{i} = c_{i}^{-} + (c_{i}^{+} - c_{i}^{-})\, p_{i},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}^{-} + C\,\mathbf{p},\quad C = \text{diag}\lbrack(c_{i}^{+} - c_{i}^{-})\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,n}\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.2)

The probabilities of belonging are


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I} = \lbrack\mathbf{0} \leq \mathbf{p} \leq \mathbf{1}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.3)

Some statements also involve an additional constraint known as the complete set condition (the normalization condition), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}p_{i}} = 1.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.4)

The definition of the probabilities of belonging and their properties (6.3, 6.4) formally match the definition of the relative parameters (4.96, 4.97). However, there exist some differences of principle between them. The relative parameters u are the randomized variables characterized by a given PDF. In contrast, the probabilities of belonging p are nonrandom variables taking values within the unit nonnegative cube.

A dynamic model of the RPM-QuaRand class generates a unique trajectory, that is, described by the following equality at discrete times $j = \overline{0,s} = \mathcal{T}_{s}$:


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{s}\lbrack j,\mathbf{p}\rbrack} & {= \mathcal{S}\lbrack\mathbf{x}(j,\tau),\,\mathbf{c}^{-} + C\,\mathbf{p};(j,\tau) \in \mathcal{T}_{s}\rbrack,} \\ \mathbf{c} & {= \mathbf{c}^{-} + C\,\mathbf{p}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.5)

Here 𝒮 means an integral functional.

This problem has an additive model of measurements: in each jth measurement, the noises are characterized by an interval-type vector


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\zeta}}^{(j)} \in \mathcal{Z}^{(j)} = \otimes_{i = 1}^{m}\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{(j)},\text{\quad\quad}\mathcal{Z}_{i}^{(j)} = \lbrack\zeta_{-}^{(j)}(i),\zeta_{+}^{(j)}(i)\rbrack,\quad j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.6)

Introduce the probability of belonging qi(j) that the element ζi(j) of the noise vector takes some value from the interval 𝒵i(j). The probabilities qi(j) lie within the unit nonnegative interval and the probability vector is


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{q}^{(j)} \in \mathcal{I} = \lbrack\mathbf{0} \leq \mathbf{q}^{(j)} \leq \mathbf{1}\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.7)

In some cases, like for the probabilities of belonging of the model parameters, it is necessary to consider the normalization conditions


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}q_{i}^{(j)}} = 1,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.8)

The noise vector can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. {\overline{\zeta}}^{(j)} = {\overline{\zeta}}_{-}^{(j)}(i) + L_{j}\mathbf{q}^{(j)},\text{\quad\quad}L_{j} = \text{diag}\,\lbrack\zeta_{+}^{(j)}(i) - \zeta_{-}^{(j)}(i),\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,m}\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.9)

The measurable output of the RPM-QuaRand model (6.5) is a unique trajectory w[j, p, q] composed of an additive mix of the vectors s[j, p] (6.5) and ${\overline{\zeta}}^{(j)}$ (6.9), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{w}\lbrack j,(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}^{(j)}\rbrack = \mathbf{s}\lbrack j,\mathbf{p}\rbrack + {\overline{\zeta}}^{(j)} - + L_{j}\,\mathbf{q}^{(j)},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.10)

Therefore, as its variables the RPM-QuaRand model incorporates the probabilities of belonging $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}^{j},\, j = \overline{1,s}.$

6.1.1ML algorithm for RPM-QuaRand model with normalized probabilities of belonging

Consider the case in which the vectors p and q(1), …, q(s) are normalized and there exists information about the prior probabilities of belonging, p0 and q0(1), …, q0(s).

Throughout the book, it has been repeatedly mentioned that the ML procedures operate under uncertainty measured in terms of entropy. Therefore, we will characterize the quality of estimation using the entropy approach. Since the measurement noises are additive, let us adopt the generalized Boltzmann information entropy [141]


$$\begin{array}{r} {H_{B}(\mathbf{p},Q) = - \left\langle \mathbf{p},\mathbf{ln}\frac{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{p}_{0}} \right\rangle - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle \mathbf{q}^{(j)},\mathbf{ln}\frac{\mathbf{q}^{(j)}}{\mathbf{q}_{0}^{(j)}} \right\rangle},Q = \lbrack\mathbf{q}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{q}^{(s)}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.11)

Here ln( • ) denotes a vector with corresponding elements  • . Recall that the variables in this expression are nonnegative. Then the entropy-robust estimation problem for the RPM-QuaRand model with the normalized probabilities of belonging can be written as follows:

  • maximize the entropy function (6.11)


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H_{B}(\mathbf{p},Q)\Rightarrow\max_{\mathbf{p},Q} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (6.12)

  • subject to

    • –the normalization conditions


      $$\begin{array}{r} {\left\langle \mathbf{p},\mathbf{1} \right\rangle = 1,\text{\quad\quad}\left\langle \mathbf{q}^{(j)},\mathbf{1} \right\rangle = 1,\quad j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
      (6.13)

      and

    • –the balance constraints


      $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{S}\lbrack\mathbf{x}\lbrack j,\tau\rbrack,\,\mathbf{c}^{-} + C\,\mathbf{p};(j,\tau) \in \mathcal{T}_{s}\rbrack + {\overline{\zeta}}_{-}^{(j)} + L_{j}\,\mathbf{q}^{(j)} = \mathbf{y}\lbrack j\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
      (6.14)

The constraints (6.13, 6.14) extract an admissible set Υ from the unit nonnegative (m + r)-dimensional cube ℐ.

In the general case, this problem is an entropy-nonlinear programming problem. Its nonlinear properties follow from the balance constraints (6.14), which contain a nonlinear functional 𝒮 of the parameters. Note that the randomized approach to estimation leads to the optimization problems of entropy-linear functional programming.

Consequently, the entropy-robust ML algorithm for the RPM-QuaRand model with the normalized probabilities of belonging has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. {(\mathbf{p},Q)}^{*} = \arg\max_{(\mathbf{p},Q)}\lbrack H_{B},\, \middle| \,(\mathbf{p},Q) \in \Upsilon\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.15)

6.1.2ML algorithm for RPM-QuaRand model with interval-type probabilities of belonging

For the models of this class, the probabilities of belonging take values within the nonnegative r-dimensional cube—the normalization condition is not imposed. The estimation problems arising for these RPM-QuaRand models have two modifications depending on entropy choice, namely, the statements with the Boltzmann or Fermi entropies [149].

When using the generalized Boltzmann information entropy (6.11), the Boltzmann entropy-robust estimation problem for the RPM-QuaRand model with the interval-type probabilities of belonging can be written as follows:

  • maximize the entropy function (6.11)


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H_{B}(\mathbf{p},Q)\Rightarrow\max_{\mathbf{p},Q} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (6.16)

  • subject to:

    • –the interval-type conditions


      $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{q}^{(j)} \in \mathcal{I},\quad j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
      (6.17)

      and

    • –the balance constraints


      $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{S}\lbrack\mathbf{x}\lbrack j,\tau\rbrack,\,\mathbf{c}^{-} + C\,\mathbf{p};(j,\tau) \in \mathcal{T}_{s}\rbrack + {\overline{\zeta}}_{-}^{(j)} + L_{j}\,\mathbf{q}^{(j)} = \mathbf{y}^{(j)},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
      (6.18)

The constraints (6.17, 6.18) extract an admissible set Γ from the unit nonnegative r-dimensional cube ℐ.

The Boltzmann entropy-robust ML algorithm for the RPM-QuaRand model with the interval-type probabilities of belonging has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. {(\mathbf{p},Q)}^{*} = \arg\max_{(\mathbf{p},Q)}\lbrack H_{B},\, \middle| \,(\mathbf{p},Q) \in \Gamma\rbrack. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.19)

In some applications, it is necessary to choose the generalized Fermi information entropy in order to eliminate the interval-type conditions:


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}H_{F}(\mathbf{p},Q) = - \left\langle \mathbf{p},\mathbf{ln}\frac{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{p}_{0}} \right\rangle - \left\langle (\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{p}),\mathbf{ln}(\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{p}) \right\rangle -} \\ & {- {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left( {\left\langle \mathbf{q}^{(j)},\mathbf{ln}\frac{\mathbf{q}^{(j)}}{\mathbf{q}_{0}^{(j)}} \right\rangle + \left\langle (\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{q}^{(j)}),\mathbf{ln}(\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{q}^{(j)}) \right\rangle} \right)},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.20)

where Q = [q(1), …, q(s)].

Clearly, the definition of this function explicitly considers the interval property of the variables. The admissible set is characterized by the balance constraints only.

The Fermi entropy-robust estimation problem for the RPM-QuaRand model with the interval-type probabilities of belonging can be written as follows:

  • maximize the entropy function (6.1.2)


    $$\begin{array}{r} \left. H_{F}(\mathbf{p},Q)\Rightarrow\max_{\mathbf{p},Q} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
    (6.21)

  • subject to the balance constraints


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{S}\lbrack\mathbf{x}\lbrack j,\tau\rbrack,\,\mathbf{c}^{-} + C\,\mathbf{p};(j,\tau) \in \mathcal{T}_{s}\rbrack + {\overline{\zeta}}_{-}^{(j)} + L_{j}\,\mathbf{q}^{(j)} = \mathbf{y}\lbrack j\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
    (6.22)

The constraints (6.22) extract an admissible set Θ from the unit nonnegative n-dimensional cube ℐ.

The Fermi entropy-robust ML algorithm for the RPM-QuaRand model with the interval-type probabilities of belonging has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. {(\mathbf{p},Q)}^{*} = \arg\max_{(\mathbf{p},Q)}\lbrack H_{F},\, \middle| \,(\mathbf{p},Q) \in \Theta\rbrack, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.23)

where Θ is the set defined by the balance constraints. Note that the problem (6.21, 6.22) contains (r + ms) less constraints than the problem (6.16–6.18). Due to this feature, the computational complexity of the estimation problem (6.21, 6.22) is smaller in comparison with its counterpart (6.16–6.18).

6.2Functional Description of Dynamic RPM-QuaRand Models

As established in the previous section, the estimation problems for the probabilities of belonging generally represent finite-dimensional nonlinear programming problems with entropy objective functions. The nonlinearity of these problems is caused by the nonlinearity of the functional 𝒮 that characterizes the model (6.5). Consider the models with one input and one output that are measured at discrete times from the interval 𝒯.

1. Dynamic models with unstructured power nonlinearities

A functional description of such a model has the following form


$$\begin{aligned} {s\lbrack j\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) = 0}^{K_{h}}w_{h}}}} & {\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack x\lbrack j - n_{1}\rbrack\cdots x\lbrack j - n_{h}\rbrack,} \\ & {j \geq maxK_{h}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.24)

(Also, see Fig. 4.8.)

Its dynamic and nonlinear properties are reflected by the multidimensional pulse characteristics $w_{h}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack,\, h = \overline{1,R},$ with a finite “memory” Kh, i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} {w_{h}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack} & {\neq 0,\quad\text{for}\,\, 0 \leq (n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) \leq K_{h};} \\ {w_{h}\lbrack n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}\rbrack} & {= 0,\quad\text{for}\,\,(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) > K_{h}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.25)

As the model parameters consider the ordinates of its pulse characteristics. A lexicographical ordering of the variables yields


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. (n_{1},\ldots,n_{h})\rightarrow v,\text{\quad\quad}v = \overline{1,V_{h}},\,\, V_{h} = (K_{h} + 1)\, h, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.26)

Define a vector c(h) = {c1(h),…,cVh(h)} composed of the ordinates of the pulse characteristic wh[n1, …, nh]. Perform a similar operation with the products x[j − n1]⋯x[j − nh]. Introduce another vector


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{X}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack = \left\{ x_{1}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack,\ldots,x_{V_{h}}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\}} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.27)

composed of the lexicographically ordered products x[j − n1]⋯x[j − nh]. Then the model equation (6.1.2) can be transformed into


$$\begin{array}{r} {s\lbrack j\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left\langle \mathbf{c}^{(h)},\mathbf{X}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.28)

As the result of all these manipulations, the original nonlinear model (6.1.2) has been reduced to its linear analog (6.28) of considerably higher dimension.

Using the probabilities of belonging p from Section 6.3, let us write the parameter vector c(h) as


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{c}^{(h)} = \mathbf{c}_{-}^{(h)} + C^{(h)}\mathbf{p}^{(h)},\,\, C_{h} =} & \left. \text{diag}\,\lbrack(c_{i}^{(h, + )} - c_{i}^{(h, - )})\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,V_{h}}\rbrack, \right. \\ & {h = \overline{1,R}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.29)

Substituting (6.29) into (6.28) gives the equation


$$\begin{aligned} {s\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left\langle C_{h}\,\mathbf{p}^{(h)},\mathbf{X}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle},} \\ {.\hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left\langle \mathbf{c}_{-}^{(h)},\mathbf{X}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.30)

2. Dynamic models with structured power nonlinearities

For this class of dynamic models, a functional description has the following form:


$$\begin{array}{r} {s\lbrack j\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{K_{h}}\left( {w_{h}\lbrack n\rbrack x\lbrack j - n\rbrack} \right)^{h}}},\text{\quad\quad}j > K.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.31)

(Also, see Fig. 4.11a.) Here the dynamic properties are reflected by the pulse characteristics $w_{h}\lbrack n\rbrack,\, h = \overline{1,R},$ with a finite “memory” Kh, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {w_{h}\lbrack n\rbrack \neq 0,\quad\text{for}\,\, 0 \leq n \leq K_{h};\text{\quad\quad}r_{h}\lbrack n\rbrack = 0,\quad\text{for}\,\, n > K_{h}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.32)

As the model parameters consider the ordinates of the pulse characteristics. In other words, the parameters make the vector


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{c}^{(h)} = \left\{ c_{1}^{(h)},\ldots,c_{K_{h}}^{(h)} \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.33)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {c_{n}^{(h)} = w_{h}\lbrack n\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}n = \overline{0,K_{h}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.34)

Using the probabilities of belonging p, write the parameter vector c(h) in the form (6.29). Substituting these equalities into (6.31) yields the model equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {s\lbrack j\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left( {\left\langle \mathbf{c}_{-}^{(h)},\mathbf{x}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle + \left\langle C_{h}\,\mathbf{p}^{(h)},\mathbf{x}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle} \right)^{h}},} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.35)

where x[j] = {x[j],…,x[j−Kh]}.

Thus, the relation between the model's output and parameters is essentially nonlinear (more specifically, a power function).

3. Dynamic models with structured power nonlinearities

For this class of dynamic models, a functional description has the following form:


$$\begin{array}{r} {s\lbrack j\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{K_{h}}w_{h}}}\lbrack n\rbrack x^{h}\lbrack j - n\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}j > K.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.36)

(Also, see Fig. 4.11b.) Its dynamic properties are described by the pulse characteristics $w_{h}\lbrack n\rbrack,\, h = \overline{1,R},$ with a finite “memory” Kh (6.32). As the parameters of this model adopt the ordinates of its pulse characteristics, i.e., the parameter vector is c(h) (6.34). Define a vector ${\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}}^{h}\lbrack j\rbrack$ composed of xh[j], …, xh[j − Kh]. Then the model equation (6.36) can be transformed into


$$\begin{array}{r} {s\lbrack j\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left\langle \mathbf{c},{\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle},\text{\quad\quad}j > K.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.37)

Using the expression (6.29) in this equality, write


$$\begin{aligned} {s\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left\langle C_{h}\,\mathbf{p}^{(h)},{\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle},} \\ {\hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left\langle \mathbf{c}_{-}^{(h)},{\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack \right\rangle}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.38)

Thus, the models of this structural class are linear in their parameters.

6.3Optimality Conditions and Structure of Entropy-Optimal Probabilities of Belonging

The entropy-robust estimation problems for the RPM-QuaRand models are classified as finite-dimensional entropy-nonlinear programming problems. Their nonlinear properties fully depend on the nonlinearity of the RPM-QuaRand model. In particular, if the dynamic model is represented by a functional Volterra series with the structure shown in Fig. 4.11a, then the admissible set in the estimation problems is described by a system of equalities with power nonlinearities. In this case, the admissible set often has a nonconvex configuration, and the optimality conditions turn out to be local and therefore can be used only numerically. As a result, we fail in extracting common structural properties of the solutions (the probabilities of belonging) from these conditions. On the other hand, for the one-dimensional RPM-QuaRand models that are reducible to the linear form (6.30, 6.38), we can establish global optimality conditions and analyze the structural properties of the solutions.

1. Normalized probabilities of belonging

The general problem within the functional model framework is characterized by equalities (6.12–6.14). It will be adapted to the case in which the functional model is one-dimensional and reducible to the linear form (6.30):


$$\begin{aligned} {s\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{i}^{(h)}}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack + \zeta_{j}^{-} + Z_{j}q_{j},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.39)


$$\begin{aligned} {\hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}c_{-}^{(h)}}}(i)z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack,} \\ {z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \delta_{i}^{(h)}x_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}\delta_{i}^{(h)} = c_{i}^{(h, + )} - c_{i}^{(h, - )},\quad i = \overline{1,V_{h}},} \\ Z_{j} & {= \zeta_{j}^{+} - \zeta_{j}^{-},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.40)

Then the constraints (6.13, 6.14) in the estimation problem (6.12) take the following form.

  • The normalization conditions for the probabilities of belonging of the model parameters in the power blocks of the functional model are


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{i}^{(h)}} = 1,\quad h = \overline{1,R};} \\ \end{array}$$
    (6.41)

  • The normalization conditions for the probabilities of belonging of the measurement noises are


    $$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}q_{j}} = 1;} \\ \end{array}$$
    (6.42)

  • The empirical balance conditions are


    $$\begin{aligned} & {\widetilde{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{i}^{(h)}}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack + Z_{j}q_{j} - y\lbrack j\rbrack = 0,\quad j = \overline{1,s},} \\ & {\widetilde{s}\lbrack j\rbrack = \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + \zeta_{j}^{-}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
    (6.43)

The entropy function is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {H_{B}(P,Q) = - {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{i}^{(h)}}}\,\ln\frac{p_{i}^{(h)}}{{\widetilde{p}}_{i}^{(h)}} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}q_{j}}\,\ln\frac{q_{j}}{{\widetilde{q}}_{j}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.44)

Thus, the estimation problem can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. H_{B}(P,Q)\Rightarrow\max \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(6.45)

subject to the constraints (6.41, 6.42, 6.43).

In this problem, the admissible set Υ is described by a system of equalities and hence it represents a constrained optimization problem. To obtain optimality conditions, let us define the Lagrange function


$$\begin{aligned} L_{B} & {= H_{B}(P,Q) + {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\lambda_{h}}\left( {1 - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{i}^{(h)}}} \right) + \mu\left( {1 - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}q_{j}}} \right)} \\ & {+ {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\theta^{(j)}}\left( {y\lbrack j\rbrack - \widetilde{s}\lbrack j\rbrack - {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{i}^{(h)}}}\delta_{i}^{(h)}x_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack + Z_{j}q_{j}} \right).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.46)

Here λ1, …, λR; μ; θ1, …, θs denote the Lagrange multipliers for the corresponding constraints (6.41, 6.42, 6.43). The first-order optimality conditions in the direct variables (P, Q) yield the following system of equations:


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial L}{\partial p_{i}^{(h)}} & {= - \ln\frac{p_{i}^{(h)}}{{\widetilde{p}}_{i}^{(h)}} - 1 - \lambda_{h} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\theta_{j}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack = 0,} \\ h & {= \overline{1,s};\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,V_{h}}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.47)


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_{j}} = \ln\frac{(1 - q_{j}){\widetilde{q}}_{j}}{q_{j}} - \mu - Z_{j} = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.48)

In combination with the normalization conditions (6.41, 6.42), equations (6.47, 6.48) lead to the following expressions for the entropy-optimal probabilities of belonging of the model parameters and measurement noises that are parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers θ1, …, θs:


$$\begin{aligned} {\lbrack p_{i}^{(h)}\rbrack}^{*} & {= \frac{{\widetilde{p}}_{i}^{(h)}\exp\left( {- {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\theta_{j}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack} \right)}{{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{V_{h}}{\widetilde{p}}_{k}^{(h)}}\exp\left( {- {\sum\limits_{m = 1}^{s}\theta_{j}}z_{k}^{(h)}\lbrack m\rbrack} \right)},} \\ q_{j}^{*} & {= \frac{{\widetilde{q}}_{j}\exp( - \theta_{j}Z_{j})}{{\sum\limits_{m = 1}^{s}{\widetilde{q}}_{m}}\exp( - \theta_{m}Z_{m})}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.49)


$$\begin{array}{r} {h = \overline{1,R},\quad i = \overline{1,V_{h}},\quad j = \overline{1,s}} \\ \end{array}$$

Introduce Vh functions of integer argument $P^{(h)}\lbrack i\rbrack,\, i = \overline{}1,V_{h},$ whose values are defined by the entropy-optimal probabilities of belonging. By this definition, $P^{(h)}\lbrack i\rbrack,\, i = \overline{}1,V_{h},$ represent distribution functions for the probabilities of belonging. According to (6.49), they are exponential functions.

The Lagrange multipliers θ1, …, θs are calculated from the empirical balance constraints (6.43) after substitution of the entropy-optimal probabilities of belonging (6.49). For notational convenience, introduce


$$\begin{aligned} {S\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + \zeta_{j}^{-} - y\lbrack j\rbrack,} \\ {\varphi^{(h)}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s})} & {= {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{(V_{h})}{\widetilde{p}}_{k}^{(h)}}\,\exp( - {\sum\limits_{l = 1}^{s}\theta_{l}}z_{k}^{(h)}\lbrack l\rbrack),} \\ {\psi_{j}^{(h)}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s})} & {= {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{(V_{h})}{\widetilde{p}}_{k}^{(h)}}\, z_{k}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack\,\exp( - {\sum\limits_{l = 1}^{s}\theta_{l}}z_{k}^{(h)}\lbrack l\rbrack),} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.50)

and


$$\begin{aligned} {\mu(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s}) = {\sum\limits_{l = 1}^{s}{\widetilde{q}}_{l}}} & {\exp( - \theta_{l}Z_{l}),\quad\nu_{j}(\theta_{j}) = {\widetilde{q}}_{j}Z_{j}\exp( - \theta_{j}Z_{j}),} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.51)

With these notations, the empirical balance constraints take the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\frac{\psi_{j}^{(h)}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s})}{\varphi^{(h)}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s})}} + \frac{\nu_{j}(\theta_{j})}{\mu(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s})} + S\lbrack j\rbrack = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.52)

2. Interval-type probabilities of belonging

The entropy-optimal estimation problem for the RPM-QuaRand model can be stated using the generalized Boltzmann information entropy (6.16–6.18). This form of the estimation problem involves a considerably larger number of constraints than the previous one (some of them are inequalities). Therefore, it moves to the class of finite-dimensional mathematical programming problem, and optimality conditions are defined by the Kuhn–Tucker theorem [134].

The solution procedure of the entropy-optimal estimation problem can be significantly simplified if we use the generalized Fermi information entropy (6.1.2) as the objective function. The interval properties of the probabilities of belonging for the model parameters and measurement noises are embedded in the entropy function, which makes the estimation problem a constrained optimization problem. Like before, optimality conditions can be derived using Lagrange's method of multipliers.

The Lagrange function for the problem (6.21, 6.22) takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {L_{F} = H_{F}(P,Q) + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\theta^{(j)}}\left( {y\lbrack j\rbrack - \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack - {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{i}^{(h)}}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack + \zeta_{j}^{-} + Z_{j}q_{j}} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.53)

The first-order optimality conditions are given by the system of inequalities


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial L}{\partial p_{i}^{(h)}} & {= \ln\, p_{i}^{(0,h)}\frac{1 - p_{i}^{(h)}}{p_{i}^{(h)}} - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\theta_{j}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack,} \\ h & {= \overline{1,R},\, i = \overline{1,V_{h}};} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.54)


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_{j}} = \ln\, q_{j}^{0}\frac{1 - q_{j}}{q_{j}} - \theta_{j}Z_{j} = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.55)

Then the entropy-optimal probabilities of belonging of the model parameters and measurement noises that are parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers have the form


$$\begin{aligned} p_{i}^{(h),*} & {= \frac{p_{i}^{(h,0)}}{p_{i}^{(h,0)} + \exp\left( {{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\theta_{j}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack j\rbrack} \right)},} \\ h & {= \overline{1,R},\quad i = \overline{1,V_{h}},} \\ q_{j}^{*} & {= \frac{q_{j}^{0}}{q_{j}^{0} + \exp(\theta_{j}Z_{j})},\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.56)

Clearly, the entropy-optimal probabilities of belonging lie within the unit intervals. To find the Lagrange multipliers, substitute the expressions (6.56) into the empirical balance constraints (6.22). By analogy with the previous case, introduce the following notations:


$$\begin{aligned} {S\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + \zeta_{j}^{-} - y\lbrack j\rbrack,} \\ {\varphi_{j}(\theta_{j})} & {= Z_{j}\frac{q_{j}^{0}}{q_{j}^{0} + \exp(\theta_{j}Z_{j}},} \\ {\psi_{j}^{(h)}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s})} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}\frac{p_{i}^{(h,0)}}{p_{i}^{(h,0)} + \exp\left( {{\sum\limits_{l = 1}^{s}\theta_{l}}z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack l\rbrack} \right)}}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(6.57)

Then the empirical balance equations can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\psi_{j}^{(h)}}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{s}) + \varphi_{j}(\theta_{j}) + S\lbrack j\rbrack = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(6.58)

The left-hand sides of equations (6.52, 6.58) incorporate strictly monotonically decreasing functions, which guarantees the existence of a unique solution. (The proof of this fact is left to the interested reader). Chapter 7 below describes an algorithm for solving such multiplicative-type equations.

CHAPTER 7 COMPUTATIONAL METHODS OF RANDOMIZED MACHINE LEARNING

DOI: 10.1201/9781003306566-7

The general randomized machine learning problem is formulated in terms of functional entropy-linear programming, which allows us to obtain the optimal solution structure parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers. To calculate their values, we have to solve the nonstandard nonlinear equations with the so-called parameterized integral components, which can be found only numerically. Therefore, it is impossible to analytically estimate such important parameters of computational procedures as the Lipschitz constant, the Hölder constant, the degree of smoothness, and others. For solving these equations, our idea is to extend the randomization approach to the computational algorithms intended for solving the RML problems. The randomization approach itself was declared and repeatedly used before; see [135]. However, the major properties of the randomized problem-oriented algorithms arise in the course of their implementation. In what follows, we will develop the algorithms for solving the empirical balance equations and calculating the multidimensional integrals on the basis of “packet” Monte Carlo simulations, which are implemented using heterogeneous-structure computing aids.

An important special class of the RML problems includes the machine learning problems with the probabilities of belonging and linear models. For this class, it is possible to obtain a structural representation of the optimal solutions parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers. The resulting balance constraints have a nonlinear form but without the integral components. For solving these equations, the multiplicative algorithms [140, 142] will be employed.

7.1Classes of Balance Equations in RML and ML Procedures

In Chapters 4 and 5, we have derived the empirical balance equations for the RPM-Orig, RPM-Rel and RPM-CauRand models, in which the role of variables is played by the Lagrange multipliers. An analysis of these equations (more specifically, of the functions that form their components) allows us to separate out two classes of the nonlinear equations for further study.

1. Equations with integral components

The equations of this class arise in the RML procedures with the RPM-Orig and RPM-Rel models (5.74–5.76). Recall that the equations under consideration contain the definite multidimensional integrals that are parameterized by the Lagrange multipliers. For example, for the RPMs with the original parameters (RPM-Orig), the integral components have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbb{M}_{j}(\theta) - \mathbf{y}^{(j)} = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.1)

where


$$\begin{aligned} & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\quad\mathbb{M}_{j}(\theta) = \mathcal{P}^{( - 1)}(\theta){\int_{\mathcal{A}}P_{0}}(\mathbf{a}) \times} \\ & {\times \exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.}\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack \times} \\ & \left. \quad \times \mathcal{B}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h})\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}\rbrack d\mathbf{a} + {\mathbb{Q}}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}), \right. \\ {j = \overline{1,s}.} & \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.2)

In these equalities, the matrix $\theta = \lbrack{\overline{\theta}}^{(1)},\ldots,{\overline{\theta}}^{(s)}\rbrack$ and the functions $\mathcal{P}(\overline{\theta})$ and ${\mathbb{Q}}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)})$ are given by (5.4.1) and (5.75), respectively.

A similar situation also occurs for the randomized parametric models with the relative parameters (RPM-Rel). The balance equations for this class of models can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{N}}_{j}(\overline{\theta}) - \mathbf{y}^{(j)} = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.3)

where


$$\begin{aligned} {{\mathbb{N}}_{j}(\theta) = \mathcal{W}^{( - 1)}(\theta){\int_{\mathcal{U}}W_{0}}(\mathbf{u}) \times} & \\ {\times \exp\left\lbrack \left. - {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{s}\left\langle {\overline{\theta}}^{(j)},\mathcal{D}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h}) \right.}\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + \Delta\mathbf{u}\rbrack \right\rangle \right\rbrack \times} & \\ \left. \times \mathcal{D}\lbrack\mathbf{x}((t_{j},\tau_{h})\, \middle| \, h = \overline{1,(j-1)}),\mathbf{a}^{-} + \Delta\mathbf{u}\rbrack d\mathbf{u} + \mathbb{G}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)}), \right. & \\ {j = \overline{1,s}.} & \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.4)

These expressions include 𝒲(θ) (5.4.2) and $\mathbb{G}_{j}({\overline{\theta}}^{(j)})$ (5.4.3). Note that the functionals ℬ and 𝒟 are of the power type.

Equations (7.1, 7.3) have a similar structure; using them, construct a class of nonlinear equations of the following form:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{B}\left\lbrack {{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbf{f})} \right\rbrack = \mathbf{0},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.5)

with the integral components


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbf{f}) = {\int_{\mathcal{E}}\exp}\left( {- E(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{e})} \right)d\mathbf{e},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.6)

or


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbf{f}) = {\int_{\mathcal{E}}E}(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{e})\exp\left( {- \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{e})} \right)d\mathbf{e},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.7)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {E(\mathbf{f},\mathbf{e}) = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) = 1}^{m}A_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h})}}}(\mathbf{f})\,{\prod\limits_{k = 1}^{h}e_{n_{k}}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.8)

The notations are as follows: f ∈ Rs as the vector of the desired variables, i.e., the parameters of the integral components; B(u) as a vector function that contains the vectors of the integral components (7.6) or (7.7); e ∈ E ⊂ Rr as the vector of the integration variables in (7.6, 7.7); finally, E as the r-dimensional parallelepiped.

A numerical solution procedure for equation (7.5) consists of the following steps: (a) calculating the integral components ℂ(f) under fixed variables f and (b) calculating the new vector of the variables that is the solution of the corresponding balance equations. This procedure corresponds to an iterative process with the structure illustrated in Fig. 7.1. It has the main iterative loop (see double lines) intended for solving equation (7.5) using the algorithm


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{f}^{(k + 1)} = \Omega\left( {\mathbf{f}^{k},\mathbf{B}\left\lbrack {{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbf{f}^{k})} \right\rbrack} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.9)

and also the secondary loop (see single lines) intended for calculating the function B with the integral components (7.6, 7.7).

Get back to equation (7.5), reducing it to a more convenient form for calculations. Introduce a change of variables that maps the space Rs and the domain ℰ ∈ Rr into the unit nonnegative cubes of proper dimensions. Since the domain ℰ is the r-dimensional parallelepiped, this transformation can be performed with the linear change of variables


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{w} = L\,\mathbf{e} - \mathbf{e}^{-},} & \left. \quad L = \text{diag}\,\lbrack 1/(e_{i}^{+} - e_{i}^{-}),\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,r}\rbrack, \right. \\ & {\mathbf{w} \in I^{r} \subset R_{+}^{r} = \lbrack\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1}\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.10)

The space Rs can be mapped into the unit nonnegative s-dimensional cube by nonlinear transformations, e.g.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{z} = \left\{ \frac{1}{1 + \exp f_{i}},\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,s} \right\},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z} \in I^{s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.11)

Using these transformations in (7.5), write


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{0},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z} \in I^{s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.12)

The integral components in this equation are


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{z}) = {\int_{I^{r}}\exp}\left( {- E(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w})} \right)d\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z} \in I^{s},\quad\mathbf{w} \in I^{r},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.13)

or


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z}) = \int_{I^{r}}} & {\exp\left( {- E(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w})} \right)\exp\left( {- E(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w})} \right)d\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z} \in I^{s},\quad\mathbf{w} \in I^{r},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.14)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {E(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w}) = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}{\sum\limits_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h}) = 1}^{m}A_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{h})}}}(\mathbf{z})\,{\prod\limits_{k = 1}^{h}w_{n_{k}}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.15)

Equation (7.12) will be solved by minimizing the residual function


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. F(\mathbf{z}) = \|\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{z})\|\Rightarrow\min_{\mathbf{z}},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{z} \in I^{s}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.16)

Note that it is impossible to establish any characteristics of the residual function analytically due to its integral components. Thus, we have to hypothesize several local minima of the function F(z) on the admissible set Is. Hence, the problem (7.16) comes to a global minimization of this function.

2. Equations with analytical functions

The balance equation of this class arise in the ML problems with the RPM-QuaRand models. The probabilities of belonging that characterize the parameters of these models can be normalized or interval-type. In the former case, the ML-based estimation algorithm is formulated as a constrained maximization problem for the generalized Boltzmann information entropy. In the latter case, it seems more convenient to choose the generalized Fermi information entropy.

Write the empirical balance equations for the normalized probabilities of belonging (6.52) in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {m_{j}(\mathbf{v}) = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\frac{\beta^{(h)}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s};\, j)}{\alpha^{(h)}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s})}} + \gamma_{j}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s}) = 0,\quad j = \overline{1,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.17)

where


$$\begin{aligned} {\alpha^{(h)}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s})} & {= {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{V_{h}}p_{k}^{(h,0)}}{\prod\limits_{l = 1}^{V_{h}}v_{l}^{z_{k}^{(h)}\lbrack l\rbrack}},} \\ {\beta_{k}^{(h)}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s};\, j)} & {= {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{V_{h}}z_{k}^{(h)}}\lbrack j\rbrack p_{k}^{(h,0)}{\prod\limits_{l = 1}^{V_{h}}v_{l}^{z_{k}^{(h)}\lbrack l\rbrack}},} \\ {\gamma_{j}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s})} & {= S\lbrack j\rbrack + \frac{q_{j}^{0}Z_{j}v_{j}^{Z_{j}}}{{\sum\limits_{l = 1}^{s}q_{j}^{0}}v_{j}^{Z_{l}}} - y\lbrack j\rbrack,} \\ v_{l} & {= \exp( - \theta_{l}),\text{\quad\quad}l = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.18)

The variables in these equations are defined on the nonnegative orthant R+s. Sometimes, they are called the exponential Lagrange multipliers.

Consider the empirical balance equations for the interval probabilities of belonging (6.58) and represent them in terms of the variables (v1, …, vs) ≥ 0 (7.18). Introduce the following notations:


$$\begin{aligned} {\varrho_{j}^{(h)}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s})} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{V_{h}}\frac{p_{i}^{(h,0)}}{p_{i}^{(h,0)} + {\prod\limits_{l = 1}^{s}v_{l}^{z_{i}^{(h)}\lbrack l\rbrack}}}},} \\ {\vartheta_{j}(v_{j})} & {= Z_{j}\frac{q_{j}^{0}}{q_{j}^{0} + v_{j}^{Z_{j}}},} \\ {\omega\lbrack j\rbrack} & {= \vartheta_{j}(v_{j}) + \hat{s}\lbrack j\rbrack + \zeta_{j}^{-} - y\lbrack j\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.19)

Write equations (6.58) as


$$\begin{array}{r} {n_{j}(\mathbf{v}) = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\varrho_{j}^{(h)}}(v_{1},\ldots,v_{s}) + \omega\lbrack j\rbrack = 0,\text{\quad\quad}j = \overline{1,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.20)

The final forms of the empirical balance equations allow us to identify some general properties of these equations, which can be fruitful for choosing appropriate computational methods.

7.2Monte Carlo Packet Iterations for Global Optimization

The RML algorithms for the RPM-Orig and RPM-Rel models are intended for solving the empirical balance equations, in which the role of variables is played by the Lagrange multipliers or by the auxiliary variables taking their values within the unit nonnegative cube. An approach to design numerical methods proceeds from minimization of a residual function (generally, a quadratic norm). In an RML problem, there exists an algorithmically defined relation between the residual function and variables, and this feature of the problem finally reduces it to a global minimization problem. Under such conditions, the Monte Carlo method seems to be an suitable design tool for RML algorithms.

Vast amounts of literature have been published dealing with applications of the Monte Carlo method in different global optimization problems. Some insight into these problems and methods to solve them can be gained from [135, 158, 171–173, 196, 199].

In contrast to the existing methods, the idea put forward here is to use simple Monte Carlo simulations, i.e., the generation of independent random vectors with the uniform distribution on the nonnegative unit cube.

7.2.1Canonical form of global optimization problem

Consider the global minimization problem


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. f(\mathbf{x})\Rightarrow\text{globmin} \right. \\ & \text{subject~to~the~following~constraints:} \\ & {\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{x}} = \left\{ \mathbf{x}:\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \mathbf{0},\,\mathbf{x} \in R^{d} \right\},\quad\mathbf{g} \in R^{r},\, r < d.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.21)

The objective function f(x) satisfies the Hölder condition with constants H > 0 and w > 0, i.e., its modulus of continuity has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \omega(t) = \max_{(\widetilde{\mathbf{v}},\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \in R^{d}\mspace{2mu}:\|\widetilde{\mathbf{v}} - \widetilde{\mathbf{y}}\| \leq t} \middle| f(\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}) - f(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}) \middle| \leq Ht^{w}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.22)

The functions g(x) in (7.22) are assumed to be continuous.

Write the canonical form of the problem (7.21) as


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. F(\mathbf{z})\Rightarrow\text{globmin} \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.23)


$$\begin{aligned} & \text{subject~to~the~following~constraints:} \\ & {\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{K}_{\mathbf{z}} = \mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{z}}{\cap Z_{+}^{d}},} \\ & {Z_{+}^{d} = \left\{ \mathbf{z}:\mathbf{0} \leq \mathbf{z} \leq \mathbf{1} \right\} \subset R^{d},} \\ & {\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{z}} = \left\{ \mathbf{z}:\mathbf{w}(\mathbf{z}) \leq \mathbf{0},\,\mathbf{z} \in Z_{+}^{d} \right\},\quad\mathbf{w} \in R^{r},\, r < d.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.24)

A relation between the original problem and its canonical form is defined by a continuously differentiable bijective transformation of the variables, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x}),\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x} = \mathcal{T}^{( - 1)}(\mathbf{z}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.25)

In fact, quite a few transformations answer these conditions, e.g.,


$$\begin{aligned} & {\mathbf{z} = \left\{ \frac{1}{1 + exp( - a_{i}x_{i})},\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,d} \right\},} \\ & {\mathbf{x} = \left\{ \frac{1}{a_{i}}\ln\frac{z_{i}}{1 - z_{i}},\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,d} \right\}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.26)

In many applications, the domain of definition of the variables x is not the entire space Rd but its subset—the d-dimensional parallelepiped Πx. Then the problem (7.21) is stated as follows:


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. f(\mathbf{x})\Rightarrow\text{globmin} \right. \\ & \text{subject~to~the~constraints} \\ & {\mathbf{x} \in \Pi_{\mathbf{x}}{\cap \mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{x}}},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.27)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Pi_{\mathbf{x}} = \left\{ \mathbf{x}:\mathbf{a} \leq \mathbf{x} \leq \mathbf{b} \right\},\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x} \in R^{d}.} \\ \\ \end{array}$$
(7.28)

In these expressions, the d-dimensional vectors a and b have fixed elements ai and $b_{i},\, i = \overline{1,d}.$ The transformation (7.26) is simplified to


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{z} = \left\{ \frac{x_{i} - a_{i}^{-}}{a_{i}^{+} - a_{i}^{-}},\, \middle| \, i = \overline{1,d} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.29)

Due to the continuity of the transformation (7.26), the function F(z) is bounded below on 𝒦z, i.e., there exists a constant c such that


$$\begin{array}{r} {F^{*} \geq c.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.30)

The constant c is generally unknown but equals 0 in some special global minimization problems. For example, this takes place for the problems in which the function F(z) is defined as the residual between the left- and right-hand sides of a certain system of equations.

The function F(z) also satisfies the Hölder condition with other constants L and p, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \omega(h) = \max_{(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}) \in \mathcal{K}_{\mathbf{x}}\mspace{2mu}:\|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{y}\| \leq h} \middle| F(\mathbf{v}) - F(\mathbf{y}) \middle| \leq Lh^{s}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.31)

Denote by ℤ* the set of all global minimum points z* and by F(z*) = F* the global minimum value in the problem (7.23). In other words, assume that a global minimum is achieved not at a unique point but on a finite set ℤ*.

How should we comprehend the solution of the problem (7.23)? This issue is of crucial importance, as its obviousness disappears for real computational processes. Actually, it is impossible to achieve an exact value of the global minimum F* even with an arbitrarily high accuracy of calculations. We can speak about getting into some r-neighborhood of the exact global minimum value. In other words, the matter concerns an approximate global minimum value F̃* within the r-neighborhood. At the very beginning, we have declared to employ the Monte Carlo method for global minimization. Hence, the value F̃* gets into the r-neighborhood with a certain probability, less or equal to 1.

Also note that computations are implemented through iterative procedures that represent a sequence of steps with numbers k. Each step yields an intermediate result. In the problem (7.23), the intermediate results are the values $\widetilde{F_{1}^{*},\ldots,\widetilde{F_{k}^{*},\ldots}}.$ Assume that at some step k* an approximate global minimum value F̃k** has entered an r-neighborhood. Nevertheless, this event is random and it may happen that at step (k* + 1), the value leaves the neighborhood. For increasing the reliability of approximate global minimization, introduce a positive number ϱ that characterizes the number of steps during which the values F̃k**, F̃(k* + k1)*, …, F̃(k* + k𝜚)* stay within the r-neighborhood after first getting into it at step k*.

7.2.2Idea of method and concept of solution

Consider a simplified statement of the problem (7.23) in which the admissible set is the d-dimensional cube Z+d. This problem is solved by an algorithm that represents an iterative procedure to construct a sequence of records

At step k, the algorithm generates a batch 𝒵k of the Nk = Mkd independent random vectors z1, …, zNk obeying the uniform distribution on Z+d. Here Mk denotes the number of independent uniformly distributed random variables on the interval [0, 1] that are produced at step k by a random generator for each of the d coordinates.

For the kth batch, the algorithm calculates the values of the function $F(\mathbf{z}^{j}),\, j = \overline{1,N_{k}},$ as well as its minimum value Fk* (the kth record) and argument zk*. Due to a random character of the Monte Carlo simulations, the value Fk* is also random.

Transition to step (k + 1) consists in increasing the number of random vectors by the rule


$$\begin{array}{r} {M_{k + 1} = \alpha M_{k},\text{\quad\quad}\alpha > 1,} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.32)

and calculating a new record Fk + 1* for the (k + 1) th packet. This yields a monotonically decreasing sequence


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{F} = \left\{ F_{0}^{*} \geq \ldots, \geq F_{k}^{*},\ldots \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.33)

In addition to the records sequence (7.33), the algorithm constructs a sequence of their decrements


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{U} = \left\{ u_{1},\ldots,\, u_{k},\ldots \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.34)

where uk=|Fk*−Fk + 1*|.

The algorithm stops when the sequence of random variables uk stays within a given δ-neighborhood of the origin during ρ successive steps, i.e., the number of steps till its termination is


$$\begin{array}{r} {\tau = \min\left\{ k:\max_{k - \rho \leq s \leq k}u_{s} \leq \delta \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.35)

In the sequel, this algorithm will be called the GFS algorithm (Generation, Filtration, Selection).

The solution of the problem (7.23) is represented by the quadruple


$$\begin{array}{r} {S = \left\{ F_{\tau}^{*},\mathbf{z}_{\tau}^{*},r_{\tau}^{*},\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{E}_{r_{\tau}}) \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.36)

where

  • Fτ*, zτ* indicate an approximate global minimum value and its argument, respectively, at the stop time τ;

  • rτ* is the estimated size of the neighborhood of the exact global minimum value at the stop time τ;

  • the event


    $$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{E}_{r_{\tau}^{*}} = \left\{ F_{\tau}^{*} - F^{*} \leq r_{\tau} \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
    (7.37)

    where F* gives the exact global minimum value on the set Z+d;

  • P(ℰrτ*) denotes an estimated probability of the event (7.37).

A real algorithm involves a strictly monotonically decreasing subsequence


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbb{F}^{*} = \left\{ F_{1}^{*} > \ldots, > F_{k}^{*},\ldots \right\}} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.38)

of the sequence ℱ* (7.33). A theoretical analysis below is based on exploring the properties of the sequence ℱ*. As 𝔽* forms a subsequence of ℱ*, in qualitative terms the analysis results remain the same for the subsequence 𝔽*.

7.2.3Probabilistic characteristics of random sequences ℱ and 𝒰

A study of the random sequences generated by the packets of simple Monte Carlo simulations is an important stage to investigate the fundamental properties of the GFS algorithm in terms of computations. These properties include convergence analysis (in particular, convergence conditions) and estimation of the numerical characteristics of a resulting solution [35].

1. Probabilistic characteristics of packets 𝒵k

In each stage k, the algorithm generates a packet 𝒵k of Nk independent random vectors with the uniform distribution on the d-dimensional cube. The source of the packet 𝒵k is a random generator: for each of the d coordinates at step k it produces an array of Mk independent uniformly distributed random variables on the interval [0, 1] (simple Monte Carlo simulations). As a result, at step k we have a packet of (Mk)d random vectors obeying the uniform distribution on the unit cube.

Consider the unit cube Z+d (7.23) and its partition into elementary cubes using a virtual uniform lattice with the step


$$\begin{array}{r} {\eta_{k} = M_{k}^{- q}} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.39)

for each of the d coordinates. Here q specifies a lattice parameter such that


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 < \gamma \leq q \leq \beta < 1.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.40)

Denote by P(Mk, d, q) the probability that there exists an elementary virtual cube containing none of the random (Mk)d vectors generated at step k. This probability can be estimated as follows.

Lemma 1 The probability P(Mk, d, q) has the upper bound


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(M_{k},d,q) \leq {(M_{k}^{q} + 1)}^{d}\left( {1 - \frac{1}{M_{k}^{dq}}} \right)^{M_{k}^{d}} = Q(M_{k},d,q).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.41)

As k→∞,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. Q(M_{k},d,q) \right.\sim\mathbf{Q}(M_{k},d,q) = M_{k}{}^{dq}\exp\left( {- {(M_{k})}^{(1 - q)d}} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.42)

Proof. Consider a certain virtual elementary cube of the volume (ηk)d. The generated random vectors are independent and obey the uniform distribution on the unit cube; at step k, their number is (Mk)d. Hence, the probability that this elementary virtual cube contains none of these vectors makes up


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left( {1 - {(\eta_{k})}^{d}} \right)^{M_{k}^{d}} = \left( {1 - \frac{1}{M_{k}^{dq}}} \right)^{M_{k}^{d}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.43)

Let B be the event that such an elementary virtual cube exists. According to (7.41),


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(B) \leq Q(M_{k},d,q),} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.44)

because (Mkq + 1)d is an upper bound for the number of all elementary virtual cubes with the side ηk = Mk − q for each coordinate.

Due to


$$\begin{array}{r} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\,\frac{{(1 - x^{- q})}^{x}}{\exp( - x^{(1 - q)})} = 1,} \\ \end{array}$$

letting k→∞ in (7.44) gives the inequality


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. P(B) \leq Q(M_{k},d,q) \right.\sim M_{k}{}^{dq}\exp\left( {- M_{k}{}^{(1 - q)d}} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.45)

■

Corollary 1 With a probability not smaller than (1 − Q(Mk, d, q)), each elementary cube with the side Mk − q contains at least one of the random vectors from the packet generated at step k.

2. Probabilistic properties of sequence ℱ*

Consider a sequence of “quasi global” minimum values ℱ* = {F0*,…,Fk*,…} and a sequence of the corresponding arguments 𝒵* = {z0*,…,zk*,…}.

Denote by ℤ* the set of all global minimum points of the function F( ⋅ ) on the unit cube. Introduce the distance l( ⋅ ) between an arbitrary point z and the compact set ℤ* in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {l(\mathbf{z},{\mathbb{Z}}^{*}) = \min_{\mathbf{y} \in {\mathbb{Z}}^{*}}\|\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{y}\|.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.46)

Lemma 2 With a probability not smaller than (1 − Q(Mk, d, q)),


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 \leq F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} \leq \omega(h_{k}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.47)

where ω( ⋅ ) is the modulus of continuity of the function F(z), $h_{k} = \eta_{k}\,\sqrt{d}/2,$ and F* gives an unknown value of the global minimum of the function F( ⋅ ) on the set Z+d.

Proof. Let $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ be the closest point (in terms of the distance (7.47)) to the set ℤ* from the packet of the random points generated at step k. Recall that, with a probability not smaller than (1 − Q(Mk, d, q)), at least one of the generated points gets into each virtual elementary cube with the side ηk. Therefore, the distance is


$$\begin{array}{r} {h_{k} = \|\mathbf{z}^{*} - \hat{\mathbf{z}}\| \leq \eta_{k}\,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{2}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.48)

This happens if the point z* ∈ ℤ* implementing the distance to the set ℤ* is at the center of the cube with the side ηk. In addition, the closest random points are located at the corners of this cube and also each cube contains at least one random point.

Then, by the Hölder condition,


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 \leq F(\hat{\mathbf{z}}) - F^{*} \leq \omega(h_{k}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.49)

On the other hand,


$$\begin{array}{r} {F^{*} = F(\mathbf{z}^{*}) = \min_{\mathbf{z} \in Z_{+}^{d}}F(\mathbf{z}) \leq \min_{1 \leq s \leq k}F_{s}^{*} \leq F_{k}^{*} \leq F(\hat{\mathbf{z}}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.50)

It follows from (7.50) that


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 \leq F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} \leq F(\hat{\mathbf{z}}) - F^{*}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.51)

Finally, the expressions (7.51) and (7.49) yield the relation


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 \leq F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} \leq \omega(h_{k}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.52)

which holds with a probability not smaller than (1 − Q(Mk, d, q)). ■

Corollary 2 For the functions satisfying the Hölder condition (7.31), there exist constants


$$\begin{array}{r} {D = L\left( \frac{\sqrt{d}}{2} \right)^{s},\text{\quad\quad}p = qs} \\ \end{array}$$

such that the upper bound


$$\begin{array}{r} {0 \leq F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} \leq DM_{k}^{- p} = r_{k}(q)} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.53)

is valid with a probability not smaller than 1 − Q(Mk, d, q), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {P\left\{ 0 \leq F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} \leq r_{(}q) \right\} \geq 1 - Q(M_{k},d,q).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.54)

Note that the upper bounds (7.53)–(7.54) depend on the parameter q, which affects the volume of the virtual elementary cube with the side (7.39) for each coordinate. The constants β and γ in (7.40) should be adjusted for reaching an acceptable result in terms of the size of the desired neighborhood and the corresponding probability.

7.2.4Convergence of GFS algorithm

Using the probabilistic characteristics of the records sequence ℱk*, we can establish the following result on its convergence.

Theorem 1 For the functions that satisfy the Hölder condition,

(i) the sequence ℱk* of the records Fk* converges with probability 1 to the true global minimum F* with the exponential rate;

(iii) the sequence of the record arguments zk* converges to the set ℤ* (in terms of the distance (7.48)) with probability 1.

Proof. Use the bound Q(Mk, d, q) (7.42), which is asymptotically equivalent to Q(Mk, d, q). Therefore, further considerations will rest on the assumption that k is sufficiently large. The parameter q has a fixed value within the interval (7.40).

(i). Choose a sufficiently small value ε > 0 and find K(ε) from the condition K(ε) = min {k:rk(q)≤ε}, where rk(q) is defined by (7.53).

Then, for k > K(ε),


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left\{ F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} > \varepsilon \right\} \subset \left\{ F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} > r_{k} \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.55)

It follows from (7.54) and (7.42) that the probability of the latter event can be estimated as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{P}\left\{ F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} > \varepsilon \right\} \leq \mathbf{Q}(M_{k},d,q)} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.56)

for sufficiently large k. According to (7.32), the obvious inequality is


$$\begin{array}{r} {\alpha^{s} > s\,\text{for}\,\alpha > 1,\, s > 0.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.57)

In this case, write the estimate (7.42) as


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{Q}(M_{k},d,q)} & {= \alpha^{qkd}M_{0}^{qd}\,\exp\left( {- \frac{1}{2}\alpha^{(1 - q)kd}M_{0}^{(1 - q)d}} \right) \times} \\ & {\times \exp\left( {- \frac{1}{2}\alpha^{(1 - q)kd}M_{0}^{(1 - q)d}} \right).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.58)

Using (7.57), one of the exponents can be assigned an upper bound of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\exp\left( {- \frac{1}{2}\alpha^{(1 - q)kd}M_{0}^{(1 - q)d}} \right) < \exp\left( {- \frac{kd(1 - q)}{2}M_{0}^{(1 - q)d}} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.59)

Next, denoting x = αkdM0d, from (7.2.4) and (7.59) write


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\mathbb{Q}}(M_{k},d,q) \leq \widetilde{Q}\exp\left( {- \frac{kd(1 - q)}{2}M_{0}^{(1 - q)d}} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.60)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {\widetilde{Q} = \max_{x \geq 0}x^{q}\exp\frac{- x^{(1 - q)}}{2}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.61)

Let


$$\begin{array}{r} {C = \frac{(1 - q)d}{2}M_{0}^{(1 - q)d}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.62)

Then the probability (7.56) can be estimated in the following way:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{P}\left\{ F_{k}^{*} - F^{*} > \varepsilon \right\} \leq \widetilde{Q}\exp( - Ck)\quad\text{for}\, k > K(\varepsilon).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.63)

Due to (7.63),


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathbf{P}\left\{ \sup\limits_{s \geq 0} \middle| F_{k}^{*} - F_{k + s}^{*} \right|} & {\left. > \varepsilon \right\} \leq 2\mathbf{P}\left\{ \sup\limits_{s \geq k}(F_{s}^{*} - F^{*}) > \varepsilon/2 \right\} \leq} \\ {\leq 2{\sum\limits_{s = k}^{\infty}\mathbf{P}}\left\{ (F_{s}^{*} - F^{*}) \right.} & {\left. > \varepsilon/2 \right\} \leq \leq 2\widetilde{Q}{\sum\limits_{s = k}^{\infty}\exp}\left( {- Cs} \right)} \\ & {\text{for}\quad k > K(\varepsilon/2).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.64)

For sufficiently small ε > 0, the latter inequality implies


$$\begin{array}{r} {\lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}\mathbf{P}\left\{ \sup\limits_{s \geq 0} \middle| F_{k}^{*} - F_{(k + s)}^{*} \middle| \geq \varepsilon \right\} = 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.65)

which is a necessary and sufficient condition for the almost sure convergence of the sequence {Fk*}. In addition, the derived estimates show that this convergence has the exponential rate.

ii. This item of Theorem 1 is proved by contradiction. Assume on the contrary that there exists a subsequence $\left\{ {\hat{\mathbf{z}}}_{k}^{*} \right\}$ of the sequence {zk*} (without loss of generality, the sequence {zk*} itself) that converges to a point $\widetilde{\mathbf{z}} \in {\mathbb{Z}}^{*}$ with a positive probability. Since the function F( ⋅ ) is continuous, it follows that $\lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}F(\mathbf{z}_{k}^{*}) = F(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}) > F^{*}$ with a positive probability (on the one part) and also $\lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}F(\mathbf{z}_{k}^{*}) = \lim\limits_{k\rightarrow\infty}F_{k}^{*} = F^{*} = F(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}})$ with probability 1 by item i (on the other part). This contradiction concludes the proof. ■

Corollary 3 A strictly monotonic subsequence 𝔽* of the records sequence ℱ* converges with probability 1 to the exact global minimum value with the exponential rate.

Corollary 4 The decrements sequence 𝒰k (7.34) vanishes with probability 1 with the exponential rate.

7.2.5Study of decrements sequence 𝒰

For the Hölder-type functions, the upper bound (7.53) holds with the probability 1 − Q(Mk, d, q); see Corollary 2. Because rk + 1(q) < rk(q),


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. u_{k} = \middle| F_{k + 1}^{*} - F_{k}^{*} \middle| \leq DM_{k}^{- p}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.66)

Then it follows that, for sufficiently large k,


$$\begin{array}{r} {u_{k} \approx DM_{k}^{- p}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.67)

Let us take the logarithm of both sides of this approximate expression:


$$\begin{array}{r} {v_{k} = \log u_{k} \approx \log D - p\log M_{k}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.68)

An example of the relation vk(nk) for a computational process is illustrated in Fig. 7.2.

Consider a sequence of independent random variables ζk with zero mean and a finite variance σ2. Add this sequence to the right-hand side of the approximate expression to simulate a random character of the sequence of vk's, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {v_{k} = A - Bn_{k} + \zeta_{k},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.69)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {A = \log D,\text{\quad\quad}B = p,\quad n_{k} = \log M_{k}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.70)

The parameters A and B related to the Hölder constants and σ2 are unknown. Their estimates Â(k), B̂(k) and σ̂2(k) will be constructed using the least-squares method based on the available information about the elements of the sequence {Fk*}. This is easy to implement, since (7.69) represents a linear model (in this context, note once again that the linear regression (7.69) in the log-log scale directly follows from the upper bound (7.53)).

With these estimates, we can also estimate the size rk(q) of the corresponding neighborhood of the exact global minimum. According to (7.53),


$$\begin{array}{r} {r_{k}(q) = \log{\hat{A}}^{(k)}M_{k}^{(\frac{{\hat{B}}^{(k)}}{q})}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.71)

Clearly, the relation rk(q) is monotonically decreasing on the interval [γ, β] (7.40). Hence, it achieves minimum at q = β. The estimated size of the neighborhood at the stop time τ is


$$\begin{array}{r} {r_{\tau}(\beta) = \log{\hat{A}}^{(\tau)}M_{\tau}^{(\frac{{\hat{B}}^{(\tau)}}{\beta})},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.72)

and a lower bound for its probability (7.54) (see Corollary 2) has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {P\left\{ 0 \leq F_{\tau}^{*} - F^{*} \leq r_{\tau} \right\} \geq M_{\tau}^{\beta d}\exp\left( {- M_{\tau}^{(1 - \beta)d}} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.73)

7.2.6Admissible set 𝒦(z) of general form

Up to this point, we have considered the global minimization problem in which the domain of definition of variables z and the admissible set coincide.
