Now let us address the general case, where the admissible set 𝒦(z) (7.23) represents a part of the unit cube 𝒵+d. More specifically, it forms an intersection of the unit cube and a subset 𝒢 described by a system of inequalities with continuous functions.

The admissible set under study has a smaller volume, and hence the number of elementary cubes in its virtual partition is decreased. However, this number necessarily does not exceed the number of such cubes in the unit cube partition. Therefore, the derived probability estimates (ergo, the propositions on the algorithm convergence) remain valid for a compact set that is defined by a system of continuous functions and has a positive Lebesgue measure.

Consider the admissible domain 𝒦z (7.23) in the unit cube. Assume that it contains no isolated points and its d-dimensional Lebesgue measure ν is nonzero, i.e., 0 < ν0 ≤ ν ≤ 1.

First, analyze the case in which the value ν is known. Then the probability that a specific vector from a generated sequence of independent random vectors with the uniform distribution on the unit cube gets into the admissible domain is ν. Let Nk independent random vectors be generated at step k with the uniform distribution on Z+d, including N̂k vectors within the admissible domain. Denote by κNk the frequency with which the generated vectors occur within the admissible set 𝒦z, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\kappa_{N_{k}} = \frac{{\hat{N}}_{k}}{N_{k}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.74)

By the law of large numbers, for any (sufficiently small) ϵ > 0, η > 0 and the given value ν, there exists a number N0(ϵ, η, ν) such that, for all Nk > N0(ϵ, η, ν), the deviation |κNk−ν| is less than ϵ ν with a probability not smaller than (1 − η).

Thus, for Nk > N0(ϵ, η, ν), the inequality


$$\begin{array}{r} {\kappa_{N_{k}} \geq (1 - \epsilon)\nu} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.75)

holds with a probability not smaller than (1 − η). Hence, the number N̂k of admissible vectors in a packet composed of Nk vectors satisfies the inequality


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\hat{N}}_{k} \geq N_{k}(1 - \epsilon)\nu} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.76)

with a probability not smaller than (1 − η).

Consequently, in all the formulas incorporating the number Nk of generated vectors, we should replace it (for Nk > N0(⋅)) by the number N̂k = (1 − ϵ)νNk.

Now let us estimate the number N0(ϵ, η, ν). For η > 0, define a function c(η) using the condition


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\int_{- c(\eta)}^{c(\eta)}\exp}( - x^{2}/2)dx = 1 - \eta.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.77)

Then the number N0(ϵ, η, ν) can be found from the relation


$$\begin{array}{r} {N_{0}(\epsilon,\eta,\nu) \geq \frac{c^{2}(\eta)(1 - \nu)}{\epsilon^{2}\nu}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.78)

Second, consider the case in which the value ν is unknown but we know a value ν0 such that 0 < ν0 ≤ ν. Replacing ν by ν0 in (7.78) yields an estimate for the minimum number of generated vectors under which the frequency of admissible vectors differs from the unknown value ν at most by ϵ ν with a probability not smaller than (1 − η). In this case, for N > N0(ϵ, η, ν), the value ν can be estimated as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\hat{\nu} = \kappa_{N},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.79)

and, with a probability not smaller than (1 − η), |κN−ν|≤ϵ ν, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\kappa_{N}}{1 - \epsilon} \geq \nu \geq \frac{\kappa_{N}}{1 + \epsilon}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.80)

The lower bound from this estimate can be used instead of ν in formula (7.78).

7.2.7Logical structure of GFS algorithm

The GFS algorithm is intended for calculating a global minimum in the canonical form of the problem (7.23). It comprises two procedures, SeqLocMin and EstProb. The SeqLocMin procedure yields a sequence of records and their decrements and includes a stopping rule. The EstProb procedure estimates a minimum size for the neighborhood of the exact global minimum and also calculates a lower bound for the probability of getting into this neighborhood.

The procedures consist of a sequence of k steps, each performing t operations. Therefore, paired indexes (k, t) will be associated with the stages of each procedure.

SeqLocMin procedure

  1. Generation—creation of a packet of random vectors:

    1. (k, 1) generate a sequence of Nk independent random vectors with the uniform distribution on the unit cube;

    2. (k, 2) form a packet 𝒵k = {z1,…,zNk} of these random vectors.

  2. Filtration—choice of admissible vectors:

    1. (k, 3) choose vectors from the packet 𝒵k that belong to the admissible set 𝒦z and form an admissible packet ${\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}}_{k}$ of size Ñk.

  3. Selection—definition of the quasi global minimum for the packet and calculation of the decrements:

    1. (k, 4) calculate the values $F({\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}}^{i}),\, i = \overline{1,{\widetilde{N}}_{k}},$ of the objective function for the vectors from the packet ${\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}}_{k};$

    2. (k, 5) choose the minimum value $F_{k}^{*} = \min F({\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}}^{i}),\, 1 \leq i \leq {\widetilde{N}}_{k};$

    3. (k, 6) calculate the decrements uk=|Fk + 1*−Fk*| and the decrement logarithms vk = log uk and nk = log Nk; form the sequences 𝒰 = {uk}, 𝒱 = {vk}, 𝒩 = {nk}.

If vk ≤ log δ, the value vk is included in the sequence $\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}.$ As soon as the sequence ${\overset{\text{˜}}{\mathcal{V}}}_{k}$ accumulates ρ elements, k = τ and the algorithm stops. Then a transition to the EstProb procedure is performed.

EstProb procedure

The computational scheme of this procedure consists in the following.

  1. Parameter estimation for the regression model of decrements:

    1. (τ, 1) using sequences 𝒩 and 𝒱, estimate parameters Âτ and B̂τ by the least-squares method.

  2. Estimation of solution characteristics (quality indicators):

    1. (τ, 2) estimate the size rτ (7.72) for the neighborhood of the global minimum value;

    2. (τ, 3) calculate the lower bound for the probability P̂τ (7.73).

The logical structure of the GFS algorithm is presented in Fig. 7.3.

7.2.8Experimental study of GFS algorithm

According to the previous subsections, the probabilistic properties of the GFS algorithm established by analytical study possess an asymptotical character. In other words, they hold for a sufficiently large number of iterations. Even the estimates derived under a finite number of steps assume that it is great enough. The aim of an experimental study, which always has a finite number of steps, is to test the operability of this algorithm in typical problems. More specifically, we will check the estimates for the size of the exact global minimum neighborhood and the probability of getting into it. Recall that these estimates have been obtained using the least-squares-based estimation of the Hölder constants for the objective function. Therefore, in the course of a computational experiment, we will confirm or doubt the hypothesis about the linear regression in the log-log scale.

In the general statement, the GFS algorithm is intended for solving the global minimization problems in which it is possible to calculate the values of the associated functions (the objective function and constraints). Below we will consider the entropy estimation problem for the PDFs of the parameters of a randomized model that possesses these properties. Let us begin the experimental study of the GFS algorithm with test problems using analytical functions.

1. Analytical tests

Our testing employs some minimization problems from [4, 5, 58, 173], in which the admissible domain is the d-dimensional parallelepiped Πz.

A1. The Shekel function


$$\begin{aligned} {F(\mathbf{x}) =} & {- {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\left( {c_{i} + {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{d}{(x_{j} - a_{ji})}^{2}}} \right)^{- 1}},\quad m = 10,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x}^{*} = \mathbf{4}.\mathbf{0},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}F^{*} = - 10.5364,\quad d = 4,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}F^{*} = - 11.0216,\quad d = 2,} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.81)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {A = \left( \begin{array}{llllllllll} 4 & 1 & 8 & 6 & 3 & 2 & 5 & 8 & 6 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & 8 & 6 & 7 & 9 & 3 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & 8 & 6 & 3 & 2 & 5 & 8 & 6 & 7 \\ 4 & 1 & 8 & 6 & 7 & 9 & 3 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \end{array} \right),} \\ \end{array}$$

and


$$\begin{array}{r} {c = \frac{1}{10}(1,2,2,4,4,6,3,7,5,5).} \\ \end{array}$$

A2. The Rosenbrock function


$$\begin{aligned} {F(\mathbf{x})} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{d}1}00{(x_{i + 1} - x_{i})}^{2} + {(x_{i} - 1)}^{2},} \\ & {\mathbf{x}^{*} = \mathbf{1},\, F^{*} = 0\,\text{for~any}\, d.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.82)

A3. The Powell function


$$\begin{aligned} {F(\mathbf{x})} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{d - 2}{(x_{i - 1} + 10x_{i})}^{2}} + 5{(x_{i + 1} - x_{i + 2})}^{2} +} \\ & {+ {(x_{i} - 2x_{i + 1})}^{4} + 10{(x_{i - 1} - x_{i + 2})}^{4},} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x}^{*} = \mathbf{0},\, F^{*} = 0\,\text{for~any}\, d.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.83)

A4. The trigonometric function


$$\begin{aligned} {F(\mathbf{x})} & {= 1 + {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{d}8}\sin^{2}7{(x_{i} - 0.9)}^{2} + 6\sin^{2}14{(x_{i} - 0.9)}^{2} + x_{i} - 0.9,} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x}^{*} = \mathbf{0}.\mathbf{9},\, F^{*} = 1\,\text{for~any}\, d.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.84)

A5. The Griewank function


$$\begin{aligned} {F(\mathbf{x})} & {= 1 + {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{d}\frac{x_{i}^{2}}{4000}} - {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{d}\cos}\left( \frac{x_{i}}{\sqrt{i + 1}} \right),} \\ & {\mathbf{x}^{*} = \mathbf{0},\, F^{*} = 0\,\text{for~any}\, d.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.85)

For all computations, N0 = 10, α = 10, δ = 0.01, a = 10, ρ = 2, τ = 13, and ετ=|F*−Fτ*|. 2. Algorithmic test (entropy-based estimation for PDFs of randomized model parameters [149])

Consider an array of input and output data for some dynamic nonlinear object. Denote by y = {y[m],…,y[m+s]} the vector (packet) of output data and by x{x[0],…,x[m],…,x[m+s]} the vector (packet) of input data. Assume that the input measurements are perfect whereas the output measurements have errors that are simulated by a random vector $\overline{\xi} = \left\{ \xi\lbrack m\rbrack,\ldots,\xi\lbrack m + s\rbrack \right\}$ with independent elements. Let the elements of this vector be of the interval type, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\xi\lbrack j + m\rbrack \in \Xi_{j} = \lbrack\xi_{j}^{-},\xi_{j}^{+}\rbrack,\,\,\text{for~all}\, j = \overline{0,s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.86)

In addition, there exist PDFs $q_{j}(\xi\lbrack j + m\rbrack),\, j = \overline{0,s},$ on these intervals.

The relation between the input and output packets is described by a discrete dynamic randomized model with second-order structured nonlinearities and an additive random noise of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {v\lbrack j + 1\rbrack = {\sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\left( {{\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{m}w^{(h)}}\lbrack n\rbrack x\lbrack j + m - n\rbrack} \right)^{h}} + \xi\lbrack j + m\rbrack,\quad j = \overline{0,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.87)

which has memory of capacity m = 1, s = 1 and R = 2.

The discrete random weight functions (random pulse characteristics) w(1)[n] = w(2)[n] = 0, n > 1, reflect the dynamic properties of the linear and nonlinear blocks of this model. Introduce the notations


$$\begin{aligned} & {a_{0}^{(1)} = w^{(1)}\lbrack 0\rbrack,\, a_{1}^{(1)} = w^{(1)}\lbrack 1\rbrack;\quad\mathbf{a}^{(1)} = \left\{ a_{0}^{(1)},a_{1}^{(1)} \right\};} \\ & {a_{0}^{(2)} = w^{(2)}\lbrack 0\rbrack,\, a_{1}^{(2)} = w^{(2)}\lbrack 1\rbrack;\quad\mathbf{a}^{(2)} = \left\{ a_{0}^{(2)},a_{1}^{(2)} \right\};} \\ & {\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x}\lbrack j\rbrack = \left\{ x\lbrack j + 1\rbrack,x\lbrack j\rbrack \right\}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.88)

Choose x[0] = {0.39;0.19} and x[1] = {0.93;0.39}.

The random parameters an(h) take their values within the intervals


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(h)} = \lbrack - A_{n}^{(h)},A_{n}^{(h)}\rbrack,\quad A_{n}^{(h)} = \beta_{n}^{(h)}\exp( - \alpha_{n}^{(h)}\, n).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.89)

The parameters of the above-mentioned intervals are given in Table 7.2.

Table 7.2: Parameters of intervals.

The PDFs P(1)(a(1)) and P(2)(a(2)) are defined on the intervals (7.89).

According to the RML algorithm, the entropy-optimal PDFs of the model parameters and measurement noises have the form


$$\begin{aligned} {{\widetilde{P}}^{(h)}\left( \mathbf{a} \right)} & {= \frac{1}{\mathcal{R}^{(h)}(\theta)}\,\exp\left( {- {\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{s}\,}\theta_{j}\, V_{j}^{(h)}\left( {\mathbf{a}^{(h)},\mathbf{x}\lbrack j\rbrack} \right)} \right),\quad h = \overline{1,R};} \\ {{\widetilde{q}}_{j}(\xi)} & {= \frac{1}{\mathcal{Q}_{j}(\theta_{j})}\,\exp\left( {- \theta_{j}\,\xi} \right),\, j = \overline{0,s},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.90)

where


$$\begin{aligned} {\mathcal{R}^{(h)}(\mathbf{\theta})} & {= {\int\limits_{\mathcal{A}^{(h)}}\exp}\left( {- {\sum\limits_{j = 0}^{s}\,}\theta_{j}\, V_{j}^{(h)}\left( {\mathbf{a}^{(h)},\mathbf{x}\lbrack j\rbrack} \right)} \right)d\mathbf{a}^{(h)},} \\ {\mathcal{Q}_{j}(\theta)} & {= {\int\limits_{\Xi_{j}}\exp}\left( {- \theta_{j}\,\xi_{j}} \right)d\xi_{j},\quad j = \overline{0,s},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.91)

and


$$\begin{aligned} {V_{j}^{(1)}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{x})} & {= a_{0}^{(1)}x\lbrack j + 1\rbrack + a_{1}^{(1)}x\lbrack j\rbrack,} \\ {V_{j}^{(2)}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{x}) =} & {\left( {a^{(2)}x\lbrack j + 1\rbrack} \right)^{2} + \left( {a^{(2)}x\lbrack j\rbrack} \right)^{2} +} \\ & {+ 2a_{0}^{(2)}a_{1}^{(2)}x\lbrack j + 1\rbrack x\lbrack j\rbrack.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.92)

The Lagrange multipliers θ0 and θ1 are calculated by solving the system of equations


$$\begin{array}{r} {\Phi_{j}(\theta) = \sum\limits_{h = 1}^{R}\frac{{\overset{\text{˜}}{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}^{(h)}(\theta)}{\mathcal{R}^{(h)}(\theta)} + \frac{{\overset{\text{˜}}{\mathcal{B}}}_{j}(\theta_{j})}{\mathcal{B}_{j}(\theta_{j})} - y\lbrack j + 1\rbrack = 0,\quad j = \overline{0,s},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.93)

where the integral components have the form


$$\begin{aligned} {{\overset{\text{˜}}{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}^{(h)}(\theta)} & {= \int\limits_{\mathcal{A}^{(h)}}V_{j}^{(h)}\left( {\mathbf{a}^{(h)},\mathbf{x}\lbrack j\rbrack} \right)\exp\left( {- \sum\limits_{i = 0}^{1}\theta_{i}V_{i}^{(h)}\left( {\mathbf{a}^{(h)},\mathbf{x}\lbrack j\rbrack} \right)} \right)d\mathbf{a}^{(h)},} \\ {{\overset{\text{˜}}{\mathcal{B}}}_{j}(\theta)} & {= \int\limits_{\Xi_{j}}\,\xi_{j}\exp\left( {- \theta_{j}\,\xi_{j}} \right)d\xi_{j}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.94)

The measured values of the object's output vector are y[1] = 0.5 and y[2] = 2.2.

For solving equations (7.93), minimize the residual function


$$\begin{array}{r} {J(\theta) = \|\Phi(\theta)\|_{L_{2}}} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.95)

on the cube Πθ.

The results of computations are presented in Table 7.3 and also illustrated in Fig. 7.6. Due to the existing integral components (7.94), the objective function was defined algorithmically. For this collection of tests, the algorithm was implemented in MATLAB using Parallel Computing Toolbox. The integral components (7.94) were calculated by integral2 function whereas the minimum value by the GFS algorithm. All computations were performed with 32 working processors (often called workers) on the same computing system as in the case of analytical tests. The solution of equations (7.95) was obtained for the two search domains Πθ: θ ∈ [ − 10, 10] × [ − 10, 10] for Variant 1, and θ ∈ [ − 3,  − 2] × [ − 0.5, 0.5] for Variant 2; see Table 7.3.

7.3On Calculation of Multidimensional Integrals Using Monte Carlo Method

The equations of the Lagrange multipliers that are induced by the empirical balance constraints contain the integral components (7.13, 7.14) on the domains with unit volumes.

These integrals will be calculated using the Monte Carlo method with a random generator as follows. For each element of a vector w ∈ In ⊂ Rn, it produces sequences of random numbers of length M to form N = Mn random vectors (points) $\mathbf{w}^{(i)},\, i = \overline{1,N}.$ The details can be found in [147].

A major difficulty of the Monte Carlo method is to estimate the length M of the sequence of random numbers (the number N of random points) that is sufficient for integrals calculation with a given error δ. Obviously, such an estimate has a random character and should be equipped with a corresponding probability.

For obtaining these estimates, two implementation strategies of the Monte Carlo method will be compared with one another. The first strategy involves a uniform orthogonal lattice S constructed in In from the uniform lattices 𝕊k for each element wk with the step


$$\begin{array}{r} {h = \frac{1}{M}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.96)

The elementary cubes in In have the same volumes


$$\begin{array}{r} {v = h^{n} = \left( \frac{1}{M} \right)^{n}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.97)

Then equalities (7.13, 7.14) can be written as


$$\begin{aligned} {\widetilde{\mathbb{B}}(\mathbf{z})} & {\approx v{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\phi}(\mathbf{w}^{i},\mathbf{z}),} \\ {\widetilde{\mathbb{G}}(\mathbf{z})} & {\approx v{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\varphi}(\mathbf{w}^{i},\mathbf{z}),} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.98)

where


$$\begin{aligned} {\phi(\mathbf{w}^{i},\mathbf{z})} & {= \exp\left( {- E(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w}^{(i)})} \right),} \\ {\varphi(\mathbf{w}^{i},\mathbf{z})} & {= E(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w}^{(i)})\exp\left( {- E(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w}^{(i)})} \right).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.99)

The second strategy is based on a nonuniform (random) orthogonal lattice $\hat{\mathbb{S}}$ constructed from the product of nonuniform (random) lattices ${\hat{\mathbb{S}}}_{k}$ for each kth element of the vector w. In contrast to the uniform lattice, the step of the nonuniform one makes up


$$\begin{array}{r} {h_{k}^{(i)} = w_{k}^{(i + 1)} - w_{k}^{(i)},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.100)

thereby representing a random variable. The elementary cubes in the lattice $\hat{\mathbb{S}}$ have random volumes v(1), …, v(N), i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {v^{(i)} = {\prod\limits_{k = 1}^{n}h_{k}^{(i)}},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,N}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.101)

According to the mean value theorem, the exact values of the integrals on the nonuniform lattice (7.100, 7.101) are given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbb{B}(\mathbf{z}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}v^{(i)}}\phi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z}),} \\ {\mathbb{G}(\mathbf{z}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}v^{(i)}}\varphi(\xi^{(i)},\mathbf{z}),} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.102)

where ζ(i) and ξ(i) denote the mean points of the elementary cubes of the lattice $\hat{\mathbb{S}}$ for the integrals (7.13) and (7.14), respectively.

Define the error between the exact (7.102) and approximate (7.98) values of these integrals as


$$\begin{aligned} \left| \mathbb{B}(\mathbf{z}) - \widetilde{\mathbb{B}}(\mathbf{z}) \right| & \left. = \middle| \sum_{i = 1}^{N}v^{(i)}\phi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) - v\sum_{i = 1}^{N}\phi(\mathbf{a}^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \right. \\ & \left. \leq \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \middle| v^{(i)} - v \middle| \middle| \phi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z} \middle| + \right. \\ {v\sum_{i = 1}^{N}} & \left| \phi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) - \phi(\mathbf{a}^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) \middle| = \epsilon(N), \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.103)

and


$$\begin{aligned} \left| \mathbb{G}(\mathbf{z}) - \widetilde{\mathbb{G}}(\mathbf{z}) \right| & \left. = \middle| \sum_{i = 1}^{N}v^{(i)}\varphi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) - v\sum_{i = 1}^{N}\varphi(\mathbf{a}^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \right. \\ & \left. \leq \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \middle| v^{(i)} - v \middle| \middle| \varphi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) \middle| + \right. \\ {v\sum_{i = 1}^{N}} & \left| \varphi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) - \varphi(\mathbf{a}^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) \middle| = \kappa(N). \right. \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.104)

First, let us derive upper bounds ϵ̃(N, n) and κ̃(N, n) for ϵ(N) and κ(N), and then solve the inequalities


ϵ(N) ≤ ϵ̃(N) ≤ δ,  κ(N) ≤ κ̃(N) ≤ δ.
(7.105)

Here δ is a given error. We should bear in mind that ϵ(N) and κ(N) are random variables. Therefore, inequalities (7.105) may hold with some probability only.

1. Consider inequality (7.3) and estimate the first term:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \left. \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N} \right|v^{(i)} - v \middle| \middle| \phi(\zeta^{(i)},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \max_{\zeta \in I^{n}} \middle| \phi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) \middle| \left. \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N} \right|v^{(i)} - v \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.106)

By the definition of the function ϕ(w, z), under fixed z (7.98) write


$$\begin{array}{r} \left| \phi(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \max_{\mathbf{w} \in I^{n}}\exp( \middle| E(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}) \middle| ) \leq \exp(G), \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.107)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. G = {({\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{T}A^{(t)}})}^{2},\text{\quad\quad}A^{(t)} = \max\left. \sum\limits_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{t}) = 1}^{n} \right|A_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{t}} \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.108)

Next, estimate the difference between the random elementary volume v(i) (7.101) and the elementary volume v of the uniform lattice.


$$\begin{array}{r} \left| v^{i} - v \middle| = \middle| {\prod\limits_{k = 1}^{n}h_{k}^{i}} - h^{n} \middle| \leq h^{(n - 1)}\,\max_{i} \middle| h_{k}^{i} - h \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.109)

Note that the variable hki is random. Consider the event


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{V}^{k} = \left\{ \max_{i} \middle| h_{k}^{i} - h \middle| < \gamma \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.110)

and also the union of the events 𝒱1, ..., 𝒱m,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{V} = {\underset{k = 1}{\overset{n}{\cup}}\mathcal{V}^{k}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.111)

Here γ specifies a small positive value. A lower bound for the probability of the event 𝒱 will be established below.

Choosing γ = h2, write


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \max_{i} \middle| v^{i} - v \middle| \leq h^{(m - 1)}\gamma = h^{(m + 1)}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.112)

Thus, by (7.106–7.108) the inequality


$$\begin{array}{r} \left| {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{(v_{i} - v)}}\phi(\zeta^{i},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq N\left( \frac{l}{N} \right)^{n + 1}\,\exp(G). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.113)

holds with the probability of the event (7.111).

2. Find a lower bound for the probability of the event (7.111). Consider the difference |hk(i)−h| and take a small positive value γ such that |hk(i)−h|>γ for all steps hk(i) of the random lattice $\hat{\mathbb{S}}.$ Calculate the probability of this event. If the number of random points is large (small h) and they have a uniform spread, then the distance between these points must be close to h.

The event maxi|hk(i)−h|>γ means that it is possible to find a pair of random variables (ξ, η) ∈ [0, 1] with the following property: if one of them (e.g., ξ) takes a value y ∈ [0, 1], then the other η ≠ ℒ = [y + h − γ, y + h + γ]. Hence, the interval ℒ of length 2γ that has center at the point y + h is empty. Actually, assume the random variable η gets into the interval ℒ, i.e., η = ξ − h ± δ, where 0 < δ < γ; in this case, it follows that |hk(i)−h|<γ.

Due to the independence of the uniformly distributed random variables, the probability of the event maxi|hk(i)−h|>γ is the same for all elements of the vector a and does not exceed [1 − 2γ + ψ(N)]N, where ψ(N) gives an empirical probability correction for a specific random generator, which is found experimentally. An analysis of the standard random generators indicates that the function ψ(N) almost vanishes starting from N = 1000. Therefore,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \widetilde{P}(\max_{i} \middle| h_{k}^{(i)} - h \middle| > \gamma) = \widetilde{P}(\mathcal{V}^{k}) = {(1 - 2\gamma)}^{N}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.114)

The probability of the event 𝒱 (7.111) has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\widetilde{P}(\mathcal{V}) = \widetilde{P}(N,n) = {(1 - 2\gamma)}^{Nn}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.115)

The probability of the opposite event $\underset{k = 1}{\overset{m}{\cup}}\left. (\max_{i} \middle| h_{k}^{(i)} - h \middle| < \gamma) \right.$ makes up


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(\mathcal{V}) = 1 - {(1 - 2\gamma)}^{Nn}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.116)

Choosing γ = h2, from (7.116) we establish that the probability of the event (7.111) is


$$\begin{array}{r} {P(\mathcal{V}) > 1 - ({\lbrack - 2\left( \frac{l}{N} \right)^{2}\rbrack}^{Nn}) = P(N,n).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.117)

Consequently, inequality (7.113) holds with a probability not smaller than P(N, m).

3. Consider the second term in (7.3). The following estimate is valid:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. v\left. \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N} \right|\phi(\zeta^{i},\mathbf{z}) - \phi(\mathbf{w}^{i},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \left( \frac{1}{N} \right)^{n}\,\max_{(\zeta,\mathbf{w}) \in I^{n}} \middle| \phi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) - \phi(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}) \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.118)

The expression under the summation sign defines the modulus of continuity of the function ϕ(w, z); see [61]. Since this function is differentiable,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \max_{(\zeta,\mathbf{w}) \in I^{n}} \middle| \phi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) - \phi(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \max_{\mathbf{w} \in I^{n};\mspace{2mu} k \in \lbrack 1,n\rbrack} \middle| \frac{\partial\phi(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z})}{\partial w_{k}} \middle| \,\max_{(\zeta,\mathbf{w}) \in I^{n}}\|\zeta - \mathbf{w}\|. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.119)

The distance between any random point and its nearest neighbors does not exceed the diagonal of the elementary cube, i.e.,


$$\begin{aligned} {\max_{(\zeta^{i},\mathbf{w}^{i}) \in I^{n};i \in \lbrack 1,N\rbrack}\|\zeta^{i} - \mathbf{w}^{i}\|} & {\leq \sqrt{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}{(\zeta_{k}^{i} - w_{k}^{i})}^{2}} \leq \sqrt{n}\max_{k}\delta_{k}^{i},} \\ & {\delta_{k}^{i} = \zeta_{k}^{i} - w_{k}^{i}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.120)

Take a sufficiently small positive value γ. According to (7.100) and the definition of ζi as the mean point of the elementary cube of the nonuniform random lattice, consider the chain of inequalities


$$\begin{array}{r} {\max_{k}\delta_{k}^{i} < \max_{k}h_{k}^{i} < \gamma.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.121)

Let γ = h2, where h is the step of the uniform lattice. The latter inequality holds with the probability P(N) (7.117).

Estimate the value


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial w_{k}} = - E(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z})\exp( - E(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}))\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{k}},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.122)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{k}} = {\sum\limits_{t = 1}^{T}{\sum\limits_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{t}) = 1}^{n}A_{(n_{1},\ldots,n_{t})}}}(\mathbf{z}){\prod\limits_{r = 1,n_{r} \neq k}^{t}x_{n_{r}}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.123)

Using (7.106–7.108), write


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \max_{\mathbf{w} \in I^{n}}\max_{k} \middle| \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial w_{k}} \middle| \leq G^{2}\exp(G). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.124)

Then the estimate (7.119) takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \max_{(\zeta,\mathbf{w}) \in I^{n}} \middle| \phi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) - \phi(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \sqrt{m}\left( \frac{l}{N} \right)^{2 + n}G^{2}\exp(G) = \frac{n}{N}\sqrt{n}G^{2}\exp(G). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.125)

Substitute (7.107) and (7.119) into (7.3) to establish that the inequality


$$\begin{array}{r} \left| \mathbb{B}(\mathbf{z}) - \widetilde{\mathbb{B}}(\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq N\exp(G)\left( \frac{l}{N} \right)^{m}\left\lbrack {1 + \sqrt{m}\left( \frac{l}{N} \right)^{2}G^{2}} \right\rbrack = \widetilde{\epsilon}(N,m) \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.126)

holds with a probability not smaller than P(N, m) (7.117).

4. Now switch to inequalities (7.3). They are structurally similar to inequalities (7.3), and the only difference consists in the function φ(w, z) (7.98). Hence,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \left. \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N} \right|v^{i} - v \middle| \middle| \varphi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \max_{\zeta \in I^{n}} \middle| \varphi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) \middle| \left. \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N} \right|v^{i} - v \middle| \leq N\left( \frac{l}{N} \right)^{n + 1}\max_{\zeta \in I^{n}} \middle| \varphi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.127)

By the definition of the function φ(a, z) (7.98),


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \max_{\zeta \in I^{n}} \middle| \varphi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \max_{\mathbf{w} \in I^{n}} \middle| E(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \exp(E(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z})) = G\exp(G), \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.128)

where G is given by equalities (7.108). For the second term in (7.3), the estimate takes the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \max_{(\zeta,\mathbf{w})} \middle| \varphi(\zeta,\mathbf{z}) - \varphi(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq \max_{\mathbf{w} \in I^{n},\mspace{2mu} k \in \lbrack 1,n\rbrack}\, \middle| \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial w_{k}} \middle| \max_{(\zeta,\mathbf{w}) \in I^{n}}\|\zeta - \mathbf{w}\|. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.129)

According to the definition of the function φ(w, z) (7.98), also write


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial w_{k}} = \frac{\partial E(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z})}{\partial w_{k}}\exp( - E(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z}))(1 - E^{2}(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{z})),} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.130)

which yields the estimate


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \max_{\mathbf{w} \in I^{n},\mspace{2mu} k \in \lbrack 1,n\rbrack}\, \middle| \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial w_{k}} \middle| \leq G(1 + G^{2})\,\exp(G). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.131)

Thus, the inequality


$$\begin{array}{r} \left| \mathbb{G}(\mathbf{z}) - \widetilde{\mathbb{G}}(\mathbf{z}) \middle| \leq N\left( \frac{l}{N} \right)^{n + 1}G\exp(G)\left\lbrack {1 + \frac{l}{N}(1 + G^{2})} \right\rbrack = \widetilde{\kappa}(N,n) \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.132)

takes place with a probability not smaller than P(N, m) (7.117).

An upper bound for the value N (or M) can be calculated from the condition


$$\begin{array}{r} {N^{*} = \max(\widetilde{\epsilon}(N,n) = \delta;\,\,\widetilde{\kappa}(N,n) = \delta).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.133)

7.4Multiplicative Algorithms with p-Active Variables

Many problems arising in RML and ML procedures are reduced to systems of nonlinear equations, e.g., the balance equations (7.9–7.12). Let us illustrate a method for solving such equations that are associated with the entropy maximization problems on polyhedrons [140].

Consider a system of equalities that are interpreted as the balance constraints between data q ∈ Rr and an output y ∈ Rn of some linear parametric model:


$$\begin{array}{r} {T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{q},\quad(T,\mathbf{y}) \geq 0,\,\,\mathbf{q} \geq \varepsilon > 0,\text{\quad\quad}r < n.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.134)

Here T denotes a matrix of full rank r. For the system (7.134), there exists a set of solutions and a unique solution among them that maximizes the entropy


$$\begin{array}{r} {H(\mathbf{y}) = - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}y_{i}}\ln\frac{y_{i}}{ea_{i}},\text{\quad\quad}e = 2.71,} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.135)

with a1, …, an acting as parameters.

Consider the following constrained optimization problem for the entropy (7.135):


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. H(\mathbf{y})\Rightarrow\max, \right. \\ & {T\,\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{q}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.136)

The corresponding Lagrange function has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {L(\mathbf{y},\overline{\lambda}) = H(\mathbf{y}) + {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{r}\lambda_{k}}\left( {q_{k} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}t_{ki}}y_{i}} \right).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.137)

The first-order optimality conditions are given by


$$\begin{aligned} {\nabla_{y_{i}}L(\mathbf{y},\overline{\lambda})} & {= \frac{\partial H(\mathbf{y})}{\partial y_{i}} - {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{r}\lambda_{k}}t_{ki} = 0,\quad i = \overline{1,n};} \\ {\nabla_{\lambda_{k}}L(\mathbf{y},\overline{\lambda})} & {= q_{k} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}t_{ki}}y_{i} = 0,\quad k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.138)

The first group of equations yields a relation between the variables y and the Lagrange multipliers $\overline{\lambda}$ in the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {y_{i}(\overline{\lambda}) = \frac{a_{i}}{{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{r}\exp}(t_{k}i\lambda_{k})},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,n}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.139)

This relation allows us to eliminate the primal variables y from the definition of the Lagrange function (7.137), leading to the following expression for the dual function (which depends on the dual variables—the Lagrange multipliers):


$$\begin{array}{r} {\widetilde{L}(\overline{\lambda}) = L\lbrack\mathbf{y}(\overline{\lambda}),\overline{\lambda}\rbrack.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.140)

The elements of its gradient are


$$\begin{array}{r} {\nabla_{\lambda_{k}}\widetilde{L}(\overline{\lambda}) = q_{k} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}y_{i}}(\overline{\lambda}),\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.141)

In terms of the dual function, the second group of the optimality conditions (7.138) can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\nabla_{\lambda_{k}}\widetilde{L}(\overline{\lambda}) = 0,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.142)

Hence, the balance constraints take the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda}) = \frac{1}{q_{k}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}t_{ki}}\frac{a_{i}}{{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{r}\exp}\left( {\lambda_{j}t_{ji}} \right)} = 1,\quad\overline{\lambda} \in R^{r},\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.143)

Often it seems convenient to transform these equations using the nonnegative variables $z_{k} = \exp(\lambda_{k}),\, k = \overline{1,r},$ known as the exponential Lagrange multipliers. Then equations (7.143) are reduced to


$$\begin{array}{r} {B_{k}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{q_{k}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}t_{ki}}a_{i}\left( {\prod\limits_{j = 1}^{r}z_{k}^{- t_{ji}}} \right) = 1,\quad\mathbf{z} \in R_{+}^{r},\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.144)

Now, for the dual function (7.140), the Hessian matrix has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \Gamma(\overline{\lambda}) = \lbrack\nabla_{\lambda_{j},\lambda_{l}}\widetilde{L}(\overline{\lambda})\, \middle| \,(j,l) = \overline{1,r}\rbrack, \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.145)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {\nabla_{\lambda_{j},\lambda_{l}}\widetilde{L}(\overline{\lambda}) = - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}t_{kj}}\frac{\partial y_{j}}{\partial\lambda_{l}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.146)

The primal variables expression (7.139) implies the inequality


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial y_{j}}{\partial\lambda_{l}} \leq 0,} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.147)

holding for all λ ∈ Rr. Therefore, the Hessian matrix (7.143) consists of nonnegative elements. Taking into account (7.145), the quadratic form $K = \left\langle \Gamma\overline{\lambda},\,\overline{\lambda} \right\rangle$ is strictly positive definite for any $\overline{\lambda} \in R^{r}.$ This means that the dual function L̃ is strictly convex. The system of equations 7.143 guarantees boundedness of its solution, i.e., there exists a constant c > 0 such that $\left| \overline{\lambda} \middle| \leq c < \infty. \right.$ Consequently, L̃ ≥ Lmin.

For solving equations (7.138), utilize the multiplicative algorithm with p-active variables as follows.

Initial step:


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{z}^{0} > \mathbf{0}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Iterative step:


$$\begin{aligned} z_{k_{1}(s)}^{(s + 1)} & {= z_{k_{1}(s)}^{s}B_{k_{1}(s)}^{\gamma}(\mathbf{z}^{s}),} \\ \cdots & {= \cdots\cdots\cdots,} \\ z_{k_{p}(s)}^{(s + 1)} & {= z_{k_{p}(s)}^{s}B_{k_{p}(s)}^{\gamma}(\mathbf{z}^{s})} \\ z_{k}^{(s + 1)} & {= z_{k}^{s},\quad k \neq k_{1}(s),\ldots,k_{p}(s),} \\ & {(k,k_{1}(s),\ldots,k_{p}(s)) \in \overline{1,n}.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.148)

Further analysis will need an additive form of the algorithm (7.148) in the variables λk = ln zk. This form is written in the following way.

Initial step:


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\overline{\lambda}}^{0} \in R^{n}.} \\ \end{array}$$

Iterative step:


$$\begin{aligned} \lambda_{k_{1}(s)}^{(s + 1)} & {= \lambda_{k_{1}(s)}^{s} + \gamma\ln{\widetilde{B}}_{k_{1}(s)}({\overline{\lambda}}^{s}),} \\ \cdots & {= \cdots\cdots\cdots,} \\ \lambda_{k_{p}(s)}^{(s + 1)} & {= \lambda_{k_{p}(s)}^{s} + \gamma\ln{\widetilde{B}}_{k_{p}(s)}({\overline{\lambda}}^{s})} \\ \lambda_{k}^{(s + 1)} & {= \lambda_{k}^{s},\quad k \neq k_{1}(s),\ldots,k_{p}(s),} \\ & {(k,k_{1}(s),\ldots,k_{p}(s)) \in \overline{1,n},} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.149)

where ${\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda}) = B_{k}(\exp(\overline{\lambda})),\, k = \overline{1,r}.$

A major difficulty for such algorithms is to select active variables. This selection can be organized by a cyclical rule, e.g., for p = 1,


$$\begin{array}{r} {k_{1}(s) = s(\text{mod}\, n + 1).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.150)

A more efficient approach involves residual feedback, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \vartheta_{k}(\mathbf{z}^{s}) = \middle| 1 - B_{k}(\mathbf{z}^{s}) \middle| ,\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,n}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(7.151)

Introduce the following notations:


$$\begin{aligned} \frac{r}{p} & {= I + \delta,\text{\quad\quad}\rho = s\lbrack\text{(}mod)\,(I + 1)\rbrack,} \\ I & {= \left\lbrack \frac{r}{p} \right\rbrack,\text{\quad\quad}0 \leq \delta \leq p - 1.} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.152)

Here [ ⋅ ] indicates the integer part of value  ⋅ . Consider the index sets


$$\begin{array}{r} {K = \left\{ 1,\ldots,r \right\},\text{\quad\quad}K_{m}(s) = \left\{ k_{1}(s),\ldots,k_{m}(s) \right\},} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.153)

where


$$\begin{array}{r} {m = \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {1,\ldots,p\text{if}\,\rho < I;} \\ {1,\ldots,\delta\text{if}\,\rho = I.} \\ \end{array}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.154)

Let


$$\begin{aligned} {P_{m - 1}(s)} & {= \left\lbrack {{\underset{v = 1}{\overset{\rho}{\cup}}K_{p}}(s - v)} \right\rbrack{\cup K_{m - 1}}(s),} \\ {G_{m - 1}(s)} & {= K\smallsetminus P_{m - 1}(s),} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(7.155)

where K0(s) = P0(s) = G0(s) = ⌀.

Now we can state the selection rule of active variables: the packet of active variables is formed by the p variables whose indexes correspond to the maximum residuals, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {k_{m}(s) = \arg\max_{i \in G_{m - 1}(s)}\vartheta_{i}(\mathbf{z}^{s}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.156)

This rule yields the chain of inequalities


$$\begin{array}{r} {\vartheta_{k_{p}(s)}(\mathbf{z}^{s}) < \vartheta_{k_{p - 1}(s)}(\mathbf{z}^{s}) < \cdots\vartheta_{k_{1}(s)}(\mathbf{z}^{s}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.157)

Application of the rule (7.156, 7.157) makes all variables active in (I + 1) iterations, and this situation occurs again and again with period (I + 1).

Our convergence analysis of the algorithm (7.149) will begin with an important notion as follows.

Definition The algorithm (7.4) is called Gλ-convergent if there exist a subset Gλ ∈ Rn and positive scalars a(Gλ), γ such that, for all γ ∈ (0, a(Gλ)) and ${\overline{\lambda}}^{0} \in G_{\lambda},$ the algorithm converges to the solution ${\overline{\lambda}}^{*}$ of equation (7.143) with the linear rate.

A similar definition can be introduced for the algorithm (7.148), in which the variables are the exponential Lagrange multipliers z ∈ R+r.

Consider a subsequence ${\overline{\lambda}}^{(I + 1)s}$ of the elements that are generated by the algorithm (7.149) and also an auxiliary system of nonlinear differential equations that is obtained from (7.149) as γ→0, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{d\lambda_{k}}{dt} = \ln{\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda}),\text{\quad\quad}\overline{\lambda}(0) = {\overline{\lambda}}^{0},\text{\quad\quad}k = \overline{1,r}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.158)

Lemma 1 The singular point ${\overline{\lambda}}^{*}$ of the system (7.158) is asymptotically stable for any initial deviations ${\overline{\lambda}}^{0} \in R^{r}.$

Proof. Consider the dual function (7.140) and define its derivative along the trajectory of the system (7.158):


$$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{d\widetilde{L}}{dt} = \sum_{k = 1}^{r}\frac{d\widetilde{L}}{d\lambda_{k}}\frac{d\lambda_{k}}{dt} = \sum_{k = 1}^{r}\lbrack 1 - {\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda})\rbrack\,\ln{\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(7.159)

Then $\frac{d\widetilde{L}}{dt} < 0$ for all ${\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda}) \neq 1$ and $\frac{d\widetilde{L}}{dt} = 0$ for ${\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda}) = 1.$ Since there exists a unique minimum point of the dual function, its gradient vanishes only at this point. Hence, $\frac{d\widetilde{L}}{dt} < 0$ for all $\overline{\lambda} \in R^{r},$ and $\frac{d\widetilde{L}}{dt} = 0$ for $\overline{\lambda} = {\overline{\lambda}}^{*}.$

Therefore, L̃ (7.140) is a Lyapunov function for equation (7.158), and this property holds for any ${\overline{\lambda}}^{0} \in R^{r}.$ ■

The convergence conditions of the iterative process (7.149) are defined by Theorem 1. Assume that:

(a) the functions $\Phi_{k}(\overline{\lambda}) = \ln{\widetilde{B}}_{k}(\overline{\lambda}),\,(k = \overline{1,n}),$ are continuously differentiable;

(b) the Jacobian matrix $J({\overline{\lambda}}^{*}) = \left\lbrack \frac{\partial\Phi_{k}(\overline{\lambda})}{\partial\lambda_{i}} \right\rbrack_{{\overline{\lambda}}^{*}}$ is a Hurwitz matrix;

(c) the set Gλ is compact;

(d) there exists ε > 0 such that the inequality $\|\overline{\lambda}(t) - {\overline{\lambda}}^{*}\| \leq \varepsilon,$ where $\overline{\lambda}(t)$ is the solution of the system (7.156) with the initial condition $\overline{\lambda}(0) = {\overline{\lambda}}^{0},$ holds for all ${\overline{\lambda}}^{0} \in G_{\lambda}$ starting from some t > 0.

Then the process generated by the algorithm (7.4) is Gλ-convergent.

Under the hypotheses of this theorem, the algorithm (7.149) gives a Euler polygon approximation for the solution of the system (7.158).

Proof. Choose a countable everywhere dense set of points {ζs} in Gλ. Let t1 be the first time when the solution of equation (7.158) with the initial condition ζ1 gets into the ε/2-neighborhood of the point ${\overline{\lambda}}^{*};$ this time t1 exists by condition (d). Choose a neighborhood 𝒢1 of the point ζ1 so that the points from it will reach the 3ε/4-neighborhood of the point ${\overline{\lambda}}^{*}$ along the trajectory of the system (7.158) after the time t1. Note that condition (a) guarantees that the solution is continuously dependent on the initial conditions.

Choose a point ζ2 among the ones not belonging to 𝒢1. Like for the point ζ1, define t2 and a neighborhood 𝒢2 for the point ζ2. Continue this process to obtain a cover of the set Gλ by open sets 𝒢1, 𝒢2, ... Due to condition (c), from these sets it is possible to choose a finite subcover 𝒢i1, …, 𝒢im. Let T = min {ti1,…,tim}. Finally, using condition (a), take a sufficiently small value γ > 0 so that on the interval 0, T the solution of the system (7.158) is approximated by the Euler polygons with the accuracy ε/4.

CHAPTER 8 GENERATION METHODS FOR RANDOM VECTORS WITH GIVEN PROBABILITY DENSITY FUNCTIONS OVER COMPACT SETS

DOI: 10.1201/9781003306566-8

The final stage of the RML procedure is to generate an ensemble of random vectors or trajectories using the entropy-optimal randomized model. Here of crucial importance are the methods that allow to generate these random objects with given PDFs of arbitrary form. In the general statement, the generation problem of random sequences and random vectors is classical for the Monte Carlo method. There exist many methods for generating “standard” sequences of random numbers with given probabilistic characteristics (uniform, Gaussian, Poisson distributions, etc. [159, 168]). However, when the matter concerns the sequences obeying arbitrary-form PDFs and also the sequences of high-dimensional random vectors, just a few methods can be suggested. At the beginning of this chapter, we will give a brief survey of generation methods, which does not claim to be exhaustive and provides an insight into the main concepts underlying these methods. Our attention will be focused on a method for generating random vectors with PDFs defined on compact sets. It approximates a given PDF by n-dimensional piecewise constant functions, in which the step depends on the Lipschitz constant of this PDF. A major aspect of random object generation is to perform a statistical check whether the probabilistic properties of the generated objects match the given PDF.

8.1A Survey of Generation Methods for Random Objects

The problem to generate random variables, vectors and trajectories has a growing significance because the Monte Carlo method is a real tool for solving different problems of numerical integration, optimization, control and machine learning, including randomized machine learning. Therefore, it would be useful for the reader to get acquainted with some generation methods that are frequently mentioned in the literature. This survey consists of two parts, the first being devoted to the generation of random variables and the second to the generation of random vectors.

8.1.1Random variables

1. Continuous random variables

Consider a random variable ξ that takes values within an interval [a,b] and has a continuous PDF w(x). Its probability distribution function has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {F(x) = {\int_{a}^{x}w}(y)dy.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.1)

The range of the function F is the interval [0,1]. Define a random variable η obeying the uniform distribution on the interval [0,1] and study the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {F(\xi) = \eta.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.2)

The solution of this equation—a random variable ξ—has the PDF w(x), see [168].

2. The method of inverse functions

Consider a random variable ξ distributed on an interval [a,b] with a continuous PDF w(x). Its probability distribution function F(x) has the form (8.1). Assume that it possesses the inverse function G(y) = F − 1(y). As established in [159, 168], the random variable ξ = G(η), where η is given by (8.2), has the PDF w(x). This result applies to the PDFs with discontinuities of the first kind.

3. The composition method of inverse functions

Let a random variable ξ be distributed on an interval [a,b] with a PDF w(x) (possibly, with discontinuities of the first kind). In addition, assume that this PDF represents the sum of PDFs wi(x) with the same properties, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {w(x) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}p_{i}}w_{i}(x),\text{\quad\quad}p_{i} \geq 0,\quad{\sum\limits_{i = n}^{n}p_{i}} = 1.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.3)

The random variables ξi with the PDFs wi(x) are generated using one of the above-mentioned methods. The non-random variables p1, …, pn take values within the unit interval. They will be interpreted as probabilities; to this end, introduce an integer random variable Y such that Pb(Y = i) = pi. Then the random variable ξ can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {\xi = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\xi_{i}}\Delta(Y = i),\text{\quad\quad}\Lambda(Y = i) = 1\text{~if~}\, Y = i;\,\,\Lambda(Y = i) = 0\text{~if~}\, Y \neq i.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.4)

4. The acceptance-rejection method (AR method)

This method was developed by S. Ulam and J. von Neumann. In contrast to the previous methods, it is based on simulations of generated random variables, including their checking subject to a given PDF. Let us study the main idea of the AR method. Consider a random variable ξ distributed on an interval [a,b] with a PDF w(x). Introduce the number


$$\begin{array}{r} {c = \max\left\{ w(x),\, x \in \lbrack a,b\rbrack \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.5)

Generate a pair of independent random variables η, γ obeying the uniform distribution on the intervals [a,b] and [0,c], respectively. If γ < w(η), then ξ = η. Otherwise, repeat the generation procedure.

A pair (γ, η) corresponds to a point on the (y, x) plane, which contains the set 𝒲 = {(y,x):y≤w(x), x∈[a,b]}. The points generated by the AR method are uniformly filling the rectangle [0, c] × [a, b]. However, many of them do not belong to the requisite set 𝒲. This leads to a natural desire to put the set 𝒲 into a closer set. A general approach to solve this problem was proposed in [159].

5. Generation of common PDFs: several examples

The exponential PDF. Consider a random variable ξ distributed with the PDF w(x) = λexp ( − λx), x ≥ 0. The corresponding probability distribution function has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {F(x) = 1 - \exp( - \lambda x).} \\ \end{array}$$

The inverse function is


$$\begin{array}{r} {G(y) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1 - y).} \\ \end{array}$$

Generating the random variable Y with the uniform distribution on the interval [0,1], obtain the random variable


$$\begin{array}{r} {\xi = \frac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1 - Y).} \\ \end{array}$$

The Gaussian PDF. A Gaussian random variable is ξ ∼ N(μ, σ2), where μ denotes its mean and σ2 its variance. Assume that a generator of a standard Gaussian random variable Ξ ∼ N(0, 1) is available. Then


$$\begin{array}{r} {\xi = \mu + \Xi\sigma.} \\ \end{array}$$

The generation methods of random variables with the Gaussian, gamma and beta PDFs distributions (with continuous and discrete “sharpness” parameters) were described, e.g., in the book [159]. These methods are based on generators of uniformly distributed random variables on the interval [0,1].

8.1.2Random vectors

1. Independent elements

If a random vector $\overline{\xi}$ consists of independent elements ξi, then its PDF and probability distribution function have a multiplicative structure, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {w(\mathbf{x}) = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}w_{i}}(x_{i}),\text{\quad\quad}F(\mathbf{x}) = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}F_{i}}(x_{i}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.6)

Therefore, each element ξi can be generated independently by solving the equation


$$\begin{array}{r} {F_{i}(\xi_{i}) = \eta_{i},\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,n},} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.7)

where η1, …, ηn are the independent random variables that obey the uniform distribution on the interval [0,1].

2. Dependent elements

If a random vector $\overline{\xi}$ has dependent elements ξi, then its PDF can be written as the product of the conditional PDFs:


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. w(\mathbf{x}) = w_{1}(x_{1})w(x_{2}\, \middle| \, x_{1})\cdots w_{n}(x_{n}\, \middle| \, x_{1},\ldots,x_{n - 1}). \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(8.8)

Let us introduce the conditional probability distribution functions


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. F_{i}(x_{i}\, \middle| \, x_{1},\ldots,x_{i}) = {\int_{- \infty}^{x_{i}}w_{i}}(x\, \middle| \, x_{1},\ldots,x_{i})dx,\text{\quad\quad}i = \overline{1,n}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(8.9)

Consider the system of equations


$$\begin{aligned} {F_{1}(\xi_{1}) = \eta_{1},} & \\ \left. F_{2}(\xi_{2}\, \middle| \,\xi_{1}) = \eta_{2}, \right. & \\ {\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots} & \\ \left. F_{n}(\xi_{n}\, \middle| \,\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n - 1}) = \eta_{n - 1}. \right. & \\ \end{aligned}$$
(8.10)

Note that (η1, …, η, n) are the independent random variables with the uniform distribution on the interval [0,1]. Solving these equations sequentially, find a collection of the desired random variables, i.e., a vector $\overline{\xi} = \left\{ \xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n} \right\}$ with the PDF w(x) [168].

3. The multidimensional AR method

Consider a given PDF w(x), where the vector x ∈ G ⊂ Rn. Denote


$$\begin{array}{r} {c = \max(w(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{x} \in Q).} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.11)

Consider a set 𝒬 in space R(n + 1) that contains the points {y≤w(x,x∈Q)}, and also a cylindrical set with height c and base Q, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {W = \left\{ c,Q \right\}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.12)

Following the general idea of the AR method (see above), generate a random variable γ with the uniform distribution on the interval [0,c] and also a random vector $\overline{\eta}$ with the uniform distribution on the set Q. This yields a random point $(\gamma,\overline{\eta})$ in the set W (8.12). If it gets into the set 𝒬, then $\mathbf{x} = \overline{\eta}.$ Otherwise, the generation procedure is repeated.

Clearly, the efficiency of this method essentially depends on the configuration of the set that contains the set 𝒢. It seems that the cylindrical sets are not best. Therefore, the generation method under study is sensitive to the quality of approximation for the set 𝒢.

4. The Metropolis-Hastings (MH) method

Unlike the previously considered ones, this method involves a specially designed Markov chain for generating each element of a sample with a given PDF. Assume that it is necessary to generate an element of a sample with a PDF w(x). Since the generation procedure is based on a Markov chain, each new value x(s + 1) of this element depends on its preceding value xs only. Consider an auxiliary conditional PDF q(y | xs). A reasonable choice is using a PDF with a rather simple generation of random objects. As a rule, the Gaussian PDF works well.

At step s of the MH method, one should generate a random vector ys and calculate the parameter


$$\begin{array}{r} {u = \frac{w(\mathbf{y}^{s})}{w(\mathbf{x}^{s})}\,\frac{\left. q(\mathbf{x}^{s})\, \middle| \,\mathbf{y}^{s} \right.}{\left. q(\mathbf{y}^{s})\, \middle| \,\mathbf{x}^{s} \right.}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.13)

The transition rule has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {u \leq 1,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x}^{(s + 1)} = \mathbf{y}^{s},} \\ {u > 1,\text{\quad\quad}\mathbf{x}^{(s + 1)} = \mathbf{x}^{s}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.14)

Similarly to the AR method, the efficiency of the MH method depends on the form of the auxiliary function. In particular, if the Gaussian distribution is used as the auxiliary one, then its parameters are adjusted for a better approximation of a given PDF. For details, the reader is referred to [31, 32, 64, 120, 121].

8.2Direct Generation Method for Random Vectors with Given Probability Density Function

This method uses an approximation of a given PDF by a step function, with a subsequent generation of the uniformly distributed independent random vectors inside a randomly chosen elementary cube. Consider a PDF w(x), x ∈ Q ⊂ Rn.

8.2.1Unit cube Q

Introduce a uniform lattice with step h for each coordinate of the unit cube Q. Then this cube is partitioned into the elementary cubes of volumes Vi = hn. Let (1/h) be an integer value. Then the number of elementary cubes is N = (1/h)n and $i = \overline{1,N}.$ For each elementary cube, introduce another lattice with step η. As a result, each elementary cube consists of inner subcubes of volumes vij = ηn. Denote their number by M = (1/η)n, $j = \overline{1,M}.$ Assume that the total volume of all elementary cubes coincides with the total volume of all their subcubes. Choose an arbitrary point xij in each inner subcube and define the value


$$\begin{array}{r} {C_{i} = \frac{1}{M}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}w}(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{j}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.15)

For a sufficiently large number M,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. C_{i} \right.\sim\frac{1}{V_{i}}{\int_{V_{i}}w}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.16)

Therefore,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. C_{i} \right.\sim w(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{if}\,\mathbf{x} \in V_{i}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.17)

Denote by ${\overline{\xi}}^{i},\, i = \overline{1,N},$ the independent random vectors obeying the uniform distribution on the elementary cubes. The density of such a vector is 1/Vi inside an elementary cube and 0 outside it. These vectors can be generated using the method (8.6, 8.7).

Let β be an integer random variable that does not depend on $\left\{ {\overline{\xi}}^{i} \right\}$ and takes values 1, …, N with the probabilities pi = CiVi. Then the generated vectors have the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {\mathbf{x} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\overline{\xi}}^{i}}\Lambda(\beta = i),} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.18)

where Λ(A) means the indicator function of a set A. The PDF of the vector x can be written as


$$\begin{aligned} & \left. P(\mathbf{x} = d\mathbf{x}) = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}P}(\mathbf{x} = d\mathbf{x}\, \middle| \,\beta = i)P(\beta = i) = \right. \\ & {\left. \text{\quad\quad}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}C_{i}}d\mathbf{x}\Lambda(V_{i}) \right.\sim{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}w}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}\Lambda(V_{i}).} \\ \end{aligned}$$
(8.19)

8.2.2Compact set Q

1. Q—parallelepiped Π

Consider the set Pi = {x:a≤x≤b}, where a and b are given vectors. Denote the lengths of their edges by $l_{i} = b_{i} - a_{i},\, i = \overline{1,n}.$ Introduce a nonuniform lattice on this set, which can be designed either with a fixed number K of elements for each coordinate or with a fixed step h. In the former case, there are different steps for all coordinates, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {h_{i} = l_{i}/K;} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.20)

in the latter case, different numbers of elements for all lattices, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {K_{i} = l_{i}/h.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.21)

In fact, the fixed-step statement has been considered above. Hence, we will study the former case with a variable step. Because the lattice has the same number of elements for each coordinate, the number of all elementary parallelepipeds Πi is N = Kn. The elementary parallelepipeds have the same volume


$$\begin{array}{r} {V = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}h_{i}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.22)

Inside each parallelepiped, introduce another lattice with M elements for each coordinate. Then for each coordinate the lattice step is


$$\begin{array}{r} {\eta_{i} = h_{i}/M,} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.23)

and the volume of the jth inner subparallelepiped πij makes up


$$\begin{array}{r} {v = {\prod\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\eta_{i}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.24)

(here j denotes the index of an inner subparallelepiped inside the ith elementary parallelepiped). The number of all inner subparallelepipeds πij inside the elementary parallelepiped Πi is


$$\begin{array}{r} {L = M^{n}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.25)

Choose an arbitrary point xij in πij and calculate the value


$$\begin{array}{r} {C_{i} = \frac{1}{M}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{M}w}(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{j}).} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.26)

Under a sufficiently large number M,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\left. C_{i} \right.\sim\frac{1}{V_{i}}{\int_{V_{i}}w}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.27)

The remainder of this generation procedure is organized in the same way as for the unit cube; see above.

2. Arbitrary compact set Q

In this case, put the set Q into the parallelepiped Π = {x:a≤x≤b}. The edges can be defined arbitrarily, but in such a way that Q ⊂ Π. A more efficient approach to generate random vectors is putting the set Q into a hull in form of the parallelepiped Π*. These possibilities are illustrated in Figs. 8.1(a) and 8.1(b) (a—arbitrary parallelepiped Π, b—hull). Clearly, hull construction requires a preliminary calculation of the extreme points (A, B, C, D).

Recall that the PDF w(x) is defined on the set Q. Introduce an auxiliary PDF of the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {W(\mathbf{x}) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {w(\mathbf{x})} & {\text{if}\,\mathbf{x} \in Q,} \\ 0 & {\text{if}\,\mathbf{x} \in \Pi\smallsetminus Q.} \\ \end{aligned}~ \right.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.28)

It is immediately obvious that the parallelepiped Π forms the domain of definition of the PDF W(x). We will use the generation procedure of item 2 for the PDF W(x). Note that W(x) = 0 on the elementary parallelepipeds Πi and also on the inner subparallelepipeds πij inside the set Π* ∖ Q. Hence, P(x = dx) = 0 by (8.2.1).

8.3Approximation of Given Probability Density Function

The suggested generation procedure for random vectors with a given probability density function has such important aspects as approximation accuracy and lattice step.

1. Estimation of approximation accuracy

Consider a PDF w(x), where x ∈ Q ⊂ Rn. The set Q is compact, i.e., has a nonzero volume VQ ≠ 0. Assume that the set Q is put into an n-dimensional parallelepiped Π. The function w(x) is square integrable.

To generate random vectors with the PDF w(x), it will be approximated by a piecewise constant function g(x), x ∈ Π. The quality of this approximation will be measured by the functional


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. J(A) = \middle| {\int_{A}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - g(\mathbf{x})} \right)}d\mathbf{x} \middle| , \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(8.29)

where A indicates an arbitrary set in Π.

Define a uniform lattice with a step $h_{k},\, k = \overline{1,n},$ for each coordinate on the set Π of the volume VΠ. Each element of this lattice is an elementary parallelepiped $\Pi_{i},\, i = \overline{1,N},$ with the sides hk. Without loss of generality, assume that


$$\begin{array}{r} {N = \frac{V_{\Pi}}{V_{\Pi_{i}}} = \frac{V_{\Pi}}{\prod\limits_{k = 1}^{n}h_{k}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.30)

Moreover, let this value be integer. Note that all the elementary parallelepipeds Πi have the same volumes. In each set Πi, replace the function w(x) with a constant Bi. Performing this operation for all the elementary parallelepipeds, obtain a piecewise constant linear approximating function g(x).

Consider a certain set A ∈ Π. It is covered by the union of the elementary parallelepipeds, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {A = {\underset{i = 1}{\overset{N}{\cup}}\Pi_{i}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.31)

Then, using the Cauchy–Bunyakovsky–Schwarz inequality, write the upper bound


$$\begin{array}{r} {J(A) \leq \sqrt{{\int_{A}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - g(\mathbf{x})} \right)^{2}}d\mathbf{x}{\int_{A}\Lambda}(A)d\mathbf{x}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.32)

Here Λ(A) denotes the indicator function of the set A. It follows from (8.32) that


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{A}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - g(\mathbf{x})} \right)^{2}}d\mathbf{x} \leq {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\int_{\Pi_{i}}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - B_{i}} \right)^{2}}}d\mathbf{x}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.33)

Hence,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sup\limits_{A}J(A) \leq {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\int_{\Pi_{i}}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - B_{i}} \right)^{2}}}d\mathbf{x}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.34)

As a result, the best estimates of the constants B1, …, BN can be derived by minimizing the functional


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\int_{\Pi_{i}}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - B_{i}} \right)^{2}}}d\mathbf{x}\Rightarrow\min_{B_{1},\ldots,B_{N}} \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(8.35)

subject to the condition


$$\begin{array}{r} {V_{\Pi_{i}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}B_{i}} = 1.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.36)

This equality expresses the normalization condition of the PDF. The solution of the minimization problem is given by


$$\begin{array}{r} {B_{i}^{*} = \frac{1}{V_{\Pi_{i}}}{\int_{\Pi_{i}}w}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.37)

Thus, the described approximation procedure yields the optimal piecewise constant PDF g*(x) with the approximation accuracy


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sup\limits_{A}J(A) \leq \sqrt{V_{\Pi}}\sqrt{{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\int_{\Pi_{i}}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - B_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2}}}d\mathbf{x}} \leq \delta.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.38)

2. Optimization of lattice step (estimation of Lipschitz constant)

The procedure suggested below employs an estimate of the Lipschitz constant for the function w(x), which is assumed to be continuous. We have Bi* = w(xi*), where xi* ∈ Πi but the point xi* is unknown. Let the function w(x) satisfy the Lipschitz condition with a constant L, i.e.,


$$\begin{array}{r} {\max_{\mathbf{x} \in \Pi_{i}}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - B_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2} \leq L^{2}\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{i}^{*}\|.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.39)

The integral form of this inequality on the intervals [0, h1] × [0, h2] × ⋯ × [0, hn] can be written as


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{|pi_{i}}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - B_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2}}d\mathbf{x} \leq L^{2}{\int_{0}^{h_{1}}\cdots}{\int_{0}^{h_{n}}\left( {x_{1}^{2} + \cdots + x_{n}^{2}} \right)}dx_{1}\cdots dx_{n} =} \\ {L^{2}\left( {\frac{h_{1}^{3}}{3}h_{2}h_{3}\cdots h_{n} + \frac{h_{2}^{3}}{3}h_{1}h_{3}\cdots h_{n} + \cdots + \frac{h_{n}^{3}}{3}h_{1}h_{2}\cdots h_{n - 1}} \right) = L^{2}\varrho.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.40)

The variable ϱ is independent of the index i of an elementary parallelepiped because all of them have the same sizes. Taking into account (8.40), transform inequality (8.34) into


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sup J(A) \leq L\sqrt{V_{\Pi}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\varrho}} = L\sqrt{V_{\Pi}N\varrho}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.41)

Then


$$\begin{array}{r} {V_{\Pi} = NV_{\Pi_{i}} = N{\prod\limits_{j = 1}^{n}h_{j}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.42)

Hence, using (8.40), the right-hand side of inequality (8.41) can be reduced to


$$\begin{array}{r} {L\sqrt{V_{\Pi}N\varrho} = L\sqrt{V_{\Pi}}N\varrho = L\sqrt{V_{\Pi}^{2}}\frac{\varrho}{\prod\limits_{j = 1}^{n}h_{j}} = \frac{L}{\sqrt{3}}V_{\Pi}\sqrt{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}h_{j}^{2}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.43)

Denote h = max1 ≤ j ≤ nhj. Then it follows from (8.41, 8.43) that


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sup J(A) \leq L\sqrt{n/3}hV_{\Pi}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.44)

For a given approximation accuracy δ of the PDF w(x), the corresponding maximum lattice step is


$$\begin{array}{r} {h = \frac{\delta}{L\sqrt{\frac{n}{3}}V_{\Pi}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.45)

The maximum step for the longest edge of the parallelepiped allows us to find the number N of points and, using it, the steps hj for all other coordinates.

3. Rough estimate of step

The estimation method of the Lipschitz constant L and the maximum step h for elementary parallelepipeds design rests on the assumption that the integral in (8.37) can be calculated analytically (without errors). Unfortunately, this is not always the case. A given PDF often has a complex structure, which requires numerical calculation of the integral in formula (8.37). Such calculations are performed using an inner lattice with a step ηi that is considerably smaller than the step hi of the main lattice.

The step ηi can be chosen using a simple technique as follows. First, specify a certain step ηij, and calculate the number Mij = li/ηij of points in the integral sum Sij. Then repeat these operations, and check the variability of the resulting integral sums. If |Sij−Si(j − 1)|≤δ, where δ is a given accuracy, then stop further partition of the inner lattice. The integral can be estimated by


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{\Pi_{i}}\left( {w(\mathbf{x}) - {\hat{B}}_{i}^{*}} \right)^{2}}d\mathbf{x} \leq {\hat{J}}_{i} = S_{i}^{j^{*}} + \delta/2.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.46)

Here j* denotes the index of the inner lattice for which the calculations are stopped. Then, according to (8.38),


$$\begin{array}{r} {\sup\limits_{A}J(A) \leq \sqrt{V_{\Pi}}\sqrt{{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\hat{J}}_{i}} + N\delta/2}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.47)

The constants B̂1*, …, B̂N* and the estimates Ĵ1, …, ĴN are obtained numerically.

Because all the calculations have a rough character, it makes sense to consider an accuracy estimate based on another metric. Let $A \subseteq {\underset{i = 1}{\overset{N}{\cup}}Q_{i}}.$ Since VQi is independent of i,


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \sup\limits_{A}J(A) \leq V_{Q}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\max_{\mathbf{x} \in Q_{i}}} \middle| w(\mathbf{x} - C_{i}) \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(8.48)

The optimal constants $C_{i},i = \overline{1,N},$ are yielded by solving the optimization problem


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\max_{\mathbf{x} \in Q_{i}}} \middle| w(\mathbf{x} - C_{i}) \middle| \Rightarrow\max_{C_{1},\ldots,C_{N}}. \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(8.49)

The solution has the form


$$\begin{array}{r} {{\widetilde{C}}_{i} = \frac{\max_{\mathbf{x} \in Q_{i}}w(\mathbf{x}) + \min_{\mathbf{x} \in Q_{i}}w(\mathbf{x})}{2}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.50)

Recall that these constants are used to construct an approximating function for the PDF. Hence, they must be normalized in the following way:


$$\begin{array}{r} {C_{i}^{*} = \frac{{\widetilde{C}}_{i}}{V_{Q}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}{\widetilde{C}}_{i}}}.} \\ \end{array}$$
(8.51)

In the final analysis, the error can be estimated as


$$\begin{array}{r} \left. \sup\limits_{A}J(A) \leq V_{Q}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\max_{\mathbf{x} \in Q_{i}}} \middle| w(\mathbf{x} - C_{i}^{*}) \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$$
(8.52)

Consequently, we have derived two estimates for the approximation error, (8.47) and (8.52). In applications, it is necessary to calculate both estimates and compare them with a given accuracy. If at least one of the estimates fails, calculations should be repeated with a smaller lattice step.

CHAPTER 9 INFORMATION TECHNOLOGIES OF RANDOMIZED MACHINE LEARNING

DOI: 10.1201/9781003306566-9

By now the computer systems of various performance levels have evolved towards a heterogeneous structure that is characterized by an availability of computing devices of different types. A standard system includes a universal multi-core processor in combination with a massive-parallel architecture accelerator (also called a computational processor or a coprocessor). An overwhelming majority of modern high-performance systems is based on the concept of horizontal scaling, integrating thousands of heterogeneous computation modules within a uniform organization.

The heterogeneous architecture of computation modules considerably complicates an efficient utilization of computer systems, which is often comprehended as an almost 100% load of all computing devices. Here a main difficulty consists in architectural features and, in many cases, in significant distinctions of the application programming interfaces (API) available for computing devices of different types. For massive-parallel accelerators, the former factor causes the need for parallel data processing and use of corresponding algorithms. The latter factor predetermines a high complexity of the software tools implementing different models of programming, in terms of their development and integration.

Therefore, a topical problem of contemporary computer science is to suggest new approaches to the development and implementation of the algorithms and technologies intended for a wide range of heterogeneous computer systems.

In the recent times, machine learning has achieved a definite level of maturity, being now applicable to many practical problems that had been considered unsolvable or far too computationally intensive. Much of the current advancements in this science lie in the field of software engineering, due to a high computational complexity of most real problems. These are high-dimensional optimization problems that demand efficient computational algorithms.

In some aspects, randomized machine learning imposes even tougher requirements to computational efficiency, which is associated with the difficult mathematical problems in the foundation of this theory. Thus, an efficient implementation of RML methods comes to parallel calculations using heterogeneous structure computing systems.

9.1Architecture of Modern Computer Systems

The present-day computer systems based on von Neumann's architecture may have different configuration depending on the number and type of processors, the capacity and structure of memory, and the presence of accelerators (coprocessors). These systems can be classified using a logical structure of memory, which defines memory access rules for the program codes executed by a processor. Such an approach discriminates between two classes of the systems, namely, the ones with shared and distributed memory. Of course, this classification suffers from certain drawbacks but yields a convenient and efficient representation of computer systems for the development and analysis of system-oriented algorithms.

Within this classification, the address space of memory accessed by processors is either uniform or separate. This property predetermines an appropriate programming model for utilization of computer system resources.

Note that the classification under study is not unique. There exist technologies allowing a user to treat a computer system with physically distributed memory as a system with a uniform address space. Conversely, a system with distributed memory can be emulated on a system with shared memory.

Two standard programming models have become widespread in these classes to date, namely, the model based on shared memory and the model based on message passing. The former model has the advantages of a uniform address space owing to a direct usage of shared memory for data transmission between processors. The latter model incorporates a data blocking mechanism, and data blocks are sent to other processors in the form of messages. For the time being, a detailed organization of these mechanisms is not so important: note that message transfer is a slower operation than direct memory access. This property must be taken into account in the course of algorithm development.

First and foremost, further advancement of computer systems aims at reducing the time required to solve the existing problems or at formulating and solving new (or current) of larger scale. Historically, computer performance has been improved using two approaches that finally formed the concepts of vertical and horizontal scaling. Vertical scaling is implemented by increasing the performance of one computation module whereas horizontal scaling by increasing the number of computation modules.

As a rule, a computation module represents a single- or multi-processor system with shared memory, i.e., a computer system with a uniform address space that can be accessed by any processor. Such a general description covers common single-processor workstations and also rather large multi-processor computer systems.

At the initial phase, the computation modules were developed within the concept of vertical scaling, since a rapid progress of microelectronics yielded faster and faster processors and memory modules. As soon as the physical limits were achieved, making further speed-up of a single processor impossible, the evolution moved towards horizontal scaling, i.e., multi-core processors. Note that horizontal scaling was also used for increasing the number of processors with identical access to shared memory.

An accumulated experience in the design of large multi-processor systems with shared memory demonstrated that many processors cannot be utilized with good efficiency within the framework of a common memory model. Therefore, the only way for a theoretically unrestricted growth of computer performance is horizontal scaling applied to the computation modules operating in the shared memory model. Obviously, at the upper level a system with this architecture represents a system with distributed memory. Most modern high-performance computer systems are designed using this principle and architecture.

As a result, a parallel execution of programs at different levels of computer systems became a basic approach to improve their performance. A real feasibility of program code parallelization led to the uprise of a new science called parallel computing. This science studies hardware tools for a parallel execution of programs and also a wide circle of issues related to the efficient exploitation of such systems.

The modern computer systems have a support of program parallelism, at the level of hardware and also at the level of system software (operating system). Users of such a computer system are developing programs that are implemented and executed using a functionality provided by its operating system. Thus, we can identify three main layers for a program that implements a given algorithm; see Fig. 9.1.

The lower layer answers for hardware support (hardware layer); in accordance with von Neumann's architecture, this layer can be described by a command handling node (processor) and storage memory for commands and data. Of course, the real systems have a more complicated organization, but this simple diagram suffices for our level of detail. The second layer, called the system layer, forms system software required for an abstract operation of all hardware tools by a user regardless of their functionality. Finally, user (or application software) occupies the upper level of the architecture, which is known as the user layer.

Now let us discuss the elements of this architecture in more depth, as illustrated in Fig. 9.2. The commands executed by a processor have a certain organization and are coming sequentially, thereby forming a thread of execution. This is a major concept for parallelization at the hardware level of a computer system [45].

Parallelism is implemented through a simultaneous execution of several commands or threads. Here a widespread approach is the so-called simultaneous multi-threading (SMT), in particular, the Hyper-Threading Technology developed by Intel. This approach allows to execute several threads on a single processor (processor core), thereby implementing not physical but logical parallelization. Nevertheless, a considerable increase in performance can be gained because in most programs the execution process also includes latent operations (working with memory and storage devices). Waiting for their completion, a processor may execute several commands from another thread. If there exist many available processors or cores (processing elements (PEs) in the terminology of large-scale computer systems), then it is possible to organize a real parallelism for threads.

A user manages hardware tools (in our case, processor threads) through an application programming interface (API) provided by corresponding software tools. Therefore, for a user processor threads as physical objects are represented in the form of logical objects independent of hardware support. These objects implement a program code created by a user of a computer system. The main objects of this class are threads and processes of an operating system.

A process is a basic element of execution for an operating system that is implemented by a special program object. All contemporary operating systems can run several processes via a simultaneous execution. A program code is executed in a processor, and a real parallelism is impossible for a single processor. However, in this case, a logical parallelism can be organized.

For safe execution, the processes of an operating system are isolated from each other in computer memory. In particular, this feature imposes some restrictions on their interaction, which are implemented using special mechanisms. A concrete form of these mechanisms bears computational cost, as it is necessary to guarantee a safe functioning of all processes. Thus, a process is a “heavy” object consuming considerable computational resources for their creation, functioning and elimination. At the same time, a thread is a “light” program object that operates within the framework of the resource sharing model of a process (memory, file descriptors, etc.). Hence, threads do not need much resources for their functioning. A process contains at least one thread.

Being fundamental objects at the system level, the threads and processes also define an abstraction level for a user-friendly development of algorithms and programs. Therefore, the system-level architecture of a computer system that is implemented by an operating system has a hierarchical organization. In accordance with this architecture, a major task for the system level is to map system objects into hardware ones, i.e., to support an execution of the system (logical) threads within the hardware threads directly on a processor.

The contemporary operating systems are multitasking, which means that they can support many simultaneously running processors by sharing the address space of memory among them to guarantee their safe execution. This leads to a parallel execution of tasks and hence a logical parallelism. A physical parallelism can be achieved if a computing device (processor) features a real execution of a process or thread. Consequently, for a successful parallelization of several processes a computer system must have several computing devices (processors or cores).

Note that multitasking can be implemented with a single computing device, e.g., based on time sharing: an operating system executes each process during a fixed period of time, then suspends it and switches to another process. Clearly, this approach gives no real increase in performance, and the advantages of parallelism are not gained.

9.2Universal Multithreaded Architecture
